Document [0]As such, 2D NMR experiments, including 1H-13C heteronuclear multiple-quantum correlation (HMQC), 1H-15N heteronuclear multiple-bond correlation (HMBC), correlation spectroscopy (COSY), and diffusion-ordered spectroscopy (DOSY), have also been used for gaining more detailed information about the identities of degradation byproducts.30, 31 It is worth noting that solution-state NMR experiments require extraction of the residual polymeric material from the solid support.30, 31 This introduces the possibility of sampling errors (e.g., not all components of the degraded sample are equally soluble in the extraction solvent, potentially resulting in misrepresentation of the full breadth and proportions of chemical changes) and further degradation of unstable or more sensitive intermediate species (e.g., via reaction with water in the atmosphere or extraction solvent, reaction with the extraction solvent itself, or quenching of otherwise persistent radical species). Moreover, for amine-functionalized resins and other aminopolymer networks, dissolution is unlikely for most of the material. Solid-state NMR, on the other hand, can be used for directly analyzing aged sorbents without the need for polymer extraction. Solid-state NMR is typically less sensitive and has lower resolution than solution-state NMR but is advantageous for directly investigating amine-functionalized resins and additional key details (such as support-polymer interactions and polymer dynamics in confinement), including evaluating these parameters as a function of temperature. That is important because side reactions between the amine phase and surface hydroxyls or silanols on the solid support can create bound interfacial species that consume CO2-reactive functionality and contribute to long-term capacity loss. Beyond NMR and IR spectroscopy, tracking the change in elemental distribution can provide additional corroboration for the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., carbonyls) and loss of nitrogen-containing species (e.g., NH3).32 Performance and spectroscopic measurements can be complemented by quantum-chemical calculations for simulating spectroscopic signatures, evaluating the reaction thermodynamics and activation free-energy barriers of potentially relevant elementary reactions, and evaluating the plausibility of various degradation mechanisms.10, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37 These methods have been applied for evaluating plausible radical-based oxidation reactions, the foundation of which lies in the basic autooxidation scheme (BAS), originally proposed by Bolland and Gee (Figure 3A).38, 39, 40 The BAS is widely accepted as a general set of reactions governing the autooxidation of polymers and is most likely applicable to the oxidative degradation of aminopolymers, evidenced by the presence of an oxidative induction period attributed to the accumulation of reactive oxidation intermediates.10, 32 However, compared with hydrocarbon polymers, the presence of N in the backbone affects the potentially relevant reactions in the degradation mechanism.
Document [1]Traditional techniques for measuring degradation-reaction-induced changes in aminopolymer molecular weight (e.g., size-exclusion chromatography [SEC] and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry [MALDI-MS]) could also be useful in determining the relative extents of chain scission and radical recombination (crosslinking), which decrease and increase molecular weight, respectively, and thereby affect polymer mobility. Measuring gas diffusion in supported aminopolymer systems remains a challenge and is further complicated by polymer-mobility changes that occur upon CO2 or H20 adsorption and degradation. Changes in polymer mobility can also physically redistribute amines, causing them to migrate, volatilize, or become trapped in pore regions that CO2 cannot readily access, which lowers capacity even without complete chemical destruction of the amines. The extent to which O2 diffusion controls the overall rate of degradation is unknown, and measurements in well-controlled environments are needed for generating a more accurate understanding of the relevance of mass transport versus degradation reaction rates. Measuring CO2 diffusion could also be useful for understanding the relative rates of gas diffusion and reaction, and non-reactive probe molecules, such as N20, can be used for isolating transport effects.111 Finally, researchers should continue to comprehensively characterize the performance of partially degraded sorbents to form a holistic understanding of the effects of degradation. For example, if oxidative degradation results in a disproportionate loss of primary amines, the average heat of adsorption and the shape of the CO2 and H20 adsorption isotherms could be affected. As highlighted previously, a comprehensive understanding of the interconnected effects of sorbent composition and environmental and process variables is still being developed. As this knowledge is established, identifying how specific variations in sorbent chemistry can be beneficial for use under particular environmental or process conditions is a critical next step toward a more flexible deployment of DAC technology. For example, do the most significant degradation mechanisms differ depending on the chemical structure of the aminopolymer? Do certain design modifications suppress specific degradation mechanisms, which could be more prominent under certain conditions?
Document [2]Given the implication of radicals in the oxidation mechanism, it is reasonable to expect that incorporating antioxidants or radical scavengers into the composite would have a beneficial effect. A key challenge associated with using these kinds of additives is that alkylamines themselves are fairly effective radical scavengers, so an additive must be able to prevent propagation back to the aminopolymer for long enough to allow radical quenching. In some cases, conventional antioxidants (such as quinones, phenols, or ascorbic acid) can accelerate oxidative degradation, as has been demonstrated for amine-based solvents.96, 97, 98 Conversely, sulfur-based antioxidants, which react with alkylhydroperoxides to form sulfides, sulfoxides, and thiosulfinates, as well as free-radical scavengers that trap chain-branching species, have been demonstrated to inhibit oxidative degradation in amine-based sorbents.99, 100 For example, Vu et al. found that sulfur-based compounds 2, 2-thiodiethanol (TDE), 3, 3′-dithiodipropionic acid (DTDP), and 2-hydroxyethyl disulfide (HEDS) significantly increased the ability of TEPA/SiO2 sorbents to retain CO2 adsorption after accelerated oxidative aging and long-term ambient storage (Figure 7A). After 15 months of storage at room temperature, the regular TEPA/SiO2 sorbent retained 52% of its initial adsorption capacity, whereas TEPA/SiO2 sorbents containing TDE, DTDP, and HEDS retained 69%, 76%, and 84% of their capacities, respectively. TEPA/SiO2 sorbents containing traditional antioxidants, such as butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), however, retained less than 48% of their original capacities.99 In another recent example, Guta et al. demonstrated that radical scavengers, such as 4, 4′-bis(α, α-dimethylbenzyl)diphenylamine (BDDPA), inhibited degradation in PEI/Al2O3 sorbents under dry CO2-free air, dry CO2 air, and humid CO2 air and proposed that they could neutralize the alkyl, aminyl, alkoxyl, and hydroxyl radicals formed during degradation processes.100 It is hard to envision a simple strategy for effectively replacing these additives, which must be close to the aminopolymer and are consumed as part of its protective mechanism, suggesting that the amount incorporated must be optimized alongside technoeconomic analysis given the potential trade-off between CO2 capacity and stability.
Document [3]Among them, Alesi and Kitchin and Yu et al. studied the oxidative degradation of the sorbent in air at 120 °C for seven days and three days, respectively. They both found a reduction of ca. 80 % in CO2 adsorption capacity. For the degradation mechanisms, the former linked this loss in capacity to irreversible amine loss, while the latter related it to the formation of nitrite and amide species under oxidative conditions. Similarly, Sonnleitner et al. examined degradation of the sorbent in air, further indicating the importance of oxidation for sorbent stability. In summary, for resin-based sorbents, there is still no systematic report on their degradation characteristics in CFB-TSA processes. In particular, it remains difficult to form widely accepted conclusions on oxidative degradation mechanisms in the open literature. Moreover, there is still no systematic utilization strategy of this type of sorbent in the design of an industrial CFB-TSA process. In this study, based on a commercial resin-based solid amine sorbent (DRC-Ⅰ) from Beijing DERUNCHEN Environmental Protection Technology Co., Ltd, a new industrial CFB-TSA carbon capture process for large-scale commercial units with high-rate flue gas is under developing through an academic-industrial collaboration program.
Document [4]DAC removes CO2 from the atmosphere by passing ambient air through a material (sorbent) that selectively binds CO2 (adsorption step). One of the leading DAC technologies being deployed globally at the pilot scale is adsorption using amine-rich solid sorbents (e.g., solid-supported aminopolymers, grafted amines, and amine-functionalized resins). These sorbents offer high CO2 capacities because they contain high densities of CO2-reactive amines.5, 6 The adsorption process occurs through acid-base chemistry to form chemisorbed species, such as ammonium carbamates or, in the presence of water, ammonium bicarbonates. During repeated CO2 uptake and regeneration, some carbamate-derived intermediates can rearrange or condense into strongly bound urea-type and other carbamate-derived species that fail to desorb, irreversibly tying up amine sites and lowering working capacity. After adsorption, the sorbent is subjected to a stimulus or combination of stimuli—such as heat (∼80°C–130°C), steam, or vacuum—that release the CO2 for downstream use or sequestration (desorption step), regenerating the material for another adsorption step. Within this overall framework, the specific process design can vary widely; factors such as sorbent composition, ambient temperature, relative humidity, and temporal or seasonal variations can all play a role in defining the optimal process operating conditions for adsorption or desorption (e.g., adsorption and desorption times and temperatures).7 Ultimately, exposure to this repeated cycling process in air, and thus to oxygen, is a key driver of oxidative sorbent degradation (Figure 1A).9 *Figure 1 Overview of CO2 direct air capture (DAC) using amine-based sorbents (A) Repeated exposure to adsorption-desorption cycles can cause amine-based sorbents to lose their ability to capture CO2. (B) Loss of sorbent working capacity leads to increased levelized cost of CO2 capture over relevant timescales.
Document [5]The C–H bond dissociation energy for CH2 adjacent to N is reduced, potentially making these more vulnerable to radical attack.34, 41 In turn, a radical in this position significantly reduces the free-energy barrier for C–N bond cleavage, making this an important new radical-propagation reaction that also results in loss of amine content. For example, Figure 3B shows a free-energy profile for radical-facilitated NH3 formation in triethylenetetramine (TETA). The free-energy barrier for the radical-facilitated process was calculated by metadynamics simulations to be ∼90 kJ mol−1, significantly lower than the barrier calculated for the thermally driven reaction to form NH3 (∼282 kJ mol−1).10 Yan et al. used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy to directly observe radical formation in oxidized PEI/SiO2 sorbents for the first time (see “future outlook and conclusions” for further discussion), 42 further supporting that radical-based reactions can form the basis for understanding oxidative degradation of aminopolymers and the mechanisms underlying formation of products that are identified. *Figure 3 Mechanisms of radical-based oxidation of amine-based sorbents (A) Overview of the different reaction types within the basic autooxidation scheme (BAS) (left) and corresponding structural examples in an aminopolymer fragment (right). Computational investigations have been used for evaluating the thermodynamics of various reactions within the BAS and their applicability to aminopolymers, complementing experimentally observed sorbent degradation. Document [6]Acknowledging that translating accelerated-aging studies into real-world lifetimes continues to be a grand challenge across many material classes and applications, we also advocate for efforts to standardize accelerated degradation protocols. Ensuring that relevant environmental factors and process conditions, depending on the specifics of the DAC process, are accurately reflected in the protocol will allow the production of comparable datasets for material comparison across different labs. These protocols will encourage researchers developing new materials to go beyond single-point performance metrics, such as CO2 capacity, and develop a more comprehensive understanding of their materials. Experimental validation of computationally proposed degradation mechanisms requires characterization of species that might not be easily identified by standard *ex situ* techniques reported in the literature. *In situ* spectroscopic characterization, combined with selective isotopic labeling, can deepen our understanding of intermediates formed and help validate or rule out proposed degradation mechanisms. For example, the use of isotopically labeled gases (e.g., D20, 17O2, 13CO2, C17O2, and H2170) or aminopolymers (e.g., 15N, 13C-, and D-PEI) in degradation studies involving characterization via FTIR (kinetic isotope effects and vibrational band shifts due to isotopic labeling) and solid-state NMR (sensitivity improvement) can allow for improved ability to observe specific functional groups and the mechanisms by which they are formed. *In situ* EPR spectroscopy techniques have the potential to significantly expand our knowledge of transient species in the degradation mechanism because oxidative degradation is speculated to be (at least partially) radical based. However, only recently was EPR used for probing the oxidative degradation of aminopolymers.42 Yan et al. treated a BPEI/SiO2 sorbent under air at 110°C for 24 h and observed a peak at 336.3 mT, providing direct evidence for the presence of radical species.
Document [7]Innovative solutions are critical for rapidly reducing atmospheric CO2 levels and slowing global warming, ultimately helping to mitigate the worst impacts of climate change. . Direct air capture (DAC) is a promising carbon removal technology that is projected to play a crucial role in capturing CO2 from the atmosphere and mitigating the rise in CO2 levels.[ , , , ]. To achieve the critical goal of limiting global surface temperature increase to below 2 °C, it is essential to expedite the development and large-scale deployment of DAC technology, in conjunction with other negative emission technologies, which is vital for climate stabilization. . The development of practical sorbents with high CO2 adsorption capacity, selectivity, and stability under atmospheric conditions is imperative. Amine-functionalized sorbents are promising materials in DAC processes, displaying high CO2 adsorption capacity, selectivity, and the ability to perform under both dry and humid conditions with moderate regeneration energies. Well-known examples of amine-functionalized sorbents include poly(ethylenimine) (PEI) supported on porous γ-Al2O3/silica and polymeric sorbents.[ , , ]. However, one of the obstacles faced by amine-functionalized sorbents is their susceptibility to losing CO2 adsorption capacity over repeated cycles of adsorption/desorption in the DAC. In a typical cycle of adsorption/desorption in DAC, the sorbent is exposed to various atmospheric components, such as O2, N2, H20, and CO2, alongside other process parameters (e.g., temperature), which affect the long-term stability of the sorbent The presence of appreciable O2 concentrations together with elevated temperatures associated with sorbent regeneration has been linked to observations of oxidative degradation, which affects the adsorption performance longevity of the sorbent.[ , , ].
Document [8]Amine-based sorbents are highly effective for direct air capture (DAC) due to their excellent CO2 capture efficiency under ultra-dilute conditions. However, these sorbents can suffer degradation when exposed to combinations of heat, oxygen, and other atmospheric components, indicating a need for improved sorbent stability. In this study, we developed amidoxime functionalized polymer of intrinsic microporosity (PIM-1-AO) fibers with tethered amines, specifically tris(2-aminoethyl)amine (TAEA) and tris(3-aminopropyl)amine (TAPA), denoted as PIM-1-AO-TAEA and PIM-1-AO-TAPA, respectively. In addition, large scale sorbent fiber spinning has been successfully performed by producing meters of fibers in the lab. We demonstrated that substituting TAEA with TAPA, which has propyl chains instead of ethyl chains, reduces oxidative degradation under regeneration conditions. The findings revealed that PIM-1-AO-TAPA not only significantly outperforms PIM-1-AO-TAEA after accelerated aging process, but also outperforms any other sorbent used in DAC aged under similar conditions. Moreover, PIM-1-AO-TAPA sorbent fibers showed one of the highest amine efficiencies (0.25) considering the low amine loading (21 %) coupled with robust CO2 uptake performance (1.12 mmol/g) under DAC conditions. Currently, ∼ 40 billion metric tons of CO2 are emitted annually, primarily from fossil fuel combustion and industrial activities, adding to the staggering total of 3, 200 billion metric tons accumulated since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution. If current emissions continue, global temperatures are projected to rise by more than 1.5 °C in the near future. To offset continuing CO2 emissions and CO2 reduce legacy atmospheric CO2, deploying carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies is essential.
Document [9]ABSTRACT: Direct air capture (DAC) technologies, particularly adsorption-based systems, are advancing rapidly as a form of negative emission technologies (NETs). DAC technologies represent a promising engineering approach to addressing diffuse CO2 emissions and provide several deployment advantages, including flexibility and scalability. However, a critical yet often overlooked challenge of adsorption-based DAC is the limited stability of CO2 sorbent materials, which undermines sustainability and hinders largescale deployment. While most research has focused on developing adsorbents with high CO2 selectivity and capacity, stability remains a crucial criterion, investigated in some studies through multicycle testing and exposure to accelerated degradation environments. This review provides a brief overview of DAC adsorbent types, followed by a detailed analysis of existing studies on the stability of solid sorbents under DAC operating conditions, highlighting key findings and research gaps. The stability of different adsorbents is discussed, along with the influence of operational variables on degradation behavior. Findings indicate that oxidative degradation in the presence of oxygen can be severe, particularly for the amine functionalities in amine-based sorbents under DAC conditions. Ultimately, this review aims to guide the development of efficient and durable CO2 adsorbents, contributing to the design of more sustainable DAC systems. Mitigating the negative effects of global warming and preventing further anthropogenic climate change are among the most critical challenges of the 21st century. The concentration of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere has increased by about 50% since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution, from 280 to 427 ppm in December 2025.1 Prospects of human population and economic growth point toward a steady increase in atmospheric CO2 concentration unless a rapid global response is deployed. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), and in parallel to other actions, it now appears essential to employ negative emission technologies (NETs) to meet the strict 1.5°C temperature increase target.2 With 2024 marking the first calendar year where global mean temperature rose by more than 1.5°C (approximately by 1.55 °C) above preindustrial levels, 3 the role of NETs becomes even more critical to avoid exceeding the upper limit of a 2 °C temperature increase.

Document [0]As such, 2D NMR experiments, including 1H-13C heteronuclear multiple-quantum correlation (HMQC), 1H-15N heteronuclear multiple-bond correlation (HMBC), correlation spectroscopy (COSY), and diffusion-ordered spectroscopy (DOSY), have also been used for gaining more detailed information about the identities of degradation byproducts.30, 31 It is worth noting that solution-state NMR experiments require extraction of the residual polymeric material from the solid support.30, 31 This introduces the possibility of sampling errors (e.g., not all components of the degraded sample are equally soluble in the extraction solvent, potentially resulting in misrepresentation of the full breadth and proportions of chemical changes) and further degradation of unstable or more sensitive intermediate species (e.g., via reaction with water in the atmosphere or extraction solvent, reaction with the extraction solvent itself, or quenching of otherwise persistent radical species). Moreover, for amine-functionalized resins and other aminopolymer networks, dissolution is unlikely for most of the material. Solid-state NMR, on the other hand, can be used for directly analyzing aged sorbents without the need for polymer extraction. Solid-state NMR is typically less sensitive and has lower resolution than solution-state NMR but is advantageous for directly investigating amine-functionalized resins and additional key details (such as support-polymer interactions and polymer dynamics in confinement), including evaluating these parameters as a function of temperature. That is important because side reactions between the amine phase and surface hydroxyls or silanols on the solid support can create bound interfacial species that consume CO2-reactive functionality and contribute to long-term capacity loss. Beyond NMR and IR spectroscopy, tracking the change in elemental distribution can provide additional corroboration for the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., carbonyls) and loss of nitrogen-containing species (e.g., NH3).32 Performance and spectroscopic measurements can be complemented by quantum-chemical calculations for simulating spectroscopic signatures, evaluating the reaction thermodynamics and activation free-energy barriers of potentially relevant elementary reactions, and evaluating the plausibility of various degradation mechanisms.10, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37 These methods have been applied for evaluating plausible radical-based oxidation reactions, the foundation of which lies in the basic autooxidation scheme (BAS), originally proposed by Bolland and Gee (Figure 3A).38, 39, 40 The BAS is widely accepted as a general set of reactions governing the autooxidation of polymers and is most likely applicable to the oxidative degradation of aminopolymers, evidenced by the presence of an oxidative induction period attributed to the accumulation of reactive oxidation intermediates.10, 32 However, compared with hydrocarbon polymers, the presence of N in the backbone affects the potentially relevant reactions in the degradation mechanism.

Document [4]DAC removes CO2 from the atmosphere by passing ambient air through a material (sorbent) that selectively binds CO2 (adsorption step). One of the leading DAC technologies being deployed globally at the pilot scale is adsorption using amine-rich solid sorbents (e.g., solid-supported aminopolymers, grafted amines, and amine-functionalized resins). These sorbents offer high CO2 capacities because they contain high densities of CO2-reactive amines.5, 6 The adsorption process occurs through acid-base chemistry to form chemisorbed species, such as ammonium carbamates or, in the presence of water, ammonium bicarbonates. During repeated CO2 uptake and regeneration, some carbamate-derived intermediates can rearrange or condense into strongly bound urea-type and other carbamate-derived species that fail to desorb, irreversibly tying up amine sites and lowering working capacity. After adsorption, the sorbent is subjected to a stimulus or combination of stimuli—such as heat (∼80°C–130°C), steam, or vacuum—that release the CO2 for downstream use or sequestration (desorption step), regenerating the material for another adsorption step. Within this overall framework, the specific process design can vary widely; factors such as sorbent composition, ambient temperature, relative humidity, and temporal or seasonal variations can all play a role in defining the optimal process operating conditions for adsorption or desorption (e.g., adsorption and desorption times and temperatures).7 Ultimately, exposure to this repeated cycling process in air, and thus to oxygen, is a key driver of oxidative sorbent degradation (Figure 1A).9 *Figure 1 Overview of CO2 direct air capture (DAC) using amine-based sorbents (A) Repeated exposure to adsorption-desorption cycles can cause amine-based sorbents to lose their ability to capture CO2. However, these sorbents can suffer degradation when exposed to combinations of heat, oxygen, and other atmospheric components, indicating a need for improved sorbent stability. In this study, we developed amidoxime functionalized polymer of intrinsic microporosity (PIM-1-AO) fibers with tethered amines, specifically tris(2-aminoethyl)amine (TAEA) and tris(3-aminopropyl)amine (TAPA), denoted as PIM-1-AO-TAEA and PIM-1-AO-TAPA, respectively. question: Which physical processes govern the movement of water and the exclusion of ions within graphene-oxide membranes used for desalination?
perspectives: Interlayer capillary transport through hydrated nanochannels
Defect-dominated transport through holes and edge pathways
Solution-diffusion through oxidized graphene domains
Surface diffusion along functionalized gallery walls

Document [0]Graphene oxide membranes show exceptional molecular permeation properties, with a promise for many applications. However, their use in desalination technologies is limited by a permeation cutoff set by the interlayer spacing d ≈ 13.5 Å, typical for graphene oxide laminates that swell in water. Achieving smaller d for laminates immersed in water has proved to be a challenge. Here we describe how to control d by physical confinement. Membranes with d from 9.8 Å to 6.4 Å are demonstrated. Importantly, water transport is weakly affected despite the reduced interlayer spacing.
Document [1]Different dimensional intercalation materials may be used to tune membrane structure, but the transport picture considered here still centers on two coupled routes: permeation through hydrated interlayer nanochannels and shortcut flow through holes in the basal plane or gaps at sheet edges. Development of bio-inspired materials/GO composite membranes can improve water resistance and structural stability, for example through coatings inspired by adhesive biological materials. Lee et al. found that dopamine is capable of forming polymer-like coatings on a variety of substrates through oxidized self-polymerization . The rich oxygen-containing functional groups of GO nanosheets provided the possibility of combining them with bionanomaterials; for instance, dopamine could be coated on the surface of GOMs . Combination with bionic materials will increase the mechanical stability and surface flexibility of GOMs, which may help preserve the membrane architecture in which these transport pathways operate. Such structural stabilization does not itself define a separate transport mechanism here, but instead helps maintain the channel network through which permeation and exclusion are expressed. Because holes in the basal plane and gaps at sheet edges provide direct shortcuts, membranes with many such defects exhibit transport dominated by flow through holes and edge pathways rather than by the regular interlayer galleries. This shortcut contribution complements, rather than replaces, the interlayer pathway, and it can shorten the effective path length available for water permeation. At the same time, water molecules can permeate through the interconnected nanochannels formed between GO nanosheets and follow tortuous paths mainly on the hydrophobic non-oxidized surface of GO rather than in the hydrophilic oxidized region . Within this description, the hydrated interlayer nanochannel network remains the capillary route through which water is transmitted across stacked GO sheets. By regulating pore size and the charge around the pore, hydrated ions can be effectively hindered while water continues to permeate through the hydrated nanochannel network. Taken together, the present description therefore retains defect-mediated shortcut transport together with interlayer capillary transport as the main explanation of water permeation and ion rejection in GOMs.
Document [2]To gain an insight into ion permeation through our membranes, we carried out permeation experiments at different temperatures, T (Fig. 2c). For both channel sizes, d = 9.8 and d = 7.9 Å, the permeation rates follow the Arrhenius equation, exp(-E/kBT), i.e., show activation behaviour. The data yield E = 72 ± 7 and 20 ± 2 kJ/mol for K+ ion permeation through PCGO membranes with d ≈ 7.9 and 9.8 Å, respectively. The exponential dependence explains the fact that the observed ion diffusion rates are orders of magnitude smaller than those given by eq. (1) at room temperature. Qualitatively, transport occurs through the membrane’s atomic-scale, hydrated capillaries or nanochannels. In a bulk solution, ions and water are surrounded by water molecules, but permeation is governed by confinement within these channels. Accordingly, channel size strongly influences ion transport, whereas water can still pass through the membrane nanochannels.
Document [3]The water permeability in GO membrane is governed through interlayer channels, in which the layered galleries provide sufficient interlayer distance to accommodate water molecules and support flow through the stacked structure. Moreover, the graphene oxide membrane’s selectivity and permeability are further influenced by the interlayer d spacing of GOms. Supplementary to this, GO membranes are mechanically reliable, inexpensive, and suitable for industrial-scale production, making them a perfect candidate for water desalination. GOms with two-dimensional water channels in a stacked-layer form, including the intercalated GOms, have therefore attracted attention for their water selectivity and permeability. Although there has been extensive research on these two-dimensional GOms, both chemically treated and physically intercalated, the stacking of graphene oxide laminates remains an important structural consideration in describing membrane transport. Recent studies have therefore continued to examine how this laminar framework affects water transport and selectivity in GO membranes.
Document [4]Advanced membrane systems are widely used for separation processes, such as water treatment, gas purification, chemical industry as well as food and pharmaceutical processing , . The membrane plays the key role in determining the separation efficiency, working stability and maintenance costs. Polymeric membranes are successfully applied in industry but they deserve further improvement in terms of permeability, selectivity and working stability . Recently, graphene oxide (GO) has been recognized as a promising candidate for efficient aqueous separation owing to the high permeability and high selectivity , , . The interconnected nanochannels formed by the non-oxidized regions of GO sheets offer low friction transport of water molecules so that they pass through with an extremely fast speed , . In addition, high selectivity can be obtained because of the uniform distribution of the interlayer spacing. Unmodified GO membranes are not suitable for desalination because the interlayer distance is larger than the diameters of common hydrated ions . What’s more, the hydration of GO in aqueous environment makes it more challenging to constrain the interlayer spacing within a sub-nanometer range , . According to the pristine interlayer spacing of GO membranes reported in current literature, they should be categorized as nanofiltration membranes. Also, larger interlayer distances can be conveniently achieved by sandwiching soft polymeric chains , , functional groups , or nano-sized materials between GO sheets , , , , . One of the major challenges in the application of GO membranes for nanofiltration is the improvement of the water flux without scarifying the rejection . Several strategies have been tried, including (i) reducing the thickness of GO membranes , , , (ii) introducing controllable nanopores into GO sheets , , (iii) inserting nano-spacers into GO laminates to widen the interlayer spacing , .
Document [5]Currently, graphene oxide (GO) membrane is becoming a new-generation material for desalination application with high water permeability and ion rejection rate. The unusual 2D interlayer nanostructure in GO membrane provides a reliable and precise transport environment for fast water permeation and ion rejection. However, the studies on molecular mechanisms for water and ion transport in the 2D interlayer nanochannels of GO membrane are far from adequate, and the trade-off between selectivity and permeability is another problem significantly restraining the further development of GO membrane for desalination. In this work, molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to investigate the atomic mechanism of water and ion transport in 2D nanochannels of GO membrane, and the influences of interlayer space and nanostructure on water and ion transport were also revealed. We find that transport depends strongly on the hydrated interlayer nanochannels formed by neighboring GO sheets, while water transport can also proceed by solution-diffusion through oxidized graphene domains after sorption into oxygen-rich regions. Within this picture, the oxidized domains provide an additional route embedded in the broader interlayer transport architecture rather than a separate competing framework. Both the capillary channel network and the oxidized domains therefore contribute to the same membrane-level balance between permeability and rejection. The role of nanostructure in this account is to modulate how these two allowed routes are expressed, rather than to introduce a third mechanistic class of transport. By combining the influences of interlayer space and nanostructure on water and ion transport, a new design principle for high-efficient GO desalination membrane is proposed. The findings in this work expand our understanding of water and ion transport in GO membrane and may also greatly promote the development of desalination membrane prepared by other 2D materials. Nowadays, fresh water shortage has become a worldwide problem because of water pollution and waste . Seawater, which covers 71% of the surface area of our earth, provides an adequate fresh water supply if advanced desalination method is developed.
Document [6]Among which, desalination through reverse osmosis (RO) membrane has become a widely applied technology due to its high-energy efficiency [ , , ]. Currently, preparing advanced RO membranes with robust mechanical property, high separation performance (i.e. high water flux and high ion rejection rate), and low operation cost and energy consumption are the main developmental direction for seawater desalination technology . Recently, nanofiltration RO membranes prepared from two-dimensional (2D) materials have presented great potential for desalination application [ , , , ]. Especially for graphene oxide (GO), the interlayer gallery assembled from atomic-thin GO nanoflakes offers unique 2D nanochannels for fast water transport meanwhile rejecting the transport of other small molecules and ions [ , , , , ]. Up to now, many theoretical [ , , ] and experimental [ , , ] studies have shown that GO membrane presents superior desalination performance. Overall, previous studies mainly focus on the regulation of interlayer spaces of GO membrane (e.g. chemically functional group modification and physically embedding nanoparticles) to pursue more efficient desalination. Although the increased interlayer space can enhance water permeability, the corresponding ion rejection rate will decrease. Typically, these regulating methods for interlayer space of GO membrane are not easy to realize, meanwhile the trade-off relationship between water permeability and ion rejection rate is another problem needing to be reconsidered. GO is an oxidized form of graphene (GN) including epoxide, hydroxyl, and carboxylic acid groups on it [ , , ]. Normally, the epoxide and hydroxyl groups mainly distribute on the base plane of GN, whereas carboxylic acid groups distribute on the edges. However, the distribution of epoxide and hydroxyl groups is not uniform on GN plane .
Document [7]Thus, the optimum preparation method should be chosen according to the separation system and separation requirement. It is usually considered that water molecules first go to the hydrophilic “gate” (space between edges of two adjacent GO nanosheets or defects of GO) for aggregation and then enter the hydrated 2D interlayer nanochannels, as shown in Figure 3. The GO lamellae have oxidation and non-oxidation zones. The oxidation zone with abundant oxygen-containing functional groups allows for strong hydrogen bonding interactions with water molecules ; however, GOMs can be chemically modified through a chemical reaction with oxygen-containing functional groups. Along the functionalized walls of the interlayer galleries, adsorbed water can move by surface diffusion, hopping between neighboring oxygen-containing groups. Nair et al. found that submicron-thick GOMs can impede the flow of liquid and gas molecules while allowing the penetration of water vapor; this is probably attributed to the presence of interlayer gaps between GO sheets, which allow the transport of water vapor through the membrane . Based on isotope labeling, it was demonstrated that liquid water can permeate at ultrafast speeds through millimeter-long interlayer nanocapillaries in GO membranes . The abundant oxygen-containing groups at the edges and defects of GO layers have good hydrophilicity, which could allow water molecules to preferentially enter the two-dimensional channels between GO layers and migrate through the hydrated interlayer galleries; thus, GOMs can be used for ultrafast water permeation .
Document [8]To analyze transport in our PCGO membranes, we employ the previously suggested model of a network of hydrated graphene capillaries, which was developed to account for the fast permeation of water through GO membranes12, 18, 19. Within this model, we performed molecular dynamics simulations to find energy barriers for various ions entering graphene capillaries of different widths (supplementary section 6). As seen in Fig. 2c the energy barrier E exhibits a sharp increase for d < 9 Å and is considerably larger for divalent ions compared to monovalent ones, in agreement with our experiments and the above discussion (Fig. 2a). Quantitatively, the obtained E are of the same order of magnitude as those found experimentally; the discrepancy in exact values can be expected because realistic GO channels contain non-stoichiometric functionalities, rough edges, etc. which are difficult to model accurately. We also performed simulations to evaluate a possible contribution of diffusion rates through capillaries themselves into the overall permeation rates. Our results show that the diffusion coefficient for K+ changes with d but the effect is small compared to the exponential decrease in permeation rates, which was observed experimentally (supplementary section 6). Taken together, these results are consistent with transport in our case proceeding through sub-nm graphene capillaries. Finally, the exponential suppression of ion permeation combined with fast water transport in PCGO membranes makes them an interesting candidate for water filtration applications. Even though scalable production of such membranes is difficult, one can envisage alternative fabrication techniques to control d in GO laminates. To this end, we show that it is possible to restrict the swelling of GO membranes in liquid water, for example, simply by incorporating graphene flakes into GO laminates (see supplementary section 7). The resulting composites referred to as GO-Gr membranes exhibit notably less swelling (difference in d of ≈ 4 Å) with respect to the standard GO laminates.

question: Which mechanisms of mass transfer account for the exceptional increases in CO2 separation performance observed in superior mixed-matrix membranes?
perspectives: Molecular sieving primarily through the filler micropores
Solution-diffusion mainly through the polymer with filler-induced chain rigidification
Interfacial free-volume pathways at polymer-filler boundaries
Facilitated transport via reversible CO2-binding sites on the filler or polymer
context:
Document [0]Membrane process is a robust technology for CO2/CH4 separation. To achieve the energy-efficiency necessary for a cost-effective membrane-based CO2/CH4 separation, high-performance membranes are often desirable. There are several approaches that can be undertaken to realize such membranes. In this study, we focused on zeolite 5A, with the microporous domains providing the molecular-sieving function. These efforts afforded membranes with results confirming that our membrane at 30 wt% loading of zeolite 5A was able to surpass the 2008 Robeson upper bound limit given a performance of 2450 barrers CO2 permeability and 19.3 CO2/CH4 selectivity. Notably, at this loading, the negative effect brought by the interfacial nanogaps between the filler and matrix diminished, allowing the contribution of the zeolite micropores to be more fully expressed. Despite a decrease in the CO2/CH4 selectivity, zeolite 5A is effective in alleviating the intensity of the permeability-selectivity trade-off. Also, benchmarking of the filler effectiveness is first demonstrated using a new filler enhancement index, *F**index*. The largest *F**index* value in this study was 1.97. This attaches a label of “competent” to our zeolite 5A filler at 30 wt% loading, demonstrating its effectiveness.
Document [1]One way to achieve higher permeability and selectivity is by functionalizing GO nanosheets with amino groups. Zhang et al. modified GO nanosheets with aminosilane to obtain amino-GO/Pebax MMM. The surface modification improved the filler distribution and membrane mechanical strength. More importantly, the surface amino groups increased the membrane affinity for CO2. Those amino groups also serve as reversible CO2-binding sites, enabling a facilitated transport contribution through the membrane, especially under humid conditions. In the dry state, with the addition of 0.5 wt.% of the amino-functionalized GO nanosheet, the CO2 permeability increased from 95.4 Barrer to 172 Barrer. The performance is even more impressive under the humid state. With 0.9 wt.% of inorganic filler in the humid state, the MMM showed improved CO2 permeability from 424 Barrer to 934.3 Barrer at 2 bar and 35 °C, while the CO2/CH4 selectivity increased to 40.9 and the CO2/N2 selectivity increased to 71.1 . Another way to improve the permeability of GO-based MMMs is by using porous reduced GO (PRG). Dong et al. prepared PRG-based MMMs based on a Pebax 1657 matrix with a finely tuned degree of GO reduction to ensure sufficient residual amounts of functional groups on the reduced GO. The narrow gas flow galleries with an average gap of 0.34 between neighboring reduced GO sheets ensured a high molecular sieving effect. As a result, the MMM showed substantially improved CO2 permeability (119) as well as CO2/N2 selectivity (104) at 0.2 MPa and 30 °C . In another work, He et al. reported a layer-by-layer Pebax MMM that was functionalized with both PGO and o-POPs (Figure 13).
Document [2]Recently, Atalay-Oral et al. proposed a comparative study about the effect of different zeolites on the transport properties of polyvinylacetate (PVAc). They compared four different zeolites: 4A (pore size 4.2 Å), Ferrierite (pore size 4.2 Å), 5A (pore size 5.2 Å), and Silicalite-1 (pore size 5.5 Å). For all of the different fillers, the CO2-selective features of the mixed matrix membranes were increased. Ferrierite showed the better improvement in terms of performance: the selective feature (both CO2/CH4 and CO2/N2) increased proportionally to the inorganic content (Table 7), whereas the permeability increased at 20 wt.% loading, but negligible differences were observed at higher inorganic content. The authors suggest the size-selective character of the Ferrierite pores to be the main reason for the superior performance of the Ferrierite-based hybrid membranes. Another study compared the performance of Zeolite A and zeolite ITQ-29 when embedded in PTMSP . Surprisingly, when single gas tests were performed on a hybrid membrane containing 20 wt.% Zeolite A loading, a 35% drop in CO2 permeability was observed being combined with a 70-fold enhancement of the CO2/N2 selectivity (Table 7), surpassing the Robeson’s upper bound. Such behavior is also consistent with solution-diffusion remaining mainly through the polymer phase, while the zeolite rigidifies nearby PTMSP chains and suppresses the passage of larger gases more strongly than CO2. The extraordinary performance was attributed to the molecular sieving ability of the nanoparticles. A much lower improvement was observed in the case of ITQ-29 zeolite. These results highlighted that choosing the proper zeolite is extremely important in the design of hybrid membranes.
Document [3]Upon filler incorporation, the CO2/CH4 separation factor was increased from 23 to 40 as compared to pristine PSF. Similar to the previous MOFs, the MILs’ family also represents a group of nanoporous particles that is suitable for the development of mixed matrix membranes for CO2 capture. Document [0]The growing demand for energy calls for a rapid shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources, such as wind, solar, biomass, hydropower, and geothermal energy . In the path toward a low-carbon energy society, hydrogen plays an important role as a secondary energy carrier [ , , , , , ]. In this context, water electrolysis has the potential to be a key element in coupling the electrical supply, transportation, heating, and chemical sectors via power-to-gas in a future sustainable energy system . While PEM water electrolysis offers several advantages over traditional electrolysis technologies, further advancement is impeded by insufficient stability of the membrane electrode assembly (MEA) at high anodic potential and high current . The degradation of the MEA in PEMWE has been discussed in several reviews [ , , ] as well as studies of high – Pt and Ir – loaded MEAs [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , ] which focus on different components of the MEA. The membrane can also undergo chemical attack by HO• and HOO• radicals, and the resulting thinning and loss of proton conductivity increase ohmic losses during long-term operation. The state-of-the-art anode catalyst for PEM water electrolyzers is iridium oxide. However, iridium suffers from dissolution at high anodic potentials albeit being the most corrosion-resistant metal known. The iridium dissolution in a MEA is evidenced by the iridium deposits in the electrolyte membrane accompanied by a decrease in both anode exchange current density and overall cell performance . It is proposed that the dissolution of iridium shares the same Ir (III) intermediate species with the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) [18, , , , , , ] (Eqs (1), (2), (3), (4), (5), (6), (7)).
Document [1]The failure of anode catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzers poses a significant barrier to their commercial deployment. In PEM electrolyzers, anode catalysts typically degrade due to the extremely oxidative environment and low local pH at the anode. Under these harsh conditions, catalysts may dissolve into the electrolyte, leading to progressive catalyst loss. These degradation processes are interconnected and complex, rather than isolated issues. Consequently, improving catalyst materials remains important for overall system performance. In this perspective, we systematically review dissolution-driven anode catalyst failure and its effects on PEM electrolyzer stability. We pay special attention to the limitations of current approaches, including material durability and gaps in system-level strategies. A thorough understanding of these challenges is crucial. Achieving a stable anode for acidic OER requires deep insight into these failure mechanisms under real PEM operating conditions. By integrating advances in catalyst design, electrochemical characterization, engineering solutions, and data-driven methods, we can address these challenges effectively. This comprehensive approach is essential to accelerate the development and enable the widespread adoption of PEM electrolyzers. Document [8]The main challenges associated with a large-scale application of proton exchange membrane (PEM) based water electrolysis are the reduction of the iridium loading at the oxygen evolution electrode (anode) to prevent supply constraints as well as the minimization of hydrogen generation costs to increase economic competitiveness while retaining a sufficient system lifetime. These topics are addressed by an optimization of the electrode composition and by a reduction of catalyst loading in the membrane electrode assembly (MEA), accompanied by a rigorous analysis of voltage losses and an investigation of degradation phenomena during an accelerated stress test. First, the influence of ionomer content in anode electrodes with an IrO2/TiO2 catalyst on the electrolyzer performance is investigated. It is shown that by optimizing the ionomer content, voltage losses, e.g., due to mass transport phenomena, can be minimized, thereby enabling high performance at current densities up to 6 A cm-2. In the second part of this thesis, the effect of a reduced catalyst loading is investigated, and we show that a significant reduction of the platinum loading on the hydrogen evolution electrode (cathode) is possible without a decrease in performance. In contrast, lowering the iridium loading on the anode leads to thin, inhomogeneous catalyst layers, resulting in a significant performance drop. Based on these findings, future catalyst material requirements are discussed in the context of a large-scale application of PEM water electrolysis. Finally, the influence of a fluctuating power supply on electrolyzer performance and durability is simulated by an accelerated stress test including load cycles and operation interruptions. It is shown that avoiding current interruptions and resulting open circuit voltage periods is crucial to prevent catalyst dissolution and enable a sufficient long-term stability. perspectives: Coke deposition that blocks active sites and pores

Document [0]However, catalytic cracking plastics into fuel oil is not only the reuse of waste, but also can alleviate the depletion of petroleum, thus realizing the renewability of resources. The advancement of the plastics field has led to the upgrading of plastic thermal cracking technologies. This article provides a summary of the pyrolysis method for converting waste plastics into fuel oil, and proposes optimized path. Pyrolysis is the simplest and most basic plastic cracking method. Catalytic pyrolysis is a development approach that is more applicable under current technological circumstances, and research into more efficient, environmentally friendly, and cost-effective catalyst is the key. Catalytic hydropyrolysis and supercritical water liquefaction have the ability to generate liquid fuels with a more focused range of products. These methods show promise for further advancement, while their demanding reaction conditions impose constraints on the scalability of production. Solvolysis is an appropriate method for breakdown oxygen-containing polymers. The recently introduced series technique has the capability to decompose waste polymers at low temperature and low pressure. Facing with issues such as catalyst carbon deposition inactivation, high melt viscosity, low product selectivity, and low heat conductivity of waste polymers. Feed-derived inorganic fillers, pigments, and dirt can leave ash or metal-rich residues on the catalyst, fouling pores and covering active surfaces. From feedstock composition (co-pyrolysis), structure-activity relationship of pore structure and activity, reactor, and other processes, we can optimize the oil production technology. Only by amplifying the excellent results of plastic pyrolysis at laboratory level can the sustainable utilization of waste plastics be realized. Advancing the already well-established catalytic cracking technique is a crucial approach to address the disposal of enormous quantities of waste plastics. It is believed that with the continuous efforts of scientific researchers, the strategy of turning waste into treasure will be better. Conceptualization, L. A.; validation, Z. Z. and R. As mentioned before, many zeolites, such as HZSM-5, ZSM-5 and H-Beta zeolites, have been well used in the study of catalytic pyrolysis. The structure of zeolites changes with the pore size and their connectivity. Zeolite has Bronsted and Lewis acid sites and Bronsted acid site is the main catalytic center. The active sites and different pore sizes of molecular sieves can promote the deoxidation of oxygen-containing compounds and improve the yield of aromatics. In the rapid pyrolysis of zeolite catalyst, the main reaction pathway is hydrocarbon pool mechanism, deoxidation, cracking, aromatization, aldehyde condensation and ketone reaction. The conversion of oxygen-containing compounds into hydrocarbons in the framework of the molecular sieve depends on the shape selectivity of pore space and pore size of the molecular sieve. If the hydrocarbon generated in the pyrolysis reaction cannot be desorbed, they will oligomerize into coke in the zeolite pore, blocking the active site and causing the deactivation of the catalyst. Metal modification is another way to improve the catalytic activity of zeolite catalysts. Adding metals to the hierarchical ZSM-5 catalyst can promote deoxidation through decarboxylation and decarbonylation process and can further improve the performance of CFP of biomass to aromatics . Recent studies of metal modified zeolite catalysts in CFP are shown in Table 2. Chen et al. found that treating HZSM-5 with an appropriate amount of nickel and copper can improve the activity of catalyst and obtain more aromatics, but the high metal loading will reduce the aromatics yield .
Document [2]Research has been carried out to understand the mechanisms under which coke formation occurs and to search for solutions to reduce or eliminate coke deposition. Significant efforts have been exerted over the past twenty years in developing coke-inhibiting methods. Coke inhibitors, i.e., chemical additives, or special coating of metal surfaces which suppress coke formation. Coke inhibitors/surface coating work by passivating catalytically active metal sites through chemical bonding interactions, and/or forming a thin layer to physically isolate the metal sites from coke precursors in a process stream, and/or interfering with those radical reactions leading to coke formation by blocking active radical sites on surfaces. This review paper investigates the effect of the most important methods such as new chemical additives, tube material construction, pretreatment of surface on the coke formation of pyrolysis furnaces.

Document [5]The work presented in this PhD thesis is embedded in a strategy for the development of innovative processes to answer contemporary challenges, such as the energetic transition of chemical industry. The research project aims to investigate ozonation as an alternative process to classical combustion for the regeneration of coked catalysts. The scope therefore presents a very high industrial relevance as almost 80% of industrial processes involve heterogeneous (or solid) catalysts. The formation of coke over such material leads to an important decrease of catalytic performances during the process. In order to recycle spent catalysts, which are often rare or expensive materials, different regeneration methods were investigated over the years. The most common and industrially implemented process is the combustion of coke with air or oxygen-enriched air at around 500°C, whose main drawbacks are the important energy consumption and the thermal degradation risk for thermo-sensitive catalysts. Due to its high oxidative power, use of ozone for the regeneration of catalysts allows to remove coke in milder conditions at around 100°C. After promising results obtained in the laboratory team, many challenges remain unanswered to acquire a deeper understanding of the ozonation process. This project aims to investigate catalyst deactivation by coke formation and catalyst regeneration with ozone. The study of ozonation process for the regeneration of coked catalysts was conducted in this work with a combined experimental and numerical approach. Coked catalysts used in this study were industrial HZSM-5 zeolites exposed to pyrolysis of polyethylene at 450°C. This reaction was identified as a promising process for the revalorization of plastics wastes. Comprehensive study of catalysts deactivation by coke formation during pyrolysis and their reuse after regeneration showed the ability of ozonation to restore complete catalytic efficiency and characteristics. The influence of operating conditions on coke removal efficiency was investigated with a lab-scale parametric study in a fixed-bed reactor and by developing robust analytical methodology.

The yield and composition of liquid and gas products over various FCCs were studied quantitatively. Document [8]Coke deposition rate strongly depends on the physicochemical properties of the catalysts (the presence of functional groups—acid-base character, porosity, the presence of metal and degree of its dispersion, type of support in the case of supported catalysts, incorporation of promoters). Therefore, studies devoted to the increase in the efficiency of biomass pyrolysis and bio-oil upgrading are focused on the design of the catalytic systems possessing the structure and composition which allows maintaining of the satisfying activity with simultaneous reduction in susceptibility to carbon deposit formation (Table 1). Generally, the mechanism of coke formation involves several paths depending on the temperature: arising of metal carbides (150–400 °C), formation of amorphous films with a polymeric character (250–500 °C), production of graphitic carbon (about 500 °C), or growth of carbon filaments (above 300 °C). In the case of heterogeneous catalysts, coke can be located on the surface of metal particles, the metal–support interface, or support (Figure 3). Deactivation of the catalyst may follow through the encapsulation of metal particles due to polymerization or condensation of the primary products of the thermal decomposition of biomass (i.e., oxygenates, aromatics) which usually occur below 500 °C or the formation of carbon fibers at higher temperature range. Encapsulating carbon can be formed due to adsorption of oxygenated and/or nonoxygenated products produced in the initial step of the process on the metal sites. In these conditions, carbon atoms are not only dissolved in the metal crystallites and adsorbed on the bottom of metal grains (at the interface between active phase and the support), but primary decomposition products can be subjected to subsequent condensation or polymerization over the metal particle surface. It results in the formation of a polymeric or amorphous coke film, which covers or encapsulates the metal particles. This limits their capacity for the adsorption of reactants and causes a rapid loss of catalyst activity due to the decrease in active metallic surface .
Document [9]The extension of aromatization reactions at acid centers during catalytic pyrolysis of mixed plastic waste can produce coke, which further seals internal acid sites. This blocks subsequent reactions, reduces aromatics selectivity, and promotes the persistence of intermediate species. Cracking vapors can also form coke on the outer surface of ZSM-5, which leads to the inactivation of surface cracking ability, but does not fully prevent access to acid sites in the microchannels. The results also confirm that the coke generated during catalytic pyrolysis is a main reason for the reduction of aromatics. Studies have also shown that contaminant-derived species can poison the Brønsted acid sites of the catalyst . Halogenated, sulfur-containing, and nitrogen-containing additives or contaminants in the feed can generate species that strongly poison Brønsted acid or metal sites. In addition to blocking the pores or active sites of the catalyst with carbonaceous materials and causing deactivation of the zeolite catalyst, accumulated solid residues further limit catalyst accessibility. According to research, the degree of coke formation can vary substantially . For example, under a certain feed-to-catalyst ratio, larger coke deposition is observed in some upgrading runs than in others. Lower solid-residue formation correspondingly lessens blockage of pores and active sites. More severe coke formation accelerates catalyst deactivation, which can be explained by two aspects . On the one hand, more continuous reaction sequences increase the possibility of condensation and finally accelerate the formation of coke. On the other hand, rapid conversion of coke precursors also leads to acceleration of the coking process.

Document [0]Surface fouling poses a significant challenge that restricts the analytical performance of electrochemical sensors in both in vitro and in vivo applications. Biofouling resistance is paramount to guarantee the reliable operation of electrochemical sensors in complex biofluids (e.g., blood, serum, and urine). Seeking efficient strategies for surface fouling and establishing highly sensitive sensing platforms for applications in complex media have received increasing attention in the past. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent research efforts focused on antifouling electrochemical sensors. Initially, we present a detailed illustration of the concept about biofouling along with an exploration of four key antifouling mechanisms. Subsequently, we delve into the commonly employed antifouling strategies in the fabrication of electrochemical sensors. These encompass physical surface topography (micro/nanostructure coatings and filtration membranes) and chemical surface modifications (PEG and its derivatives, zwitterionic polymers, peptides, proteins, and various other antifouling materials). The progress in antifouling electrochemical sensors is proposed concerning the antifouling mechanisms as well as sensing capability assessments (e.g., sensitivity, stability, and practical application ability). Finally, we summarize the evolving trends in the field and highlight some key remaining limitations. The alternative text for this image may have been generated using AI. PEG is the most widely used antifouling interface design material and is considered the “gold standard” of antifouling performance .

Following intravenous administration of nanoparticles, blood proteins adsorb onto the nanoparticle surface forming a protein corona134–136, which impacts its biological trajectory in vivo137. The protein-coated nanoparticles then circulate and interact with different cells and tissues on their way to the tumour. Cell-surface receptors may bind to the protein corona for cellular uptake108, 138, 139, with apolipoproteins and complement proteins playing key roles139. Cell-surface receptors may also recognize the nanomaterial itself. For example, CD36 mediates the uptake of lipid micelles and may be involved in the uptake of clinically relevant liposome formulations140, CD206 mediates the uptake of mannose-coated nanoparticles141, and receptor gp60 mediates the uptake of albumin particles142. In addition, non-specific uptake mechanisms such as macropinocytosis may drive cellular uptake87. Most injected nanoparticles are sequestered by the liver and spleen, rendering them unavailable for tumour delivery143–145. Nanoparticles smaller than 5.5 nm are filtered out of the bloodstream via the kidneys146. Nanoparticles that reach the tumour cross the blood endothelium predominantly via active endothelial transcytosis88, 89, 93. Transcytosis is mediated by specific endothelial cell phenotypes89. Abnormal tumour vessels may also permit passive nanoparticle passage through endothelial fenestrae or transcellular pores that connect the lumen to the tumour interstitium. Once the nanoparticles are inside the tumour, they transport through the tumour microenvironment and interact with cellular and acellular tumour components.

Document [0]Extra-hepatic delivery is an important issue in the field of DDS. Recently, there has been increasing research studies regarding tissue-selective delivery without attaching specific ligands, via the recruitment of endogenous ligands after protein-corona formation and subsequent receptor-mediated endocytosis.14–16 Such a strategy is considered to be based on inter-organ trafficking mechanisms in the human body. Herein, we summarize information from the literature on tissue-selective delivery of nanoparticles without the use of specific ligands. In some cases, the endogenous ligands have been clarified. However, in others, no information is available concerning the precise mechanism of tissue-selective delivery and future analysis is required. Differences in endothelial fenestration and local blood-flow patterns can also influence vascular filtration and residence time of circulating LNPs before uptake occurs. Specific and efficient delivery of therapeutic agents such as RNA into the spleen is a key technology for the treatment of a variety of diseases such as cancers, infectious diseases, autoimmune disorders, and other immune-related conditions. In studies of selective organ targeting (SORT), formulations have included 20–30 mol% of negatively charged phospholipids such as phosphatidic acid (PA) or bis(monoacylglycerol)phosphate (BMP) as a fifth lipid component.78 Among hepatotropic counterparts, apolipoprotein E (ApoE) is most frequently adsorbed, consistent with protein-corona-mediated recognition in the liver.

However, realizing this potential requires direct evidence of corona–receptor interactions *in vivo*; a challenge hampered by the limitations of *in vitro* settings. This opinion instead emphasizes the role of plasma proteins acquired by NPs in shaping receptor interactions. Corona components derived from selected plasma proteins, including apolipoproteins, can retain their properties *in vivo*, enabling specific receptor targeting after corona formation. Document [5]The major challenge for developing LNP-based gene therapies, however, is finding effective, tissue-specific delivery strategies (beyond the liver). In fact, many nanomedicines have limited accumulation in extrahepatic tissues or tumors, with only a small percentage of the injected dose actually reaching its target.16 Many approaches have been devised to enhance tissue- or cell-specific delivery, particularly for targeting tumors, 17 including grafting targeting moieties onto the nanoparticle surface or modulating nanoparticle surface properties.18 Both strategies assume that LNPs will directly interact with the cell surface once administered; however, this is not the case.19 In fact, LNPs first interact with biological fluids, whose nature depends on the administration site: from lung surfactants when inhaled, to interstitial fluid when locally injected, to blood plasma following intravenous administration. The biomolecules in these fluids include electrolytes, lipids, and most importantly proteins, which adsorb on the LNP surface, forming a layer that defines the new biological identity of an LNP: the “biomolecular corona” (Figure 1).19, 20 This surface coating can be formed by hundreds of biomolecules including apolipoproteins, immunoglobulins, coagulation factors, and many others (Table 1).21−23 Some of these biomolecules might associate almost irreversibly to the LNP surface, in either their native or denatured form, 24 affecting, de facto, subsequent interactions. It has been proposed that the corona comprises both these tightly bound proteins (“hard” corona), which presumably bind directly to the LNP surface with high affinity, and also a looser, more dynamic layer (“soft” corona) which constantly exchanges with proteins in the environment. Among corona components, apolipoproteins are especially relevant because their retention can promote receptor-mediated uptake by hepatocytes. This phenomenon enabled the success of Onpattro, which efficiently targets hepatocytes due to the retention of one particular protein, namely, apolipoprotein E (ApoE), in its corona.10, 32, 33
Document [6]Certain surfactant- or peptide-modified nanoparticles (NPs), such as poly(ethylene glycol)-, polysorbate-, or amyloid β-protein (Aβ)-CN peptide-modified NPs, can absorb apolipoproteins (Apos) like ApoE or ApoB, forming Apo-rich protein coronas. These absorbed proteins interact with lipoprotein receptors on the blood–brain barrier (BBB), thereby facilitating NP entry into the brain.99–101 One example of protein corona-mediated targeting involves modifying the binding pattern of apolipoproteins on the surface of liposomes, which has been shown to enhance accumulation in the brain and demonstrate therapeutic effectiveness in a mouse model of glioma.100 This report details how the liposomal surface was altered using a short, non-toxic peptide derived from beta-amyloid (Aβ1–42). This modification specifically targets the lipid-binding domain of apolipoproteins to control their adsorption patterns. This engineered liposomal system enables brain-targeting proteins to associate within the bloodstream, effectively exposing their receptor-binding domains on the liposomal surface as they circulate.

For example, liposomes containing phospholipids with high phase transition temperature display differences in blood behavior.78, 79 It will be interesting to investigate whether these differences can be attributed to distinct protein adsorption onto the nanoparticle surface. Figure 3. Effect of blood-protein association on LNP systemic fate and biodistribution. PEG lipids can be incorporated into LNPs, but the resulting particles are defined biologically by the proteins that associate with their surface. Following intravenous LNP injection, surface lipids can exchange while proteins present in the blood, including apolipoproteins such as ApoE, associate with the nanoparticle, allowing receptor-mediated interactions with cells. LNPs therefore present biomolecular coronas in blood. A common surface component in this literature is a hydrophilic polymer with a neutral charge at physiological pH. The most commonly used polymer is polyethylene glycol (PEG). PEGylation has long been discussed in simplified terms, but it is now recognized that the proteins associated with PEGylated nanomedicines are important determinants of their biological identity (Figure 3). These interactions shape how nanoparticles are encountered by cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system.80−82 Conversely, avid capture by resident phagocytes such as Kupffer cells and splenic macrophages can dominate the initial fate of circulating LNPs and thereby determine their downstream tissue accumulation. However, it is now recognized that it is the presence of certain proteins, such as clusterin (apolipoprotein J), in the corona of PEGylated nanomedicines that is central to their biological identity.83, 84 These observations emphasize that the surface-presented protein corona, rather than the bare material alone, is essential to understanding LNP fate (Figure 3).85, 86

Abstract: Many potential therapeutic compounds for brain diseases fail to reach their molecular targets due to the impermeability of the blood-brain barrier, limiting their clinical development. Nanotechnology-based approaches might improve compounds pharmacokinetics by enhancing binding to the cerebrovascular endothelium and translocation into the brain. Adsorption of apolipoprotein E4 onto polysorbate® 80-stabilized nanoparticles to produce a protein corona allows the specific targeting of cerebrovascular endothelium. This strategy increased nanoparticle translocation into brain parenchyma, and improved brain nanoparticle accumulation 3-fold compared to undecorated particles (119.8 vs 40.5 picomoles; p<0.01).

Document [0]These lipids demonstrate excellent safety and efcacy for in vivo delivery of therapeutic nucleic acids of any size (Figure 1) [46–49]. We illustrate the concept of pHsensitive amphiphilic membrane disruption and endosomal escape, and highlight the potential of nonlamellar ionizable lipids with precisely controlled pH-sensitive amphiphilicity for efcient cytosolic nucleic acid delivery. The cell and subcellular membranes consist of a lipid bilayer containing phospholipids, cholesterol, and transmembrane proteins, playing a critical role in regulating the transport of substances into and out of cells and subcellular compartments. Nucleic acids, being negatively charged macromolecules, cannot pass through cell membranes unaided. Amphiphiles or surfactants can interact with the lipid bilayer, disrupting the membrane to facilitate the delivery process. Cationic lipids, such as DOTAP (1, 2-dioleoyl-3-trimethylammonium propane), are positively charged amphiphiles that have been incorporated into cationic liposomes for nucleic acid delivery . These cationic liposomes form stable LNPs with negatively charged nucleic acids, enabling intracellular transfection. An overly stable association between the lipid carrier and its nucleic-acid cargo after uptake can also limit delivery, because the nucleic acid may remain trapped in the LNP instead of dissociating into the cytosol for productive activity. However, these cationic lipids generally exhibit relatively low transfection efciency and signifcant toxicity. Figure 1 Nonlamellar ionizable lipid nanoparticles facilitate safe and efcient cytosolic delivery of a variety of therapeutic nucleic acids, including small RNA, mRNA, plasmid DNA, and gene editors into target cells. Ionizable lipids demonstrate promise in overcoming the limitations of cationic lipids, ofering a more efective and safer approach for in vivo cytosolic delivery of nucleic acids. These lipids mitigate cytotoxicity concerns, providing a pathway for efcient nucleic acid delivery in therapeutic applications .

The branched ionizable lipids also induce more efcient endosomal escape than lamellar lipid MC3 in mRNA LNPs . A study compared the cellular uptake and endosomal escape of MC3 with lipid 5, an analogue of SM-102, using single molecule fuorescence microscopy. MC3 LNP produced higher cellular uptake than Lipid 5, however, lipid 5 resulted in a 6-fold increase of endosomal escape efciency as compared to MC3 LNP, about 15% and 2.5% cytosolic delivery efciency for Lipid 5 and MC3, respectively, Figure 9 . Parallel-tempered metadynamics simulations confrmed that the branched ionizable lipids SM-102 and ALC-0315 possessed low free energy value and high capacity to penetrate a lipid bilayer, while MC3 did not have the ability to pass through a bilayer . Consequently, the branched ionizable lipids were more likely to mediate mRNA transfection for vaccines . The results further demonstrate that nonlamellar ionizable lipids are more efective in inducing endosomal escape than lamellar ionizable lipids. Biocompatibility and hemocompatibility of the delivery systems are essential for nucleic acid therapeutics because they are mostly administered systemically or locally. Document [0]As the mechanisms of action and immunomodulation of MSCs are being unveiled, a whole new range of potential clinical applications of these cells is also being established. Although MSCs are being studied and explored in virtually every field of health and medical research, autoimmune diseases have characteristics that make them especially important targets in these new therapeutic approaches. Autoimmune diseases are chronic diseases and systemic disorders in which an overactivation of the immune system occurs and a chronic inflammatory environment is established, leading to damage and general organic changes. Due to their ability to adapt to inflammatory microenvironmental conditions and to exert immunomodulatory activity through a paracrine route, MSCs are excellent candidates to be applied in these treatments. Through the secretion of soluble mediators, MSCs can positively influence the autoimmune process, including the inhibition of B and T cells, the decrease in Th1/Th2, Th17/Treg, and M1/M2 ratios, and the downregulation of inflammatory cytokines and factors such as IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, TNF-α, IFN-γ and the upregulation of others such as IL-4, IL-10 and TGF-β . Considering the COVID-19 pandemic that has affected the world in recent years, MSCs have also been explored as experimental treatments in patients with severe acute respiratory syndrome, revealing promising results. One of the great difficulties in establishing an effective strategy in these patients is the ability of the virus to stimulate a severe storm of cytokines in the lungs, a mechanism against which MSCs have advantageous effects as they help establish an immunomodulated environment by secreting several immunomodulatory factors with a synergistic effect on different cytokines simultaneously . In this setting, these MSC-derived soluble factors act within the pro-inflammatory pulmonary environment caused by virus replication and the consequent cytokine storm.
