Document [4]Based on karyotype analysis using G-banding, a number of hiPSC lines present aneuploidies; including recurrent ones mainly acquired during long term culture such as trisomy of chromosome 12, 17 or X or amplification of specific locus. Prolonged passaging can also impair telomere maintenance and mitotic chromosome segregation, creating the recurrent aneuploidies observed in hiPSC cultures. These abnormalities have been extensively reviewed . It is now accepted that these chromosomal and sub-chromosomal aberrations are common features of both hESCs and hiPSCs, however it is unclear if this trend is a specific feature associated with pluripotency or whether it would also be observed in non-pluripotent cells hypothetically maintained in long term culture if possible. In addition to the more commonly known chromosomal abnormalities, an aberration known as uniparental disomy (UPD) has been reported in iPSCs . UPD occurs when a daughter cell inherits two copies of a chromosome (or part of a chromosome) from one parental cell and no copy of the corresponding chromosome (or part of the chromosome) from the other parental cell. UPD can be associated with various clinical symptoms: it may lead to the acquisition of homozygosity of a recessive allele involved in a genetic disorder or to an imbalance of paternal versus maternal epigenetic information which may lead to dysfunction in case of the presence of imprinted genes . For example, UPD of chromosome 15 leads either to Angelman Syndrome (if both copies of a section of chromosome 15 are obtained from the father) or to Prader-Willy Syndrome (if both copies are obtained from the mother), both serious developmental disorders. UPD has never been reported in the context of hiPSCs until recently when Bershteyn et al used fibroblasts from patients affected with Miller Dieker Syndrome, a genetic disease characterized by the presence of a ring chromosome 17 and linked with congenital malformations. Authors reprogrammed these fibroblasts into hiPSCs using episomal vectors.
Document [5]A large-scale study as well as several individual studies have investigated chromosomal aberrations in both human ESCs and human iPSCs, and reported that trisomy 12 is most recurrently observed in both cell types. Because chromosome 12 contains cell cycle-related genes and harbors the pluripotency-associated gene NANOG , trisomy 12 might contribute to a selective proliferative advantage in pluripotent stem cells. Mayshar et al. also reported that a gain of the 12p region was caused by prolonged culture . Interestingly, the gain of 12p is a hallmark of testicular germ cell tumors . Other frequently recurrent aneuploidies in both cell types are amplifications of chromosome 8 and X . In addition, frequencies of chromosomal aberrations were not remarkably different between human iPSCs and ESCs . Although many common chromosomal aberrations are reported, different types of chromosomal aberrations are also identified . The reason for these differences remains to be elucidated (for review see Lund et al. ). The first CNV analysis of human iPSCs was conducted by Chin et al. using array CGH . Chin et al. found a few CNVs in each iPSC line, but none of the CNVs were shared between iPSC lines . Several larger-scale studies later identified an amplification of 20q11.21 as the most recurrent CNV hotspot . This CNV was also found in human ESCs . Duplication of 20q11 is also frequently found in several cancer types . This region is enriched with genes associated with pluripotency and anti-apoptosis, such as DNA methyltransferase 3B (DNMT3B), inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1), and BCL2-like1 (BCL2L1).

However, prolonged propagation *in vitro* subjects the cells to genetic changes that accompany adaptation to culture.3 It is now known that many of these occur repeatedly because they provide the aberrant cells with growth advantages, allowing them to gradually take over the culture.4, 5, 6 The genetic aberrations observed in cultured hPSCs include large chromosomal aberrations, sub-chromosomal and copy number variations (CNVs), and nucleotide point mutations, all of which require different methodologies to be detected. Previous reviews have discussed in detail the major types of recurrent genetic changes observed in hPSCs7; we summarize them here. The first type of genomic instability detected in hESCs (human embryonic stem cells) was reported over 15 years ago, with findings of karyotypic changes involving the gain of chromosome 17q and chromosome 12.4 Since then, it has been widely accepted that hPSCs may become aneuploid during prolonged culturing. In fact, studies have estimated that up to one-third of hPSC lines acquired chromosome abnormalities over time.8 Karyotypic changes in hPSCs are not acquired randomly, as a small number of particular aberrations occur more frequently than others. Specifically, the gain of part or entire chromosomes 12 and 17 remains the most common alteration detected by chromosomal banding alongside aberrations in chromosomes 1, 20, and X (Figure 2.9, 10 It is notable that gain of the short arm of chromosome 12, typically as an isochromosome (chromosome containing two short arms), is almost always found in embryonal carcinoma cells, the malignant counterparts of hPSCs.11 Loss of chromosomes was also observed in cultured hPSCs, though not as commonly, with recurrent loss in 10p and 18q (Figure 2.10

However, recurrent chromosomal aberrations are still observed, indicating that, while the overall mutation rate is low, culture-associated selective pressures can enrich chromosomal gains that provide a survivability advantage. This signifies that recurrent CNVs need not arise at high frequency to become prominent during expansion. 5. Altered Differentiation Propensity as a Result of Genetic Abnormalities The differentiation capacity of hPSC is crucial to their potential application. However, significant variation exists in the differentiation capacity of the cells as a result of a wide range of factors, including the multitude of CNVs found in the cells (recently reviewed in ). Until recently, the majority of findings pertaining to the impact of CNVs on hPSC differentiation have been based on single cell lines, did not control for genetic background, and/or failed to identify a mechanism of differentiation impairment. Two recent reports by our group bridge these shortcomings by using multiple isogenic cell lines to evaluate the impact of gains of 12p and 20q, two of the most common recurrent CNVs in hPSCs, on differentiation . In Keller et al., we described a general reduction in differentiation capacity in cells carrying a 12p13.31 gain. Furthermore, we demonstrated that residual pluripotent cells regularly form during hepatic progenitor differentiation in these cells.
Document [8]We found that karyotypic differences could be seen in fibroblast and iPSC cultures in material from our patient. One reason for the differences observed during culture is that the cultured cell population is subject to selective growth. Growth in culture increases the likelihood that a pre-existing variant providing a proliferative advantage will become enriched. Under these conditions, abnormal variants already present in the donor fibroblast population before reprogramming can be clonally selected and expanded during iPSC derivation. Such observations indicate that the composition of cell populations can shift during derivation and expansion. The origin of these minor cell populations is not always clear. Thus, fibroblast culture may preferentially reveal subclones that are already present at low frequency in donor cells and that expand more readily under culture conditions.

This could pave the way for their use in transplantation therapies benefiting patients with kidney disorders. PSC-derived kidney organoids have been generated via patterning to intermediate mesoderm (IM) using various protocols, and these progenitors self-organize and pattern to develop organoids that variably consist of nephrons, endothelial cells, ureteric epithelium, and stroma.3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 As such, none of these models represent a complete developing kidney. Although organoid transplantation has been performed, considerable hurdles remain to develop an efficient clinical therapy, mainly related to maturation state and vascular integration. Broadly, there are 2 main approaches. The first involves generating a large number of nephrons and transplanting them into the host to enable vascularization and filtration. This review explores the field of organoid vascularization, examining the biological principles that inform bioengineering approaches. To bridge these gaps, we developed Cell2Spatial, a computational framework that segments spatial spots at single-cell resolution, even when SC and ST datasets are not fully matched in cell types. The method integrates information-theoretic gene selection, spatially weighted likelihood modeling, and spatial hotspot detection to improve signal fidelity. A corrected saturation model calibrates library size against gene complexity, ensuring accurate cell count estimation in ST data. Low-resolution ST analyses therefore remain sensitive to reference incompleteness and to expression patterns that are not well captured in the reference used for deconvolution. Structures such as axons and dendrites are especially difficult to preserve during dissociation, so the associated cells or states may be under-represented in the reference rather than defining a separate source of deconvolution error here. Indeed, it has been estimated that over 40% of the total transcriptome of an adult mouse brain may be missed by sc/snRNA-seq22. First, they can bias analyses that do not take them into account. An example with dramatic implications is that deconvolution estimates of cell-type proportions can be invalid if the reference is missing any cell types23, as we illustrate later in this work. Second, biologically important signals may be assigned incorrectly when either the reference is incomplete or contamination is not modeled. For example, cell populations such as adipocytes5 and neutrophils25 may be missed in dissociation-based references, and the resulting mismatch can distort interpretation. Analyzing ST data typically proceeds by extracting cell-level information from the spatial expression data, as cells are natural units of analysis. With high-resolution platforms such as MERFISH3, 10x Visium HD4, or 10x Xenium5, this is usually done using cell segmentation6-8. Document [6]**Background** Spot-based Spatial transcriptomics (ST) allows for unbiased gene expression analysis within tissue architecture, overcoming the limitations of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) by preserving spatial context. Spot-based measurements nevertheless require computational deconvolution to infer cellular compositions from aggregated expression profiles. While scRNA-seq serves as a key reference for deconvolution, the impact of incompletely captured tissue cell states on its accuracy is still unclear. In this study, we systematically evaluate how reference state coverage affects cellular deconvolution and give helpful guide-lines to researchers to address this task. **Methods** We systematically evaluate the impact of single-cell reference state coverage for global and cell type-specific deconvolution performances in primary and metastatic breast cancer ST datasets. Focusing on state-of-the-art deconvolution tools Cell2location and Robust Cell Type Decomposition (RCTD), we assess the influence of how completely references capture relevant breast cancer cell states, as well as the usage of breast cancer atlases with broader state coverage. **Results** Our findings demonstrate that deconvolution accuracy depends on whether the reference captures the cellular states present in the assayed tissue, with RCTD and Cell2location exhibiting similar performances across cell-types. Cell populations whose dominant transcriptional states were less completely represented, such as myeloids, presented greater challenges for accurate deconvolution than cell types whose states were better captured, such as epithelial cells. Differences in per-cell mRNA output can also bias mixed-spot estimates, because within the same spot, transcript-rich cell types contribute more counts than equally abundant but transcriptionally smaller cells. Spatial domains associated with prominent cell types like cancer and stromal cells were detected, although their contributions were systematically under- or over-estimated when reference states were coarse or incomplete. Finally, breast cancer single-cell atlases were also able to provide reliable deconvolution results when they covered the relevant tissue states. **Conclusion** This study provides important insights into optimizing reference state coverage for ST deconvolution, highlighting the strengths and limitations of current computational tools when relevant cell states are incompletely represented in spatial transcriptomics analyses.
Document [7]Cancer remains one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, with glioblastoma (GBM) standing out as an especially aggressive and treatment-resistant malignancy. A central driver of this resistance lies in the tumor microenvironment (TME)—a complex, spatially organized ecosystem of diverse cell types and signaling pathways. Understanding cellular heterogeneity and intercellular communication within the TME is crucial for developing more effective therapies. Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, in which human tumors are engrafted into immunocompromised mice, preserve essential tumor characteristics and provide a valuable platform for studying TME dynamics. However, accurately resolving cell-type mixtures in such complex samples remains analytically challenging, especially when the single-cell reference used does not fully reflect the states present in the assayed tissue. This thesis presents two major computational innovations to address these challenges using spatial transcriptomics (ST) data. First, it introduces spOT-NMF, a novel unsupervised deconvolution method that integrates Optimal Transport with Non-negative Matrix Factorization. In contrast to popular reference-based approaches that depend on single-cell reference datasets and can be sensitive to reference mismatch in complex tissues, spOT-NMF is fully reference-free. It disentangles mixed gene expression profiles among samples by leveraging the Wasserstein distance, enabling accurate and scalable analysis across varying spatial resolutions and sequencing depths. Extensive benchmarking against established unsupervised methods such as LDA, NMF, and cNMF demonstrates that spOT-NMF consistently outperforms these models, particularly in low-signal and heterogeneous xenograft settings. Second, a computational framework (XenoSignal) is developed to discover and enhance interpretability of ligand-receptor (LR) interactions in xenografts. An analytic pipeline was established to better characterize which interactions can be interpreted with confidence.
Document [8]Deconvolution methods are broadly classified into reference-based and reference-free approaches. Reference-based approaches such as Robust Cell Type Decomposition, cell2location, and SPOTlight deconvolve a spatial spot based on its inferred cellular composition by referring to scRNA-seq data . While these approaches generally achieve higher accuracy, they require high-quality, well-matched scRNA-seq reference datasets that may not be available or may not fully capture the cell states present in the assayed tissue . Conversely, reference-free methods such as STdeconvolve and Conditional Autoregressive Deconvolution characterize cellular composition without external references, instead relying on spatial gene expression patterns to identify distinct cell populations . At the same time, neighboring spots often share spatially correlated expression, violating models that assume each spot is an independent mixture . While these methods are more flexible, they can still struggle when spatial dependence between neighboring spots is not adequately modeled . Benchmarking analysis demonstrated that hybrid approaches, particularly Bayesian and graph-based models incorporating spatial transcriptomic data and biological priors, outperform purely data-driven methods . Importantly, the study provides practical guidelines for selecting appropriate deconvolution methods based on reference availability and the extent of spatial dependence in the dataset . Deconvolution tools are critical for distinguishing malignant, stromal, and immune cell populations within the tumor microenvironment . This capability enables precise characterization of cellular composition, ultimately enhancing ST's utility for understanding disease progression, treatment response, and identification of novel therapeutic targets .

Document [0]Difficulty in obtaining and preserving samples, and the quality of genome annotation in non-human primates have restricted the scope of most comparative studies in primates to characterizing patterns of gene regulation across a small set of species using bulk transcriptomic data from a limited number of tissues10–14. Moreover, recent analyses15, 16 highlight the difficulty of disentangling functional gene co-regulation confounded with co-expression because of variation in cell-type abundance across tissue samples. Comparative co-expression analysis at single-cell resolution has the potential to systematically trace the origin and diversity of cell types across animal evolution. Representing cells by conserved gene-module or pathway activity profiles can likewise provide a shared space for cross-species alignment of homologous cell types when individual orthologues vary. Single-cell transcriptomics has become a powerful tool to identify regional and interspecific variation in gene expression underlying the evolution of brain regions and cell types within17–19 and across species20–24. For example, aligning human and mouse samples from homologous brain regions revealed extensive divergence in gene expression of cortical cell types2 , and the presence of a primate-specific striatal interneuron population25, highlighting the need to study primate brains at high resolution to uncover the mechanisms behind evolutionary innovations in the human lineage. To identify human-specific patterns of gene activity driving brain evolution, we used the gene expression resource recently generated by the BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network consortium26. This dataset contains high-quality single-nucleus transcriptomic atlases of the middle temporal gyrus (MTG) sampled from five primates (human, chimp, gorilla, macaque and marmoset), spanning an evolutionary period of \~45 million years. The essence of our approach was to identify cell types shared across species, and then use this common sample space to determine where and how orthologues change their expression pattern. In this study, we identified 57 homologous cell types by aligning single-nucleus MTG atlases of five primates. We observed high cross-species similarity in expression variability over 57 consensus cell types for orthologous genes, suggesting conserved transcriptional patterning across primates.

Early microarray-based comparative studies noted that divergence in gene activity in the same tissue between species reflects their evolutionary relationships12, 33. Similarly, concordance among orthologous genes decreases with evolutionary distance between human and non-human primates, while remaining high among the great apes. Many marker genes and, in particular, transcription factors also show high functional conservation across species, suggesting a highly conserved molecular landscape of the MTG region across primates (Fig. 3e; see Methods for details on marker and transcription factor selection). Such conservation means that homologous cell types can also be aligned in a shared regulatory-network space defined by transcription-factor programs rather than only by raw expression of orthologous genes. For each gene with multiple isoforms in a pair of species, we calculated the ability of each isoform to correctly predict itself across species. Document [8]Cross-species comparisons can use one-to-one ortholog gene expression to map cell types across extensive collections of datasets. A learned cross-species latent embedding can similarly bring transcriptionally corresponding cells together in a common space for homologous cell-type alignment. Spurious cross-dataset correspondences are minimized—only cells mapping consistently across multiple datasets are used to identify common subpopulations (Barkas et al., 2018). It will be important in the near future for ortholog-based and latent-space tools to be benchmarked for different kinds of data, and against each other extensively. I foresee that careful evaluation of these approaches will likely be critical for achieving robust performance across many species. Though the above approaches offer exciting possibilities for comparing single-cell data across species, many caveats exist for their implementation. All current approaches require that only the orthologous genes between the species are used during analysis. These genes are used during feature selection and downstream analysis (Figure 1A). Non-homologous genes expressed in only one dataset contribute heavily to variation, and can drive cells to cluster with their own species rather than the same cell type across species (Figure 2C; Stuart and Satija, 2019). However, this ortholog-restricted comparison does not capture every aspect of species-specific transcriptional variation. Indeed, clade-specific genes are known to drive species-specific cell type diversification (Santos et al., 2017; Florio et al., 2018), and sub- or neo-functionalization in expression patterns of one gene copy following gene duplication is common (Figure 2D; Farrè and Albà, 2010). For closely related species, such as humans and mice, gene symbols can be easily matched to identify orthologs. For more distantly related organisms, databases such as ENSEMBL can be used to identify one-to-one matches (Zerbino et al., 2018). This works well for closely related species, but becomes more difficult as the amount of evolutionary time between species increases, and the relationship between genes becomes less clear (Thornton and Desalle, 2000).

Wong 1, 2 Deciphering how DNA sequence specifies cell-type-specific regulatory activity is a central challenge in gene regulation. We present Bag-of-Motifs (BOM), a computational framework that represents distal cis-regulatory elements as unordered counts of transcription factor (TF) motifs. This minimalist representation, combined with gradient-boosted trees, enables the accurate prediction of cell-type-specific enhancers across mouse, human, zebrafish, and Arabidopsis datasets. Despite its simplicity, BOM outperforms more complex deep-learning models while using fewer parameters. We validate BOM’s predictions experimentally by constructing synthetic enhancers from the most predictive motifs, demonstrating that these motif sets drive cell-type-specific expression. By providing direct interpretability and broad applicability, BOM reveals a highly predictive sequence code at distal regulatory regions and offers a scalable framework for dissecting cis-regulatory grammar across diverse species and conditions. A fundamental goal of biology is to understand how genetic information is translated into the diverse phenotypes observed across organisms. At the heart of this process lies an intricate regulatory network that controls gene expression with remarkable spatial and temporal precision. Cis-regulatory elements (CREs)—including promoters, enhancers, insulators, and silencers—coordinate the recruitment of transcription factors (TFs) and cofactors to DNA. Enhancers are of particular importance as they act as integrators of developmental and environmental cues to establish and maintain cell identity1–3 . These elements are can be located far from their target genes and contain clusters of short TF binding motifs (\~8–10 bp)4 , whose number can influence the strength of TF binding5 . Representations that encode three-dimensional chromatin contacts can therefore capture which distal CREs physically engage their target promoters in a cell-type-specific manner. Advancements in genome-scale experimental profiling of the regulatory genome have enabled researchers to map CREs across diverse mammalian cell types systematically.

Using gradient-boosted trees, BOM captures the combinatorial contributions of TF motifs while remaining computationally efficient. Importantly, the motif-centric representation yields a vocabulary of regulatory features that is biologically interpretable and can be linked directly to gene expression and TF expression. This also supports trans-regulator abundance-aware regulatory representations, in which cis-motif features are paired with the cell-type-specific expression or abundance of the TFs and cofactors that read them. This can yield feature importance scores, motifs (k-mers or PWMs, depending on the provided input features, Figure 2A) and motif interactions (Ghandi et al., 2014; Keilwagen and Grau, 2015), all of which comprise a compendium of regulatory grammar, informative for understanding the regulation of gene expression. Due to the inherent capability of DNNs to learn predictive motif representations and rules for cooperative TF binding interactions (Avsec et al., 2021), they represent a powerful approach to uncover the detailed *cis*-regulatory grammar of genomic sequences (Figure 2C) (Koo and Ploenzke, 2020a; He et al., 2020). This is achieved by interpreting the models using approaches that include: 1) CNN kernel visualization, where typically motifs in the initial layers are visualized, 2) input perturbation-based (sensitivity) analysis, which highlights the parts of a given input sequence that are most influential for the model prediction by occluding or mutating them (Alipanahi et al., 2015; Ancona et al., 2017), 3) gradient-based methods that estimate feature importance with iterative backward and forward propagations through the network (Shrikumar et al., 2017; Montavon et al., 2018; Shrikumar et al., 2018), yielding e.g. saliency maps (Simonyan et al., 2013) and 4) higher-order interactions among sequence elements, which can be assessed e.g. by using association rule analysis (Naulaerts et al., 2015; Zrimec et al., 2020), second-order perturbations (Koo et al., 2018), self-attention networks (Ullah and Ben-Hur, 2020) or by visualizing kernels in deeper layers (Maslova et al., 2020); interested readers are referred to (Eraslan et al., 2019a; Koo and Ploenzke, 2020a).
Document [6]This can be useful in complicated tasks, such as learning DNA regulatory grammar, because a wider array of representations can be combinatorially constructed from partial representations to capture the rich array of biologically important sequence patterns *in vivo* (Siggers and Gordân, 2014; Zrimec et al., 2020). Successive layers (e.g. Third layer) then learn to recognize motif interactions (i.e. associations in predicting the target variable) across the regulatory structure (Zeng et al., 2016; Zrimec et al., 2020). The extent to which sequence motif representations are learned by first layer kernels is influenced by kernel size and pooling, which enforce a spatial information bottleneck either from the sequence to the CNN or between successive CNN layers, respectively. For instance, large max-pooling (≥10) was shown to force kernels to learn whole motifs, whereas CNNs that employ a low max-pool size (≤4) capture partial motifs (Koo and Eddy, 2019). Similarly, the size of successive convolutional kernels can also affect the ability to assemble whole motifs in deeper layers. Moreover, the number of kernels in the first layer sets a hard constraint on the number of different sequence patterns that can be detected (Koo and Eddy, 2019). Since the scope of initial characterized sequence features limits the range and complexity of grammar representations that can be built downstream, this parameter was generally found to have the greatest impact on CNN performance (Zeng et al., 2016). Therefore, in contrast to learning tasks where the main features are simple, such as occurrence of a PWM-like motif in TFBS prediction, using multiple parts of the regulatory structures requires deeper and more complex architectures that learn distributed motif representations to address the more complex sequence patterns (Koo and Eddy, 2019; Trabelsi et al., 2019) (Figure 2D).
Document [7]However, it does require representing the categorical nucleotide sequence data numerically using an encoding scheme, such as one-hot, which transforms the sequence into a binary matrix with columns corresponding to each category. DNNs have thus been applied mostly on one-hot encoded nucleotide sequences as input (Eraslan et al., 2019a; Alipanahi et al., 2015), with recent reports showing that the use of k-mer embedding to represent the input sequences can improve model performance compared to one-hot encoding (itself a special case of k-mer embedding where *k* = 1) (Trabelsi et al., 2019). These inputs are well suited for comprehending the base DNA motif information as well as higher order interactions that describe the DNA regulatory grammar of gene expression (Eraslan et al., 2019a; Zrimec et al., 2020). Thus, DNNs achieve high predictive accuracies often surpassing those of models based on engineered features and, in our experience, using structural DNA properties does not lead to improved predictive performance with DNNs (Zrimec et al., 2020). Due to the large amount of model *hyper*parameters, such as network structure (e.g. number and size of kernels, Figure 2B) and training algorithm (e.g. learning rate), a special step termed hyperparameter optimization (Bergstra et al., 2015) is required for finding the best combinations of these hyperparameters and is an integral part of DNN training. To train DNNs, the data is typically split into training, validation, and testing datasets, where: 1) the model is trained on the training set by minimizing a loss function commonly MSE for regression and cross entropy for classification (Géron, 2019), 2) hyperparameter tuning is performed on the validation set and the best performing model on the validation set is chosen, and 3) the performance of the final model is evaluated on the testing set, also verifying if it overfits the data (Eraslan et al., 2019a; Zrimec et al., 2020) (Figure 2A).

Document [2]ISD is a Bayesian probabilistic framework that views biomolecular structure determination as an inference problem. At the core of the ISD approach is a probability distribution over conformational space representing and combining both noisy and possibly incomplete data as well as prior knowledge about the unknown structure. Several Bayesian approaches have been developed to model the structure of chromosomes based on ensemble Hi-C data . These methods try to infer a consensus structure of the population data, which is only of limited use. Moreover these approaches have not fully benefited from the Bayesian approach to chromosome structure inference. Wang et al. calculate structural ensembles using a Bayesian approach, but only optimize the posterior probability and do not apply the full Bayesian inference machinery, which allows for the quantification of parameter uncertainties and the comparison of alternative models. Here we report on the application of ISD to infer statistically well-defined ensembles of chromosome structures from single-cell Hi-C data. We show that Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling allows us to compute diverse ensembles of coarse-grained chromosome conformations that reflect the sparsity of single-cell Hi-C contacts. MCMC techniques and the flexibility of our Bayesian approach also allow us to compare different models of the chromatin fiber as well as alternative models for Hi-C contacts. We use the conformational ensembles to map epigenetic marks into three-dimensional space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ISD outperforms alternative methods on simulated data. Finally, we show how to extend the approach to diploid chromosomes and infer the structures of two chromosome copies simultaneously. We model the chromatin fiber with a beads-on-a-string representation. Owing to the sparsity of single-cell Hi-C contacts, we use a highly coarse-grained model in which every bead represents 500 kb of chromatin and has a radius of approximately 215 nm. Beads are connected such that they form a linear chain. The connectivity is enforced by a harmonic backbone potential, which penalizes distances between consecutive beads as soon as they exceed the bead diameter a.

Then an initial random conformation is equilibrated to minimize the energy of overstretched bonds and turns into one of the conformations corresponding to the provided single cell Hi-C contact map. DPDchrom and the Stevens method use interaction potentials softer than those in CMD, hence preventing vitrification during equilibration. The significant limitation of the Stevens method is its restricted conformational range with additional constraints, whereas DPDchrom can sample a broader range due to the presence of explicit solvent. We have determined the set of parameters that are optimal for the reconstruction of chromatin conformations. The constraints, such as connectivity along the chain and additional bonds from the list of spatial neighbors, define a family, i.e., an ensemble, of multiple conformations. Within such families, at least some of the observed variation is best described as transient stochastic contact configurations. Families may have different sizes. A family size is defined by conformational freedom of the units (mostly, free of additional bonds) and soft nature of the entire system (bends, twists, etc.). Such maize genotypes also show greater plasticity in lateral rooting and root system expansion under low N conditions, allowing more effective foraging for scarce soil nitrogen. Maize performance under reduced fertilizer input is influenced by N supply and the level of N uptake from soil , and genotypic differences in response to low N are commonly observed among hybrids . Sustained N uptake under limited N supply is an important trait in maize . The efficiency of maize in accessing soil N depends on its ability to acquire N from the soil solution, which is influenced by how the root system is deployed in the soil . Nitrogen uptake efficiency (total aboveground N accumulation at a given level of N supply) can be separated into constituent traits that describe root characteristics associated with genetic variation in N uptake . The amount and placement of root tissue active in N acquisition influence the rate of N uptake, and these component traits differ genetically . Development of the root system affects nitrate acquisition from the soil . Genotypic differences in lateral root development can influence where active root tissue is positioned for nitrate uptake and subsequent transport . High NUE is critical for sustainable maize production , and better understanding of genotypic differences in root foraging under low N can help explain why maize RE globally is only about 35% to 55% .

Document [0]Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) enhance nutrient provision in exchange for carbon. However, a shift from nutrient to carbon limitation, induced by repeated or intense defoliation, can represent a trade-off between plant regrowth and the maintenance of mycorrhiza. The combined effects of AMF, phosphorus and defoliation on growth of *A**gropyron* *elongatum* (C3 grass, low mycorrhizal responsiveness) and *B**rachiaria* *brizantha* (C4 grass, high mycorrhizal responsiveness) were explored. Each species was subjected to a manipulative experiment with AMF inoculation (non-inoculated, inoculated), soluble P supply (low, high) and defoliation (non-defoliated, 60% defoliated). In *A. elongatum*, at low P supply, mycorrhizal plants showed increased growth rates following defoliation without substantial changes in AMF colonization. Plants under phosphorus limitation can maintain growth by remobilizing phosphorus from older tissues and using each unit of internal phosphorus more efficiently. At high P supply instead, we found a clear trade-off between regrowth and the maintenance of mycorrhiza evidenced by growth depression (biomass and tillers) and lower AMF activity (reduction of arbuscules). In contrast, in *B. brizantha*, defoliation effects on plant regrowth were independent from AMF at any P supply (no trade-off). This indicates that cost-benefit relationship in defoliated plants is highly context-dependent and may vary with mycorrhizal responsiveness of species. This variation of responses can play a decisive role on plant recovery in pastures and natural grasslands subjected to herbivory. Many experiments have demonstrated the growth stimulation of plant crops in the greenhouse, resulting in increased yield parameters and in the control on soil-borne pathogenic organisms. However, the replication of successful results of PGPR applications under field conditions has been limited by the lack of knowledge about their ecology, survival and activity in the plant rhizosphere. Part of this ecological uncertainty arises because plant genotypes differ in root-exudate chemistry, creating host–inoculant mismatches when a strain adapted to one host is applied to another in the field. The main aspects related to the application of bacterial inoculants are discussed below. **Efficacy of PGPR inoculation** PGPR efficacy is dependent on establishing an effective population density of active cells in plant rhizosphere. As this is a simple principle, it has proved to be difficult to establish dose response effects in which the degree of plant growth promotion or disease suppression can be directly correlated with size of the PGPR population. In general, bacterial suspensions of PGPR are prepared at densities of 108 to 109 CFU ml-1 for root dipping and soil inoculation.

question: Which types of organic materials are responsible for the enduring sequestration of carbon in soils under agricultural management?
perspectives: Microbial necromass associated with mineral surfaces
Plant-derived compounds associated with mineral surfaces
Particulate organic matter protected within aggregates

Document [0]Physical fractionation of soil organic matter (SOM) is usually used to explain the dynamics of SOC as affected by land-use change (von Lützow et al., 2007), Li et al., 2013). The particulate organic matter (POM, particle size > 0.05 mm) is considered to be dominated by plant residues at different levels of decomposition. Therefore, it is an active or labile SOM pool and thus changes quickly to plant C inputs and microbial decomposition (von Lützow et al., 2007), Li et al., 2013). However, particulate organic matter occluded within stable aggregates can be physically protected from decomposers and thereby contribute to longer-term carbon persistence in managed cropland soils. Given the larger plant C inputs after cropland abandonment (Guan et al., 2018), Liu et al., 2018), a reduction in the content of this pool can be ascribed to increased mineralization in abandoned compared with conventionally cultivated soils (i.e., with tillage but without the returning of stubble). In contrast, the mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM, particle size < 0.05 mm) mainly consists of microbially derived compounds (Cotrufo et al., 2013), Kleber et al., 2021). This microbial substance–dominated fraction of SOC is believed to be stable in the short term (over a decade), because it is absorbed on surfaces of fine minerals or encapsulated in micropores (von Lützow et al., 2007), Kleber et al., 2021). Recent advances emphasize the role of microbially synthesized compounds (e.g., microbial necromass carbon, MNC) in the formation and stabilization of SOC (Miltner et al., 2012, Liang et al., 2017), Liang et al., 2019). The microbial necromass contains substantial amounts of N (over 60 % of total soil N) (Mengel et al., 1996; Cui et al., 2020).

Bacterial taxa may also influence necromass retention on mineral surfaces by interacting with fungal morphology or chemistry39. To resolve these contradictions, we anticipate that future studies may compare species effects in terms of forming mineral-associated C. Here, we hypothesized that decomposition rates, necromass formation20, and necromass-mineral association would vary among treatments. In this laboratory incubation, the substrate-derived C and N remaining in the bulk soil pool represent C and N that were not released as gaseous efflux.
Document [2]Natural wetlands store 20–30 % of soil organic carbon (SOC), and conversion of croplands to wetlands is thus an effective strategy for SOC restoration. However, the contribution of microbial necromass carbon to mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) during this conversion process remains unclear. We collected samples of topsoil (0–20 cm) and subsoil (40–60 cm) from croplands, rewetlands (i.e., rewetting croplands) and natural wetlands in 20 different sites in Baiyangdian Lake to compare changes in SOC fractions (particulate organic carbon, POC; mineral-associated organic carbon, MAOC) and microbial contributions to these fractions. Both SOC and POC in the topsoil gradually decreased from croplands to wetlands. Microbial necromass carbon (MNC) mirrored the decline in SOC, but its contribution to MAOC gradually increased in the subsoil. Depth-dependent regulation of SOC fractions was observed, with conversion indirectly affecting soil microbe and necromass accumulation through regulating soil properties, thereby influencing SOC fractions in the topsoil. In contrast, in the subsoil, soil properties had a more direct impact on SOC fractions, with microbial effects being less apparent. This study confirms the critical role of MNC within MAOC in regulating SOC fractions during conversion of croplands to wetlands, and highlights the potential to enhance SOC stability. Enhancing and protecting soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and its stability is a highly effective strategy for reducing atmospheric CO2 levels and mitigating global warming (Yang et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2023).
Document [3]Microbes are the central players in decomposition, acting on both labile carbon and more recalcitrant materials in ways that shape the transformation of organic inputs. Importantly, microbial activity is key to decomposition responses and to the fate of carbon in the soil. The formation of microbial necromass, dead microbial cells that can become associated with mineral surfaces, is a major component of stable SOM and contributes as a key mechanism in long-term carbon sequestration through the MCP. An enhanced knowledge of these microbial processes directly supports a mechanistic understanding of soil carbon persistence. This highlights the importance of considering soil and climate context in interpreting SOM dynamics. This paper therefore links theoretical developments with their application. In principle, it integrates a mechanistic, multi-scale approach to SOM dynamics, moving beyond simplistic conceptualizations by emphasizing the MCP and mineral-associated microbial residues. Operationally, it provides a framework for understanding stable SOM formation.
Document [4]Carbon transformation and stabilization within these fractions are strongly influenced by climate and soil texture . For example, higher temperature and optimum moisture content trigger particulate organic carbon (POC) degradation by stimulating microbial activity and enzyme kinetics, thereby reducing turnover times . However, simultaneously, these climatic conditions can indirectly promote the formation of mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) by stimulating the degradation of complex organic matter and the subsequent formation of microbial necromass, which can adsorb on mineral surfaces . Additionally, fine-textured soils (such as clays) provide greater surface area and pore spaces for organo–mineral associations and physical protection, thereby promoting MAOC formation and stability compared to sandy soils . This is further mediated by microbial processing, because microbial turnover generates necromass that forms MAOC, including under nutrient limitation or during drying–rewetting cycles that induce cell lysis and subsequent adsorption . Therefore, the interaction between microbial processing and soil mineralogy helps channel carbon from labile POC into stable MAOC pools . Recent studies have demonstrated that cropland soils typically contain lower SOM concentrations than natural ecosystems owing to frequent disturbances and reduced carbon inputs . In agricultural systems, the persistence of SOM is closely tied to the extent to which organic matter is transformed into mineral-associated forms rather than remaining as more labile material . Crop residues contribute varying amounts of carbon with different chemical compositions, some of which can become associated with minerals after processing . Some of these plant-derived compounds can also adsorb onto mineral surfaces and enter the MAOC pool, allowing plant inputs to contribute to long-term carbon persistence in cropland soils. This broader decline in SOC under cultivation highlights why the mineral-associated fraction is critical for retention in managed cropland .

Document [0]Control plots received no straw or biochar as a soil amendment. The authors also examined two rates of nitrogen fertilizer: 0 kg N per ha (N0) and 210 kg N per ha (N1). Total methane emissions were highest on the plots receiving straw at 5.05 t per ha. The biochar amendments reduced methane emissions, relative to the straw treatment, for both levels of nitrogen. Biochar also increased total soil carbon at higher rates than returning straw to the soil. The carbon in biochar can exist in soils over long time scales, and biochar increases soil porosity, while reducing soil bulk density . Changing the cropping pattern from continuous paddy rice to paddy rice followed by maize or aerobic rice production can substantially reduce methane emissions. Weller et al. examined methane and nitrous oxide emissions from three cropping patterns on experimental plots in Los Baños, Philippines. Replacing the second paddy rice crop with an upland crop (maize or aerobic rice) reduced methane emissions by 66% to 81%. Methane emissions were reduced also in the subsequent wet season, when paddy rice was again planted, by 54% to 60%. Annual emissions of nitrous oxide increased with the planting of an upland crop, yet the substantial reductions in methane emissions resulted in a smaller global warming potential with the diversified cropping pattern . Zhang et al. also examine methane and carbon dioxide emissions from fields planted in a rice-rapeseed rotation in Central China. The authors assess the implications of alternative tillage practices and of incorporating plant residue into the soil, following harvest. This study highlights how rhizospheric emissions respond to water-regime-induced redox shifts, providing a deeper theoretical foundation for developing targeted low-carbon management strategies for rice paddy cultivation. Water resources represent one of Earth’s most invaluable natural assets and are fundamental to both human sustenance and agricultural productivity.

question: Which biological processes are responsible for the decline in wheat grain productivity when heat and drought stress occur simultaneously after flowering?
perspectives: Reduced source photosynthesis from stomatal closure and photoinhibition
Impaired grain sink strength and starch synthesis
Accelerated leaf senescence shortening grain filling
Reduced assimilate transport and stem-reserve remobilization
context:
Document [0]Drought stress severely hampered the gas exchange parameters of crop plants and this could be due to decrease in leaf expansion, impaired photosynthetic machinery, premature leaf senescence, oxidation of chloroplast lipids and changes in structure of pigments and proteins (Menconi et al., 1995). Anjum et al. (2011a) indicated that drought stress in maize led to considerable decline in net photosynthesis (33.22%), transpiration rate (37.84%), stomatal conductance (25.54%), water use efficiency (50.87%), intrinsic water use efficiency (11.58%) and intercellular CO2 (5.86%) as compared to well water control. Many studies have shown the decreased photosynthetic activity under drought stress due to stomatal or non-stomatal mechanisms (Ahmadi, 1998; Del Blanco et al., 2000; Samarah et al., 2009). Stomata are the entrance of water loss and CO2 absorbability and stomatal closure is one of the first responses to drought stress which result in declined rate of photosynthesis. Stomatal closure deprives the leaves of CO2 and photosynthetic carbon assimilation is decreased in favor of photorespiration. Considering the past literature as well as the current information on drought-induced photosynthetic responses, it is evident that stomata close progressively with increased drought stress. It is well known that leaf water status always interacts with stomatal conductance and a good correlation between leaf water potential and stomatal conductance always exists, even under drought stress. It is now clear that there is a drought-induced root-to-leaf signaling, which is promoted by soil drying through the transpiration stream, resulting in stomatal closure. The "non-stomatal" mechanisms include changes in chlorophyll synthesis, functional and structural changes in chloroplasts, and disturbances in processes of accumulation, transport, and distribution of assimilates. In wheat after flowering, simultaneous heat and drought can also slow phloem assimilate transport and weaken remobilization of stem water-soluble reserves to the ears, leaving less carbohydrate available for grain filling.
Document [1]The decreasing carbon assimilation rate (*P**N*) observed in the present study was attributed to heat stress, which, in turn, led to a drastic reduction in grain yield in all the genotypes investigated. Photosynthesis is one of the cellular functions most sensitive to high-temperature stress (Wahid et al. 2007; Wang et al. 2016). On the other hand, photo-inhibition in wheat plants occurs during heat stress to cause ROS generation, damage to PSII components, chlorophyll degradation, inactivation of enzymes involved in CO2 assimilation, and, ultimately, reduction in *P**N* (Djanaguiraman et al.).
Document [2]Decreased photosynthetic rate under high temperature in wheat has been linked to damage to the photosynthetic apparatus. The results of the current study indicate that terminal heat stress reduced PN, gs, and E, which led to iWUE and WUE losses, although these changes varied in severity among the tested genotypes. The strong relationship observed between gs and E is of particular interest because gs directly regulates water loss from the leaves. The decrease in E is therefore consistent with stomatal limitation under stress. Decreasing gs under high temperature has already been noted in wheat, together with effects on chlorophyll fluorescence.
Document [3]The effects of extreme high temperatures on crops have been widely analyzed in several species; wheat , cowpea , soybean , and rice . In the case of wheat, Asseng et al. provided a detailed impact assessment of high temperatures on yield and how critical the adverse effects will be on the production of this crop. Although most of these studies focus on the flowering stage, many evaluations have also been carried out on the other stages of plant development . For example, Wang et al. found differences in photosynthesis and stomatal conductance values between pre-anthesis high temperature acclimated wheat plants and those that had not experienced pre-anthesis heat exposure. As Hay and Walker described, crop yield is affected by heat stress. In this regard, effects on leaf gas exchange and photosynthetic performance have been repeatedly identified in plants . In the first instance, extreme temperatures can affect photosynthesis at the stomatal level under heat stress conditions. In fact, by controlling water vapor and CO2 diffusion, stomata largely contribute to both the rate and the temperature dependence of photosynthesis . Several studies have analyzed plant behavior at the stomatal conductance level under heat-stressed situations, with most indicating inhibition of photosynthesis . Yang et al. also suggested that stomatal responses to high temperature are strongly influenced by water vapor pressure in maize plants.
Document [4]These traits should be prioritized in programs developed for the genetic breeding of wheat that aims at the development of heat-tolerant cultivars. High-temperature stress at the reproductive phase is a most important factor limiting grain yield in wheat. The problem is further worsened by global warming. As such, the results of the current study pave the way for exploring the effects of terminal heat stress on leaf photosynthesis and photosystem II activity in wheat. It was found that terminal heat stress left negative effects on both leaf gas exchange and chlorophyll fluorescence to cause drastic losses in wheat grain yield. Such losses are intensified under combined post-flowering heat and drought in wheat, when developing kernels lose sink strength because endosperm starch-synthesizing enzymes are inhibited, reducing starch deposition in the grain. Given the appropriateness but complex nature of grain yield as the most desirable selection criterion for screening heat-tolerant genotypes, the results from this study will be useful in identifying the most reliable predictors of yield. Hence, sub-stomatal CO2 concentration (*C**i*) and Fv/Fm could be suggested as the most important criteria for screening heat-tolerant genotypes in wheat. ABA promotes the efflux of K+ ions from the guard cells, which results in the loss of turgor pressure leading to stomata closure. Dehydration of plants has been shown to cause ABA level increase up to 50-fold due to loss of cell turgor or cell membrane perturbation (Guerrero and Mullet, 1986). Overall, ABA is a dominant signal in controlling growth and transpiration under drought stress. Environmental stresses have a direct impact on the photosynthetic apparatus, essentially by disrupting thylakoid electron transport and the stomatal control of the CO2 supply (Allen and Ort, 2001). The ability of crop plants to acclimate to different environments is directly or indirectly associated with their ability to acclimate at the level of photosynthesis, which in turn affects biochemical and physiological processes and, consequently, the growth and yield of the whole plant (Chandra, 2003).
Document [6]Drought and heat stress causes significant reductions in growth and yield of several important crops; however, the extent of damage depends upon crop growth stage and severity of the stress. In general, the reproductive phase is more sensitive to the stresses causing a substantial reduction in the yield. Water relations are influenced by certain factors including the leaf water potential, leaf and canopy temperature, transpiration rate, and stomatal conductance. Exposure to drought stress disturbs all these factors in plants however, stomatal conductance is affected the most (Farooq et al., 2009b). A significant reduction in the leaf water potential and transpiration rate was observed under the drought conditions which ultimately increased the leaf and canopy temperature (Turner et al., 2001). Another important feature for plant physiological regulation is water use efficiency which is the ratio of the dry matter accumulated to the water consumed (Monclus et al., 2006). Efficient cultivars of wheat have higher water use efficiency under drought stress (Abbate et al., 2004). This improvement in the water use efficiency is mainly due to the accumulation of the dry matter by consuming less amount of water due to the closing of stomata and less rate of transpiration. A reduced water use efficiency was observed in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) when exposed to an early season water shortage and it ultimately resulted in poor biomass accumulation and yield (Costa et al., 1997).

Photosynthetica 57: 9–17), leading to reduced transpiration rates (Wang et al. 2016 Timing effects of heat-stress on plant ecophysiological characteristics and growth. J Agron Crop Sci 204: 49–61). Reduced net photosynthesis (PN) is often caused by reduction of CO2 concentration at the carboxylation sites inside the chloroplast (Evans et al. 2009 Resistances along the CO2 diffusion pathway inside leaves. Document [8]Heat stress also affects plant growth and function (Wahid et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2012). Very little information is available regarding some of these broader effects in crops (Basirirad, 2000; Rennenberg et al., 2006). Overall, drought and heat stresses hamper different physiological functions of plants (Table 2). One of the key physiological phenomena affected by the drought and heat stress in plants is photosynthesis (Farooq et al., 2009b). It is mainly affected due to stomatal limitation, greater susceptibility to photoinhibition and leaf senescence (Wahid et al., 2007). Under combined post-flowering heat and drought in wheat, leaf senescence is accelerated, which shortens the grain-filling period and reduces the time available for assimilate supply to developing kernels. Stomatal closure under drought reduces the CO2 availability, which makes plant more susceptible to photoinhibition (Lawlor and Cornic, 2002). Similarly, heat stress also impairs the process of photosynthesis under these conditions, further reducing assimilate supply during grain filling.
Document [9]Photosynthesis is limited by reduced stomatal conductance under drought stress (Bota et al., 2004). Under heat stress, light-dependent chemical reactions taking place in the thylakoid are among the main sites of damage as a result of high temperature stress. Increased leaf temperature and photon flux density affect the thermo-tolerance adjustment of PSII (Crafts-Brandner and Salvucci, 2002). Together, restricted stomatal conductance and damage to PSII reduce source photosynthesis under combined heat and drought stress.

question: Which biological characteristics of current crops act as barriers to achieving maximum theoretical yields within vertical farming environments?
perspectives: Sink-size limitations of existing cultivars bred for field conditions
Canopy architecture poorly matched to multilayer artificial-light systems
Photoperiod and spectral-response traits not optimized for indoor regimes
Root-zone constraints on nutrient and oxygen acquisition in dense hydroponic systems
context:
Document [0]However, this assumption neglects that photosynthesis is responsive to sink demand: Without adequate partitioning of assimilates to grain and other sinks, the source, or photosynthetic potential, will be underutilized (e.g., [85–89. Yield is the cumulative result of both source and sink strength over the course of development. Source strength is determined by both net photosynthetic rate and the rate of assimilate remobilization from source tissues [90. Sink strength is the product of the size, number, and activity of sink organs; the latter refers to the specific uptake rate of resources. In dense hydroponic systems used for vertical farming, restricted root-zone volume together with oxygen depletion and nutrient gradients can limit nutrient and oxygen acquisition, making root traits a direct constraint on yield realization. Although difficult to measure, methodologies are being proposed to estimate sink activity [91. The concept of source or sink limitation is quantitative, and the important question is to what extent source or sink limits yield realization during seed set and filling. The source–sink balance during the time of economic sink development may be defined as the difference between the amount of assimilate available and the capacity to store it. Studies show source strength is in excess in both winter and summer cereals, such as barley [92, wheat and barley [86, and maize [93. This is consistent with the facts that (i) yield tends to be far better related to the number than to the average weight of seeds [219 and references quoted therein, (ii) seed weight tends to be insensitive or only marginally responsive to source strength per seed during seed filling [15, 94, 95, and (iii) photosynthesis and RUE are upregulated when sink strength is increased through breeding or treatments [85–87, 96.
Document [1]Historically, increases in yield potential have been mainly related to increases in grain m−2 rather than to greater individual grain weight, implying that grain yield in wheat is sink-limited during grain filling . Aisawi et al. reported that grain yield in spring CIMMYT germplasm was associated with grain weight rather than grain m−2; in this case, yield potential also appeared to be associated with increasing grain sink strength through potential grain weight. Borrás et al. reviewed 18 experiments imposing source-manipulation treatments in wheat, including shading, grain removal or spike trimming, defoliation and chemical leaf desiccation, concluding that wheat grains appeared to grow mostly at saturated assimilate availability, so yield was generally sink-limited in favorable growing conditions. Experiments where sink capacity was boosted—in one case by a light treatment and in another study in response to the 7Ag.7DL chromosome translocation —likewise indicated that sink capacity constrains the realization of yield potential post-anthesis. Degraining experiments carried out in wheat by Gaju et al. also indicated sink rather than source limitation during grain filling. Consistent with sink limitation of grain growth, Ahmadi et al. showed that post-anthesis defoliation did not affect grain yield or individual grain weight in one high-yielding winter bread wheat cultivar.
Document [2]Consequently, photosynthesis of leaves and spikes is down-regulated by lack of sink strength. Sink strength is set by the number of grains and their potential size, which are determined immediately before anthesis and depend on source availability (as resource allocation to inflorescences affects survival of developing florets and growth of ovaries). The concept that yield is limited by both source and sink strength therefore becomes clear when integrated over time (Figure I. While studies and funding have mainly focused on improving photosynthesis, sink strength remains a critical research bottleneck. In vertical farming systems, photoperiod and spectral-response traits of many cultivars remain tuned to field daylengths and solar spectra, so developmental and photosynthetic responses are not optimized for indoor regimes with fixed photoperiods and LED light quality. Increasing photosynthesis (e.g., during the stem-elongation phase; Figure I will improve yield through increasing sink strength (with the proviso that the partitioning towards the juvenile inflorescences is maintained). Traits that would improve yield with current levels of photosynthesis include the following: Increasing seeds set per unit inflorescence dry matter through hormonal regulation (see also previous section ‘Roles of Hormone Crosstalk: Regulating Root Growth and Source–Sink Relationships’) Improving floret survival through accelerating rates of floret development Setting larger grain weight potential Enhancing phloem loading *Figure I Schematic Diagram Illustrating that in Preanthesis of Cereals, Source Strength Determines the Sink Strength during Postanthesis, which in Turn may Affect Source Activity during Grain Filling (top left), and Four Candidate Traits to Further Raise Sink Strength.* While the role of photosynthesis in crops is reasonably well documented and has led to development of screening protocols with potential for routine application in field research such as chlorophyll fluorescence [117, the same cannot be said for respiration. This bottleneck in understanding is profoundly troublesome, since many field data sets show that crop yields are significantly more influenced by night than day temperature [18, 19, which could relate to effects on respiration and/or crop development.
Document [3]Sink limitation during storage organ development is not limited to grain crops but also applies to tuber and root crops such as potato or cassava [97, 98. The widespread sink limitation for yield realization during seed filling may reflect the evolutionary reward of modulating reproductive output through number rather than size [99. This implies that stable seed size would have been adaptive [100, as size may have a marked effect upon fitness. Indeed, stabilizing selection (natural selection force in a population towards a particular value) would reduce intraspecific variability of seed size towards an optimal seed size, balancing between survival of the individuals and the number of progeny produced. As seed set precedes seed growth (even in indeterminate crops, the overlap is small), plants have tended to be conservative to ensure reaching critical seed size for survival. This would explain why breeding has consistently increased yield through increasing sink strength (seed number or potential weight) in major grain crops (e.g., in wheat [15, rice [101, and maize [102 but not necessarily via increased leaf photosynthesis (e.g., [103. A solid proof of concept comes from the widespread boosts to yield of semidwarf cereals. The decrease in stem elongation increased partitioning of assimilates to the developing inflorescence, improving floret development and fertility and therefore increasing sink strength [104, 105. The resultant boost to harvest index [106–109 was likely the most important architectural change in crops for increasing yield. Document [1]Starch films have attracted increasing attention due to their biodegradability, edibility, and potential use as animal feed from post-products. Applications of starch-based films include food packaging, coating, and medicine capsules. However, a major drawback of starch-based films is their brittleness, particularly under dry conditions, caused by recrystallization of amylopectin within the starch matrix during retrogradation. To address this challenge, various strategies and methodologies have been developed to regulate structure, compatibility, and performance. This review covers fundamental aspects, such as the microstructures, phase transitions, and compatibility of starch, as well as application-oriented techniques, including processing methods and formulation design. Intermolecular interactions play a crucial role in developing starch-based materials, as they strongly affect processability and final properties. Given the abundance of hydroxyl groups in starch, compatibility among components depends strongly on polar interactions. The extent of amylopectin recrystallization is therefore an important factor in determining film brittleness. Additional formulation approaches have also been explored to improve the mechanical properties of starch film. Drawing upon both the literature and our expertise, this review not only summarizes the advancements in this field but also identifies the limitations of current technologies and outlines promising research directions for future development. The invention of plastic is a double-edged sword, as it has significantly enhanced the quality of human life while concurrently engendering severe ecological pollution through plastic waste. The packaging industry stands out as one of the foremost driving forces behind the exponential proliferation of plastics usage; thus, transitioning towards sustainable alternative packaging materials derived from renewable resources should be embraced as a more circular and eco-centric approach. Consequently, an urgent imperative arises to foster novel materials that offer commensurate functionalities to plastic products but are environmentally benign. Starch is a widely available natural polysaccharide found in all grain crops, offering several benefits such as low cost, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and ease of processing.

question: How do variations in the food matrix account for the divergent bioaccessibility of micronutrients in processed products that share a comparable overall composition?
