However, although these mechanisms operate across different spatial scales and timescales, they are not mutually exclusive. Prebiotic organic feedstock could likewise have been synthesized in terrestrial hydrothermal systems and other water-rock reaction environments on the early Earth. Thermally processed deposits of exogenous organic matter may have degassed HCN into lake systems fed by glacial meltwater rich in P and S sourced from locally dissolving cosmic dust. Taken together with recent findings from geology, astronomy and prebiotic chemistry, our results provide support for the fertilization of prebiotic chemistry by cosmic dust on early Earth. Furthermore, cosmic dust is potentially a widespread and flexible planetary fertilizer, being accreted in quantities that may be assessed by observation9, 65 to potentially habitable exoplanets. Cosmic dust grains in pristine modern sedimentary systems appear to derive mainly from undifferentiated carbonaceous chondrite or cometary precursor bodies66, 67. Cosmic dust that appears to originate from differentiated asteroids represents less than 5% by mass of all cosmic dust in most deposits68. The compositional disparity between modern accretion fluxes of cosmic dust and predicted early fluxes must be considered in interpreting the relevance of our results for understanding the supply of bioessential elements to early Earth’s surface. Bridging this gap requires us to make assumptions, both about the parent bodies of cosmic dust falling to Earth today and how those precursor objects are represented in our simulations. We assume that all cometary material is well represented by the compositions of unmelted micrometeorites and apparently cogenetic carbonaceous chondrite meteorites68. Dust from asteroids is conservatively assumed to sample differentiated precursor bodies. Cosmic dust grains from differentiated material is considered to represent an equal mixture of crust and core material and to be well represented by the compositions of silicate and iron-type grains arriving on Earth, today69. These assumptions inform the values in Supplementary Table 1.

According to our present understanding, the universe is some twelve to fifteen billion years old. It now appears that throughout almost all of that very extended time period there has been abundant molecular material present, and that much of that material is organic. This review discusses the nature of this matter, in the interstellar medium of our own Milky Way Galaxy and other galaxies, and in our Solar System. Particular attention attaches to the questions of whether interstellar molecular material survived the processes associated with the origin of the Solar System and was incorporated into comets and asteroids, whether some of these organics were subsequently delivered to the Earth, and whether such matter played a role in the origin of life. The references given are primarily to reviews and recent articles, and are intended to be representative rather than complete. Of the chemical elements that play a role in terrestrial biology, only hydrogen is primordial. All of the carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorous, metals and other trace elements were produced by nucleosynthesis in the cores of evolved stars or in stellar explosions (e.g., Matteucci 1991; Trimble 1991), 1997). Although the abundance of these elements has increased significantly over the age of the universe (Songaila and Cowie, 1996), there appear to be at least some galaxies which already contained significant amounts of molecular material based predominantly on these elements less than one billion years after the Big Bang; that is, when the universe was 7% or less of its present age. Such a galaxy was recently detected at a red shift of 4.69 in both emission from carbon monoxide and with a continuous spectrum presumably attributable to thermal emission from interstellar dust grains (Ohta et al., 1996; Omont et al., 1996). From what is known of our own Milky Way Galaxy and other relatively nearby galaxies, such dust grains are in significant measure organic in their composition, while carbon monoxide serves as a tracer of the gas in dense interstellar clouds which also contains a wide variety of more complex organic molecules (see below).

According to our present understanding, the universe is some twelve to fifteen billion years old. It now appears that throughout almost all of that very extended time period there has been abundant molecular material present, and that much of that material is organic. One possibility is a simple mechanism in which sulfur is liberated from condensed phases into the gas phase. Perhaps atomic sulfur is being released from Venus’s surface. Less likely, the sulfur could be coming from the cloud droplets as they evaporate at the bottom of the clouds. This seems less likely because the bulk of the droplet chemistry is believed to be more oxidizing than the surrounding atmosphere (Krasnopolsky 2012; Jiang et al. 2024). The surface seems more likely, though the exchange of atoms, or really, electrons, between the lower atmosphere and the surface is uncertain: it may well be the atmosphere and surface is not in redox equilibrium (Bierson & Zhang 2020). It is also possible that, at the higher temperatures below the clouds, some sulfur chains become strained or develop terminal sulfur atoms bound by a single bond, analogous to loose threads. Although such fragments would constitute only a minor fraction of the sulfur inventory, they may nonetheless be sufficient to supply the sulfur required for this chemistry. The S3 and S4 observations are highly uncertain, because it is difficult to infer specific species from such broad observed features. If the observations are accurate, then our predictions favor the presence of some lower-boundary source of active sulfur. This hypothesis can be tested either by lower-atmosphere observations of the sulfur cycle, for example, by DAVINCI (Garvin et al. 2022), in tandem with further laboratory and theoretical exploration into the behavior of elemental sulfur under high temperatures and thick CO2 gas, or with minerals in contact with supercritical CO2.
Document [7]The abundance of elemental sulfur and polysulfur species in the upper atmosphere of Venus and their implications for the enigmatic ultraviolet absorption has been investigated in several studies over the past few years. However, the photochemistry of sulfur species in the upper atmosphere of Venus is still not well understood and the identity of the missing ultraviolet absorber(s) remains unknown. Iron chloride or other metal-halide aerosols have also been proposed as candidate materials for Venus’s missing ultraviolet absorber. Here we update an existing photochemical model of Venus’ upper atmosphere by including sulfur pathways relevant to ultraviolet absorption. It is more likely that sulfur allotropes produced by this chemistry could contribute more substantively. Photochemical reactions are found to be important sources of elemental sulfur and polysulfur allotropes, Sn. These species absorb in the critical ultraviolet region and are expected to be found in both the aerosol and gas phase, indicating that in-situ high resolution aerosol mass spectrometry might be a useful technique for identifying the ultraviolet absorber on Venus. The photochemistry of sulfur species in the upper atmosphere of Venus is not well understood and is poorly quantified. Near and above the cloud tops, sulfur-bearing molecules are photolyzed, leading to the production of Sn (n = 1–7) and Sx (x = 8+).
Document [8]The large backscattering cross section of the particles composing the upper clouds on Venus suggests that a small quantity of high refractive index material is present in the clouds. We propose that this material is elemental sulfur and that sulfur also accounts for the absorption of uv-visible radiation at wavelengths outside of the SO2 absorption bands. A physical-chemical model of the clouds shows that sulfur, with a mass comparable to that of the observed Mode 1 particles, can be produced in oxygen-poor regions of the upper clouds and in rising air columns. Sulfur production from SO2 can be rapid, which explains the observed correlation between SO2 and the uv absorber. The sulfur is properly located to be the uv absorber uv absorber since its calculated concentration rapidly increases with depth in the upper clouds, but it is largely absent in the middle and lower clouds. Sulfur nucleation provides a means of generating the observed bimodal particle size distribution in the upper clouds. Chemical modeling shows that the sulfur vapor is rich in short-chain allotropes such as S3 and S4. These allotropes have absorption bands centered near 4000 and 5300 Å, respectively. We suggest that the sulfur particles on Venus are largely composed of S8, but also contain a few percent of S3 and S4. Such particles could account for the wavelength dependence of the albedo of Venus and for the solar energy deposition profile in the clouds. These allotropes are metastable and relax to S8 over periods of hours to days, providing a simple explanation for the relatively short lifetime of the uv absorber. Document [0]This review underscores the pervasive nature and multifaceted health implications of PFAS, emphasizing their potential to disrupt metabolic regulation. Due to their persistent and bio-accumulative properties, PFAS present significant challenges for both environmental and public health. This comprehensive evaluation highlights the molecular mechanisms through which PFAS may contribute to metabolic dysfunction, with particular attention to evidence implicating PPARα-associated pathways in hepatic lipid handling. Epidemiological studies suggest a correlation between PFAS exposure and adverse metabolic outcomes, particularly among vulnerable populations such as children and expectant mothers. These studies also illustrate the complexities in establishing causal relationships, given the heterogeneity of PFAS compounds and numerous confounding factors in human health research. In vitro and in vivo studies provide further insights into the biochemical pathways influenced by PFAS, reinforcing their potential to disrupt hepatic metabolic homeostasis and contribute to conditions like dyslipidemia and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. In silico models offer valuable insights into the binding affinities and interaction mechanisms of PFAS with biological targets, complementing traditional experimental methods. Although these computational tools enhance our understanding of PFAS toxicity and support the development of safer chemical alternatives, the limitations of in silico studies, including the need for validated models and comprehensive datasets, highlight the necessity of integrating these findings with empirical research. The evolving regulatory frameworks for PFAS reflect a growing recognition of their health risks. The global variability in PFAS regulation underscores the need for a unified strategy to manage these contaminants effectively. Regulatory measures, combined with innovative remediation technologies and policy-driven approaches, are crucial for mitigating PFAS pollution and reducing its metabolic impact. Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies to better understand the long-term health effects of PFAS exposure on liver and metabolic function. Developing advanced methodologies for detecting and remediating PFAS in the environment is also essential. Addressing the multifaceted challenges posed by PFAS will help safeguard public health and foster more effective regulatory and remediation strategies to mitigate their impact.
Document [1]Consequently, assessments of human toxicity rely on a multidisciplinary approach that includes epidemiological studies, computational modeling (in silico methods), in vitro assays, and in vivo animal studies. Computational modeling, in particular, serves as a pivotal tool in elucidating the potential risks and toxicological profiles of these contaminants, thereby reducing the reliance on invasive human sampling techniques . Despite extensive research on the toxicity and bioaccumulation of individual PFAS compounds, the effects of PFAS mixtures reflective of environmental conditions remain poorly understood . Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) are among the most extensively studied PFAS, primarily due to their historical widespread use and their persistence as stable degradation products of other PFAS precursors . Contemporary studies on “legacy PFAS” and their “alternative” replacements employ animal models, cellular assays, epidemiological data, and computational simulations to elucidate further the endocrine-disrupting properties and overall toxicity of PFAS compounds . A representative selection of legacy and alternative PFAS compounds is depicted in Figure 1. The structural similarity between PFAS and fatty acids has raised concerns about their potential to disrupt lipid metabolism in the liver . In hepatic tissue, this concern has focused in part on PPARα-related pathways involved in lipid regulation . These pathways are essential regulators of hepatic lipid metabolism. Disturbance of these pathways during PFAS exposure may contribute to conditions like dyslipidemia and steatosis . Additionally, PFAS exposure has been linked to altered expression of lipid-metabolism genes across various species, indicating widespread effects from both legacy and emerging PFAS compounds .
Document [2]Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc., Bethesda, MD, United States, 3 Sciome LLC, Research Triangle Park, NC, United States, 4 Division of Translational Toxicology, National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, Research Triangle Park, NC, United States Toxicants with the potential to bioaccumulate in humans and animals have long been a cause for concern, particularly due to their association with multiple diseases and organ injuries. Per- and polyfluoro alkyl substances (PFAS) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH) are two such classes of chemicals that bioaccumulate and have been associated with steatosis in the liver. Although PFAS and PAH are classified as chemicals of concern, their molecular mechanisms of toxicity remain to be explored in detail. In this study, we aimed to identify potential mechanisms by which an acute exposure to PFAS and PAH chemicals can induce lipid accumulation and whether the responses depend on chemical class, dose, and sex. To this end, we analyzed mechanisms beginning with the binding of the chemical to a molecular initiating event (MIE) and the consequent transcriptomic alterations. We collated potential MIEs using predictions from our previously developed ToxProfiler tool and from published steatosis adverse outcome pathways. Most of the MIEs are transcription factors, and we collected their target genes by mining the TRRUST database. To analyze the effects of PFAS and PAH on the steatosis mechanisms, we performed a computational MIE-target gene analysis on high-throughput transcriptomic measurements of liver tissue from male and female rats exposed to either a PFAS or PAH. The results showed peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-α targets to be the most dysregulated, with most of the genes being upregulated. Furthermore, PFAS exposure disrupted several lipid metabolism genes, including upregulation of fatty acid oxidation genes (Acadm, Acox1, Cpt2, Cyp4a1-3) and downregulation of lipid transport genes (Apoa1, Apoa5, Pltp). Such shifts in oxidative metabolism are also consistent with PFAS-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, which can impair beta-oxidation and increase reactive oxygen species in hepatocytes.
Document [3]Complementing these findings, Cui et al. demonstrated that chronic low-level PFOS exposure in adult zebrafish (F0) led to hepatic steatosis and structural abnormalities in liver and intestinal tissues. In their offspring, altered expression of genes such as lepa and dgat1b was consistent with disturbed metabolic regulation. Similar findings were reported with F-53B, a PFOS analog, where parental exposure induced hepatotoxicity and—critically—altered the PPAR signaling pathway in unexposed offspring . Given the central role of PPAR signaling in hepatic lipid metabolism and inflammatory gene regulation, these findings suggest that PFAS analogs can durably perturb PPAR-controlled metabolic circuits relevant to liver injury. Although some studies did not directly define every upstream step linking exposure to transcriptional change, the persistence of metabolic dysregulation and hepatic phenotypes supports sustained disruption of PPAR-linked lipid homeostasis. Zebrafish, in particular, have proven to be a powerful model for detecting compound-induced alterations in such hepatic metabolic programs .
Document [4]Some studies even associated PFAS exposure with sex-dependent outcomes, such as thyroid dysfunction and reproductive disorders (Melzer et al., 2010; Blake et al., 2018; Hammarstrand et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2021; Sang et al., 2024). Studies using serum measurements of liver injury markers, however, do not provide insights into the PFAS-induced molecular mechanisms of liver injury, particularly for specific endpoints, such as steatosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and inflammation. One plausible upstream event is PFAS-induced endoplasmic-reticulum stress, which can trigger inflammatory signaling and exacerbate hepatocellular injury. Of all the possible toxicity-induced liver injury phenotypes, many rodent and human studies have consistently linked PFAS exposure with various degrees of lipid accumulation in the liver (Wan et al., 2012; Bagley et al., 2017). The increased buildup of lipids in the liver leads to an adverse outcome called hepatic steatosis, which can progress to liver cirrhosis or non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Thus, understanding the progression from exposure to steatosis can help elucidate the molecular mechanisms of PFAS-induced liver injury via steatosis. Steatosis adverse outcome pathways (AOPs) are frameworks that link a molecular initiating event (MIE) (such as molecular binding to a toxicant) to steatosis through a sequence of biological steps organized into intermediate effects (e.g., upregulation of specific genes or increased fatty acid synthesis) and key events (such as liver triglyceride accumulation) (Ankley et al., 2010; Mellor et al., 2016). Although researchers have described various steatosis AOPs, how PFAS exposure leads to steatosis via the previously described AOPs remains underexplored to our knowledge. While existing studies report various metabolic pathways and mechanisms by which PFAS cause steatosis, they do not describe the effect of dose response or organism sex and include an analysis of only a limited set of pathways.

Serum levels of these enzymes are markers of dyslipidemia; thus, their elevation suggests that PFOS may induce dyslipidemia in murine models . PFAS can significantly influence lipid metabolism through their interaction with nuclear receptors of the PPAR family, which regulate the expression of genes involved in lipogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and adipocyte differentiation . PPAR activation by PFAS may therefore contribute to changes in hepatic and systemic lipid composition, including increased cholesterol levels and triglyceride accumulation, effects observed in both experimental studies and epidemiological investigations. Together, these findings support a mechanism in which PFAS perturb hepatic lipid homeostasis through PPAR-regulated metabolic pathways.

In silico studies demonstrated that PFAS carbon chain length and the nature of the functional group play a crucial role in determining their affinity towards this receptor . Molecules with longer carbon chains and higher degrees of fluorination and branching exhibit increased binding efficacy, which is a crucial aspect considered in QSAR models. PFAS show target-specific binding affinities, with detectable affinity towards PPARα, delineating part of their hepatic toxicological profile . However, transcriptomic studies and in silico analyses suggested that PPARα is the principal transcription factor regulated by PFOA, influencing not only lipid metabolism-related genes but also differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the liver . Advances in integrative systems biology have facilitated the construction of molecular networks that illustrate the intricate interplay between PFAS exposure, hepatic signaling pathways, and gene expression alterations. These computational frameworks have been instrumental in identifying specific gene sets and regulatory modules implicated in PFAS-associated hepatic responses, including modules relevant to bile-acid handling . Such alterations suggest that PFAS can perturb signaling programs that are crucial for hepatic lipid homeostasis and bile-acid handling. Document [0]This review underscores the pervasive nature and multifaceted health implications of PFAS, emphasizing their potential to disrupt metabolic regulation. Due to their persistent and bio-accumulative properties, PFAS present significant challenges for both environmental and public health. This comprehensive evaluation highlights the molecular mechanisms through which PFAS may contribute to metabolic dysfunction, with particular attention to evidence implicating PPARα-associated pathways in hepatic lipid handling. Epidemiological studies suggest a correlation between PFAS exposure and adverse metabolic outcomes, particularly among vulnerable populations such as children and expectant mothers. These studies also illustrate the complexities in establishing causal relationships, given the heterogeneity of PFAS compounds and numerous confounding factors in human health research. In vitro and in vivo studies provide further insights into the biochemical pathways influenced by PFAS, reinforcing their potential to disrupt hepatic metabolic homeostasis and contribute to conditions like dyslipidemia and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. In silico models offer valuable insights into the binding affinities and interaction mechanisms of PFAS with biological targets, complementing traditional experimental methods. Although these computational tools enhance our understanding of PFAS toxicity and support the development of safer chemical alternatives, the limitations of in silico studies, including the need for validated models and comprehensive datasets, highlight the necessity of integrating these findings with empirical research. The evolving regulatory frameworks for PFAS reflect a growing recognition of their health risks. The global variability in PFAS regulation underscores the need for a unified strategy to manage these contaminants effectively. Regulatory measures, combined with innovative remediation technologies and policy-driven approaches, are crucial for mitigating PFAS pollution and reducing its metabolic impact. Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies to better understand the long-term health effects of PFAS exposure on liver and metabolic function. Developing advanced methodologies for detecting and remediating PFAS in the environment is also essential. Addressing the multifaceted challenges posed by PFAS will help safeguard public health and foster more effective regulatory and remediation strategies to mitigate their impact.

One plausible upstream event is PFAS-induced endoplasmic-reticulum stress, which can trigger inflammatory signaling and exacerbate hepatocellular injury. Of all the possible toxicity-induced liver injury phenotypes, many rodent and human studies have consistently linked PFAS exposure with various degrees of lipid accumulation in the liver (Wan et al., 2012; Bagley et al., 2017). Thus, understanding the progression from exposure to steatosis can help elucidate the molecular mechanisms of PFAS-induced liver injury via steatosis. Steatosis adverse outcome pathways (AOPs) are frameworks that link a molecular initiating event (MIE) (such as molecular binding to a toxicant) to steatosis through a sequence of biological steps organized into intermediate effects (e.g., upregulation of specific genes or increased fatty acid synthesis) and key events (such as liver triglyceride accumulation) (Ankley et al., 2010; Mellor et al., 2016). Although researchers have described various steatosis AOPs, how PFAS exposure leads to steatosis via the previously described AOPs remains underexplored to our knowledge. Document [0]Female mice exposed to PFOA for 15 days showed a reduced IgM response to a T-cell-independent antigen at doses of 1.88 mg/kg or above. Suppression also occurred in T-cell-dependent assays, despite little change in the proportion of splenic B cells. The investigators therefore proposed impaired B-cell or plasma-cell function as a possible route from PFOA exposure to lower antibody output. This is experimental support for a B-cell functional mechanism; it does not establish that every PFAS has the same effect at ordinary human exposure levels.
Document [1]Human peripheral-blood mononuclear-cell cultures provide a way to examine antibody production after PFAS exposure. In one study, a TLR9 agonist together with IL-2 stimulated a T-cell-independent response, and PFOA, PFOS, PFNA and PFHxS showed suppressive trends in IgG and IgM release. A parallel antigen-dependent assay also detected reduced antibody production. These findings connect the chemicals to antibody output during B-cell activation. Because the cultures contain several immune-cell types, the results support B-cell-associated dysfunction without isolating a strictly B-cell-intrinsic cause.
Document [2]In the human Namalwa B-lymphoma cell model, PFOA, PFOS, PFNA and PFHxS reduced expression of RAG1 and RAG2 in time- and concentration-dependent experiments. These genes participate in assembling antigen-receptor genes during lymphocyte development. Their altered expression provides a possible developmental route by which PFAS could affect the B-cell repertoire available for an antibody response. The measurements were made in a transformed cell line at the tested concentrations; they are not direct measurements of antibody loss after vaccination in people.

HFPO-TA was particularly potent for these endpoints, whereas some other tested compounds did not produce the same response. This is a candidate developmental mechanism supported by a cell-based assay, rather than proof that the full PFAS class uniformly blocks vaccine responses.
Document [4]Adult mice given PFOA at 7.5 mg/kg/day for 15 days showed sex-dependent changes in splenic B-cell populations. Female mice had fewer plasmablasts and several other B-cell subsets. Remaining isolated B cells displayed increased metabolic responses after stimulation, so the findings do not support a simple claim that all B-cell activation was abolished. The authors linked the altered populations to reduced primary IgM output. This experimental route concerns B-cell development, survival and the supply of antibody-producing cells, with dose and sex limiting its scope.
Document [5]PFAS exposure can affect the cells that initiate an adaptive immune response. The evidence is from a cell model, and the strength of the response depended on the compound and concentration; reduced vaccine responses in people were not measured directly in this experiment.

The result establishes chemical exposure followed by impaired humoral output in that model; it does not identify every intervening molecular step or a universal human threshold.

The high exposure and in-vitro setting limit direct extrapolation to ordinary vaccination conditions.

Document [1]Harmonized protocols for sample collection, digestion, and MP identification will be essential to ensure consistency and reliability. Another important gap concerns human exposure assessment. Very little is known about MP concentrations in drinking water, food, and indoor air at levels relevant to renal exposure. Future studies should aim to quantify MP loads in human urine, blood, and kidney tissues across diverse populations and link them to dietary habits or environmental exposures. A controlled human study involving MP supplementation could provide valuable insight into absorption and distribution mechanisms, but such an approach would raise significant ethical concerns. Animal studies to date have mostly used relatively high doses of MPs, typically in the range of 2-10 mg per kilogram for several weeks. A major limitation in the current toxicological data is that many experimental studies employ exposure levels that are far higher than plausible human environmental exposures. At such high doses, mechanisms such as oxidative stress, lysosomal overload, and particle-induced inflammation may dominate, but these responses may not scale linearly to the low, chronic exposures typical in humans. Thus, quantitative extrapolation from rodent high-dose experiments to human risk must be done with caution. In regulatory toxicology practice, effects observed in animals are typically adjusted by safety (uncertainty) factors, often 100-fold or more, to account for interspecies differences and variability among humans. Until more data become available on internal human micro- and NP burdens, exposure kinetics, and dose-response at environmentally relevant levels, it is prudent to interpret high-dose animal findings as hazard signals rather than direct risk predictions. There is a need for long-term experiments with environmentally realistic doses to determine whether MPs contribute to chronic kidney disease or fibrosis. Mechanistic studies are also lacking. Another underexplored mechanism is the leaching of plastic-associated additives or residual monomers, which may diffuse out of MPs and NPs and contribute toxic effects independently of the particles themselves. Further work should clarify the involvement of ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and complement activation, while exploring how particle size, shape, polymer type, and surface chemistry influence renal toxicity. Document [5]Microplastics and nanoplastics (MNPs) have rapidly emerged as pervasive environmental contaminants with direct relevance to human physiology. Once regarded as biologically inert, it is now clear that these particles can enter the bloodstream, cross cellular barriers, accumulate in tissues, and trigger persistent cellular stress and inflammatory responses. Their effects have been well documented in marine and ecological systems, but only recently have mechanistic and clinical data revealed their implications for the cardiovascular system . Cardiovascular injury induced by MNPs is increasingly linked to their presence within vascular and cardiac tissues and the resulting chronic inflammation and cellular injury . These processes are recognized drivers of atherosclerotic plaque initiation and progression, plaque instability and thrombosis, and myocardial structural and functional remodeling. Importantly, MNPs have now been detected in human arteries, atherosclerotic plaques, coronary thrombi, saphenous vein grafts, pericardium, and myocardium, providing direct evidence of their bioavailability within cardiovascular tissues .
Document [6]Once in the bloodstream, particles can be filtered by the glomerulus, reabsorbed in the tubular epithelium or translocated across the nephron. Particle size influences nephrotoxicity: Toxicity does not scale linearly with size, and there is a specific range where renal toxicity is greatest . MPs can reach the kidney through several routes, including ingestion, inhalation, and medical exposure. Ingestion of contaminated food and water is considered the dominant pathway. Chronic ingestion may also disrupt the gut microbiome and impair epithelial-barrier integrity by weakening tight junctions, thereby increasing intestinal permeability and systemic uptake of MPs. Once in the gastrointestinal tract, small particles, particularly those < 10 μm, are able to cross the intestinal barrier and enter systemic circulation. Mechanisms include paracellular leakage through impaired tight junctions, transcytosis by enterocytes or specialized M cells in Peyer’s patches, and transport *via* chylomicrons through the lymphatic circulation . Inhaled airborne MPs may deposit in the lungs, cross the alveolar epithelium, and enter the bloodstream, from which they are subsequently distributed to peripheral organs, including the kidney . In addition, iatrogenic sources have been reported: MPs and NPs have been detected in infusion and dialysis fluids, providing a direct route into circulation without the need to cross epithelial barriers . Once in systemic circulation, the renal fate of MPs is dictated by particle size, surface charge, and protein corona formation . Some particles undergo glomerular filtration and become retained in the glomerular basement membrane, while others are internalized by proximal tubular epithelial cells through endocytosis . The “filtration-reabsorption-translocation” hypothesis suggests that MPs can be filtered at the glomerulus, partly reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, and subsequently translocated to the renal interstitium or back into systemic circulation . At the cellular level, MPs are readily taken up by proximal tubular epithelial cells, as demonstrated *in vitro* with human cultured cells; internalization leads to lysosomal accumulation, defective degradation, and release of reactive oxygen species (ROS), triggering oxidative stress and mitochondrial injury .

question: Which primary triggers account for the occurrence of idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity associated with various major pharmaceutical agents?
perspectives: Reactive-metabolite formation that creates neoantigens or danger signals
Direct pharmacologic interaction with immune receptors such as specific HLA complexes
Mitochondrial stress followed by failure of adaptive hepatocellular responses
Bile-acid transporter inhibition that initiates cholestatic stress

Document [0]In the case of IDILI, as the primary site of drug metabolism, many reactive metabolites can be formed and then bound to liver proteins. This drug-modified protein adduct can then be taken up by antigen presenting cells (APC) and presented to T cells on the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) to produce signal 1 of an immune response (Figure 2A). The drug-modified proteins are seen as “foreign” by the immune system, and that is what leads to an immune response. Endogenous liver proteins are recognized by the immune system as “self”, but when the proteins are bound to drugs the immune system can recognize it as “nonself”. An active immune response is activated towards “nonself”, while tolerance results from recognizing “self”. Small molecules do not elicit an immune response unless they covalently bind to proteins because in most cases small molecules do not bind with sufficient affinity to the MHC . Most drugs that are associated with a significant incidence of IDRs are metabolized to reactive metabolites that could act as haptens and lead to an immune response. However, not all drugs that are metabolized to reactive metabolites are associated with a significant incidence of IDRs. Therefore the Hapten Hypothesis is likely only a part of the mechanism because it is still not clear what determines which drugs will cause IDILI . Figure 2. Hypotheses of immune mediated IDRs. A) The Hapten hypothesis: a reactive drug or reactive metabolite acting as a hapten binds to endogenous proteins, creating drug-modified proteins and generating Signal 1 of the immune response. B) The Danger hypothesis: reactive species damage cells, resulting in the release of danger signals and leading to Signal 2 of the immune response. Immune cells such as CD8 T cells that have received Signal 1 and 2 can then cause cell death.
Document [1]Figure 1Furthermore, the abnormalities of the above-mentioned immune cells and associated molecules affect the status of acute liver injury (Vega et al., 2017; García-Cortés et al., 2018; Stravitz and Lee, 2019). Recently, numerous clinical and experimental studies have found that immune responses are closely related to the development of DILI (Woolbright and Jaeschke, 2018). In particular, HLA alleles have been reported strongly associated with liver injury caused by a series of other drugs, e.g., flucloxacillin, clavulanic acid-amoxicillin, and Polygonum multiflorum, providing new insights for uncovering the mystery of DILI. For some drugs, the initiating event may be direct pharmacologic interaction with particular immune receptors, including specific HLA complexes, which triggers T-cell activation. In addition, some HDS-induced liver injuries have commonly observed antibodies or active T cells that support the immune system play a key role in the pathogenesis of liver injury (Manso et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019). Here, we integrate the progress of the immune mechanisms of DILI and provide a reference for the prevention and treatment of DILI. The innate immune system is the first line of host defense, and its activation is much more rapid than the adaptive immune system (Patel et al., 2016). The innate immune system is a natural immune defense system, which is gradually formed in the long-term phylogenetic evolution of organisms, and is mainly composed of tissue barriers, innate immune cells, and molecules. Drugs or active metabolites could form new antigens to initiate innate immune responses and ultimately mediate immune liver damage. Damaged hepatocytes release related danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) to activate innate immune cells, which secrete related cytokines and chemokines that recruit amounts of neutrophils and monocytes to the injured sites to clear necrotic cell debris. DAMPs include high-mobility group box protein 1 (HMGB1), S100 proteins, heat shock proteins, ATPs, and some others like mitochondria-derived DAMPs, reported to induce inflammasomes via binding Toll-like receptors 2 and 4 (Vénéreau et al., 2015).
Document [2]In addition, for many published DILI cases, it is unclear whether the liver injury was induced by drugs or due to alternative causes (17, 21-23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 35) not carefully excluded by the use of a strong causality assessment tool such as the updated RUCAM (34). Concern also exists that for most drugs, there are too few cases available for investigators to evaluate (24). The details of how a drug initiates DILI are unknown and likely different for different drugs (24, 78). Among the possible general mechanisms are that reactive metabolites can act as haptens to form neoantigens, and they can also cause cell damage leading to the release of DAMPs and activate inflammasomes. There is a large amount of circumstantial evidence for the involvement of reactive metabolites in the mechanism of idiosyncratic DILI; however, it is very difficult to prove that a specific reactive metabolite is responsible for human idiosyncratic DILI caused by a specific drug. Drug metabolism occurs in the liver preferentially via CYP (79, 80) and to a lesser extent through non CYP pathways (81). CYP is primarily localized in the liver and degrades many drugs to harmless metabolites; however, it also has the potential to produce toxic metabolites (79, 80), which have the potential to initiate idiosyncratic DILI. To further evaluate this issue, top drugs causing idiosyncratic DILI as assessed in 48 cases worldwide with verified causality by RUCAM were analyzed for their possible metabolism via (83-100) CYP (101-118) (*Table 2*).
Document [3]In addition, it should be possible to design better treatments when drug-induced liver injury does occur. **Keywords: ** idiosyncratic drug reactions, idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury, immune mediated, immune tolerance Idiosyncratic is defined as peculiar to an individual and describes idiosyncratic drug reactions (IDRs) as reactions that only affect specific individuals. In most cases, whether pharmacology, genetics, environment, or all three determine who will develop an IDR is currently not well understood. IDRs pose a significant issue for healthcare and drug development, as these reactions are often not detected in clinical trials . The incidence of these reactions may only be clear after millions of people have taken the drug, where only a small percentage of patients will experience a reaction (generally <1%). In 2004 in the United Kingdom, adverse drug reactions accounted for 6.5% of hospital admissions with an overall mortality of 2% . Although the percentage of IDRs is only about 10% of the total adverse drug reactions , given the total number of drugs prescribed, IDRs are common and represent a major and increasing cause of candidate failure in drug development. Over 10% of drugs approved during 1975-1999 acquired a black box warning or were withdrawn . IDRs are especially difficult to deal with because the mechanism of injury is not well understood, and current testing is not effective in predicting their risk . IDRs are described as type B adverse drug reactions, which means that they do not generally involve the pharmacological effect of the drug and do not occur in most patients. Additionally, most IDRs appear to involve the bioactivation of the drug into a reactive metabolite . This is in contrast to type A reactions, which are generally a consequence of a drug’s pharmacological effect, and therefore more predictable. An example of a type A reaction is excess bleeding caused by warfarin, which is an anticoagulant.
Document [4]Although inflammasomes are important in innate immunity to fight off infection, excess inflammation can lead to a variety of autoinflammatory conditions. In relation to IDILI, danger signals or drug-modified proteins may signal the activation of inflammasomes and lead to immune mediated liver injury (Figure 3). Figure 3. Inflammasome activation. Drugs have the potential to activate the inflammasome, leading to release of IL-1ß and IL-18, which can further stimulate an immune response. Recently an in vitro experiment was designed to evaluate the ability of certain drugs that cause idiosyncratic skin rashes to activate inflammasomes. THP-1 cells (a human monocyte cell line) were treated with two pairs of chemically similar drugs. Telaprevir has a “black box” warning for severe skin rashes while boseprevir does not, and dimethyl fumarate causes contact sensitization and ethacrynic acid does not cause idiosyncratic reactions even though it covalently binds to proteins. Telaprevir and dimethyl fumarate activated inflammasomes while boseprevir and ethacrynic acid did not . This suggests that inflammasome activation with production of IL-1ß may be a biomarker of IDR potential. Drugs that require bioactivation into their respectful reactive metabolites need to be tested in this model, as well as drugs that cause other forms of IDRs such as IDILI or blood disorders. IDILI may be difficult to study in this model because drugs that cause IDILI generally need to be converted to their reactive metabolite in order to cause liver injury. However, inflammasomes appear to be an intriguing hypothesis of how reactive metabolites activate the immune system leading to an IDR.
Document [5]Although the incidence of serious IDRs is low, their unpredictable nature make them scary. Also, because the mechanism of these adverse reactions is poorly understood, there is no specific treatment other than withdrawal of the offending drug and supportive care . While IDRs can affect a multitude of sites in the body, the three most common targets are the liver, skin, and blood cells. Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (IDILI) is the type of IDR most likely to lead to drug withdrawals . In addition, IDILI accounts for 13% of all cases of acute liver failure in the USA . Therefore significant research has been conducted to better understand these reactions in order to prevent future drug candidates from causing IDILI . Unfortunately, as with other IDRs, the mechanism of IDILI is still poorly understood. The liver is a multifaceted organ involved in metabolism, catabolism, and digestion. In terms of metabolism, anything that is absorbed by the intestines must travel through the portal vein to the liver, where it is subject to metabolism before it enters the general circulation. Specifically, the liver plays a major role in decomposition of endogenous products and is the primary site of drug metabolism in the body. The liver is a prime target for IDRs because drug metabolism can result in the formation of reactive metabolites, and injury is most likely to occur where reactive metabolites are formed. The two major types of IDILI are hepatocellular necrosis and cholestatic liver injury. For cholestatic cases, the initiating event may be inhibition of bile-acid transporters such as the bile salt export pump, which causes bile acid accumulation and initiates cholestatic stress. Although a specific drug usually produces a characteristic pattern of injury, it can vary in different patients. Multiple clinical characteristics make the mechanism of IDILI difficult to define. One important characteristic is that the onset of these reactions is generally delayed. Such a delay is consistent with the need for hepatic drug metabolism before injury becomes apparent and, in cholestatic cases, with interference in bile-acid transport.
Document [6]Little is known with certainty about the mechanisms of idiosyncratic drug reactions (IDRs); however, there is substantive evidence that reactive metabolites are involved in most, but not all, IDRs. In addition, evidence also suggests that most IDRs are immune mediated. That raises the question of how reactive metabolites induce an immune response that can lead to an IDR. The dominant hypotheses are the hapten and danger hypotheses. These are complementary hypotheses: a reactive metabolite can act as a hapten to produce neoantigens, and it can also cause cell damage leading to the release of danger-associated molecular pattern molecules that activate antigen presenting cells. Both are required for an immune response. There are also hypotheses involving mitochondrial injury. For some drugs, the initiating event may be mitochondrial stress, with injury following when adaptive hepatocellular responses fail to restore energy and redox homeostasis. With some possible exceptions, mitochondrial stress alone is unlikely to be able to completely explain IDRs. However, some types of mitochondrial injury could produce danger signals. Clarifying the contribution of these mechanisms to IDRs has therefore been difficult, and rigorous testing of mechanistic hypotheses was impossible in the past.
Document [7]Despite the strong association with HLA, the positive predictive value of HLA allele polymorphisms in drug-induced adverse reactions is limited (Rao et al., 2020). These results suggest that there are other factors, other than the HLA allele, that contribute to the progression of IDILI. Despite a lot of research in this field, the precise activation of the immune system and how it affects liver injury remain to be deeply defined, given extremely limited sample sizes, lack of prospective studies, randomized controlled trials, and excessive confounding factors. Idiosyncratic liver injury caused by drugs such as tienilic acid and halothane is associated with antibodies against drug-modified proteins (Pohl et al., 1989; Bourdi et al., 1996; Robin et al., 1996), as has been observed in DILI. The antibodies against amodiaquine (AQ) were detected in patients with liver injury induced by AQ, suggesting that AQ-induced idiosyncratic reactions involve immune recognition of AQ-modified proteins (Christie et al., 1989). Recently, exosomes as extracellular vesicles from various cells, secreted as membranous structures, have been studied as an important tool for intercellular communication. Exosomes are usually characterized as small membrane vesicles (diameter: 40–150 nm; density: 1.10–1.18 g/ml) (Kowal et al., 2016). Interestingly, some studies have considered exosomes as potential biomarkers for the early evaluation, monitoring, and detection of DILI (Bala et al., 2012; Cho et al., 2017; Royo et al.).

question: Through which mechanisms does arsenic induce cancer when encountered at concentrations typically found in the environment?
perspectives: Epigenetic reprogramming and altered gene regulation
Oxidative stress with indirect genotoxicity
Endocrine disruption affecting growth and differentiation signaling
Altered stem-cell selection or tissue-regenerative signaling

Although arsenic exposure was found to alter methylation levels in global DNA and promoters of some genes, current research is hard to understand due to the complexity and insubstantial information provided in the current studies. Further investigations are necessary to systematically explore DNA methylation on a genome-wide level in cell lines exposed to arsenic and target tissues from well-characterized arsenic-exposed populations or tumor tissues from arsenic-associated cancers. Such studies will assist in elucidating the possible biological effects of arsenic exposure on DNA methylation and carcinogenesis. In liver cells, treatment with As2O3 correlated with hypomethylation in the *cis*-regulatory sites of the promoter of *MYC* (a known cancer-associated gene), as well as hypermethylation in the promoter of *MAX* (a regulator of *MYC* and cell cycle) . Thus, As2O3-based studies not only further the targeted therapy of cancer, but also help to elucidate the mechanism of arsenic toxicity, and in turn, its role in carcinogenesis. The numerous epigenetic changes resulting from iAs exposure culminate in the deregulation of a variety of genes. Document [2]In addition to cancer, epidemiological studies have associated chronic iAs exposure with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, neurological effects, and detrimental birth outcomes . More recently, studies have also discovered that sociodemographic and regional inequalities for iAs concentrations in public water systems exist across the USA . These studies highlight the importance of iAs exposure as an environmental risk factor that likely contributes to cancer and disease disparities in human health. iAs exposure initiates and promotes carcinogenesis through epigenetic and gene-regulatory mechanisms. At environmentally relevant levels, chronic iAs exposure may also skew stem-cell selection and tissue-regenerative signaling, allowing expansion of cell populations more susceptible to malignant transformation. A growing body of evidence has identified roles for epigenetic reprogramming and altered gene regulation in mediating arsenic-induced malignant transformation of human skin, lung, bladder, kidney, liver, prostate, and breast cells. This review will focus on summarizing these gene-regulatory and regenerative mechanisms in the context of cancers resulting from chronic iAs exposure. A total of 500 studies were identified by searching PubMed in April 2023 using the terms "skin cancer and arsenic, " "lung cancer and arsenic, " "bladder cancer and arsenic, " "kidney cancer and arsenic, " "prostate cancer and arsenic, " "liver cancer and arsenic, " and "breast cancer and arsenic"; filters were applied that limited literature to those that were openly available and published within the past 5 years. Pre-exclusion criteria were applied to exclude epidemiological studies that (1) did not contain original research (i.e., reviews and editorials); (2) were case reports or case series; (3) did not measure cancer; (4) lacked reporting of the association between arsenic exposure, either by drinking water or biological measurements, and the study outcome; (5) included pregnant women because pregnancy may influence arsenic metabolism ; (6) stratified arsenic exposed populations; and (7) did not report the study in English.

Document [7]Inorganic arsenic is typically found in drinking water, soil, and some terrestrial foods such as rice, mainly as AsIII or AsV. Inorganic pentavalent arsenic AsV is absorbed by the body through drinking water and uses membrane transporters such as aquaporin and inorganic phosphate transporters (PiT) to enter cells . In the cell, arsenic AsV is converted to the more toxic form arsenite in a glutathione-dependent reaction (GSH), with subsequent methylation to mono-methylated (MMA) and di-methylated arsenicals (DMA), respectively . These methylated arsenicals are commonly considered in studies of arsenic toxicity both in vivo and in vitro . The mechanisms by which arsenic induces carcinogenesis are still a point of debate. However, it has been known that arsenical compounds contribute to carcinogenesis through altered gene expression, elevations of oxidative stress with indirect genotoxic consequences, and alterations of epigenetic regulation . At environmentally relevant exposures, elevated oxidative stress is thought to act indirectly as a genotoxic mechanism by generating DNA lesions and chromosomal damage rather than classic point mutations. There is also doubt about whether arsenic is genotoxic or not because arsenic does not cause point mutations in standard mutagenicity assays; hence it is often considered nongenotoxic . Although arsenic is viewed as a carcinogen, its non-mutagenic characteristics complicate interpretation of how it causes genetic alteration. However, a less studied mechanism, but one that is crucial for understanding arsenic-induced carcinogenesis, is the dysregulation of epigenetic modifications. Studies investigating epigenetic regulation changes upon arsenic exposure during the last decade are increasing. Researchers have attempted to explore the role of DNA methylation, histone modification, miRNAs and lncRNAs, mRNA modification, and alternative splicing in the altered gene regulation associated with arsenic toxicity and carcinogenesis.

Document [9]Arsenic is a chemical element that is toxic, and long-term exposure to it causes cancers such as lung, skin, liver, and bladder cancers. Over 150 million people around the world are affected by arsenic exposure. However, the molecular mechanism of how arsenic induces carcinogenesis is still not clear. Hence, the understanding of the dysregulation of epigenetic mechanisms caused by arsenic may help to unravel the mechanisms by which arsenic induces cancers. Arsenic is a crucial environmental metalloid whose high toxicity levels negatively impact human health. It poses significant health concerns to millions of people in developed and developing countries such as the USA, Canada, Bangladesh, India, China, and Mexico by enhancing sensitivity to various types of diseases, including cancers. However, how arsenic causes changes in gene expression that results in heinous conditions remains elusive. One of the proposed essential mechanisms that still has seen limited research with regard to causing disease upon arsenic exposure is the dysregulation of epigenetic components. In this review, we have extensively summarized current discoveries in arsenic-induced epigenetic modifications in carcinogenesis and angiogenesis. Importantly, we highlight the possible mechanisms underlying epigenetic reprogramming through arsenic exposure that cause changes in cell signaling and dysfunctions of different epigenetic elements. At environmentally relevant exposures, these changes can include endocrine disruption, with arsenic perturbing hormone-responsive growth and differentiation signaling. Document [2]In addition to cancer, epidemiological studies have associated chronic iAs exposure with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, neurological effects, and detrimental birth outcomes . More recently, studies have also discovered that sociodemographic and regional inequalities for iAs concentrations in public water systems exist across the USA . These studies highlight the importance of iAs exposure as an environmental risk factor that likely contributes to cancer and disease disparities in human health. iAs exposure initiates and promotes carcinogenesis through epigenetic and gene-regulatory mechanisms. At environmentally relevant levels, chronic iAs exposure may also skew stem-cell selection and tissue-regenerative signaling, allowing expansion of cell populations more susceptible to malignant transformation. A growing body of evidence has identified roles for epigenetic reprogramming and altered gene regulation in mediating arsenic-induced malignant transformation of human skin, lung, bladder, kidney, liver, prostate, and breast cells. This review will focus on summarizing these gene-regulatory and regenerative mechanisms in the context of cancers resulting from chronic iAs exposure. A total of 500 studies were identified by searching PubMed in April 2023 using the terms "skin cancer and arsenic, " "lung cancer and arsenic, " "bladder cancer and arsenic, " "kidney cancer and arsenic, " "prostate cancer and arsenic, " "liver cancer and arsenic, " and "breast cancer and arsenic"; filters were applied that limited literature to those that were openly available and published within the past 5 years. Pre-exclusion criteria were applied to exclude epidemiological studies that (1) did not contain original research (i.e., reviews and editorials); (2) were case reports or case series; (3) did not measure cancer; (4) lacked reporting of the association between arsenic exposure, either by drinking water or biological measurements, and the study outcome; (5) included pregnant women because pregnancy may influence arsenic metabolism ; (6) stratified arsenic exposed populations; and (7) did not report the study in English.

question: Through which mechanisms does exposure to PM2.5 induce neurotoxic effects in human populations?
perspectives: Systemic inflammatory signaling from the lung to the brain
Direct olfactory translocation of ultrafine particles into the central nervous system
Cerebrovascular endothelial injury with blood-brain barrier dysfunction
Autonomic and vascular dysregulation secondary to cardiopulmonary injury

Document [0]The lung-brain axis can propagate inflammation through systemic inflammatory signaling. Alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages, upon exposure to particulate matter, release inflammatory mediators into the systemic circulation . These circulating signals can act at the BBB interface and the cerebrovascular endothelium . In parallel, PM2.5 can injure cerebrovascular endothelial cells and disrupt tight junctions, producing blood-brain barrier dysfunction that facilitates the entry of circulating inflammatory signals into the brain. Once the neurovascular unit is compromised, peripheral inflammatory cues can more readily influence the brain parenchyma, functioning as drivers of pathological signaling . The pathogenicity of this process lies in the diverse mediators associated with systemic inflammation, including oxidized proteins, inflammatory lipids, and DAMPs . For instance, pollution-induced inflammatory signaling has been associated with molecular changes consistent with endothelial activation . By weakening vascular homeostasis, these signals effectively remove the “brakes” on inflammatory activation at the brain interface . Furthermore, DAMPs like HMGB1 (High mobility group box 1) may engage receptors at the neurovascular unit to perpetuate a sterile inflammatory response . This mechanism represents a biochemical link whereby pulmonary stress contributes to inflammation within the CNS . Components of the neurovascular unit do not act in isolation; their responses are shaped by vascular injury and altered barrier function .
Document [1]Jardim et al. demonstrated that PM2.5 induces regulatory alterations that amplify inflammatory responses. This finding suggests that responses to external damage involve a complex regulatory network, which must remain balanced to coordinate cellular responses effectively. In this review, we focus on the primary pathway by which these changes contribute to neuroinflammation. PM2.5-related inflammatory changes can cause bronchial inflammation and myocardial inflammation. Aberrant inflammatory regulation is associated with a persistent peripheral inflammatory burden. Li et al. suggested that PM2.5-induced inflammation in mice is mainly related to inflammatory dysregulation in cardiopulmonary tissues. In addition, studies have shown that PM2.5 contributes to inflammation in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B) and mice with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with increased levels of inflammation-related markers. Feng et al. demonstrated that PM2.5 exposure in cardiomyocytes (AC16) causes cardiomyocyte injury and myocardial inflammation. Secondary to this cardiopulmonary injury, PM2.5 can also provoke autonomic and vascular dysregulation, impairing cerebral perfusion and thereby contributing to neurotoxicity. These peripheral inflammations lead to the progression of the inflammatory response to the whole body, especially the brain, through inflammatory factors and cellular mediators, which leads to cognitive dysfunction. PM2.5 exposure also alters signaling in airway cells, further sustaining peripheral inflammation. Li et al. reported that PM2.5 in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B) was accompanied by enhanced pro-inflammatory signaling.
Document [2]Thus, airborne environmental exposures can initiate inflammatory cascades that extend from the lung to the brain and thereby compromise neural connectivity (Fig. 6). The elucidation of the molecular pathways linking these exposures to neuroinflammation provides a framework for developing targeted therapeutic interventions. In this account, the pathology is driven by a sequence of events beginning with alveolar irritation, propagating through systemic inflammation, and then producing downstream inflammatory effects in the central nervous system. Accordingly, therapeutic strategies can be stratified into three lines of defense: minimizing exposure, dampening the systemic inflammatory response, and limiting its downstream consequences in the brain. Given that systemic inflammation is the primary driver of this "spill-over" effect, repurposing anti-inflammatory agents represents a pragmatic clinical approach. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have shown mixed results in neurodegenerative prevention; however, agents with more specific efficacy against this inflammatory cascade warrant closer attention .

However, we must consider the caveat that in vitro cell models use direct exposure to nPM at much higher concentrations than could reach the brain by inhalation. Thus, in vitro responses might be distinctly different from the brain, which receives systemic influences, ‘lung to brain’ (see below). Thus, we also examined these inflammatory responses in vivo. In mice, a short term 3-week exposure to 300 -g/m3 nPM, but not lower concentrations, sufficed to decrease TLR4 and MyD88 mRNA, induce NF-κB localization to the nucleus, and increase proinflammatory cytokines IFN and IL1 in the cerebral cortex . Another experiment showed that initial responses to inhalation of 300 -g/m3 nPM begin as early as three weeks for induction of TNF protein in the olfactory bulb, cerebral cortex, and cerebellum of young male mice . Such early olfactory-bulb involvement supports direct olfactory translocation, with ultrafine particles deposited in the nasal mucosa moving along olfactory pathways into the central nervous system.

Therefore, new approaches with higher throughput are required. A screening strategy based on the use of relevant human cell types has been proposed by the U. S. Environmental Protection Agency and others. Because impaired neural crest (NC) function is one of the known causes for teratologic effects, testing of toxicant effects on NC cells is desirable for a DT test battery. Objective: We developed a robust and widely applicable human-relevant NC function assay that would allow for sensitive screening of environmental toxicants and defining toxicity pathways. Methods: We generated NC cells from human embryonic stem cells, and after establishing a migration assay of NC cells (MINC assay), we tested environmental toxicants as well as inhibitors of physiological signal transduction pathways. Results: Methylmercury (50 nM), valproic acid (> 10 µM), and lead-acetate [Pb(CH3CO2)4] (1 µM) affected the migration of NC cells more potently than migration of other cell types. The MINC assay correctly identified the NC toxicants triadimefon and triadimenol. Additionally, it showed different sensitivities to various organic and inorganic mercury compounds. Using the MINC assay and applying classic pharmacologic inhibitors and large-scale microarray gene expression profiling, we found several signaling pathways that are relevant for the migration of NC cells. Thus, it is necessary to carefully evaluate the developmental neurotoxicity of these emerging chemicals for their safe use. Therefore, new approaches with higher throughput are required. A screening strategy based on the use of relevant human cell types has been proposed by the U. S. Environmental Protection Agency and others. Because impaired neural crest (NC) function is one of the known causes for teratologic effects, testing of toxicant effects on NC cells is desirable for a DT test battery. Objective: We developed a robust and widely applicable human-relevant NC function assay that would allow for sensitive screening of environmental toxicants and defining toxicity pathways. Methods: We generated NC cells from human embryonic stem cells, and after establishing a migration assay of NC cells (MINC assay), we tested environmental toxicants as well as inhibitors of physiological signal transduction pathways. Results: Methylmercury (50 nM), valproic acid (> 10 µM), and lead-acetate [Pb(CH3CO2)4] (1 µM) affected the migration of NC cells more potently than migration of other cell types. Document [0]In mature soils, improving the biochemical persistence of OM is important to long-term OC stabilization. Among biota-derived OM sources, those derived from microorganisms are considered to be more persistent and prone to stabilization. As a result, enriching microbial-derived OM formation is one of the important strategies to increase OC stabilization and storage in mature soil. In managed agricultural systems, practices that foster a more active soil microbiome can contribute to this pathway. For instance, well-managed and long-term grassland practices have been shown to increase the presence of microbial necromass in MAOM fractions when compared to annual cropping systems96. Likewise, multi-species intercropping has been found to increase microbial-derived OM accumulation in macroaggregates in contrast to mono-species cropping systems97.
Document [1]Soil organic matter (SOM) represents the biggest carbon (C) reservoir within terrestrial ecosystem and is a key component of the global carbon cycle (Lal, 2004). It serves as a pivotal nutrient reservoir necessary for plant growth and significantly contributes to maintaining soil physical structure and biochemical properties (Hoffland et al., 2020). Thus, the retention of soil organic C (SOC) is essential for sustaining soil fertility, ensuring biomass production, and combating climate change. Paddy soils, accounting for approximately 9 % of global agricultural land area (Liu et al., 2021), act as a crucial component in terrestrial C sequestration. Recent studies elucidate that microbial plays a vital role in carbon dynamics in paddy soil (Li et al., 2024), Gao et al., 2024). Particularly, through biogeochemical cycling processes involving cell synthesis, growth, and death, microorganisms continuously assimilate and transform labile organic carbon into microbial necromass (Camenzind et al., 2023), Liang et al., 2017). Increasing evidence suggests that microbial necromass constitutes an important component of SOM. Using a 13C isotope tracing technique, Miltner et al. (2009) demonstrated that even after long-term incubation, a substantial proportion of microbial-derived residues remained in the soil, primarily within the non-living organic matter fraction. These findings provided direct evidence that microbial necromass is a significant contributor to SOC and can persist over the long term in soil. Building upon this understanding, recent studies have shown that long-term rice cultivation is associated with substantial microbial-derived contributions to SOC. This further supports the view that microbial residues can favor the stabilization and long-term retention of necromass in soil (Wei et al., 2022), Liu et al., 2023).
Document [2]4 | HYPHAL ESTABLISHMENT ON MINERAL SURFACES ENCOURAGES MAOM FORMATION Mounting evidence suggests that a large proportion of MAOM consists of common microbial biomolecules such as polysaccharides, lipids, organic acids, and enzymes (Grandy & Neff, 2008; Heckman et al., 2018; Miltner et al., 2012). As fungi comprise the majority of soil microbial biomass (He et al., 2020) and necromass (Liang et al., 2019; Simpson et al., 2007), they likely contribute disproportionately to microbially derived MAOM. Hyphal proliferation along soil mineral surfaces leads to the production and subsequent sorption of microbial compounds from turnover-related sources, including (1) the direct decomposition products of fungal necromass (Figure 2b) and (2) molecules originating from processes of microbial succession during hyphal necromass decomposition, such as bacterial necromass products (Figure 2c). The relative importance of these sources likely depends on both hyphosphere community composition (Anthony et al., 2020) and soil mineralogy (Creamer et al., 2019; Heckman et al., 2018). Decomposition of hyphae and associated microbes releases organic compounds into their surrounding environment that have the potential to interact with minerals. These compounds include microbial biomolecules generated during fungal turnover and during the succession of other microbes on decomposing necromass. Many of the compounds produced during necromass decomposition and microbial succession have the potential to form new MAOM.

Document [4]Concomitantly, SOM is brought into contact with mineral particles. Aboveground litter-derived compounds are transported downward through the soil profile in dissolved or colloidal form before sorbing to reactive mineral surfaces. Moreover, this transfer occurs through dissolved or colloidal material moving through the profile. Some of this material interacts with iron oxide mineral particles at reactive surfaces. Others bind strongly to mineral surfaces and thus remain associated with the mineral phase. Fungal biomass, in turn, also contributes substantially to the formation of SOM through necromass that is left behind after cell death. Microbial turnover may also contribute to the formation of stabilized SOM (Lehmann and Kleber, 2015). However, little is known about the forms of organic matter extracted from boreal forest soils. A recent study from our group shows that ca. 40–70% of the total organic C in DOM extracted from boreal forest is present in a colloidal size fraction (Meklesh et al., 2022). Important challenges for future research are to examine how such colloidal fractions move through soils and interact with mineral surfaces. The significance of specific molecular interactions in decomposition processes has been questioned by soil scientists, considering that soil microorganisms may not always have the energy and nutrient resources needed for every proposed mechanism (Lehmann and Kleber, 2015). This may be true in some contexts. However, attention remains on how litter-derived dissolved or colloidal compounds are sorbed to reactive mineral surfaces and how microbial turnover leaves necromass that can persist in mineral soils.
Document [5]In addition, mechanical disruption of the residual cell envelopes by physical processes, e.g., shrinking and swelling of SOM as well as soil mixing due to bioturbation by macrofauna may also determine the fate (Bohlen et al., 2004; Basile-Doelsch et al., 2020). The ultimate fate of the necromass then depends on many factors: microbial decay, clay content, Fe or Al oxides, water content and pore system of the soil aggregates (Schimel et al., 2007). Microbial necromass (including cell envelope fragments) can be stabilized within the soil matrix through its small size, spatial conformation, and by interaction with itself, e.g., by the formation of stacks of cell-wall fragments that may hamper degradation due to limited accessibility of the interior regions (Miltner et al., 2012; Buckeridge et al., 2020). Necromass may easily be occluded in soil aggregates and therefore not be bioavailable for degradation. Interactions of biomolecules with other organic and mineral matter can occur by ionic or hydrogen bonds or hydrophobic interactions (Galicia-Andres et al., 2021). However, various types of biomolecules are partly stabilized in SOM to different extents: proteins > bulk biomass C > lipids (e.g. PLFA) (Kindler et al., 2006; Kindler et al., 2009; Miltner et al., 2009; Spence et al., 2011; Miltner et al., 2012). An overarching stabilization process of SOM and necromass can also be caused by the formation of hydrophobic domains with a decreased chemical activity of water (Masoom et al., 2016) by drying processes, or by loss of pore water connectivity. The authors impressively provided evidence that around 75% of the necromass-derived SOM material is actually not in contact with water.
Document [6]As microbial necromass decomposition proceeds, more slowly decomposing aromatic components yield more complex molecules for organomineral interactions. For example, condensed aromatic residues can persist for years as particulate matter in litterbags (Fernandez et al., 2019), and related particulate residues have been shown to persist in soils for millennia (Scott et al., 2010). The formation of organo-mineral complexes from these condensed aromatic molecules remains poorly characterized. However, such complexes are likely important given the persistence of aromatic residues in soils and the fact that other complex aromatic molecules contribute substantially to mineral-bound SOM (Angst et al., 2021; Rasse et al., 2005). Pyrogenic carbon from fire residues or char amendments supplies condensed aromatic compounds that persist and become associated with mineral surfaces. In a study of microbial growth in ligninfree model soils, increased mineral-associated phenolic and aromatic compounds were observed after 18 months (Kallenbach et al., 2016), suggesting the accumulation of persistent aromatic material. Thus, microbial necromass turnover products and pyrogenic carbon likely contribute directly to new MAOM formation. Document [7]For instance, microbial processes intended to liberate organic matter or nutrients can promote the transformation of root inputs in the rhizosphere (Olagoke et al., 2019), and may therefore contribute indirectly to MAOM in some systems. Indeed, a recent comparison across Critical Zone Observatory sites in the United States highlighted extensive retention of microbially processed material on clays in deep mineral soils (Dove et al., 2020). Similarly, mineral-associated low-molecular-weight compounds are often linked to root exudates moving through soil profiles (Sokol et al., 2019), but in this context they are better viewed as intermediates in rhizosphere processing than as a distinct long-term source pathway. Root-derived compounds are often transformed within the rhizosphere into low-molecular-weight products with high mineral affinity before sorbing to mineral surfaces. Given the close proximity of roots, microbes, and mineral surfaces, the rhizosphere likely represents an important zone for the formation of MAOM in mineral soils. In the case of products with high mineral affinity, such rhizosphere transformation would lead to higher rates of sorption in deeper soils than expected based solely on leaching from surficial horizons (e.g., Mikutta et al., 2019; Sokol et al., 2019). As bacterial and fungal biomass turns over, microbial necromass presents a wide range of organic residues available for mineral sorption (Figure 2b). When microbial cells lyse, that material enters the surrounding environment and can be further transformed by decomposers before stabilization on mineral surfaces (see below). Aboveground litter-derived compounds are transported downward through the soil profile in dissolved or colloidal form before sorbing to reactive mineral surfaces. Moreover, this transfer occurs through dissolved or colloidal material moving through the profile. Some of this material interacts with iron oxide mineral particles at reactive surfaces. Fungal biomass, in turn, also contributes substantially to the formation of SOM through necromass that is left behind after cell death. Soils are the largest terrestrial reservoir of biologically fxed atmospheric carbon dioxide, comprising 3500–4800 Pg of organic carbon (OC)1 . Climate2 and geological parent material3 are well-known controls on the long-term storage and stabilization of OC. In contrast to these natural environmental factors, land-use change has a direct impact on OC storage, which can obscure the efects of climate, geology, and geochemistry4 . Sub Saharan Africa is known for ongoing land-use change, because of population growth and increasing demand for food5 . It is widely accepted that forest to cropland conversion results in carbon loss, threatening the key role of soils in ecosystem services6 .
