Document [1]Future permafrost thaw will likely lead to substantial release of greenhouse gases due to thawing of previously unavailable organic carbon (OC). Accurate predictions of this release are limited by poor knowledge of the bioavailability of mobilized OC during thaw. Organic carbon bioavailability decreases due to adsorption to, or coprecipitation with, poorly crystalline ferric iron (Fe(III)) (oxyhydr)oxide minerals but the maximum binding extent and binding selectivity of permafrost OC to these minerals is unknown. We therefore utilized water-extractable organic matter (WEOM) from soils across a permafrost thaw gradient to quantify adsorption and coprecipitation processes with poorly crystalline Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides. We found that the maximum adsorption capacity of WEOM from intact and partly thawed permafrost soils was similar (204 and 226 mg C g−1 ferrihydrite, respectively) but decreased to 81 mg C g−1 ferrihydrite for WEOM from the fully thawed site. In comparison, coprecipitation of WEOM from intact and partly thawed soils with Fe immobilized up to 925 and 1532 mg C g−1 Fe respectively due to formation of precipitated Fe(III)–OC phases. Analysis of the OC composition before and after adsorption/coprecipitation revealed that high molecular weight, oxygen-rich, carboxylic- and aromatic-rich OC was preferentially bound to Fe(III) minerals relative to low molecular weight, aliphatic-rich compounds which may be more bioavailable. This selective binding effect was stronger after adsorption than coprecipitation. Our results suggest that OC binding by Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides sharply decreases under fully thawed conditions and that small, aliphatic OC molecules that may be readily bioavailable are less protected across all thaw stages. Permafrost thaw leads to the release of organic carbon (OC), which may bind with ubiquitous ferric iron (Fe(III)) minerals.
Document [2]The largest and most persistent portion of soil organic carbon (OC) is stored with mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM), making the protection and augmentation of MAOM stocks crucial in our efforts to mitigate climate change. To achieve this goal, a sound understanding of the controls of MAOM formation and stabilization is needed. Interactions between organic matter and reactive mineral surfaces are key drivers of these processes. Persistent MAOM can also arise because microbes continually recycle fresh inputs into microbial products and other slow-turnover carbon compounds that are repeatedly replenished on mineral surfaces. Still, questions about their relative importance across large spatial scales as well as on subdecadal time scales remain unresolved, largely because their individual roles are often obscured by the complexity of mineral soils and by their concurrent operation. To address these questions, I leveraged a large-scale experimental study where permeable containers with pristine mineral phases, including goethite (iron oxide), were exposed to natural conditions at different soil depths across the three study regions of the Biodiversity Exploratories of Germany. With this setup, I sought to resolve how reactive mineral phases contribute to the formation and stabilization of soil OM and how this intersects with continued microbial recycling of inputs across soil depths. Associations with reactive mineral phases emerged as a principal mechanism contributing to MAOM formation in topsoils. Persistent OM accumulation was consistent with retention on mineral surfaces through sorptive interactions. Organic carbon persistence was also consistent with continual microbial recycling of fresh inputs into microbial products and other slow-turnover carbon compounds. Therefore, long-term MAOM reflects ongoing replenishment of compounds that remain associated with mineral surfaces.

Document [4]Iron oxides are crucial for the long-term storage of soil organic carbon (SOC) in paddy soils, making them a key factor in global carbon cycles and important for strategies aimed at combating climate change. This review examines the role of iron oxides in paddy soils, particularly their interaction with SOC, which helps stabilize carbon and contributes to mitigating climate change. These iron oxide phase transformations during wet–dry cycles help trap carbon in the soil, supporting climate change mitigation efforts. Wet–dry cycles promote iron mineral dissolution and re-precipitation, forming new reactive surfaces and OC-Fe complexes. Future research should adopt a multi-scale approach to better connect molecular mechanisms with ecosystem-level carbon processes. A deeper understanding of iron oxide behavior in paddy soils will support the development of sustainable soil management practices and improve models for predicting soil carbon sequestration under climate change. Paddy soils, a significant type of anthropogenic wetland ecosystem, are crucial for global food security, providing sustenance for more than half of the world’s population. Despite occupying a relatively small area, paddy soils play a critical role in the global carbon cycle, especially in the long-term sequestration of organic carbon . Globally, rice cultivation covers approximately 160 million hectares, accounting for about 11–12% of total cropland area . Continuous anthropogenic management through periodic flooding, ploughing, and drainage profoundly influences pedogenic processes, promoting the distinctive features of these soils, including pronounced iron and manganese mobilization, gleization, and the formation of characteristic plough-pan horizons . Paddy soils, though occupying a small area, are highly effective in storing SOC, which plays a vital role in reducing greenhouse gases and combating climate change. This carbon storage capability makes paddy soils essential for mitigating climate change . The ability of paddy soils to store carbon is largely due to the stabilization of organic carbon through interactions with soil minerals, especially iron oxides .
Document [5]Here, we refer to phases that are formed after either adsorption or coprecipitation as Fe–OC associations. The formation pathway of Fe–OC associations directly affects the properties of the Fe–OC phase. As organic matter accumulates on these associations, organo-organic coatings can develop that shield underlying mineral-associated carbon from enzymatic and microbial exposure. While adsorption of OC changes the surface properties of the mineral, coprecipitation with OC produces a resulting Fe–OC phase with distinct surface characteristics.14–18 During the binding process, part of the OC becomes associated with mineral surfaces. Past studies using forest-floor extracts, plant litter, or humic reference materials have examined Fe binding across different OC sources. These studies involved OC interacting with Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides across a range of source materials.19–22 The binding process thus leaves a fraction of OC associated with mineral surfaces in soils.20, 23 Recently, several studies have shown that substantial fractions of OC may be bound to minerals (30–82%), with the dominant mineral fraction as Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides.12, 24, 25 The amount of Fe-bound OC can also be substantial across different sites.24, 26–28 This suggests that part of the OC may remain unavailable due to binding with Fe minerals despite microbial exposure. However, our systematic understanding of the formation and composition of Fe–OC associations in soils is limited. Across soils, OC can continue to accumulate on existing Fe–OC associations. As this material builds up on Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxide surfaces, organo-organic coatings may become more developed, thereby limiting enzymatic and microbial access to the underlying mineral-associated carbon.
Document [6]Soil organic carbon (SOC) can be stabilized via association with iron (Fe) and aluminum (Al) minerals. Fe and Al can be strong predictors of SOC storage and turnover in soils with relatively high extractable metals content and moderately acidic to circumneutral pH. Here we test whether pedogenic Fe and Al influence SOC content and turnover in soils with low Fe and Al content and acidic pH. In soils from four sites spanning three soil orders, we quantified the amount of Fe and Al in operationally-defined poorly crystalline and organically-complexed phases using selective chemical dissolution applied to the soil fraction containing mineral-associated carbon. We evaluated the correlations of Fe and Al concentrations, mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean annual temperature (MAT), and pH with SOC content and 14C-based turnover times. We found that poorly crystalline Fe and Al content predicted SOC turnover times (p < 0.0001), consistent with findings of previous studies, while organically-complexed Fe and Al content was a better predictor of SOC concentration (p < 0.0001). Our results suggest that poorly crystalline Fe and Al effectively slow the turnover of SOC in these acidic soils, even when their combined content in the soil is less than 2% by mass. However, in the strongly acidic Spodosol, organo-metal complexes tended to be less stable resulting in a more actively cycling mineral-associated SOC pool. Adsorption and complexation reactions with Fe and Al soil constituents are important mechanisms of storage and stabilization of soil organic carbon (SOC; Oades 1988 The retention of organic matter in soils. Biogeochemistry 5: 35–70"), Conant et al.

These interactions promote the formation of stable organo-mineral associations (Barber et al., 2017). The free Fe/Al-(hydr) oxides (Fed and Ald), primarily composed of hematite, goethite, ferrihydrite, and gibbsite, are characterized by poor crystallinity, high specific surface area, and dense surface sites, properties that favor SOC retention (Porras et al., 2017).

Bergsma6 , Karl‑Heinz Feger1 & Karsten Kalbitz1 Clay minerals and pedogenic metal (oxyhydr)oxides are the most reactive soil mineral constituents controlling the long-term persistence of organic carbon (OC) in terrestrial ecosystems. However, their co-occurrence in most soils complicates direct assessment of their individual contribution to OC persistence. Making use of unique mineralogical combinations in soils located in the East Usambara Mountains of Tanzania, we disentangled the contribution of clay-sized aluminous minerals (kaolinite, gibbsite) and pedogenic Fe (oxyhydr)oxides (predominant goethite and hematite) on OC storage and stabilization under natural forests and croplands. Topsoil samples, varying in contents but not types of aluminous clays and pedogenic Fe (oxyhydr)oxides, were identifed by selective extractions, X-ray difraction, and Mössbauer spectroscopy. Associated abundance of particulate and mineral-associated organic matter (OM) was quantifed by density fractionation and their changes during land-use conversion were determined as a measure of OC persistence. Additionally, we assessed the resistance of OC to chemical oxidation as well as microbial decomposition in a 50-day laboratory incubation. We found that the ratio of pedogenic Fe to aluminous clay is more consequential for OC storage and stabilization than their individual contents, despite the fact that Fe (oxyhydr)oxides generally exert a stronger impact on OC than aluminous clays. Conjunction of large amounts of Fe (oxyhydr)oxides with low aluminous clay contents caused the strongest accumulation of mineral-associated OC, a low soil respiration, high OC stability against chemical oxidation, and high OC persistence during land-use change.

Document [3]Moreover, non-crystalline Fe/Al oxides, as inorganic cementing substances, are directly involved in the formation and stabilization of aggregates, but oxalic acid in root exudates can dissolve these Fe-Al oxides, leading to the aggregate's destruction (Li et al., 2018). As roots grow and expand, they can physically fracture soil aggregates, exposing fresh mineral surfaces and previously protected mineral-associated organic matter to rhizosphere attack. The combination of organic carbon and soil mineral composition is considered the most critical stabilization mechanism for soil organic carbon. In the rhizosphere, however, low-molecular-weight, chelating root exudates can interact directly with these mineral phases, and compared to plant debris with high molecular weight input, they are more likely to contact reactive surfaces. Root exudates input organic carbon into the soil by roots, accounting for up to 40% of the carbon fixed by photosynthesis (Bais et al., 2006), so these reactions occur where root-derived compounds are concentrated. Thus, dissolution of Fe/Al oxide cements together with physical aggregate disruption can weaken mineral protection and expose mineral-associated organic matter to further rhizosphere attack.
Document [4]In the presence of high proton, ligand or reductant concentrations, Fe-, Mn-, or Al-rich mineral phases (e.g., Fe oxides and imogolite-type phases) are therefore more susceptible to dissolution than those consisting of relatively Si-rich phases (e.g., phyllosilicates). Root-induced oxygen depletion and re-oxidation can also reduce or oxidize Fe and Mn, transforming iron and manganese mineral phases and thereby destabilizing mineral-associated organic matter. Moreover, because atoms in mineral phases with a greater degree of order are arranged in a repetitive pattern that minimizes the internal energy, they tend to be energetically less susceptible to dissolution39, 63. The dissolution of mineral phases with a low degree of order is also favored kinetically, as their inherently larger surface area facilitates the adsorption of protons, ligands, or reductants, thereby accelerating the subsequent dissolution reaction. Consequently, both energetics and kinetics render oligomers, short-range order phases of Fe-, Mn-, and Al-oxides, and imogolite-type materials particularly vulnerable to dissolution in the rhizosphere18, 20, 25, 28, 62, 69–72. It is important to note, however, that the dissolution of mineral phases is frequently slowed or inhibited when adsorbed or co-precipitated OM blocks the reactive sites for protons, ligands, or reductants to attack73, 74. Desorption. Desorption of MAOM occurs if chemical bonds between OM and mineral phases are broken, liberating previously bound OM into the soil solution19, 20. In principle, OM bound through all types of sorptive interactions can be subject to desorption. But the likelihood that OM will be desorbed from mineral surfaces decreases with increasing strength of the OM-mineral bond (Figure 2c). In general terms, we distinguish three types of desorption mechanisms: (i) ligand exchange reactions, (ii) sorption disequilibrium, and (iii) chemical dispersion (Figure 3a). Document [5]Low molecular weight organic anions are usually present in the form of di- and tri-carboxylate anions such as malate, citrate, and oxalate (Jones et al. 2004). They may contain varying amounts of pH-dependent negative charge, facilitating complexation with metal cations that can destabilize mineral-organic complexes. Destabilization of mineral-organic complexes mobilizes formally protected MAOM, thus making organic matter available for microbial degradation and assimilation (Clarholm et al. 2015). Fresh root exudates may thereby enhance rhizosphere microbial nutrient mining from mineral-associated organic matter and accelerate its decomposition. For example, several researchers have found that destabilization of mineral-organic complexes by simulated root exudates (e.g., oxalate) increased the bioavailability of OM, leading to greater C mineralization (Keiluweit et al. 2015) and N utilization (Yuan et al. 2018). Plants release a mixture of complex organic compounds, and exudation of organic compounds is influenced by several factors (e.g., plant species and cultivar, plant growth stage, plant nutrition, microorganisms, environmental conditions, etc.), making it difficult to generalize about the composition of organic compounds present in root exudates (Grayston et al.).
Document [6]Ligand exchange occurs when OM with relatively high affinity for mineral surfaces replaces OM with lower affinity. This exchange arises when the interaction between the newly adsorbed ligand and the mineral surface is more thermodynamically favorable than the interaction between the previously adsorbed ligand and the mineral phase. At the soil profile scale, dissolved organic matter percolating through soil can exchange between 15-32% of adsorbed OM on minerals75. In the rhizosphere, these reactions can occur when roots increase concentrations of competing ligands, including organic acids and inorganic ions such as PO43−, Al3+, H+, and OH−18, 19, 76. Consequently, OM bound by relatively weak outer-sphere complexes is particularly vulnerable to ligand exchange, for example via relatively weak organic acids released by roots18. Similarly, elevated concentrations of inorganic ions can promote exchange of OM held in outer-sphere complexes on phyllosilicate surfaces77. Importantly, ligand exchange with strong complexing agents, such as strong organic acids, is the only mechanism that effectively desorbs OM bound via strong, inner-sphere complexes commonly found in MOAs formed by Fe and Al oxides, representing a critical disruption mechanism for MOAs often perceived as the most stable.
Document [7]Additionally, diel photosynthesis cycles cause spikes in rhizodeposition and associated microbial activity during the day29, 128, 129. Moreover, at the scale of the entire root network, rhizodeposition hotspots and hot moments emerge across phenological stages130–133, seasons134, and within different locations in the root network135. At the ecosystem level, rhizodeposition is expected to vary not only quantitatively with root density and depth136, but also with root functional traits (e.g., nutrient versus water acquisition)137. The spatiotemporal variability in rhizodeposition is mirrored by observations of mineral transformations at complementary scales. For example, we observe differential mineral transformation in the rhizosphere along single growing roots30, over diel cycles33, 115, during seasonal root growth and senescence138, 139, and over pedogenic time scales1 8. Such observed patterns of root activity, associated microbial dynamics, and mineral transformations provide a clear indication for the potential of MOA disruption, but also suggest that it is extremely variable in space and time across different ecosystems. These considerations highlight that future efforts to quantify MOA disruption rates (in relation to MOA formation rates) need to consider potential hotspots and hot moments of MOA disruption within a given ecosystem. Which MOA disruption mechanisms dominate across different soil ecosystems?. If MOA characteristics are known, one can postulate which MOA disruption mechanisms may be the most prevalent across different ecosystems. For example, mechanistic considerations suggest that mineral dissolution and ligand exchange reactions are the most effective MOA disruption mechanisms for short-range order oxides and metal–organic complexes, respectively. Because humid soil systems (temperate and tropical) are often dominated by oxides, plants and associated microbes have developed nutrient scavenging strategies tailored to target these minerals21. For instance, ectomycorrhizal fungi dominating temperate and boreal forests show a strong potential for mineral weathering through the production of organic acids and ligands140, 141.

Lacroix5, Sherlynette Pérez Castro3, Per Persson7, William J. Riley8 & Marco Keiluweit5 The majority of soil carbon (C) is stored in organic matter associated with reactive minerals. These mineral-organic associations (MOAs) inhibit microbial and enzymatic access to organic matter, suggesting that organic C within MOAs is resistant to decomposition. However, plant roots and rhizosphere microbes release compounds that can exchange with mineral-bound organics at sorption sites and chelate metal cations, thereby weakening mineral–organic binding and implying that MOAs in the rhizosphere can be dynamic. Here we identify key drivers, mechanisms, and controls of MOA disruption in the rhizosphere and present a new conceptual framework for the vulnerability of soil C within MOAs. We introduce a vulnerability spectrum that highlights how MOAs characteristic of certain ecosystems are particularly susceptible to specific root-driven disruption mechanisms. This vulnerability spectrum provides a framework for critically assessing the importance of MOA disruption mechanisms at the ecosystem scale. Comprehensive representation of root-driven MOA disruption will improve model projections of soil C-climate feedbacks and guide the development of more effective soil C management strategies. Plants allocate 40–60% of their photosynthetically fixed carbon (C) to their root systems and associated microbes1, 2 via dead root cells, tissues, mucilage, and a cocktail of simple organic compounds—collectively known as rhizodeposits3, 4. This rhizodeposition is a main source of soil organic matter (OM)2, 5, 6, the largest and most dynamic terrestrial C reservoir on Earth7. The proximity of roots to their surrounding mineral matrix is thought to facilitate such interactions with reactive mineral surfaces8–10.

question: How is phosphorus deficiency maintained in intensely weathered tropical soils when exposed to increased levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide?
perspectives: Strong sorption and occlusion by iron and aluminum minerals
Microbial immobilization of newly mineralized phosphate
Slow mineralization of soil organic phosphorus compounds
Limited replenishment from deep or residual mineral weathering

Document [0]Phosphorus sorption reactions are particularly important in highly weathered soils because strong soil sorption capacities effectively reduce P availability (Uehara and Gillman 1980; Sollins et al. 1988). Intense weathering in Ultisols and Oxisols results in the prevalence of Al and Fe oxides and hydroxides that effectively sorb P (Sanchez 1976; Harrison 1987; Pant et al. 1994). As a result, sorbed inorganic P concentrations in many tropical soils often exceed those of soil solution P by several orders of magnitude (Sanchez 1976), Fig. 14.5), and fertilization studies have shown that, in highly weathered soils, P may be rapidly and nearly completely sorbed over short timescales (e.g., Sanchez 1976; Uehara and Gillman 1980; Oberson et al.).
Document [1]Is the strong P retention that we observed restricted to soils that have favorable conditions for P desorption? Deforestation transfers large quantities of P from the aboveground biomass to the soils. In the highly weathered acidic soils of the Amazon region, much of this P is retained in sorbed or occluded P pools (Garcia-Montiel and others 2000). Despite the biologically less favorable conditions in these tropical forest soils, substantial amounts of soil P remain in these retained pools. We know of no other studies that directly assess the partitioning of soil solution phosphate. Effects of Long-term Nitrogen and Phosphorus Fertilization on Phosphorus Partitioning Long-term fertilization with N substantially reduced specific P sorption and sorption capacity in both soil horizons. In field soils, we observed more Bray P1 in the N-fertilized soils than the unfertilized soils, perhaps due to this reduction in specific sorption. We do not think changes in pH are responsible for reduced sorption; a 0.2-unit increase in pH in the N-fertilized soils (Table 2) could decrease aluminum solubility and alter sorption (McBride 1994), but decreased aluminum solubility may enhance the ability of P to adsorb strongly to aluminum hydroxides. The cause of this reduction remains uncertain, but the results indicate that the amount of readily extractable P is sensitive to sorption strength in these highly weathered soils.
Document [2]In weathered tropical soils, the chemistry of the soil affects nutrient mobility in somewhat unique ways. Mobility of nutrient ions in soil is a major factor controlling nutrient cycling, because it affects the rate at which plant roots can extract nutrients and the rate at which nutrients are lost from the system. “Sorption” broadly describes any process that removes a reactant from solution, thus reducing its mobility, and includes both adsorption and precipitation. More specifically, P sorption refers to the removal of P from the soil solution into less reactive geochemical sinks, including iron- and aluminum-associated forms. In soils, both organic and inorganic forms of P are susceptible to sorption, but the extent is influenced primarily by the concentration, chemistry, and solubility of soil P. Examples of sorption include phosphate bound with iron (FePO4) or aluminum (AlPO4). Different sorption bonds vary in their stability and thus also in how readily the sorbed P can be desorbed.
Document [3]Phosphorus (P) cycling can be divided into biological and geochemical cycling (Wood and others 1984; Harrison and others 1988; Walbridge and others 1991; Yanai 1992). On the biological side, living plants and microbes take up and immobilize P that through death and senescence becomes part of soil organic P; this P can then be mineralized and taken up once again. In highly weathered tropical soils, mineralization of soil organic phosphorus compounds can be slow, constraining the release of phosphate to plants and microbes. On the geochemical side, weathering of primary rock, dust deposition, and fertilizers supply P to ecosystems, while chemical reactions with soil minerals stabilize P in the soils. In humid ecosystems with acidic soils, geochemical reactions of adsorption and precipitation bind and stabilize soil P to iron and aluminum oxide minerals; together these processes are termed “sorption” (Frossard and others 1995). Sorption and desorption of P involve chemical bonding that ranges from weak, nonspecific to very strong, specific bondings (Tiessen and Steward 1984). The biological and geochemical P cycles therefore interact through the conversion of soil organic P to orthophosphate and the subsequent stabilization of that phosphate by soil minerals. In highly weathered tropical soils, slow mineralization limits the release of phosphate, and iron and aluminum oxides can retain much of the released P through sorption.
Document [4]In contrast, bacteria and nonfilamentous fungi are relatively immobile and thus depend on phosphate released within their immediate microsites (Tate 1985). When phosphate enters soil solution, it is exposed to extremely rapid sorption, and microbes may also immobilize part of the newly mineralized P into biomass, leaving only a small dissolved pool (Bolan 1991). In zones of substantial P depletion, much P may still be weakly represented in soil solution because phosphate released there is rapidly removed from the dissolved phase (Magid and others 1996b). Against background inputs of available P from mineralization and desorption, these additions to soil solution remain transient. Newly mineralized phosphate can be rapidly immobilized by microbes into biomass before it is lost to sorption. Such flushes therefore need not alleviate limitation, because P can be redistributed quickly into microbial biomass or sorbed forms (Singh and others 1989; Lodge and others 1994; McGrath and others 2000). During larger nutrient pulse events, any temporary increase in dissolved P remains brief because sorption is extremely rapid. Sorption is an extremely rapid process, and the strength by which P is held to sorption sites tends to increase over time (Freese and others 1995; Beauchemin and others 1996). As biotic activity and growth respond to transient nutrient availability, microbial biomass can retain part of the newly available P, while strong sorption continues to constrain the size of the soil-solution pool. In this study, we evaluated how microbial immobilization and geochemical sorption affect inorganic P in a tropical soil with strong sorption. We asked whether strong geochemical sorption constrains soil solution P under low availability and whether newly mineralized phosphate is rapidly incorporated into microbial biomass before being sorbed.
Document [5]The intense weathering in tropical lowland forests also leads to the prevalence of 1 : 1 clays (e.g., kaolinite) and aluminum and iron oxides and hydroxides that effectively sorb P (Sanchez, 1976), which result in low P availability in tropical soils and strong P limitation for tropical ecosystems. Because these old, highly weathered profiles retain little easily weatherable P-bearing material, replenishment from deep or residual mineral weathering is limited. These mineralogical and profile properties generally mean that P released into the soil is readily retained on reactive surfaces rather than remaining available in solution. This provides a direct explanation for persistent P limitation in tropical lowland forests. The interactions of soil mineralogy and weathering history play important roles in regulating the availability of P in terrestrial ecosystems. There is evidence suggesting the importance of aluminum and iron minerals in regulating how much P remains available in these old soils. At the same time, the scarcity of easily weatherable P-bearing material means that new inputs from ongoing mineral breakdown remain small. Conversely, when phosphate is released, abundant reactive mineral surfaces can reduce its availability through sorption. In old, highly weathered tropical profiles, this combination of strong sorption and limited replenishment can maintain low P availability over long periods.

The sorption and release of added phosphate in soils is important for both agriculture and the environment because the availability of added phosphate affects agricultural production and phosphate leaching causes eutrophication of water bodies. Compared to carbon preservation, the effects of Al and Fe oxides/hydroxides on phosphate sorption and release have been studied in detail (e.g., Sharpley 1983 Effect of soil properties on the kinetics of phosphorus desorption. Document [7]Together, these interactions between biological and geochemical processes control how much P is biologically available versus how much is geochemically retained in the soils, and this balance still maintains P deficiency under elevated atmospheric CO2, when greater plant and microbial demand is not matched by faster mineralization, desorption, or weathering supply. Many humid tropical and volcanic soils are dominated by iron and aluminum oxide minerals that sorb P rapidly and, in some cases, irreversibly (Wada 1985; McBride 1994). Sorption is often cited as a reason for P limitation to plant productivity and for high P fertilizer requirements in tropical agricultural systems (Sanchez 1976; Yost and others 1979). Although mature forests in tropical regions are generally quite productive without substantial P inputs, several studies have found that wet tropical forest productivity, root growth, and microbial activity can be enhanced by P additions (Cuevas and Medina 1988; Tanner and others 1990; Herbert and Fownes 1995; Ostertag 2001; Cleveland and others 2002). Moreover, disruption of P cycling by conversion of wet tropical forest to pasture, agriculture, and agroforestry often reduces extractable P pools, suggesting increased geochemical retention and reduced P availability (McGrath and others 2001). In this study, we focus on how geochemical P cycling constrains the amount of phosphate free in the soil solution. At equilibrium, acidic soils with strong sorption maintain very little P free in the soil solution (Sanchez 1976); as P is mineralized from organic matter or desorbed, it must pass through the soil solution, where it remains subject to rapid sorption (Frossard and others 1995).
Document [8]Thus, the high P sorption capacity of tropical Ultisols and Oxisols can strongly influence the overall productivity of many forest and agricultural ecosystems in the tropics. Whereas permanent negative charges are typical in the 2: 1 clay-dominated soils common throughout the temperate zone, highly weathered tropical soils are dominated by 1: 1 clays and by Al and Fe hydroxides (Sollins et al. 1988 Nutrient mobility in variable- and permanent-charge soils. Biogeochemistry 6: 181–199). Surface hydroxyl groups occur at the edge of the 1: 1 clays and on the Al and Fe hydroxides that dominate highly weathered soils (Gillman 1984 Using variable charge characteristics to understand the exchangeable cation status of oxic soils. Aust J Agric Res 22: 71–80; White and Zelazny 1986 Charge properties of soil colloids. In: Sparks D (ed) Soil physical chemistry. CRC, Boca Raton, FL, pp 39–81). This mineral assemblage is associated with the strong P sorption capacity of Ultisols and Oxisols.
Document [9]It has long been assumed that soil acidification increases reactive iron and/or aluminum (Fe/Al) oxides and promotes Pi sorption onto mineral surfaces, resulting in a decrease in Pi. However, this assumption has seldom been tested in long-term field experiments. Using a 12-year acid addition experiment in a tropical forest, we demonstrated that soil acidification increased the content of noncrystalline Fe and Al oxides by 16.3 % and 27.7 %, respectively; whereas it did not alter the absorbed Pi pool and Pi sorption capacity. Furthermore, soil acidification increased the Fe/Al-bound organic matter content by 82.5 %, accompanied by a 54.9 % reduction in Pi desorption, a 42.3 % decrease in soluble Pi content, and a 9.2 % increase in occluded Pi content. Our findings demonstrate that soil acidification reduces Pi bioavailability through greater retention of Pi in Fe/Al-associated, occluded forms. However, the interactions between organomineral-Pi have not been incorporated into global land models, which may overestimate ecosystem productivity under future acid rain scenarios. question: By what processes is the non-uniform movement of water and dissolved substances produced within structured soil environments in situ?
perspectives: Continuous biopore flow through connected root channels and soil-fauna burrows
Desiccation-crack flow in shrink-swell clay soils
Fingered flow caused by soil water repellency and unstable wetting fronts
Textural or structural funneling along horizon boundaries and interaggregate voids
context:
Document [0]In 1865, Thiel observed that roots were proliferating through previously existing channels especially in the subsoil. ThielReference Thiel9 already noted that these channels (‘*canales*’) were made by roots or soil animals. He counted 5–20 channels on 900 cm2 in 2 m soil depth. However, to commence in-depth research on biopores it was necessary to research more about their functions. In other words, it was necessary to study how soil organisms (explicitly roots and earthworms) interact with each other and with their abiotic environment (mineral and organic particles, air and water). Thus, research on biopores required, by definition, *ecological thinking*. The first researcher who published studies on the properties of biopores was, using current science nomenclature, an ecologist—Victor Hensen, a marine biologist who is known as ‘the father of quantitative plankton ecology’Reference Taylor, Sears and Merriman10. In 1877, HensenReference Hensen11 reported on the burrowing activity of earthworms in his garden. He concluded that earthworms were opening channels to the subsoil and that they were coating them with humus, thus creating a beneficial environment for root growth. Moreover, HensenReference Hensen11 made the first remarks on the dynamics of the biopore properties over time, reporting that the walls of fresh pores were covered with dark humps made up of earthworm excreta, whereas the walls of older pores, no longer colonized by worms, were uniformly covered with dark soil originating from earthworms. He also mentioned pores completely filled with dark soil that he assumed to ‘diffuse’ into the surrounding soil and to weather over time, until only unfertile soil remains. HensenReference Hensen12 clearly pointed to the relevance of earthworm channels for roots as a fertile environment with a low penetration resistance, stating, ‘More beneficial conditions for the growth of plant roots may hardly be found …’.
Document [1]We explored the mechanisms through which root systems and soil macrofauna play a role on subsurface flow processes along forested hillslopes in Yunnan, China. We hypothesized that: (i) natural, mixed forests would have a greater extension of subsurface flow compared to monospecific rubber tree plantations, because biopores should be distributed throughout the entire soil profile, due to the increased diversity of macrofauna and plant species and their different root system morphologies, and (ii) a greater number of coarse roots would increase subsurface flow. To understand the processes occurring, two different scales were considered: the pattern of water infiltration throughout the soil profile, which reflected the impact of vegetation type on subsurface flow (macroscale) and a finer ‘microscale, ’ whereby the effects of the density and size of individual roots and burrows on infiltration were elucidated. Access through **your organization** Study sites were located on the Nan Lin Shan mountain of Xishuangbanna, Yunnan province, China. The intrinsic bioavailability of MAOM is illustrated by several incubation-based experiments. In a study of 156 diverse soils from across the United States, MAOM was a strong predictor of whole-soil C decomposition dynamics. Its large pool size may compensate for lower decomposition rates in some soils, creating a substantial overall contribution to CO2 flux. When SOM fractions are incubated under ideal temperature and moisture conditions, MAOM can exhibit high N and C mineralization potential. Together, these observations indicate that destabilization of mineral-associated organic matter can contribute substantially to soil C loss.
Document [1]Recently, researchers have been able to directly observe the location, distribution, and forms of C stabilized in soil pores and on mineral surfaces . This has contributed to new conceptual models of C association with mineral surfaces. The zonal structure of organo-mineral associations posits that different functional groups of SOC arrange themselves in a particular way when interacting with minerals . In this model, polar groups of amphiphilic molecules are attracted to charged mineral surfaces with hydrophobic groups facing outward creating a zone of hydrophobic interactions to which the hydrophobic groups of other molecules are attracted. Beyond lies the kinetic zone wherein organic molecules interact with multivalent cations. This model has implications for SOC stability because organic molecules within the kinetic zone likely experience higher rates of exchange with the soil solution . Recent research has shown preferential adsorption of different organic compound classes by different phases of Fe-bearing minerals and a wide variety of organic compound classes partially sorbed to minerals, supporting the zonal model . However, destabilization is not merely ‘stabilization processes in reverse.’ The persistence and vulnerability of the mineral-stabilized C is a product of C chemistry, soil environments, and time. SOC can be protected by sorption to soil minerals, in particular metal oxides, and by incorporation into organo-metal complexes . SOC concentration is positively correlated with the amount of oxalate extractable Fe and Al in soils from wet or humid climates . The age of SOC, a proxy for soil carbon stability, also positively correlates to the amount of noncrystalline Fe and Al minerals . Thus, changes to the soil environment that affect the solubility of minerals or organo-mineral complexes or change the relative surfaces charges of minerals and organic matter can destabilize SOC. Once no longer associated with minerals, SOC may become more vulnerable (figure 1).
Document [2]The strength and sign (positive or negative) of surface charges change depending on the pH and ionic strength of the soil solution. Whether SOC becomes sorbed to soil minerals depends on the relative points of zero charge (PZC) of the organic matter and the minerals, which determine whether they have opposite charges in a given soil solution and are thus likely to sorb (figure 2). For a simple example, FeOOH has a PZC at about a pH of 9 below which the acidic solution donates protons to it resulting in a positive charge and above which it is negatively charged. Carboxyl groups on organic matter have a PZC at about a pH of 4. Thus, negatively-charged carboxyl groups on organic matter will sorb to positively-charged FeOOH between a pH of 4 and 9. In reality, soil minerals are a mixture of many types of clays and oxides of varying crystallinity and capacity for surface charge and many types of organic matter, so whether sorption happens or not at any given pH is a balance of many factors, but the principle is the same. ***Figure 2.** An idealized depiction of how pH affects adsorption and desorption between organic matter (OM) and oxides. Adsorption occurs when the OM and the oxides have opposite charges. In this example, carboxyl groups with a point of zero (pzc) charge of 4 adsorbs to the Fe oxide, goethite with a pzc of 8, when the pH is between 4 and 8. In practice, multiple influences on soil C cycling under different environmental conditions are not well understood, a knowledge gap that invites this discussion. We offer this perspective to facilitate understanding the conditions under which soil C dynamics may differ as environments change. Such influences on the soil C cycle are increasingly identified as gaps in global C models . The consequences of these impacts under changing conditions can be framed through fundamental principles of soil science: physics, chemistry, and biology. While future scenarios include local conditions that could increase soil C stocks, the broader implications remain uncertain . By focusing on processes and mechanisms of soil C change, we provide a context for empirical and computational scientists to focus on questions that directly inform how soils affect the carbon cycle. Soils are highly heterogeneous, and this complexity makes it difficult to extract generalizable principles. It is also not possible to thoroughly review every cause of soil C change in soils, when one considers the range of perturbations and settings in which soils occur. However, we can categorize broad biogeochemical patterns, and in doing so, provide a framework for discussing when soil C may change.

Conceptually, MAOM is defined as a fraction of SOM where OM exists in some degree of association with soil minerals, such as via sorption, co-precipitation, encapsulation in fine, microaggregates48, or via organo-organic interactions. MAOM is typically defined in contrast to sand-sized and/or lighter, less protected plant and fungal fragments known as particulate organic matter (POM). The methodological definition of MAOM is material collected from soil (generally, operationally defined as <2 mm) with aggregates dispersed by physical (i.e., glass beads), chemical (i.e., dispersing agents like sodium hexametaphosphate), or energetic (i.e., sonication) methods and then suggests that so too are existing MAOM stocks and the overall MAOM saturation deficit19, 20. Although the majority of MAOM is likely persistent and long-lived, there is increasing evidence for a dynamic, fastcycling MAOM pool. Given the vast quantity of C and N stored in MAOM, the presence of even a small active MAOM pool can substantially influence ecosystem processes. Sokol 16 & Em D. Whalen 17 Longstanding theories and models classify mineral-associated organic matter as the large ( \~ 60%) but slow-cycling and persistent portion of soil organic matter. Strong physico-chemical interactions and diffusion limitations restrict the turnover of mineral-associated organic matter, allowing carbon and nitrogen bound therein to persist in soil for as long as centuries to millennia. However, mineralassociated organic matter is a chemically and functionally diverse pool with a substantial portion cycling at relatively fast (i.e., minutes to years) timescales. Despite a growing body of evidence for the heterogenous and multi-pool nature of mineral-associated organic matter, we lack consensus on how to conceptualize and directly quantify fast-cycling mineral-associated organic matter and its ecological significance. We demonstrate that the dynamic qualities of fast-cycling mineral-associated organic matter vary based on 1) the chemistry of the mineral particles and organic matter, 2) the complex set of interactions between organic matter and the mineral matrix, and 3) the presence and strength of destabilizing forces that lead to decomposition or loss of mineral-associated organic matter (i.e., plant-microbe interactions, agricultural intensification, and climate change). Document [9]Soil is the largest actively–cycling terrestrial carbon reservoir, storing more carbon than the atmosphere and vegetation combined (Jackson et al., 2017; Scharlemann et al., 2014; Schlesinger, 1990). Under the SSP5–8.5 scenario, global temperatures are projected to increase by 3.3–5.7℃ by 2100 (IPCC, 2023). This warming could accelerate the decomposition of soil organic carbon (SOC) and increase soil carbon dioxide (CO2) fluxes (Davidson and Janssens, 2006; Schlesinger and Andrews, 2000). Warming–induced soil CO2 fluxes could further exacerbate global warming, creating a positive feedback cycle (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). Many studies have examined SOC responses to warming and reported variable outcomes, ranging from no net cumulative changes (Giardina et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2013) to large SOC losses observed in more recent field warming experiments (Nottingham et al., 2020; Soong et al., 2021), p.2; Verbrigghe et al., 2022). The contrasting results reflect the differences in experimental approaches as well as the complexity of soil systems, where opposing mechanisms simultaneously influence SOC inputs and decomposition. As a result, bulk soil measurements alone can lack the sensitivity needed to uncover the processes driving SOC responses (Lavallee et al., 2020; Rocci et al., 2021). Instead, investigating how fractions of soil, each with distinct physical and chemical properties, respond to warming could improve our understanding of the key mechanisms that govern SOC dynamics (Georgiou et al., 2022; Lugato et al., 2021). Soil organic carbon is typically operationally–divided by size or density fractionation into two main fractions, particulate organic matter (POM) and mineral–associated organic matter (Lavallee et al., 2020). Under long-term warming, thermal activation can increase the activity of extracellular enzymes acting on particulate organic matter, accelerating depolymerization and increasing substrate supply for microbial respiration in subsoils.

Document [9]Soil is the largest actively–cycling terrestrial carbon reservoir, storing more carbon than the atmosphere and vegetation combined (Jackson et al., 2017; Scharlemann et al., 2014; Schlesinger, 1990). Under the SSP5–8.5 scenario, global temperatures are projected to increase by 3.3–5.7℃ by 2100 (IPCC, 2023). This warming could accelerate the decomposition of soil organic carbon (SOC) and increase soil carbon dioxide (CO2) fluxes (Davidson and Janssens, 2006; Schlesinger and Andrews, 2000). Warming–induced soil CO2 fluxes could further exacerbate global warming, creating a positive feedback cycle (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). Many studies have examined SOC responses to warming and reported variable outcomes, ranging from no net cumulative changes (Giardina et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2013) to large SOC losses observed in more recent field warming experiments (Nottingham et al., 2020; Soong et al., 2021), p.2; Verbrigghe et al., 2022). The contrasting results reflect the differences in experimental approaches as well as the complexity of soil systems, where opposing mechanisms simultaneously influence SOC inputs and decomposition. As a result, bulk soil measurements alone can lack the sensitivity needed to uncover the processes driving SOC responses (Lavallee et al., 2020; Rocci et al., 2021). Instead, investigating how fractions of soil, each with distinct physical and chemical properties, respond to warming could improve our understanding of the key mechanisms that govern SOC dynamics (Georgiou et al., 2022; Lugato et al., 2021). Soil organic carbon is typically operationally–divided by size or density fractionation into two main fractions, particulate organic matter (POM) and mineral–associated organic matter (Lavallee et al., 2020). Under long-term warming, thermal activation can increase the activity of extracellular enzymes acting on particulate organic matter, accelerating depolymerization and increasing substrate supply for microbial respiration in subsoils.

Document [0]Glomalin is a specific glycoprotein belonging to the group glomalin related soil protein (GRSP) which maintains a specific peculiarity of not being easily decomposable on coming in contact with soil protease. Thus this group of proteins is considered as highly recalcitrant and capable of regulating global warming by checking the release of GHGs (like CO2, NOx). This glycoprotein is exclusively metabolized by a fungal group belonging to phylum Glomeromycota (an obligate biotroph), thus it has been named glomalin. Chemical studies of glomalin says it contains 42%–49% aromatic, 24%–30% carboryl, 4%–11% aliphatic, and 4%–16% carbohydrate-type carbon indicating its difference from typical glycoprotein. This glycoprotein contains asparagines-linked carbohydrate with a signature of organic matter, amino acid, carbohydrates with aliphatic methionine, methylene, and some antifluorescent compound imparting cementing properties to the compound which enmesh soil particles and help in macroaggregate (average mean weight diameter=1–2 mm) stabilization. The aggregate formed under influence of this glue helps to protect a relatively labile carbon pool which otherwise is highly sensitive to short-term soil management practices. Normal soil contains a low concentration of glomalin at around 60 mg cm−3. This quantity of compound is good enough for binding inorganic soil fraction, chelating heavy metals in contaminated soil, imparting dispersion resistance and antierosion characteristics to soil, accruing and exchanging air and water, and ultimately enabling species composition and diversity. In addition, the hydrophobic nature of glomalin protects the hydrolysis of hyphae, thus a considerable amount of SOC (~30%) and SON (~4%–5%) is associated with mycorrhizal fungi. Hence to the era which is in urgent need of restoring SOC and rejuvenating the soil health of land that has undergone extractive farming, degradation, and degeneration, GRSP is attaining special attention as a regulator of soil fertility.

The extraradical hyphae of AM fungi can directly bring mineral particles and organic materials together to form microaggregates, and then enmesh microaggregates into stable macroaggregates by physical entanglement mechanisms (Miller and Jastrow, 1990, Tisdall et al., 1997), Wu et al., 2014). Fine roots can likewise entangle soil particles, and sticky root exudates can act as adhesives that promote stable macroaggregate formation. Most studies have manifested that the role of AM fungi in aggregate hierarchy is mainly attributed to improvement of the formation and stability of soil macroaggregates by mycelium network, which strongly influences aggregation at scales smaller than macroaggregate by GRSP (Miller and Jastrow, 1990, Rillig and Mummey, 2006, Rillig et al., 2002), Tisdall and Oades, 1982). The potential role of AM fungi in soil aggregate disruption and dispersion has not been clarified. Nevertheless, Kohler et al. (2017) reported that in carbonate-rich soils, there is a weak correlation between aggregate stability and AM fungal hyphae/GRSP. In the semi-arid soils of Mediterranean regions with abundant primary and/or secondary carbonates, there is a less significant correlation between aggregate stability and soil organic matter (Boix-Fayo et al., 2001, Bouajila and Gallali, 2008), Six et al., 2004). Therefore, clarifying the contribution of AM fungi to soil aggregation and the characteristics of aggregate hierarchy in high-carbonate and low-organic compound soils can improve our understanding of the role of AM fungi in soil aggregate formation and stability. In this study, a three-compartment growth system was employed to investigate the effect of AM fungal inoculation on soil aggregate formation and stability under drought stress and well-watered conditions.

In this way, stable macroaggregation can be maintained through the joint action of fungal hyphae or glomalin-related products together with cation bridges between minerals and organic matter. However, the responses of GRSP accumulation and associated AMF community and diversity to long-term fertilization regimes remain unclear. Here, we investigated the dynamics of GRSP contents, AMF biomass and diversity based on a 29-year fertilization experiment (including control, mineral fertilization, manuring and straw returning treatments). Results showed that GRSP contents increased over years across fertilization treatments. Compared with no fertilization, long-term manuring and straw returning significantly increased bulk soil GRSP by 100% and 80%, respectively, and altered the chemical composition of GRSP by increasing the recalcitrant (aromatic) C proportion. The proportion of aromatic C in GRSP was positively correlated with AMF biomass and diversity (Shannon and Chao1), indicating that the chemical composition of GRSP could be regulated by AMF community and diversity. Moreover, manuring facilitated the formation of macro-aggregates (>250 µm), thus increasing the physical protection of GRSP. The structural equation modeling further demonstrated that GRSP content was positively regulated by soil macroaggregates, AMF biomass and diversity and their linkage with GRSP chemical composition. Collectively, longterm manuring could facilitate GRSP accumulation by shifts in AMF-mediated GRSP chemical composition (aromatic C) along with enhanced protection of macro-aggregates. This study highlights a feasible way forward for soil quality improvement and carbon sequestration for sustainable agriculture. Document [0]In addition to plants with different species, the quantity and quality of root exudates vary considerably in the same plant at different growth stages. Zhao et al. (2021) found significant differences in Arabidopsis root exudates during slow and fast growth stages. But there was no difference in the composition of substance species in root exudates. This difference was caused by the different absolute amounts and relative abundances of each compound. Fast-growing stage plants released a higher quantity (cumulative abundance) of sugars, sugar alcohols, organic acids, amino acids, amides/amines, and unknown compounds. In contrast, the slow-growing stage plant’s root exudates had a higher relative abundance of sugars, sugar alcohols, and organic acids. Phosphorus deficiency caused white lupine to release more malic acid in the early stages of cluster root formation and less malic acid and more citric acid in the later stages of cluster root formation (Neumann et al., 1999). Root exudates act on the surrounding environment of the root system to produce rhizosphere effects. At the same time, rhizosphere microorganisms tend to colonize the plant root system and play an important role in modifying and limiting root exudates through their metabolic activities by decomposing and transforming root exudates and abscissions (Sasse et al., 2018). The root exudates have increased a lot due to the presence of microorganisms. Prikryl and Vankura (1980) found that wheat root exudates are twice as high under natural conditions as under sterilized conditions, suggesting that rhizosphere microorganisms stimulated the release of root exudates. Graham (1988) indicated that rhizosphere microorganisms could alter plants’ physiological and biochemical processes by changing the rhizosphere nutrient status and plant hormone content, thus affecting the composition and amount of root exudates. Microorganisms are involved in the decomposition and mineralization of soil organic matter, increasing the availability of soil nutrients and promoting plant growth.

Department of Agronomy and Agricultural Extension, University of Rajshahi, Rajshahi, Bangladesh - See more Article metrics View details Plant roots are major transmitters of atmospheric carbon into soil. The rhizosphere, the soil volume around living roots influenced by root activities, represents hotspots for organic carbon (OC) inputs, microbial activity, and carbon turnover. Rhizosphere processes remain poorly understood and the observation of key mechanisms for carbon transfer and protection in intact rhizosphere microenvironments are challenging. We deciphered the fate of photosynthesis-derived OC in intact wheat rhizosphere, combining stable isotope labeling at field scale with high-resolution 3D-imaging. We used nano-scale secondary ion mass spectrometry and focus ion beam-scanning electron microscopy to generate insights into rhizosphere processes at nanometer scale. Document [0]**: ** The resource budget of Earth is limited. Rare-earth elements (REEs) are used across the world by society on a daily basis yet several of these elements have <2500 years of reserves left, based on current demand, mining operations, and technologies. With an increasing population, exploration of potential extraterrestrial REE resources is inevitable, with the Earth’s Moon being a logical first target. Following lunar differentiation at ~4.50–4.45 Ga, a late-stage (after ~99% solidification) residual liquid enriched in Potassium (K), Rare-earth elements (REE), and Phosphorus (P), (or “KREEP”) formed. Today, the KREEP-rich region underlies the Oceanus Procellarum and Imbrium Basin region on the lunar near-side (the Procellarum KREEP Terrain, PKT) and has been tentatively estimated at preserving 2.2 × 108 km3 of KREEP-rich lithologies. The majority of lunar samples (Apollo, Luna, or meteoritic samples) contain REE-bearing minerals as trace phases, e.g., apatite and/or merrillite, with merrillite potentially contributing up to 3% of the PKT. Other lunar REE-bearing lunar phases include monazite, yittrobetafite (up to 94, 500 ppm yttrium), and tranquillityite (up to 4.6 wt % yttrium, up to 0.25 wt % neodymium), however, lunar sample REE abundances are low compared to terrestrial ores. At present, there is no geological, mineralogical, or chemical evidence to support REEs being present on the Moon in concentrations that would permit their classification as ores. However, the PKT region has not yet been mapped at high resolution, and certainly has the potential to yield higher REE concentrations at local scales (<10s of kms).
Document [1]Earth-raised tides can supply the young Moon with internal heat through repeated deformation and viscoelastic dissipation. An eccentric orbit varies the forcing even when the Moon keeps the same face toward Earth. Quillen and colleagues modeled a close, synchronously rotating Moon and found that higher-order terms in Earth's tidal field could make heating in its crustal shell about 10–20 percent stronger on the nearside when the separation was less than roughly eight Earth radii. Added heat reduces the energy escaping from the underlying magma ocean, delays local freezing, and can favor a thinner crust above longer-lived nearside melt. The asymmetry weakens as the Moon recedes, so this mechanism concerns early evolution. A separate thermal model by Zhao and colleagues predicts that dissipation in a partly molten magma ocean can offset cooling for more than 150 million years. Its simplified hemispheric calculation gives earlier final solidification on the farside; model cases ending near 4.4–4.3 billion years ago retain a nearside temperature advantage of about 20–60 degrees Celsius for roughly 10–20 million years. The resulting differences in residual melt and deep thermal state could influence subsequent hemispheric magmatism. Document [1]Earth-raised tides can supply the young Moon with internal heat through repeated deformation and viscoelastic dissipation. An eccentric orbit varies the forcing even when the Moon keeps the same face toward Earth. Quillen and colleagues modeled a close, synchronously rotating Moon and found that higher-order terms in Earth's tidal field could make heating in its crustal shell about 10–20 percent stronger on the nearside when the separation was less than roughly eight Earth radii. Added heat reduces the energy escaping from the underlying magma ocean, delays local freezing, and can favor a thinner crust above longer-lived nearside melt. The asymmetry weakens as the Moon recedes, so this mechanism concerns early evolution. A separate thermal model by Zhao and colleagues predicts that dissipation in a partly molten magma ocean can offset cooling for more than 150 million years. Its simplified hemispheric calculation gives earlier final solidification on the farside; model cases ending near 4.4–4.3 billion years ago retain a nearside temperature advantage of about 20–60 degrees Celsius for roughly 10–20 million years. The resulting differences in residual melt and deep thermal state could influence subsequent hemispheric magmatism. Tides can also create new melt: Nimmo and colleagues propose that an orbital transition around 4.35 billion years ago caused extensive lunar remelting and volcanic resurfacing. That remelting model is global and does not by itself establish a nearside preference. Taken together, these modeled processes provide a physical basis for sustained tidal energy input and preferential nearside melt availability. Their combination is a proposed explanation, not proof that one tidal episode accounts for all later mare eruptions; the spatial effect depends on orbital history, material properties, and how efficiently the interior mixes.

Document [3]Earth’s nearest neighbor in space, the Moon, is a logical first target both in terms of evaluating resource potential. Following formation of the Moon as the result of a giant impact between proto-Earth and an impacting Mars-sized body c. 70–100 Myrs after the onset of Solar System formation, molten material (a primordial magma ocean) began to solidify and differentiate. After ~99% crystallization a KREEP (potassium, rare-earth element, phosphorus)-rich layer concentrated incompatible elements, a geochemical signature detected in many lunar samples today. Today, KREEP-rich lithologies are associated with enrichments in thorium on the lunar near-side (in the PKT), as observed by the gamma ray spectrometer on the Lunar Prospector. The volume of KREEP-rich lithologies associated with this region of the Moon is estimated at 2.2 × 108 km3, with potential reserves of REEs at ~2.25 × 1014–4.5 × 1014 kg. The majority of lunar samples contain REE-bearing phases as minor or trace components, typically apatite and/or merrillite with KREEP-like lithologies almost always containing merrillite. The presence of merrillite has the potential to account for up to 3% of a lithologies volume in the PKT however, this does not permit the classification of REEs on the Moon as ores. While REE abundances of trace phases in lunar rocks are high, their abundances are low compared to terrestrial ores meaning there is to date, no geological evidence to support mining the Moon for REEs yet. With the development of future technologies capable of mapping at higher resolutions, and in situ exploration by future missions, economically viable lunar resources may yet be discovered. However, other potential resources do currently exist on the Moon—including helium-3, water, oxygen, and metals (Fe, Al, Mg)—which will likely be fundamental to future space exploration.

question: By what processes might methane be restored to the atmosphere of Titan in the current epoch?
perspectives: Episodic release from crustal or mantle clathrate reservoirs
Ongoing cryovolcanic outgassing from Titan's interior
Continuous abiotic methane production by water-rock reactions in the rocky core
Slow release from methane-rich subsurface liquid or porous ice reservoirs

Document [0]Titan's atmospheric methane is continually lost through photochemistry, so a stored supply must be accessed if its abundance is to persist over geological time. Tobie, Lunine and Sotin's 2006 thermal model proposes intermittent outgassing from methane clathrates in the icy shell above an ammonia-enriched ocean. Water cages retain methane between episodes; changes in the shell's thermal state permit part of that inventory to be liberated and delivered upward. The atmospheric source is therefore release of previously stored methane, rather than a requirement that every molecule be newly produced during the same event. An episode can replenish the atmosphere even though there is no uninterrupted surface eruption throughout the intervening interval. This provides a mechanism by which relatively recent geological activity could account for methane present today. The model links storage, destabilization and outgassing, but does not directly observe a present eruption or establish a unique recurrence interval. Its relevance to the current atmosphere depends on whether Titan actually contains the proposed reservoir and whether a sufficiently recent release reached the surface.
Document [1]The hydrophobic effect, the primary driver of methane confinement within crystalline water cages, stabilizes methane clathrate hydrates under a range of conditions on Earth and other planetary bodies. While high pressure is known to drastically alter both the stoichiometry and intermolecular dynamics of gas hydrates, understanding these transformations has been hindered by the limited resolution of previous studies. Here, using in situ high-pressure single-crystal X-ray diffraction, we demonstrate a pressure-driven increase in methane content and the emergence of a previously unknown clathrate hydrate stable at pressures of 1.3-2.1 GPa. The novel phase, MH-IIb, is a clathrate phase with an H20: CH4 ratio up to 3.40. We show that the transition to MH-IIb is driven by methane–methane steric repulsion, which, with pressure, overcomes classical methane–water hydrophobic interactions and forces formation of unconventional C–H···O hydrogen bonds. Our results indicate that high pressure can substantially modify methane uptake in clathrate hydrates, with possible implications for methane partitioning during the early evolution of Titan and other icy bodies. Beyond the solar system, these pressure-induced structural changes may also be relevant to volatile partitioning in water-rich exoplanets, complicating simple links between atmospheric composition and interior composition. Methane clathrate hydrates are unique compounds that bridge geoscience, planetary science, solid-state chemistry, and energy research. They are non-stoichiometric solids, which entrap variable amounts of methane within the cavities of a water framework. On Earth, they occur in deep marine sediments and permafrost, and have long been studied for their climatic and energy significance 1–3 .
Document [2]A late change in the efficiency of heat transport can reactivate a methane reservoir that was stored for much of Titan's history. In the evolution model discussed by Tobie and colleagues in 2009, cooling and ocean crystallization thicken an internal ice layer until convection begins. Convective heat transport, coupled to tidal dissipation, changes the thermal conditions beneath the clathrate-rich crust. Where those conditions destabilize stored methane hydrate, gas can be released during renewed eruptive activity. The supply is episodic because the interior passes through distinct dynamical regimes rather than maintaining a fixed release rate. This mechanism connects long-term internal evolution to a comparatively recent atmospheric replenishment episode. It does not require methane to escape directly from a stable high-pressure hydrate at great depth: transport and shallow destabilization remain necessary parts of the proposed pathway. The timing and amount of outgassing are model dependent. Surface features interpreted as possible cryovolcanic structures are relevant context, but do not by themselves demonstrate that this particular thermal history occurred or that a release is happening now.
Document [3]Impacts provide discrete triggers for methane release from Titan's crustal clathrate deposits. Wakita and colleagues' 2025 simulations follow the pressure and temperature histories of material shocked by an impact. Parcels that cross the methane-hydrate dissociation boundary are treated as releasing their trapped gas. A crater-forming event can consequently inject methane from a pre-existing solid reservoir into the atmosphere without requiring continuous chemical production in the core. The calculation explicitly separates the available reservoir from the event that destabilizes it. It also places a strong limit on this explanation: when individual impact yields are combined with estimated impact rates, the average supply remains below atmospheric photochemical loss. In the explored model, impacts can extend atmospheric methane's lifetime by up to about three percent. Impact-triggered bursts are therefore a possible contribution to present atmospheric replenishment, not a demonstrated complete replacement source. The estimate depends on the assumed clathrate layer and dissociation treatment, and a simulated gas yield should not be mistaken for an observed methane plume on Titan.
Document [4]A warm cryolava flow can release methane from clathrate already present in Titan's shallow crust. Davies and colleagues modeled this process in 2016 by tracking cooling and the growth of solid crust at the top and base of a newly emplaced flow. Heat transferred into the substrate can destabilize methane hydrate and free its trapped gas. In this pathway, the atmospheric methane need not have arrived as gas carried within the erupted liquid: the flow supplies energy that unlocks a separate crustal reservoir. An emplacement event can thus initiate an outgassing episode that continues while sufficient heat remains beneath the cooling surface. Flow thickness controls the duration of this opportunity; the model's thicker flows take longer to freeze. This offers a physical connection between intermittent resurfacing and atmospheric resupply. It remains a proposed contribution, because the study did not establish conclusive observation of ongoing volcanism on Titan. The existence of suitable hydrate deposits, heat transfer into them, and escape of the liberated methane are necessary conditions for atmospheric replenishment.
Document [5]Experiments on methane hydrate provide a specific trigger for episodic outgassing from Titan's crust. Choukroun and colleagues examined water-methane mixtures with and without ammonia and found that ammonia can lower the temperature at which the hydrate dissociates. Their 2010 application to Titan requires locally warm, ammonia-rich conditions rather than spontaneous breakdown of every clathrate deposit. They propose that an ascending warm ice plume can heat or melt shallow pockets of ammonia-water material. The resulting cryomagma destabilizes surrounding methane hydrate, releasing gas previously held in water cages. Such a localized disturbance turns a stored solid inventory into a potential atmospheric source during a geological episode. The authors estimate that a large event could supply methane sufficient for several tens of thousands of years of atmospheric persistence. This is an experimentally informed scenario, not a measurement of a current eruption. Ammonia abundance, temperature, reservoir size and a route for gas to escape all govern whether the proposed release can occur on Titan today.
Document [6]In extraterrestrial settings, deep methane clathrate reservoirs serve as a potential long-term source for atmospheric replenishment, a mechanism proposed to sustain the methane inventories of Titan4–7 , Pluton8, 9 , and potentially many other large icy worlds7 and ocean planets10. For Titan, one proposed long-term source is continuous abiotic methane production by water-rock reactions in the rocky core, which could migrate upward into overlying clathrate reservoirs and ultimately the atmosphere. Interest in the geochemical cycling of methane extends beyond our Solar System, as distinguishing between abiotic sources and biosignatures in exoplanetary atmospheres is critical to the search for habitable worlds with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)11–13. Beyond the role as volatile reservoirs, methane hydrates may govern the thermophysical state of the planet's interior, directly dictating the density, viscosity, and thermal conductivity profi les across the crust and mantle in icy worlds7 . From a chemical perspective, the stability of methane hydrates is governed by a subtle compromise between attractive and repulsive Van der Waals forces between methane and water molecules 14–18 . This unique balance makes methane hydrates a benchmark system for investigating hydrophobic hydration 19–21, which is a fundamental process in molecular biology 22 and surface chemistry 19, 23, 24 . The high-pressure fate of methane clathrate hydrates has emerged as a subject of particular interest, offering both a platform for probing fundamental van der Waals interactions and a window into the deep cycle of methane in planetary interiors 25–27. At ambient temperature, it is well established that methane hydrate crystallizes in the cubic sI structure (MH-I phase) at moderate pressures, transforming into the hexagonal sH structure (MH-II phase) around 0.9 GPa 26, 28 (Text S1). Above 1.9-2 GPa, the MH-II further transforms into fi lled ice (MH-III phase) or decomposes into ice VII and solid methane, depending on the compression rate 26. However, prior high-pressure studies of these chemically and structurally complex non-stochiometric compounds relied primarily on powder diffraction and Raman spectroscopy 5, 26, 28–36 .
Document [7]This forces the water framework to distort, highlighting that the clathrate architecture is not dictated solely by guest–host affi nity, as traditionally assumed, but guest– guest interactions are a factor of equal signifi cance. Ultimately, these fi ndings redefi ne the limits of hydrophobic encapsulation, offering a new structural model for gas hydrates. The sequence of pressure-induced transformations resolved in this study demonstrates that methane clathrate hydrates undergo substantial structural and compositional changes between \~ 0.5 and 2.1 GPa. While MH-I exhibits only a marginal increase in methane content, the MH-IIa phase displays a pronounced compositional evolution – resolving long-standing debates regarding the fi lling of its large cage 26, 58, 59 (Text S1). Within the stability fi eld of MH-IIa, its large cage (Figure 3a) accommodates 3.34 methane molecules, yielding a maximum H O/CH ratio of 3.94: 1. Conversely, the previously postulated maximum H20/CH4 ratio of 3.4: 1 corresponds to a newly identifi ed MH-IIb phase (Figure 1). While methane hydrate reservoirs on Earth, Mars, and Titan at present occur at pressures insuffi cient to stabilize MH-IIb (< 1 GPa), the appropriate pressure range can be reached during the early evolution of large icy moons (Titan, Ganymede or Callisto) in their undifferentiated interior before ice-rock separation 4, 7 as well as in the hydrospheres of Earth-size water-rich exoplanets 7, 60 . The pressure-induced enhancement of clathrate storage capacity suggests that these deep planetary interiors may host substantial 'hidden' methane reservoirs, directly infl uencing the volatile budget, redox evolution, and potential pathways for methane release from the deep interior into their oceans and atmospheres. On Titan today, one such pathway could be ongoing cryovolcanic outgassing from the interior, venting methane to the surface and atmosphere. The MH-I → MH-IIa → MH-IIb transitions, along with associated changes in H20/CH4 ratios, suggest that the phase proportions of methane hydrates may evolve continuously with depth.
