Document [5]While surface-ocean property changes can reflect near-surface forcing, property changes of the deep ocean are instead reflective of the region of deep water formation and subsequent circulation. Circulation changes can also redistribute pre-existing North Atlantic salinity anomalies, including fresh anomalies associated with increased Arctic export, moving relatively fresh waters into the subpolar basins where deep water forms. These property changes at depth often reflect surface conditions from the past, providing memory to the deep ocean. These links allow relatively fresh anomalies carried into the subpolar North Atlantic to be traced in deep waters observed farther south. The Deep Western Boundary Current (DWBC) serves as one of the main equatorward pathways that exports these deep waters to the subtropics at depths below 1000 m. The Abaco 26.5°N hydrographic line (Figure 1A) is situated at a strategic location within the Subtropical North Atlantic, capturing both the poleward flowing upperocean subtropical gyre waters and the deep-ocean equatorward return flows of the DWBC. Over the past 40 years (1985-present), the 26.5°N hydrographic line has been surveyed quasi-annually through collaborative efforts between the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Western Boundary Time Series (WBTS) project, the University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science’s Meridional Overturning Circulation and Heat-flux Array (MOCHA) project, and the National Oceanographic Centre’s Rapid Climate Change (RAPID) program. Sustained monitoring at 26.5°N has been achieved through repeat hydrographic surveys12, 13, the use of Pressure-Inverted Echo Sounders14, 15 (PIES) and continuous mooring installations dating back to 200416. Nearly four decades of sustained observations along this latitude make this hydrographic line part of the longest-running trans basin meridional overturning observation program on the planet16–18. Elsewhere in the North Atlantic, observing systems across the advective path of the DWBC have monitored circulation and variability of the deep water mass properties therein.
Document [6]Recent observations show a gradual increase in Arctic ocean freshwater content. Using salinity profiles from ships and autonomous drifting buoys, Rabe et al. (2014) report that the liquid freshwater content of the upper Arctic basins has been increasing with a trend of 600 ± 300 km3 yr-1 over the period of 1992–2012. Several studies estimate that the accumulation of liquid freshwater in the Arctic during the 2000s may have involved multiple influences, though some uncertainties remain (Serreze et al. 2006; Bamber et al. 2012; Woodgate et al. 2012; Haine et al. 2015; Wang et al. 2018b). An intensified hydrological cycle can also freshen the subpolar North Atlantic by increasing net precipitation and river discharge into the surrounding seas. While the mechanisms of this ongoing Arctic freshening remain under debate, on multidecadal timescales the low-salinity anomalies can potentially escape the Arctic and affect ocean deep convection sites in the subpolar North Atlantic, weakening the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) (Scinocca et al. 2009; Oudar et al. 2017; Sévellec, Fedorov, and Liu 2017; Liu, Fedorov, and Sévellec 2018; Liu and Fedorov 2019). Therefore, given the central role of surface freshwater input in the hydrological cycle of polar regions (Aagaard and Carmack 1989), the question of Arctic freshening becomes critical for global ocean circulation.
Document [7]Mass balance measurements quantify these processes and are directly linked to the meteorological parameters that govern accumulation and ablation. While SMB varies spatially, a broad upper region of mass surplus is the accumulation zone, and a broad lower region of mass deficit is the ablation zone, with the boundary between the two zones defined as the equilibrium line altitude (ELA). Together, SMB and ice discharge through calving represent total mass balance, which has become increasingly negative, driven by two main components increasing dramatically in the first decade of the 21st century: ice discharge and melt (Allison et al., 2009; van den Broeke et al., 2009). While interannual variability in mass balance is mostly accounted for by variation in accumulation through precipitation, anomalies in ice discharge and meltwater runoff significantly exceed decadal variability of precipitation. These runoff anomalies therefore led to a general trend of mass loss across the ice sheet margin. In the accumulation zone above the ELA, water percolating through the snow and firn can pool into slush regions and channelize into supraglacial streams. In the ablation zone beneath the ELA, meltwater pools in supraglacial lakes and flows through streams into crevasses and moulins, entering englacial and subglacial conduits that emerge into proglacial rivers and lakes. As meltwater moves through the system, erosional debris increases sediment concentration, making glacial-melt lakes and rivers sediment-rich while leaving precipitation and snowmelt lakes clear of sediment. Finally, meltwater entering the ocean produces a buoyant sediment plume in the fjord. For marine-terminating glaciers, sediment-rich subglacial discharge released tens to hundreds of meters below the water surface either rises to form a buoyant plume or forms a turbidity current beneath the surface.

Document [0]In the early stage of the simulation (?? = 2 tidal periods), the interaction between the barotropic tide and bottom topography generates distinct internal wave beams (Figure 2a, c). These beams align closely with the linear dispersion relations of the tidal harmonics, indicated by the dashed lines, and are characterized by intensified velocity, sharpened buoyancy gradients, and enhanced turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rates (??). At the later stage (?? = 460 tidal cycles), the wave field evolves into a more complex state in which individual wave beams are no longer evident (Figure 2b, d). Instead, the system is marked by layers of strong stratification and elevated dissipation, particularly near blocking sills (A time-evolving visualization of zonal velocity and dissipation rate at late stages is provided in a supplementary movie S1). Layered temperature–salinity structure can also supply energy for abyssal diapycnal mixing through double-diffusive convection and thermohaline staircase breakdown. While the enhanced buoyancy gradient near the upper boundary (?? ∼ 2100 m) may partly arise from unrealistic wave reflection processes at the upper boundary, this artifact does not affect the interpretation of the near-bottom dynamics, which is our main focus. Document [0]The biological carbon pump (BCP) is a suite of processes collectively leading to the net uptake of atmospheric CO2. It transfers dissolved inorganic carbon to organic carbon through photosynthesis by phytoplankton in the sunlit surface ocean at a rate of \~50 GtC/yr (Chavez et al., 2011; Johnson and Bif, 2021), and then delivers part of the produced particulate organic carbon (POC) into the ocean interior (Sigman and Boyle, 2000). When POC settles to depths below the mesopelagic zone (i.e., beyond about 1000 m), it can be stored and isolated from the atmospheric carbon pool for time scales of hundreds of years or even longer (Kwon et al., 2009). Without these processes, the atmospheric CO2 content would be 200 ppm higher than it is today (Parekh et al., 2006; Henson et al., 2019). The biogenic particles that sink out of the surface layer not only fuel the dark ocean and benthic ecosystem but also play a vital role in the distributions of oxygen, carbon and nutrients. Thus, it is important to develop an understanding of the layout of global deep ocean POC fluxes over a range of spatial and temporal scales. In this context, a prevalent mooring sediment trap was invented in the 1970s to intercept sinking particles settling into the ocean interior for up to a year based on a consecutive time series sequence to better understand its composition, transport and transformation in the oceans (Honjo et al., 1980; Deuser et al., 1981). This device not merely provides a direct measurement of sinking particle flux over a range of time scales but also supplies intact time-series samples for further multidisciplinary analysis, such as chemical components (Lee, 2019) and plankton taxonomy (Takahashi and Honjo, 1981; Takahashi, 1986) in sinking particles.

Document [3]Open ocean waters store (sequester) carbon out of contact with the atmosphere on decadal to millennial timescales, exerting a major control on global climate by regulating atmospheric carbon dioxide partial pressure (pCO2)1. The magnitude of ocean carbon storage is governed by well-established mechanisms that maintain a surface-to-deep ocean gradient of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC)2, 3. The biological pump globally exports particulate organic carbon (POC) from surface waters, while physical mixing and subduction can also transfer dissolved and suspended organic matter from the surface into the ocean interior, where it can remain sequestered from the atmosphere for extended periods. POC export is largely attributed to the gravitational settling of a subset of the particle assemblage1, 4 - a process we refer to as the "biological gravitational pump" (BGP). The BGP is the key link between upper ocean photosynthetic carbon fixation, the sustenance of mid-water biota, and carbon storage in the oceans' interior4, 5, and is thought to account for ~90% of the vertical DIC gradient1. In the absence of the BGP, models predict atmospheric pCO2 would be higher by nearly twofold6. Contemporary and paleoceanographic observations both reveal that carbon sequestration by the BGP is affected by environmental changes in light, temperature, stratification and nutrient availability7, 8, and can itself drive dramatic climate shifts such as glacial-interglacial cycles8. Future climate projections suggest that the functioning of the BGP will be altered by ocean global change7, 9, potentially feeding back on anthropogenic climate warming10. As a consequence, quantification of its functioning requires a reliable baseline of accurate measurements. The underlying principles of the BGP are long established11: organic particles are continually produced and recycled in sunlit surface waters, and a small fraction of these settle into the oceans' interior.

Differences in sinking behaviour among phytoplankton groups are tightly linked to their functional traits. Distinct taxa (e.g., diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria) differ in morphology, density and buoyancy-regulation strategies, leading to large interspecific variation in sinking rates . Numerous studies considering the effects of physical processes on phytoplankton at the mesoscale and sub-mesoscale levels and on the synoptic time scale in a first approximation can be divided into several directions. Most of the works are devoted to the influence of mesoscale cyclonic and anticyclonic eddies. Canonical theory assumes vertical rise of isopycnals in cyclonic eddies (the so-called eddy pumping), leading to an increase in the nutrient flow into the photic zone . In dipole structures, the rise of deep waters in a cyclonic eddy is accompanied by the sinking of waters in the adjacent anticyclonic eddy . Accordingly, in the first case, there is an increase in biological production and in the second one - a decrease. Except the aforementioned ones, there are many features of the effect of eddies on the ecosystem, associated with specific types of eddies and their parameters, as well as their interaction with other dynamic structures and the presence of atmospheric effects. So, among anticyclonic eddies, there is a special type -a mode-water or lens-shaped eddy. The orbital speed in it is maximum at a certain depth, leading to the formation of an intra-water anticyclonic lens and the rise of isopycnals to the surface .

Document [0]Halide perovskites, known for their tunable and exceptional optoelectronic properties, have been extensively explored for photovoltaics, light-emitting diodes, photodetectors, and memristors. With solar cell efficiencies closing on theoretical limits, stabilization of perovskite devices—especially via control of the ionic activity within the device—is a research gap that needs to be addressed before commercialization. Solar cell stability is directly linked to ionic activity and redistribution within the device. However, techniques to quantify and directly observe ionic migration are limited by the soft ionic lattice nature of the perovskite as well as its mixed ionic-electronic conductivity. This review examines both theoretical and experimental approaches to understand intrinsic and extrinsic ionic motion in halide perovskites at the material and device level. In addition to elemental and molecular analysis techniques that directly identify the ion in motion, spectroscopy techniques that measure properties associated with local stoichiometry changes have also been deployed. Measurement artifacts, strategies to mitigate their occurrence, as well as ways to differentiate electronic and ionic components related to specific techniques, are evaluated. Document [1]However, the behavior of defects induced by external EFs has a complex debate on intrinsic materials and devices, which hinders the advancement of EL devices. Many studies have focused on reducing the adverse effects of defects, although there is a marked absence of comprehensive investigations into the intrinsic behavior of defects under EF conditions. Therefore, it is imperative to conduct focused research to elucidate the influence of EF on defect dynamics within operational perovskite materials and devices. Recently, EF-induced ion migration has garnered significant attention in the realm of perovskite materials and LEDs due to their association with both device performance and stability.81 Within an external EF context, ion migration often either a manifestation of defects43 or mediated by them, 82 plays a double-edged sword role in halide perovskite-based electronic devices. Although mobile ions contribute to spectral impurities and compromise the stability of PeLEDs, they also have potential to partially heal defects, thereby enhancing the device performance. This section offers a nuanced perspective of the complexities of ion migration in EL devices. 3.1.1 Relationship between ion migration and defects. The phenomenon of ion migration in LHPs has its origins in perovskite solar cells (PSCs), accounting for anomalies in low-frequency dielectric constant and hysteretic behavior.83 Mobile ions can generally be categorized into two types: ionic defects inherent in the material and excess ions derived from the precursors. As outlined in Section 2.3, ionic defects often take the form of point defects that emerge during crystallization owing to inherent softness of the material, even without external stimulation. However, ion migration is predominantly facilitated by these point defects, which enhance the rate of ion movement through mechanisms such as ion hopping.82 Due to the complexity and variability in measurement and calculation methodologies, a definite, fixed value for the ionic defect activation energy (Ea) is generally elusive. The value of Ea can be used to describe the trend and rate of ion migration.
Document [2]With researchers continuing to advance the efficiency, scalability, and stability of perovskite-based devices to meet industrial standards, a complete and up-to-date evaluation of the characterization options of the ionic behavior is critical. The role of ionic behavior in determining the stability of perovskite solar cells has been established. Suppressing ionic migration by employing a polyiodide supermolecule at the interfaces has successfully increased the efficiency and stability of perovskite solar cells under diurnal cycles.19 Ionic migration suppression by cation engineering has also enhanced the efficiency and operational as well as thermal stability of perovskite solar cells.20 Employing a physical defect passivation layer, which subsequently reduces ionic migration, has also succeeded in enhancing the stability of perovskite solar cell at 85°C for at least 2, 000 h.21 Hence, an in-depth understanding of ion migration behavior—clarifying mechanisms as well as kinetics, is crucial to drive the creation of novel perovskites with tailored ion migration properties as well as device designs with high efficiency and high stability. Due to the soft lattice nature of the perovskite as well as its mixed ionic-electronic conductivity, corrections to conventional techniques are required when applying them to perovskites. The ease of perovskite degradation under external stimuli, such as light, humidity, electric field, and heat, requires tighter control over the environment as well as excitation power used during analysis to avoid measurement-induced degradation. In operating films, moisture and oxygen commonly attack first at surfaces and grain boundaries, where they initiate decomposition reactions that accelerate device failure. In addition, the mixed ionic-electronic conductivity nature requires specialized techniques that could separate ionic conductivity from its electronic counterpart. This review will focus on the various approaches to identify and quantify ion movement in halide perovskites. First, an introduction to the type of ions that migrate, their mechanism (the origin and pathways), and their mobility will be elucidated with the help of theoretical calculations based on solid-state diffusion.

Document [4]The formation of defects in PNCs and bulk films is influenced by a variety of internal and external factors. Among these factors, the study of defect behavior under EF is particularly pivotal, as an EF serves as an indispensable external operating condition for driving these devices. The behavior of defects in the presence of EF remains intricate and elusive. Under EF, defects can redistribute within the lattice and at interfaces, changing local charge environments and influencing carrier transport. These field-driven changes are particularly concerning for researchers due to their potential to cause device degradation and introduce color impurities. A more profound understanding of the EF-induced defect dynamics behavior is still relatively limited. When devices inject or generate charge carriers or photocarriers under the influence of EF or illumination, the interaction between defects and carriers becomes notably intricate. Currently, PL variation serves as the primary tool for investigating the behavior of charge carriers and defects in the presence of lateral EF. Additionally, the movement of defects under an electric field can further perturb local defect distributions. The challenge in achieving theoretical unity in understanding defect behaviors is partly due to the absence of direct visual characterization methods for defects. Although commonly used methods, such as microscopy, spectroscopy, and electrical measurements, have been reported in the literature, these methods primarily provide indirect responses to defect behaviors, which is not conducive to simple analysis. TOF-SIMS, a technique enabling the relative visualization of ion migration phenomena within devices, and a number of developed in situ characterization techniques provide valuable insights into how defect behaviors contribute to poor device performance.
Document [5]AC driving involves the frequent reversal of the applied EF, providing a useful way to examine field-dependent defect behavior in perovskite devices.270–272 Such observations underscore that defects in NCs and thin films remain highly responsive under EF conditions across different device scenarios. AC-driven devices therefore highlight how EFs influence defect behavior within perovskite materials. When subjected to an EF, defects at interfaces or within the EML can become redistributed as charged species.268 Under a DC bias, one detrimental defect behavior is ion migration, which can lead to spectral instability. Tang et al. employed square-wave alternating voltage to study mixed-halide CsPbBrxCl3−x blue PeLEDs (∼466 nm).273 Under DC operational bias, the mixed-halide perovskite film exhibited Cl-rich and Br-rich regions, resulting in spectral instability due to halide ion migration. This phenomenon was reversible upon resetting or applying a reverse bias (Fig. 13d), indicating field-driven rearrangement of halogen ions. Under sustained illumination, such mixed-halide films can also undergo photoinduced phase segregation into halide-rich domains, a form of compositional demixing that shifts the bandgap during operation. Mobile ions accumulate at the surface of the perovskite emission layer induced by EF, which reflects the broader redistribution of halides under operating conditions.

It also emphasizes that an ideal metal-oxide/perovskite passivation layer cannot simply block the interface indiscriminately. The layer must still aid efficient charge transport from the perovskite to the charge-selective contacts, because the same boundary that degrades chemically is also where extraction has to occur. In that sense, these bridging layers chemically connect the metal-oxide and perovskite layers, can introduce a tailored interfacial dipole moment, can shift the electronic band structure across the interface, and can thereby produce more efficient charge-selective contacts while remaining positioned directly at the unstable junction. The central stability claim, however, is that perovskites are chemically unstable at the metal-oxide/perovskite interface. In direct contact with a metal-oxide surface, the perovskite may react and degrade, and the cited work on charge-selective-contact engineering and on redox reactions at NiOx/perovskite interfaces is invoked specifically because those unwanted reactions must be suppressed. The passage therefore treats the interface not as a neutral support, but as a chemically active location where degradation begins unless the contact is deliberately engineered. For that reason, the double-side passivation layer must act as an intrinsically stable barrier that physically separates the perovskite from the metal-oxide surface and prevents undesired chemical reactions at this interface. Double-side passivation is presented as important for long-term stability precisely because it suppresses interfacial redox and degradation chemistry at the contact itself while still preserving electronically effective transport across the same boundary.

Document [8]Hence, as numerous ions are mobile in perovskites, comprehensive knowledge of ionic migration has to be gathered by theoretical prediction as well as running a quantification technique in conjunction with elemental- or molecular-analysis-based spectroscopy that can identify the mobile species. Although a proper selection of spectroscopy techniques and cautions during measurements are required, various success stories on the observation and quantification of ionic migration have been reported widely. Emerging techniques have been developed to study ionic migration, as the knowledge of how to quantify and modulate ionic migration is crucial for the advancement of the field. Developments in in-operando elemental- or molecular-analysis-based spectroscopy are key to simulating and observing ionic migration at device working condition. In perovskite solar cells and LEDs, a complete understanding of the ionic migration (be it intrinsic or extrinsic) that leads to degradation could enable researchers to isolate or curb ionic migration. Approaches to mitigate ionic migration, be it internal or external ions, have been elucidated. Beyond photovoltaics, control of ionic migration could enhance the memristive device’s stability and functionality—for example, by creating a new mechanism to induce a tunable memory window.

Those characterizations are presented alongside the point that oxide charge-transport contacts are not chemically inert just because they transport electrons well. SnO2 is widely used in PSCs owing to its good electron-transport ability and chemical stability, yet interactions between Cl-containing SnO2 and the perovskite still exist. Seok et al. reported that a FASnCl interlayer can form at the SnO2/perovskite interface through an interfacial reaction between Cl-bonded SnO2 and Cl-containing FAPbI3. The paragraph further relates that reaction to the easy formation of Sn-based perovskites in the presence of Cl-, FA+, and Sn2+. In other words, the contact itself can generate a new interfacial phase through direct chemistry between the transport layer and absorber. Even if the resulting coherent interlayer can reduce interfacial charge recombination and enhance charge transport or extraction, its very formation shows that operational behavior is constrained by interfacial chemical reactions at the charge-transport contact rather than by a purely passive interface.

Document [0]As the core component of solid-state batteries, neither current inorganic solidstate electrolytes nor solid polymer electrolytes can simultaneously possess satisfactory ionic conductivity, electrode compatibility and processability. By incorporating efficient Li+ diffusion channels found in inorganic solid-state electrolytes and polar functional groups present in solid polymer electrolytes, it is conceivable to design inorganic-organic hybrid solid-state electrolytes to achieve true fusion and synergy in performance. Herein, we demonstrate that traditional metal coordination compounds can serve as exceptional Li+ ion conductors at room temperature through rational structural design. Specifically, we synthesize copper maleate hydrate nanoflakes via bottom-up selfassembly featuring highly-ordered 1D channels that are interconnected by Cu2+/Cu+ nodes and maleic acid ligands, alongside rich COO− groups and structural water within the channels. Benefiting from this interconnected channel network, Li+ ions can preferably transport through these channels rapidly by ion hopping. Thus, the Li+ -implanted copper maleate hydrate solid-state electrolytes shows remarkable ionic conductivity (1.17 × 10−4 S cm−1 at room temperature), high Li+ transference number (0.77), and a 4.7 V-wide operating window. More impressively, Li+ -implanted copper maleate hydrate solid-state electrolytes are demonstrated to have exceptional compatibility with both cathode and Li anode, enabling long-term stability of more than 800 cycles. This work brings new insight on exploring superior room-temperature ionic conductors based on metal coordination compounds. Solid-state lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) comprising Li metal anode and non-combustible solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are widely recognized as one of the most promising next-generation energy storage systems with both high energy density and superior safety1–3 . As the core component, it is of critical importance to develop highperformance SSEs with high ionic conductivity, extraordinary chemical/electrochemical stability, exceptional electrode compatibility and ease of processing4–8 .
Document [1]Lithium transport in cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 can depend on the simultaneous rearrangement of neighboring Li+ ions. Jalem and colleagues used ab initio molecular dynamics to examine lithium-site occupancy and diffusion in the three-dimensional garnet framework. Their analysis associated mobility with two local features: restrictions on how closely occupied lithium sites can approach, and unstable residence at the crystallographic 24d site. Departure from that site can initiate a reconfiguration of nearby lithium ions, allowing the local group to accommodate the movement. Thus the availability of a geometrical pathway alone does not specify whether a hop is accessible; the occupations of neighboring sites also matter. The local configuration changes the transition experienced by a tagged Li+ ion. Holding all other lithium ions fixed would remove the neighbor response that this mechanism uses to accommodate displacement, so it would describe a different migration problem. For the simulated cubic material, the estimated bulk conductivity was 1.06 x 10^(-4) S cm^(-1) at 300 K, with an activation barrier of 0.331 eV. The same trajectory analysis identified concerted lithium migration, connecting the conductivity estimate to a microscopic process involving several Li ions. A useful description of such an event tracks a configuration $(\mathbf r_1,\mathbf r_2,\ldots,\mathbf r_m)\longrightarrow(\mathbf r_1+\Delta\mathbf r_1,\mathbf r_2+\Delta\mathbf r_2,\ldots,\mathbf r_m+\Delta\mathbf r_m)$, rather than following only one tagged atom while freezing its neighbors. This notation emphasizes the coordinated displacements; it is not a new measured rate. The findings concern cubic LLZO and illustrate how local lithium occupancy and neighbor reorganization can enable conducting motion within a solid electrolyte.
Document [2]Ab initio simulations of lithium superionic conductors provide direct evidence that several Li+ ions can advance in a coordinated event. In their 2017 computational study, He, Zhu and Mo examined Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS), garnet Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO), and a lithium aluminium titanium phosphate (LATP). Their trajectories showed neighboring lithium ions exchanging sites with strong temporal correlation. Representative collective paths had migration barriers of 0.20 eV, 0.26 eV and 0.27 eV, respectively. The reported framework energy landscapes instead contained barriers of 0.47 eV, 0.58 eV and 0.49 eV. The proposed explanation includes both site occupancy and Li-Li interactions. At high lithium content, some occupied sites are energetically less favorable. During a joint move, a lithium ion moving downhill can offset part of the energy cost of another moving uphill. The activation barrier is consequently determined along the collective coordinate, rather than by adding independent single-ion barriers: $\Delta E_{\mathrm{collective}}=\max_{0\leq s\leq1}E(\mathbf r_1(s),\ldots,\mathbf r_m(s))-E(\mathbf r_1(0),\ldots,\mathbf r_m(0))$. The coordinates in this expression change together, so the interaction energy also changes along the path. Here s parametrizes one coupled path of m lithium ions. The study's interacting-ion model reproduced this reduction when the relevant higher-energy sites were occupied. These findings identify correlated many-ion lithium motion as a mechanism for rapid bulk transport in the studied electrolytes. They apply to the specified structures, occupancies and migration paths; a single isolated-ion energy profile does not fully specify that collective process.
Document [3]Curiously, some materials exhibit extremely high ionic conductivities despite having relatively low defect concentrations. These materials typically possess twofold sublattice structures: an immobile ion-containing fixed crystalline skeleton and an ionic sublattice composed of mobile constituents. Three minimum requirements must be satisfied for the occurrence of fast ionic conduction: (i) the number of energetically equivalent sites for the mobile ions must be higher than that of the mobile ions; (ii) a low barrier energy for ion migration from site to site; and (iii) the available sites must provide an interconnected continuous diffusion path. Even when some structural disorder is present, short- and medium-range ordering may be preserved, and transport still begins with the excitation of ions from one site to neighboring sites, leading to macroscopic diffusion. Under an external electric field, long-range ion conductivity is generated by a sequence of such hopping processes.
Document [4]Collective lithium motion can be resolved as strings of cooperating ions rather than as a collection of unrelated jumps. Burbano and colleagues used long molecular-dynamics trajectories for cubic and tetragonal Li7La3Zr2O12 to identify persistent displacements between lithium sites. Ions participating in coordinated replacements were grouped into stringlike excitations. Such events were frequent in the more conducting cubic phase, and the distribution of the number of participating lithium ions was approximately exponential. In ordered tetragonal LLZO, the excitations were sparse and often formed closed loops. This comparison connects lithium ordering, the geometry of cooperative motion and the large conductivity difference between the phases. It also explains why observing correlation alone is insufficient to infer efficient charge transport. For a group of equally charged lithium ions, the transported charge displacement is proportional to Q = e sum_i Delta r_i. Its squared magnitude contains both individual and cross terms: |Q|^2 / e^2 = sum_i |Delta r_i|^2 + 2 sum_(i<j) Delta r_i dot Delta r_j. In a completed local cyclic exchange, ions can change sites while their total displacement cancels. An extended conducting sequence need not have that cancellation. In three dimensions the collective diffusivity can be expressed as $D_\sigma=\lim_{t\to\infty}\langle|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta\mathbf r_i(t)|^2\rangle/(6Nt)$, where N counts the mobile lithium ions. The group displacement therefore enters the transport observable directly. The trajectory evidence therefore supports a specific collective-lithium mechanism: frequent cooperative events that propagate displacement can sustain bulk conduction, whereas rare cyclic rearrangements contribute much less to long-range transport. The distinction concerns the net motion of the group as well as how many ions participate.

Developing solid electrolyte (SE) is the most crucial aspect of building high-performance solid-state batteries. Among the numerous types of solid Li-ion conductors, the NASICON-type SEs with the general formula of Li1+xAlxGe2-x(PO4)3 (0 ≤ *x* ≤ 2) show particular prospects, owning to a combination of excellent stability, high Li-ion ionic conductivity as well as a wide electrochemical window over 5.0 V vs Li/Li-ion [ , , , , , ]. Among the available candidates, the Li1.5Al0.5Ge1.5(PO4)3 (LAGP) manifests the competitive advantages, such as the electrochemical stability and fast ionic conductivity in NASICON type SEs [ , , ]. Compared to the pristine LiGe2(PO4)3 (LGP) with Li-ion occupying at 6***b*** Wyckoff site, the substitution of Al-ion for Ge-ion in LAGP results in the additional lithium ion locating at 36***f*** site based on charge compensation , which has been considered as the primary cause of the exponential growth of room temperature ionic conductivity in the LAGP lattice and partially verified by theoretical calculations . In such phosphate frameworks, Li+ motion can be paddle-wheel-assisted, with rotating PO4 polyanions transiently opening low-barrier pathways for jumps between neighboring sites. However, for the sake of the structural complexity, there still lacks an exhaustive picture of the accurate structure and the corresponding Li-ion conduction behavior in LAGP SE [ , , , , ]. In monocrystal, the alkali Li/Na-ions generally migrate through the lattice sites (vacancy-assisted) or interstitial sites (interstitial hopping), and the migration energy barrier is determined to be about 0.5 eV by the energy landscape of crystal structural framework .

Among the key challenges, the design of superionic conductors for all-solid-state batteries often faces a fundamental trade-off between stability and ionic conductivity. Random substitutional crystals, where atomic species are randomly distributed throughout a crystal lattice, present a promising route to overcome this trade-off. Although the importance of cooperative motion in ion conduction has been pointed out, there is a lack of understanding of the relationship between mesoscale structural organization and macroscopic conductivity, limiting the rational design of optimal compositions. Here, we systematically investigate the ionic conductivity of rock salt random substitutional ionic crystals LixPb1−2xBixTe as a function of Li concentration x using molecular dynamics simulations. We find that ionic conductivity increases sharply once the x exceeds a critical threshold, without disrupting the underlying crystal structure. Strikingly, this threshold aligns with the site-percolation threshold predicted by percolation theory. Our findings establish ion percolation as a universal design principle that reconciles the trade-off between conductivity and stability, offering a simple and broadly applicable strategy for the development of robust, high-performance solid electrolytes. Designing materials that enable fast and efficient ionic transport is a central challenge in physics, chemistry, and materials science, with far-reaching implications for energy storage, catalysis, and sensing technologies. Among these, all-solid-state batteries have emerged as a promising platform for next-generation energy storage due to their intrinsic safety and potential for high energy density. A key requirement for advancing such technologies is the discovery of superionic conductors and a deeper understanding of their ionic conduction mechanisms [1–3]. Various lithium-containing oxides and sulfides have been reported to exhibit high ionic conductivity , making them promising candidates for next-generation battery applications. For all-solid-state batteries to be viable in practical settings, high ionic conductivity must be coupled with excellent chemical stability.
Document [7]Typical Li-ion battery cathodes today exhibit Li+ diffusivities in the range of 10 7 to 10 12 cm2 s 1 at room temperature.13–17 The Li+ conductivity requirements in the electrolyte are significantly higher because of the larger diffusion length scales. The typical organic electrolyte used in today’s batteries, a solvent mixture of a cyclic carbonate such as ethylene carbonate and a linear carbonate such as dimethylcarbonate with LiPF6 salt, has a Li+ conductivity on the order of 10 mS cm 1 at room temperature.18, 19 Such flammable organic electrolytes are inherently unsafe and have limited electrochemical windows of ∼ 4.5 V. A promising alternative is to replace flammable organic electrolytes with solid ceramic superionic conductors to create ‘all-solid-state’ batteries. However, until recently, known solid electrolytes, such as the garnet Li7La3Zr2O12 and the perovskite Li xLa xTiO (0 ⩽ x ⩽ 0.16), have Li+ conductivities that are at least 1–2 orders of magnitude lower compared with those of organic liquid electrolytes.20, 21 The discovery of the Li10GeP2S12 superionic conductor by Kamaya et al.22 in 2011, with the highest ever reported Li+ conductivity of 12 mS cm 1, has provided renewed hope for the development of solid ceramic electrolytes with comparable transport properties with flammable organic electrolytes. Despite its great importance, the factors that determine alkali conductivity in materials remain poorly understood. In polycrystalline solid electrolytes, fast Li+ transport can also arise along interfacial or grain-boundary regions, providing non-bulk conduction pathways distinct from Li+ hopping through interconnected bulk sites in the crystal interior. Many proposed design ‘rules of thumb’ for fast alkali conductivity are limited to specific chemistries or structure types and are not readily generalizable.
Document [8]The lithium conductor Li10GeP2S12 provides an experimental and computational example in which a one-ion potential is insufficient to describe migration. A study combining neutron-diffraction-based potential analysis, impedance measurements and nudged-elastic-band calculations examined motion along its one-dimensional lithium channels. The potential inferred for a single Li+ jump suggested a barrier near 0.09 eV. A correlated multi-ion path instead gave an effective barrier of 0.33 eV, close to the 0.29 eV activation energy obtained from impedance. This diffraction-derived one-particle potential differs from a frozen-framework single-ion energy landscape; their numerical barriers should not be interchanged. The collective path had two energy maxima with an intermediate local minimum about 0.13 eV above its starting point. The authors attributed the extra difficulty to Coulomb interactions among lithium ions sharing a crowded channel: forward progress requires neighboring ions to coordinate their movements. Thus a flat potential for an individual Li ion does not remove the occupancy constraints imposed by the other Li ions. Document [5]Achieving reliable resistive switching in oxide-based memristive devices requires precise control over conductive filament (CF) formation and behavior, yet the fundamental relationship between oxide material properties and switching uniformity remains incompletely understood. Here, we develop a comprehensive physical model to investigate how electrical and thermal conductivities influence CF dynamics in TaO -based memristors. Our simulations reveal that higher electrical conductivity promotes oxygen vacancy generation and reduces forming voltage, while higher thermal conductivity enhances heat dissipation, leading to increased forming voltage. The uniformity of resistive switching is strongly dependent on the interplay between these transport properties. We identify two distinct pathways for achieving optimal High Resistance State (HRS) uniformity with standard deviationto-mean ratios (σ/¯ µ¯) as low as 0.045, each governed by different balances of electrical and thermal transport mechanisms. For the Low Resistance State (LRS), high uniformity (σ/¯ µ¯ ≈ 0.009) can be maintained when either electrical or thermal conductivity is low. The resistance ratio between HRS and LRS shows a strong dependence on these conductivities, with higher ratios observed at lower conductivity values. These findings provide essential guidelines for material selection in RRAM devices, particularly for applications demanding high reliability and uniform switching characteristics. Document [7]The control and manipulation of filamentary resistive switching (FRS) is essential for practical applications in fields like non-volatile memories and neuromorphic computing. However, key aspects of the dynamics of conductive filament formation and their influence on device resistance remain incompletely understood. In this work we study FRS in binary oxides based memristors by investigating the dynamics of oxygen vacancies (OV) on a two dimensional lattice and their role in forming low-resistance paths that facilitate the transition between high and low global resistance states. We reveal that the mere formation of an OV percolation path is insufficient to induce a transition to a low-resistance state. Instead, an OV concentration exceeding a critical threshold across all sites in the filament is required to generate a low-resistivity conducting path. Furthermore, we simulate the impact of static defects -which block OV migration and would correspond to voids in real porous samples-, on filament formation. We show that there is a range of defect density values where OV percolate through the sample, leading to the formation of OV filaments, but conductive paths remain absent. Additionally, a small concentration of defects can reduce the final value of the low-resistance state, thereby increasing the ON-OFF ratio. These findings provide valuable insights into optimizing defective nanomaterials with memristive properties, which are crucial for advancing in-memory and neuromorphic computing technologies. Memristive devices are expected to be key components in the development of neuromorphic hardware , intended to outperform current software-based algorithms by mimicking the structure and information processing mechanism of the brain . Typical devices are metal/insulator/metal (MIM) structures of micro-nanometer size that exhibit the resistive switching (RS) effect - i.e. the reversible change of the resistance upon the application of an electrical stimulus . Since almost two decades, numerous studies of RS in devices where the insulator is a transition metal oxide (TMO) -mainly binary compounds such as TiO2, NiO, HfO2, VO2 and Ta2O5, among others[7–13]- have been reported as bipolar and atributted to the formation and retraction/rupture of nanoscale OV conducting filaments upon polarity reversal of the applied stimulus [14–18]. In this work we study FRS in binary oxides based memristors by investigating the dynamics of oxygen vacancies (OV) on a two dimensional lattice and their role in forming low-resistance paths that facilitate the transition between high and low global resistance states. We reveal that the mere formation of an OV percolation path is insufficient to induce a transition to a low-resistance state. Instead, an OV concentration exceeding a critical threshold across all sites in the filament is required to generate a low-resistivity conducting path. Furthermore, we simulate the impact of static defects -which block OV migration and would correspond to voids in real porous samples-, on filament formation. We show that there is a range of defect density values where OV percolate through the sample, leading to the formation of OV filaments, but conductive paths remain absent. Additionally, a small concentration of defects can reduce the final value of the low-resistance state, thereby increasing the ON-OFF ratio. These findings provide valuable insights into optimizing defective nanomaterials with memristive properties, which are crucial for advancing in-memory and neuromorphic computing technologies. Memristive devices are expected to be key components in the development of neuromorphic hardware , intended to outperform current software-based algorithms by mimicking the structure and information processing mechanism of the brain . Typical devices are metal/insulator/metal (MIM) structures of micro-nanometer size that exhibit the resistive switching (RS) effect - i.e. the reversible change of the resistance upon the application of an electrical stimulus . Since almost two decades, numerous studies of RS in devices where the insulator is a transition metal oxide (TMO) -mainly binary compounds such as TiO2, NiO, HfO2, VO2 and Ta2O5, among others[7–13]- have been reported as bipolar and atributted to the formation and retraction/rupture of nanoscale OV conducting filaments upon polarity reversal of the applied stimulus [14–18]. Yet some oxide memristors exhibit analog resistive switching through a bulk electronic or structural phase transition in the oxide itself, which gradually changes its conductivity under bias.

The most extensively studied structural motif in SACs is the M–N4 configuration, where a metal center is coordinated by four nitrogen atoms in a planar geometry with local D4h symmetry.20–23 This configuration confers distinct electronic properties that improve electrocatalytic kinetics, and the atomic positioning around the anchored metal center strongly influences the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates.24–27 In SACs, where single metal atoms are anchored by coordination atoms or a largely static support, the immediate coordination environment defines the electronic structure and spatial configuration of the catalytic center.28–35 The coordination environment directly influences performance, regulating electronic configuration, reactant adsorption behavior, reaction activation energy, activity, selectivity, and stability.34, 36–39 Metal–support bonding also affects resistance to agglomeration and overall catalyst stability.40–42 In some SACs under turnover conditions, however, initially isolated metal atoms migrate and coalesce into subnanometre clusters formed in situ, and those aggregates become the dominant catalytic state. Distinguishing the original anchored single-atom configuration from such in situ formed cluster states is therefore important when describing the active site under operating conditions. In SAC systems, metal–ligand bond lengths and local coordination at the angstrom scale define the electronic configuration of the active site.43–48 The coordination environment surrounding the metal center is equally critical, governing catalytic properties such as activity, selectivity, and stability.49 The electronic configuration and oxidation state of the metal are strongly influenced by the first coordination shell, where variations in the identity, coordination number, and positioning of bonded atoms modulate the metal's electronic structure.50, 51 Variations in the local coordination environment modulate the polarity of metal–ligand interactions and redistribute charge density, affecting adsorption behavior and reaction kinetics.52–54 The structure of the carbon matrix support can likewise influence the bonding and electronic environment of anchored sites.55–59 Despite these advances, the fundamental mechanisms that determine whether electrocatalytic turnover proceeds at the original isolated coordination site or at subnanometre clusters formed in situ remain inadequately understood, particularly the detailed mechanistic insights into how electrochemical conditions influence the operative structure.

As has been recently demonstrated by Wen et al. , integrating machine learning with DFT offers a route to accelerate this exploration. In this Account, we provide an overview of recent findings on the critical role of solvation and electrode potential in modeling the dynamics and free energetics of SAEs, with discussions on their implications, challenges, and possible solutions. We illustrate that the SAEs, despite a relatively simple structure, have dynamic behaviors, ensemble phenomena, and interfacial chemistry as rich as those of restructuring clusters and surfaces. By leveraging state-of-the-art computational tools, we show that it is now possible to include realistic factors into the model to better understand activity and selectivity trends, elucidate reaction mechanisms, and revise SAE design principles. We highlight the importance and benefits of removing the convenient assumptions and recovering the dynamics and realistic factors that are removed in the popular simplistic activity models whenever possible. Only by doing so can we identify the applicability of the simplistic models, so that we can use them more confidently in the systems where they hold, and revise or reinvent them for the systems where they do not. The methods discussed here may seem overkill at the moment, but we believe they will become routine calculations in a decade or two. Just as periodic DFT calculations became routine and gave rise to the CHE and activity volcanoes, the methods considering the full complexity of electrochemical interfaces would form the basis for developing next-generation activity models for the design of SAEs with activity, selectivity, and stability beyond the upper limit of existing design principles. We hope this Account can inspire the modeling community to face, understand, address, and make use of the complexity of the electrochemical interface to unlock rich interfacial chemistry and open up hidden dimensions for catalyst design. It is worth the effort to go down this rabbit hole.

question: By what processes is continuous, independent healing enabled in resilient polymeric networks under room-temperature environments?
perspectives: Dynamic supramolecular rebinding through reversible noncovalent interactions
Dynamic covalent bond exchange within the network
Chain diffusion and entanglement reformation across damaged interfaces
Replenishable healing-agent delivery through vascular networks

Document [0]Examples of H-bonding responsible for self-healing of supramolecular networks include diacid and triacid associations from renewable resources forming bis-urea reversible associations, reversible association of thymine/diamino triazine (THY/DAT), thymine/2, 6-diamino-pyridine (THY/DAP), and barbiturate/Hamilton wedge (Ba/HW), reversible dimerization of urea isopyrimidone (Upy), and polyacrylate amide (PA-A) chains carrying multiple H-bonding sites. Upy units that form quadruple H-bonds are known for generating rubber-like supramolecular assemblies, which exhibit temperature-dependent mechanical strength. When incorporated into flexible poly(ethylene-co-butylene) and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), aggregate formation of multiple Upy dimers is responsible for increased mechanical strength of the hydrogels. Thermally activated dissociation and re-association of these reversible H-bonded aggregates at ambient temperatures enables repeatable self-repair. In this context, weaker binding motifs are desirable because they preserve the dynamic supramolecular exchange needed for self-healing in tough polymers.[2j, 16]
Document [1]Imine bonds provide a dynamic covalent mechanism for self-healing because their reactions can proceed through reversible formation and exchange pathways. Reactions of imine bonds can be categorized into condensation reactions, exchange reactions, and metathesis reactions (Figure 10a) . In the condensation pathway, an amine and an aldehyde react through a hydrolysis-related equilibrium to form an imine while releasing water (Figure 10b) . When water is added to the imine product, the equilibrium shifts toward the starting materials according to Le Châtelier’s principle, demonstrating that the bond is reversible . In the imine exchange reaction, two protons of the amine move to the nitrogen atom of the imine (Figure 10c) . When a second amine is introduced, the original imine undergoes transimination and the alkyl group can be exchanged, directly enabling covalent partner swapping within the material. Imine metathesis likewise involves a scrambling reaction between two preformed imines (Figure 10d) , and this process proceeds through a four-membered cyclic transition state in which imine bonds are exchanged. The formation and exchange of imine bonds are influenced by solvent, concentration, pH, temperature, steric effects, and electronic effects . Kovaříček et al. further showed that in dialiphatic diamine forms of monoimines, local motion leads to bond exchange within the molecule, and the rate of exchange is regulated by substituents, solvent composition, and temperature . Strong electron-withdrawing substituents can enhance these dynamic imine reactions by increasing bond polarity, further supporting their role as exchangeable covalent linkages in self-healing networks.
Document [2]While single H-bond is not sufficient to induce supramolecular assemblies, multiple H-bonds formed in a directional manner may offer strong binding affinity. For example, associative groups with triple H-bonds, such as thymine (Thy) and 2, 6-diamino triazine (DAT), exhibit an equilibrium constant Ka ranging from 102 to 105 m−1, but the Ka of quadruple H-bonds such as in ureidopyrimidinone (Upy) are 107 m−1, to reach 109 m−1 for sextuple H-bonds. For that very reason, multivalent H-bonding is often used to construct supramolecular polymeric networks. Self-healing phenomenon was first reported for the network consisting of fatty acid oligomeric building blocks that contain H-bonding motifs including amidoethyl imidazolidone, di(amidoethyl) urea, and diamido tetraethyltriurea.[2f, 11] Associations of the H-bonding motifs shown in Figure 2A lead to the formation of a translucent glassy plastic materials which behave like a soft rubber at temperatures up to 90 °C, and are able to self-heal under ambient conditions. Figure 2B illustrates reversible association of multiple H-bonding between thymine/ diamino triazine (THY/DAT), thymine/2, 6-diamino-pyridine (THY/DAP), and barbiturate/Hamilton wedge (Ba/HW), which have similar structural units. Polymers end functionalized with such associative groups are capable of assembling into strong rubber-like material. Enhanced mechanical strength is not simply due to the presence of multiple H-bonds, but also cluster formations from the H-bonding moieties which result in phase segregation. Self-repairing is shown in PIB networks containing Ba/HW associative pairs.[12d] These materials showed a rubbery plateau at high shear rates, and self-healing under ambient conditions by bringing two physically separated parts into contact. That interfacial contact enables chain segments to diffuse across the damaged boundary and reform entanglements that knit the two pieces back together.

It should be noted that although energy requirements for noncovalent interactions are lower, they are highly sensitive to subtle structural or electronic changes as well as the environment. Unlike bis-urea or Upy H-bonding, which leads to crystallization or clustering, making the materials brittle, difficult to process, and limiting the dynamic exchange reactions between associative groups, as shown in Figure 3A, thiourea moieties form zigzag hydrogen-bonded arrays that do not induce unfavorable crystallization. Thus, when dense H-bonds between thiourea were utilized to crosslink low-molecular-weight polymers, tough materials that self-heal at room temperature were achieved. It was postulated that triethylene glycol spacers connecting thiourea units modulate the activation energy for the exchange of H-bonded thiourea pairs via slip motion shown in Figure 3B. As a consequence, these materials, although highly cross-linked, can heal by compression without heating, highlighting the importance of dynamic supramolecular exchange under ambient conditions.

Understanding what individual neurons or directions in activation space represent is fundamental to interpretability. Feature visualization and sparse autoencoders are central tools in that effort. Traditional approaches include feature visualization, which optimizes inputs to maximally activate specific neurons (Olah et al., 2017). For LLMs, this involves finding token sequences that strongly activate target features. Another approach is collecting dataset examples that highly activate features (Bills et al., 2023). Recent work uses LMs to automatically generate natural-language descriptions of neuron behavior based on those examples (Bills et al., 2023). Sparse autoencoders address the superposition challenge by training autoencoders with sparsity constraints to decompose neural activations into interpretable features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023). These SAEs learn overcomplete feature dictionaries where individual features correspond to interpretable concepts. Recent work has successfully applied SAEs to various layers of LLMs, discovering features corresponding to topics, entities, and linguistic properties (Bricken et al., 2023). Beyond observational analysis, interventional techniques directly modify model internals to test causal hypotheses about these identified features. Activation steering directly edits activations during inference so researchers can amplify or suppress specific behavioral tendencies tied to internal features (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023). By adding carefully chosen vectors to activations, researchers can control these feature-linked tendencies during generation, and this has been applied to enhance truthfulness, reduce toxicity, and control stylistic properties (Li et al., 2023).

These factual errors can be difficult to identify since LLMs implicitly memorize facts through their parameters rather than explicitly store factual knowledge as traditional Knowledge Bases. Accessing and interpreting the computations and memories of these models can be challenging (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Belinkov & Glass, 2019), especially when APIs are the only means of interaction and many interpretation methods rely on weights and representations (Cao et al., 2021b). The presence of errors in stored factual knowledge or the incorrect induction and obsolescence of certain facts over time may be contributing factors to this limitation, which in turn affects the performance of LLMs (Elazar et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2021a). This limitation restricts the application of LLMs in some high-stakes areas, such as healthcare, finance, and law (Dong et al., 2022). Hence, exploring the degree to which LLMs hold factual information and their ability to reason with such knowledge is vital. More formally, if we view an LM M as a computational graph with features as nodes and weighted connections between them as edges, a circuit is a subgraph of M responsible for implementing specific LM behaviors (Olah et al., 2020). Although circuits were initially defined as connections between features (Olah et al., 2020), subsequent studies have generalized them as connections between the activation outputs of transformer components (Olsson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022a), where interpreting individual transformer components becomes part of circuit interpretation. Therefore, research on interpreting individual transformer components also belongs to the study of circuits. Prior work has defined circuits with various assumptions and at different levels of granularity. Some works generalize the definition further to cover general information flows in an LM (Geva et al., 2023; Nikankin et al., 2024). All of these works count as studies of circuits as long as the goal is to find computational pathways connecting transformer components or features in an LM. An example circuit discovered by Elhage et al. Mr D' -> 'urs'. Document [6]We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms in neural networks. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: we introduce SHIFT, where classifier generalization is improved by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors. The key challenge of interpretability research is to scalably explain the many unanticipated behaviors of neural networks. Much recent work explains NN behaviors in terms of coarse-grained model components, for example by implicating certain induction heads in in-context learning (Olsson et al., 2022) or MLP modules in factual recall (Meng et al., 2022; Geva et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023). However, such components are generally polysemantic and hard to interpret, making it difficult to apply mechanistic insights to downstream applications. On the other hand, prior methods for analyzing behaviors in terms of fine-grained units attempt to fit model internals to researcher-specified mechanistic hypotheses using researcher-curated data (Kim et al., 2018; Belinkov, 2022; Geiger et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023). These approaches are not well suited to the many cases where researchers cannot anticipate ahead of time how models internally implement surprising behaviors. We propose to explain model behaviors using fine-grained components that play narrow, interpretable roles.

To address this issue, inspired by the importance sampling algorithm proposed in (Alain et al., 2016; Katharopoulos and Fleuret, 2018), we allocate distinct importance weights to the training samples within D0. The importance weight is proportional to the prediction loss of each sample, serving as a measure of its memorization difficulty. This strategy prioritizes samples that are more challenging to memorize by assigning them greater importance, thereby increasing their likelihood of selection during each training iteration, leading to faster convergence speed (Zhang et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2023). The detailed algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1. As shown in the pseudo-code, we use instance loss L(ys, xs) to measure the knowledge triplet’s importance and use this importance as the sampling probability within each batch, where L is the crossentropy loss, and ys is the correct output text given input xs.

question: Which underlying processes contribute to the generation of nonexistent objects in large multimodal language models?
perspectives: Overreliance on language priors that override weak visual evidence
Insufficient visual grounding in the vision encoder or cross-modal connector
Autoregressive error propagation in which earlier hallucinated tokens bias later object mentions
Alignment tuning that favors detailed answers over calibrated abstention when visual evidence is absent

Document [0]Object hallucination is a critical issue in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), where outputs include objects that do not appear in the input image. A natural question arises from this phenomenon: Which component of the LVLM pipeline primarily contributes to object hallucinations? The vision encoder to perceive visual information, or the language decoder to generate text responses? In this work, we strive to answer this question through designing a systematic experiment to analyze the roles of the vision encoder and the language decoder in hallucination generation. Our observations reveal that object hallucinations are predominantly associated with the strong priors from the language decoder. Based on this finding, we propose a simple and training-free framework, No-Language-Hallucination Decoding, NoLan, which refines the output distribution by dynamically suppressing language priors, modulated based on the output distribution difference between multimodal and text-only inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that NoLan effectively reduces object hallucinations across various LVLMs on different tasks. For instance, NoLan achieves substantial improvements on POPE, enhancing the accuracy of LLaVA-1.5 7B and Qwen-VL 7B by up to 6.45 and 7.21, respectively. The code will be made publicly available. In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of machine learning with the ability of language understanding and content generation, offering unprecedented capabilities and potentials across a multitude of applications. The integration of LLMs with computer vision systems has given rise to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) , facilitating various applications through their capacity to produce contextually accurate textual outputs from visual data.

LVLMs generally comprise two main components: a vision encoder that perceives visual information and a language decoder that generates text responses. This model composition motivates us to analyze the contributions of the vision and language components within LVLMs to the occurrence of object hallucinations. Through a series of analytical experiments, we find that object hallucinations primarily stem from the language decoder’s priors rather than the vision encoder. Based on this insight, we focus on overcoming language priors and introduce No-Language-Hallucination Decoding (NoLan), a simple, effective, and training-free framework designed to mitigate hallucinations in LVLMs. As illustrated in Figure 1, NoLan works by contrasting the output distributions of multimodal inputs with those of text-only inputs, acting as a corrective mechanism to address the model’s over-reliance on linguistic priors embedded in the LLM. The modulation of the output distribution increases when the similarity between the token distributions of multimodal and text-only inputs is higher, as measured by a Kullback-Leibler divergence-based function. Compared to previous methods , NoLan eliminates the need for additional training or external tools, such as other pre-trained models. Our experimental results validate the effectiveness of NoLan, demonstrating consistent improvements across various object hallucination benchmarks and LVLM families, including LLaVA-1.5 , InstructBLIP , and Qwen-VL . Specifically, on the POPE benchmark , NoLan achieves significant performance gains, with accuracy improvements of up to 8.38 and F1 score enhancements of up to 8.78, highlighting its robustness and scalability in addressing object hallucinations across diverse LVLM architectures. Document [0]A major difficulty in GCRL is reward sparsity, which hinders efficient credit assignment. Techniques such as Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) (Andrychowicz et al., 2017) address this by reinterpreting failed trajectories as successes for alternative goals, yielding denser learning signals. However, standard HER assumes Markovian rewards, which often limits its applicability to the non-Markovian, long-horizon nature of web navigation. To overcome these limitations, recent research has pivoted towards on-policy GCRL and intrinsic motivation. For instance, Gong et al. (2024) introduces GCPO, an on-policy framework that leverages self-curriculum learning to handle non-Markovian reward structures, significantly stabilizing training in complex sequential environments. Complementing this, WebAgent-R1 (Wei et al., 2025) demonstrates that end-to-end on-policy RL—augmented with parallel trajectory generation and “thinking” steps—can surpass improved imitation learning baselines without the complexity of off-policy buffer management. Beyond pure RL updates, explicit subgoal scaffolding remains critical for exploration. While early efforts like VSC-RL (Wu et al., 2025) utilized subgoal-conditioned learning to boost sample efficiency, they often struggled to balance intermediate subgoal completion with final goal optimality. Newer approaches address this by learning latent subgoals or internal world models. For instance, Park et al. (2023) propose HIQL, which learns a high-level policy over latent states, effectively decoupling strategic planning from low-level control. In a parallel direction, Duan et al. (2024) utilize world models to simulate next outcomes, enabling agents to explore sparse-reward environments via predicted rollouts. These methods advance the field by enabling hierarchical reasoning, allowing agents to sustain progress in long-horizon tasks through abstract, learned objectives. However, applying these latent or model-based approaches to web agents introduces critical limitations.
Document [1]To support planning and control, recent world-model work turns generative models into interactive simulators that can forecast how the environment will change after actions. Vid2World provides a general recipe by injecting actions and enforcing state persistence, showing how a model can simulate future observations in a way that is useful for downstream control, while real-robot settings expose robustness problems under distribution shift . Physics-aware guidance reduces implausible dynamics , and explicit memory improves long-horizon consistency when the viewpoint changes , both of which matter because planning quality depends on the simulator preserving coherent state over time. CoLA-World pushes this further by jointly learning latent actions and world dynamics, making the model more controllable rather than purely realistic. A related line moves from 2D appearance toward geometry-grounded state representations. 3D and 4D observations expose stable scene structure across viewpoints, which makes future prediction more useful for action selection than view-specific pixels alone. Text2Room iteratively fuses multi-view images to generate high-quality meshes from text, 4D-fy extends scene generation into the temporal dimension by alternating supervisory signals from 3D perception and text-to-image and text-to-video models, and WonderWorld generates interactive 3D worlds while maintaining visual quality and geometric consistency. Invisible Stitch addresses monocular-depth geometric inconsistencies through depth inpainting, while PointWorld unifies state and action in a 3D point-flow space to forecast full-scene dynamics from a small number of RGB-D observations. The remaining challenge is to improve efficiency and physical consistency without losing controllability. Across these approaches, the value of the world model lies in providing a structured latent simulator of future state change that can be used to plan actions under long horizons and compare candidate continuations before acting.

Communication allows agents to describe their capabilities, and discovery depends on how those descriptions relate to the current request rather than on fixed service entry points alone. Document [4]World Model-based Exploration: Agent planning relies on interactions with the environment. However, engaging with the real world poses challenges such as low efficiency, safety risks, and the potential for irreversible changes. To address these issues, a promising approach is to construct world models that predict state transitions within the environment. These models can be leveraged to simulate or generate training data during the planning process. RAP is a search framework that regards the LLM as a world model. It does not rely on real-world environment feedback but instead uses the LLM to predict changes in the environment state and forecast the outcomes of action executions. WEBDREAMER is a web navigation search framework that uses the LLM as the world model to predict the changes in web page states after the agent actions are executed. It relies on the world model rather than real web interactions, helping to prevent security risks and irreversible environmental changes that may occur during actual web operations. Feng et al. proposes a search framework for robotic manipulation based on multi-modal world models, which uses a diffusion model as the world model to predict the state changes of objects after robotic actions. WorldCoder uses code to build a world model, where the world knowledge is represented as code to serve as a transition function for planning based on the world model. ReasonPlanner regards a world model as a temporal knowledge graph, which records factual information according to timestamps. When an agent performs planning, it can query the temporal knowledge graph to assist the model in making forward-looking decisions. Reward Model-based Exploration: The reward model plays a crucial role in reward-based exploration methods. This type of approach fixes the parameters of the policy model and constructs training data to improve the reward model’s scoring accuracy, thereby guiding the policy model toward more promising search directions. For instance, QLASS trains a Q-value network that estimates the Q-values of intermediate nodes based on environment outcome rewards.

Document [6]Planner-centric systems tackle long-horizon control by decomposing a task into subgoals or options that condition lower-level RL controllers, so action choice is organized around latent intermediate objectives rather than a flat search over primitive moves. The immediate gain is horizon reduction: instead of optimizing over entire trajectories with delayed sparse reward, the learner receives structured intermediate objectives that can be assessed earlier and used to maintain progress. In hierarchical form, the policy is conditioned on planner outputs z_t, and policy learning focuses on executing, refining, and sequencing those latent directives . This means the system is effectively planning over an internal scaffold of predicted future progress. The core design problem is planner authority. Soft planners emit candidate subgoals that the controller can ignore when local evidence says they are poor fits, while hard planners impose mandatory execution scaffolds that can speed convergence in stable settings but fail sharply when generated plans are dynamically infeasible. Hybrid authority schedules therefore increase planner influence only when feasibility confidence is high, preserving abstraction when the planner is grounded and limiting damage when it is wrong. Several supporting design patterns strengthen this latent-planning loop. Feasibility-aware planning pairs proposal generation with grounded critics that reject or repair invalid subgoals, turning planning into a closed-loop contract rather than a one-way suggestion . Option-centric planning emits discrete skills or executable program sketches, making the high-level plan explicit and easier to debug, though sometimes less adaptable when schemas are rigid . Arbitration-centric planning explicitly ties planner influence to disagreement and calibration signals, so the controller can roll back when the current latent plan no longer matches the environment . Together these designs make decision-making depend on internally modeled subgoals, their predicted executability, and the expected consequences of following them over time.

Document [0]A major difficulty in GCRL is reward sparsity, which hinders efficient credit assignment. Techniques such as Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) (Andrychowicz et al., 2017) address this by reinterpreting failed trajectories as successes for alternative goals, yielding denser learning signals. However, standard HER assumes Markovian rewards, which often limits its applicability to the non-Markovian, long-horizon nature of web navigation. To overcome these limitations, recent research has pivoted towards on-policy GCRL and intrinsic motivation. For instance, Gong et al. (2024) introduces GCPO, an on-policy framework that leverages self-curriculum learning to handle non-Markovian reward structures, significantly stabilizing training in complex sequential environments. Complementing this, WebAgent-R1 (Wei et al., 2025) demonstrates that end-to-end on-policy RL—augmented with parallel trajectory generation and “thinking” steps—can surpass improved imitation learning baselines without the complexity of off-policy buffer management. Beyond pure RL updates, explicit subgoal scaffolding remains critical for exploration. While early efforts like VSC-RL (Wu et al., 2025) utilized subgoal-conditioned learning to boost sample efficiency, they often struggled to balance intermediate subgoal completion with final goal optimality. Newer approaches address this by learning latent subgoals or internal world models. For instance, Park et al. (2023) propose HIQL, which learns a high-level policy over latent states, effectively decoupling strategic planning from low-level control. In a parallel direction, Duan et al. (2024) utilize world models to simulate next outcomes, enabling agents to explore sparse-reward environments via predicted rollouts. These methods advance the field by enabling hierarchical reasoning, allowing agents to sustain progress in long-horizon tasks through abstract, learned objectives. However, applying these latent or model-based approaches to web agents introduces critical limitations.
