Document [6]Planner-centric systems tackle long-horizon control by decomposing a task into subgoals or options that condition lower-level RL controllers, so action choice is organized around latent intermediate objectives rather than a flat search over primitive moves. The immediate gain is horizon reduction: instead of optimizing over entire trajectories with delayed sparse reward, the learner receives structured intermediate objectives that can be assessed earlier and used to maintain progress. In hierarchical form, the policy is conditioned on planner outputs z_t, and policy learning focuses on executing, refining, and sequencing those latent directives . This means the system is effectively planning over an internal scaffold of predicted future progress. The core design problem is planner authority. Soft planners emit candidate subgoals that the controller can ignore when local evidence says they are poor fits, while hard planners impose mandatory execution scaffolds that can speed convergence in stable settings but fail sharply when generated plans are dynamically infeasible. Hybrid authority schedules therefore increase planner influence only when feasibility confidence is high, preserving abstraction when the planner is grounded and limiting damage when it is wrong. Several supporting design patterns strengthen this latent-planning loop. Feasibility-aware planning pairs proposal generation with grounded critics that reject or repair invalid subgoals, turning planning into a closed-loop contract rather than a one-way suggestion . Option-centric planning emits discrete skills or executable program sketches, making the high-level plan explicit and easier to debug, though sometimes less adaptable when schemas are rigid . Arbitration-centric planning explicitly ties planner influence to disagreement and calibration signals, so the controller can roll back when the current latent plan no longer matches the environment . Together these designs make decision-making depend on internally modeled subgoals, their predicted executability, and the expected consequences of following them over time.

Document [2]Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combining statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings support a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors through sparse, functionally interpretable internal features. In recent years, research on the Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) of Large Language Models (LLMs) has received increasing attention (Ranaldi, 2025). Recent research has established a robust foundation for understanding and utilizing internal model representations through diverse methodologies. For instance, significant progress has been made in isolating interpretable components from model activations, most notably through the deployment of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) (Shu et al., 2025), which facilitate the discovery of monosemantic features and automatic feature labeling (Templeton et al., 2024). Furthermore, intervention techniques such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) (Rimsky et al., 2024) have demonstrated the possibility of steering model outputs through targeted activation interventions.
Document [3]LLMs are built on extensive training datasets and intricate model architectures, which contribute to their remarkable emergent abilities (Wei et al., 2022). However, the exact mechanisms through which these models acquire and process vast amounts of knowledge remain unclear. Additionally, the contributions of individual model components to the overall function have been largely unexplored. To fully understand LLMs, recent studies have shifted to make use of mechanistic interpretability (more details are given in Section A at the Appendix) to reverse engineer LLMs at a more granular level such as neurons, attention heads, and connections. Neurons serve as the basic units for storing knowledge and patterns within LLMs. They are observed to be polysemantic, meaning that an individual neuron can be activated on multiple unrelated terms (Olah et al., 2020a; Bills et al., 2023). This characteristic presents a significant challenge in mechanistically understanding how models operate. Despite the challenge, recent work has explored the underlying causes of this polysemantic nature. Two key concepts have emerged as instrumental in unraveling its formation: Superposition (Olah et al., 2020a) and Monosemanticity (Bricken et al., 2023). Superposition describes the phenomenon where a feature can be spread across multiple neurons, meanwhile a neuron can also be mixed up with multiple features. Some researchers believe that this mechanism originated from an excessive number of features compared to the number of neurons (Olah et al., 2020a; Elhage et al., 2022). In exploring this concept through a toy example, i.e. a ReLU network, researchers have found that superposition allows for the representation of additional features. However, to mitigate interference, a nonlinear filter needs to be introduced (Elhage et al., 2022).

Document [5]Evaluation challenges: Assessing cultural alignment requires culturally-grounded evaluation, but most interpretability researchers come from Western contexts, potentially missing important biases. Table 2 maps mechanistic interpretability approaches to specific alignment objectives, illustrating how different MI techniques enable targeted interventions while also highlighting their limitations. This demonstrates both the promise and current constraints of interpretability-based alignment. The superposition hypothesis posits that networks represent more features than dimensions by storing features in overlapping combinations of neurons (Elhage et al., 2022). This creates fundamental challenges: Polysemantic neurons: Individual neurons respond to multiple unrelated concepts, making neuron-level interpretability difficult (Cammarata et al., 2020). Research suggests models exploit sparsity—most features are inactive for most inputs—to pack many features into limited dimensions. Interference and interaction: Features in superposition can interfere with each other in complex ways, making it difficult to predict how interventions will affect behavior (Elhage et al., 2022). Computational burden: Sparse autoencoders and other decomposition methods show promise but face scalability challenges. Training SAEs for frontier models requires enormous compute, and the number of features grows combinatorially (Bricken et al., 2023). Emergence: Large models exhibit emergent capabilities not present in smaller versions (Wei et al., 2022). Whether interpretability techniques developed on smaller models transfer to frontier systems remains uncertain. Circuit interaction: Real behaviors involve complex interactions between many circuits. Understanding how circuits compose and interfere is significantly harder than understanding individual circuits in isolation (Olah et al., 2020). Computational costs: Comprehensive circuit analysis requires extensive patching experiments that scale poorly with model size. Automated methods help but still face significant computational barriers for the largest models. Lack of ground truth: Unlike in neuroscience, we cannot easily verify interpretability hypotheses through direct experimentation.
Document [6]Large language models are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without stable internal representations. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability, the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable—but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of concept representation. We propose a framework for thinking about concept encoding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework emphasizes conceptual organization in these models: a model can form relatively sparse, approximately monosemantic "features" as directions in latent space, linking recurring manifestations of a single entity or property. Mechanistic interpretability uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite this kind of feature-like unification. Some concepts in these models are best characterized as context-dependent activation manifolds whose geometry shifts with the evolving prompt. These representational forms need not collapse into a single static format. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows a more precise account of how concept representations are organized in LLMs. Keywords Large language models · Concept encoding · Mechanistic interpretability · Concepts · Philosophy of AI · Epistemology of AI The striking competence of Large Language Models (LLMs) raises an intriguing question: are they just mimicking linguistic regularities by relying on superficial statistics, or do they form internal structures that are sufficiently sophisticated and specific to sustain mechanistic analysis of concept encoding?1 A common deflationary explanation is that LLMs possess no meaningful internal conceptual organization whatsoever. This soberly deflationary view is often motivated by the surprisingly rudimentary principle upon which LLMs are built.

question: Which elements explain the observed stagnation or inconsistency in performance improvements as frontier language models continue to scale?
perspectives: Exhaustion of high-quality pretraining data at current scales
Static benchmark saturation or contamination masking real capability gains
Optimization or architecture bottlenecks at current scales
Capability gains shifting into tool use and interaction settings not captured by static benchmarks

Document [0]However, saturation becomes problematic when it reflects loss of measurement resolution rather than capability completion. If score compression arises because evaluation noise exceeds true performance gaps, or because the benchmark lacks sufficient depth or coverage to differentiate increasingly capable systems, then apparent convergence may mask unresolved weaknesses. In this scenario, models may appear indistinguishable despite meaningful differences in robustness, calibration, or generalization. Thus, the critical distinction is whether saturation reflects true capability attainment or degradation of the benchmark’s discriminative instrument. The former signals progress; the latter calls for benchmark revision or expansion. Our benchmark selection, though criteria-driven, reflects current evaluation practices and may overrepresent widelyadopted benchmarks. Top-N leaderboard snapshots may miss saturation dynamics for sparse or inconsistently evaluated benchmarks. We assume benchmark properties are time-invariant, yet attributes like annotation diversity evolve post-release. Finally, restricting to text-only limits generalizability to multimodal settings. Many annotations relied on publicly available leaderboard data, which posed several challenges. For a given benchmark, multiple leaderboards often exist, maintained either by the original publishers or by third-party platforms. This can lead to inconsistent reporting, as leaderboards may differ in evaluation setups (e.g., LLM-judge prompts) or scoring criteria. In addition, many leaderboards are not updated regularly and therefore omit newly released models. Consequently, before extracting benchmark data, we first identified trustworthy leaderboards based on their visibility, coverage of recent models, and result verification. Future work should incorporate continuous-time leaderboard data and distinguish genuine saturation from temporary plateaus. Examining saturation recovery following architectural innovations would clarify whether saturation is transient or permanent. Integrating psychometric methods could refine ceiling estimation and enable instance-level analysis beyond aggregating metrics. Benchmark Design & Evolution. The development of AI benchmarks has evolved alongside advances in models, with an increasing focus on broad coverage and rigorous design (Reuel et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024).

When we set Dsource = Dmix, large variance exists between configurations, ranging from 9.63 for FWLQ to 14.3 for FWHQ (Table 8). However, when the training setup includes a high-quality mix-in corpus, the inherent quality of Dsource becomes less dominant. In this setting, the performance delta narrows to a maximum of 1.78 points. These results demonstrate that rephrasing low-quality data can yield competitive results when the synthetic samples are paired with a robust corpus. This observation is encouraging: it suggests that the generation pipeline can successfully up-cycle noisy web text into high-utility training tokens, thereby effectively expanding the reservoir of available source data for pretraining.
Document [2]The success of LLMs heavily depends on “Scaling Law” (Brown, 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) in pre-training, which unveils the numerical relationships of the language modeling loss, model parameters, and pre-trained tokens. By fully exploiting the potential of data and parameters according to the scaling law, LLMs such as GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2024a) have significantly outperformed average humans in writing and language understanding, and have even matched the performance of undergraduate students on disciplinary examinations. As a result, the scaling law has become a critical foundation of contemporary LLMs. However, as high-quality internet corpus becomes potentially exhausted (Villalobos et al.), the pre-training scaling is facing a substantial challenge. While massively synthesizing corpus might tackle the problem, its effectiveness after scaling remains unverified and questionable (Shumailov et al., 2024). Additionally, when capabilities are increasingly expressed outside static one-shot tests, benchmark scores alone can paint an incomplete picture of continued progress. Consequently, recent benchmark plateaus may partly reflect measurement limits rather than a simple halt in capability gains. The advent of models such as OpenAI o1 (OpenAI, 2024b), together with some recent works (Snell et al., 2024; Yue et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a), has highlighted settings in which model improvements are more readily observed. Instead of being reflected mainly on standard static benchmarks, these improvements are often more visible in practical use. The probable improving aspects include tool use, multi-turn interaction, and performance in realistic task settings. Many of the resulting gains appear in tool use and multi-turn interaction, so static one-shot benchmarks often fail to capture them. In this work, we aim to present a comprehensive survey on these emerging capability patterns and their evaluation.
Document [3]As the volume of available web text plateaus, the focus of the field has moved from quantity to quality: modern development pipelines now employ neural classifiers to filter for educational content (Gunasekar et al., 2023; Penedo et al., 2023) and analyze data repetition extensively (Muennighoff et al., 2023). Synthetic data constitutes the latest step in this progression, appearing as a solution to the exhaustion of usable real-world data. Rather than merely filtering web text, recent work uses LLMs to rephrase text into variants that preserve information while optimizing the presentation (Maini et al., 2024; Kiyomaru et al., 2026), inter alia.). The community has adopted this approach at scale: Su et al. (2025) rephrased two trillion tokens for Nemotron-CC, and several recent LLMs utilized hundreds of billions of synthetic tokens during pretraining (Abdin et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Singh et al., 2026). Prior work has explored a range of such approaches. For instance, WRAP (Maini et al., 2024) focuses on stylistic rewriting; Nemotron-CC (Su et al., 2025) extracts QA pairs and knowledge lists; BeyondWeb (DatologyAI et al., 2025) proposes continuation and summarization rephrasing; and REWIRE (Nguyen et al., 2025) targets the guided transformation of low-quality documents. Collectively, these efforts reflect the field's attempt to supplement the plateauing supply of high-quality real-world text and sustain pretraining at current scales.
Document [4]While the original paper proposed retaining 30% of the data, our results show that depending on the ratio of compute to data pool size, we must adaptively make the filtering less (or more) aggressive to account for the diminishing utility of good data with repetitions. A global data pool size of 128M samples was used for these experiments. (2020) conducted a comprehensive study on scaling laws for neural language models. They observed that, given fixed computational budgets, there exists an optimal model size, training data size, and training time. Interestingly, the triple (model size, data size, batch size) tends to scale in a roughly lock-step manner, reinforcing the notion that larger models require more data and more computation to be trained effectively. At frontier scales, however, optimization inefficiencies and architectural limitations can themselves become the bottleneck, so simply adding parameters or tokens may produce unstable or diminishing benchmark gains. This observation is corroborated by Hoffmann et al. (2022); Hernandez et al. Document [1]A precise asymptotic theory has since been developed for ridgeless least squares and random feature regression [Mei and Montanari, 2022, Hastie et al., 2022], showing that risk and variance display singular behavior near the interpolation threshold N ≈ n, corresponding to ψ1 = N/d approaching ψ2 = n/d. These works reveal that the interpolation peak is driven by variance amplification as this threshold is approached. A complementary and increasingly popular viewpoint interprets ridge-regularized RF training through the way regularization reshapes this near-singular regime. In particular, the RF ridge solution can be understood as stabilizing the estimator near interpolation. In standard random-feature constructions, it moderates the variance blow-up for new responses [Baek et al., 2023, Section 2.2]. This lens naturally highlights uncertainty amplification, provides a principled route to hyperparameter selection, and connects RF models to broader statistical learning paradigms. However, the classical RF formulation still concentrates the main difficulty around the threshold itself. Small changes in outputs, features, or regularization can be strongly magnified when ψ1 approaches ψ2. Even small perturbations in this regime may yield substantially different predictive risk or variance. This motivates the question we study: How do RF conclusions change when we explicitly account for perturbations around the interpolation threshold? Our approach: a Contamination Random Features model. We address this question through the lens of sensitivity analysis [Berger, 1984] using Huber-style contamination sets [Walley, 1991, Huber and Ronchetti, 2009]. Concretely, instead of committing to a single nominal specification, we consider credal sets [Levi, 1980], i.e. convex and weak⋆-closed sets of probabilities.

In particular, in the context of deep learning, we empirically show that the spectrum of the Hessian is composed of two parts: (1) the bulk centered near zero, (2) and outliers away from the bulk. Given the vast range of literature in this field, we further categorize methods based on their additional information requirements. This categorization facilitates a fairer and more comprehensible comparison of the various approaches. Numerous existing methods strive to exploit explicit environment labels to improve OOD generalization. Here, we focus on causal learning methods within this setting. In this section, we encapsulate the fundamental concepts underlying these techniques. Causal Learning Causal learning methods aim to learn the underlying causal structure of the data and to predict the outcome variable based on the identified causal variables. By correctly identifying the cause-effect relationships, these methods are expected to perform well even when the data distribution changes, as the underlying causal structure is often assumed to remain invariant across different environments or domains. Causal learning, rooted in the causal inference literature, provides a principled approach to the problem of OOD generalization. Its primary goal is to leverage causal variables for predictions, making it increasingly practical in recent times. We start with an introduction to the foundational concepts of causal learning, followed by an exploration of various related studies. The underlying assumption of causal learning is captured in Assumption A, which originates in the causal inference literature. It postulates the existence of a causally invariant relationship between the target variable Y and its direct causes Xpa(Y ).
Document [1]In real-world applications, it is important and desirable to learn a model that performs well on out-of-distribution (OOD) data. Recently, causality has become a powerful tool to tackle the OOD generalization problem, with the idea resting on the causal mechanism that is invariant across domains of interest. To leverage the generally unknown causal mechanism, existing works assume a linear form of causal feature or require sufficiently many and diverse training domains, which are usually restrictive in practice. In this work, we obviate these assumptions and tackle the OOD problem without explicitly recovering the causal feature. Our approach is based on transformations that modify the non-causal feature but leave the causal part unchanged, which can be either obtained from prior knowledge or learned from the training data in the multi-domain scenario. In practice, this favors features that vary smoothly over a broad support of plausible perturbations, so they remain reliable even when test inputs move beyond the training domain. Under the setting of invariant causal mechanism, we theoretically show that if all such transformations are available, then we can learn a minimax optimal model across the domains using only single domain data. Noticing that knowing a complete set of these causal invariant transformations may be impractical, we further show that it suffices to know only a subset of these transformations. Based on the theoretical findings, a regularized training procedure is proposed to improve the OOD generalization capability. Extensive experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, even with only a few causal invariant transformations. The success of many machine learning algorithms with empirical risk minimization (ERM) relies on the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) hypothesis that training and test data originate from a common distribution. In practice, however, data in different domains or environments are often heterogeneous, due to changing circumstances, selection bias, and time-shifts in the distributions . Accessing data from all the domains of interest, on the other hand, is expensive or even impossible. Consequently, the problem of learning a model that generalizes well on the unseen target distributions is a practically important but also challenging task and has gained much research attention in the past decades .

First, we introduce the graph invariant learning methods for OOD generalization. Invariant learning assumes that the information of each instance for prediction includes two parts, i.e., invariant part whose relationship with the label is stable across different environments, and variant part whose relationship with the label can change across different environments. Along this line, there are mainly two types of graph invariant learning methods: invariance optimization and explicit representation alignment . These methods are built upon the invariance principle to address the graph OOD generalization problem. The invariance principle assumes the invariance property inside the data, so that it can find such invariance in multiple environments to achieve OOD generalization. The assumption can be formulated as: Assumption 1. (Invariance Assumption). There exists a portion of information Φ(X) inside input instance X such that ∀e, e0 ∈ supp(E), P e(Y |Φ(X)) = P e0 (Y |Φ(X)), where E denotes all possible environments and Φ(X) is often called as invariant rationales of input instance X.

Executing inside DisenConv, the proposed neighborhood routing mechanism is to identify the factor that may cause the link from a center node to one of its neighbors, and accordingly send the neighbor to the channel responsible for that factor. It infers the latent factors by iteratively analyzing the potential subspace clusters formed by the node and its neighbors, after projecting them into several subspaces. In the example above, the former are the features describing the context (e.g., pastures and deserts), whilst the latter are the features describing the animals (e.g., animal shape). Ideally, the representation should be a minimal sufficient statistic for the label, preserving the stable predictive signal while discarding shortcut cues tied to the context. By exploiting the varying degrees of spurious correlation naturally present in training data collected from multiple environments, one can try to identify stable features and build invariant predictors. Invariant risk minimization (IRM) seeks to find data representations (Arjovsky et al., 2019) or features (Rojas-Carulla et al., 2018) for which the optimal predictor is invariant across all environments. The general formulation of IRM is a challenging bi-leveled optimization problem, and theoretical guarantees require constraining both data representations and classifiers to be linear (Arjovsky et al., 2019), Theorem 9), or considering the special case of feature selection (Rojas-Carulla et al., 2018), Theorem 4). Ahuja et al. (2020a) study the problem from the perspective of game theory, with an approach termed invariant risk minimization games (IRMG). They show that the set of Nash equilibria for a proposed game is equivalent to the set of invariant predictors for any finite number of environments, even with nonlinear data representations and nonlinear classifiers. However, these theoretical results in the nonlinear setting only guarantee that one can learn invariant predictors from training environments, but do not guarantee that the learned invariant predictors can generalize well across all environments including unseen testing environments. We propose invariant Causal Representation Learning (iCaRL), a novel approach that enables outof-distribution (OOD) generalization in the nonlinear setting (i.e., nonlinear representations and nonlinear classifiers1). We achieve this by extending and using methods from representation learning and graphical causal discovery.
Document [8]Due to spurious correlations, machine learning systems often fail to generalize to environments whose distributions differ from the ones used at training time. Prior work addressing this, either explicitly or implicitly, aimed to reduce reliance on features whose association with the target changes across environments. This is done by leveraging a diverse set of training environments to reduce the effect of spurious features and build an invariant predictor. However, these methods have generalization guarantees only when both data representation and classifiers come from a linear model class. We propose invariant Causal Representation Learning (iCaRL), an approach that enables out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in the nonlinear setting (i.e., nonlinear representations and nonlinear classifiers). It builds upon a practical and general assumption about the data representation (i.e., a set of latent variables encoding the data), allowing a flexible conditionally non-factorized structure that can capture complicated dependences between the latent variables while promoting invariance across environments. Based on this, we derive generalization guarantees in the nonlinear setting. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms a variety of baseline methods. Modern machine learning algorithms still lack robustness, and may fail to generalize outside of a specific training distribution because they learn easy-to-fit spurious correlations which are prone to change between training and testing environments. We recall the widely used example of classifying images of camels and cows (Beery et al., 2018). Here, the training dataset has a selection bias, i.e., many pictures of cows are taken on green pastures, while most pictures of camels happen to be in deserts. After training, it is found that the model builds on spurious correlations, i.e., it relates green pastures with cows and deserts with camels, and fails to recognize images of cows on the beach.

Specifically, it first identifies the latent factors behind the input graph and derives its factorized representations by the tailored disentangled graph encoder whose key ingredient is a multi-channel messagepassing layer. Unlike generative models, contrastive learning is an instance-wise discriminative approach that aims at making similar instances closer and dissimilar instances far from each other in representation space , so that it can get rid of computationally expensive graph reconstruction and learn informative graph representations.

This study presents RhythmX™, a hybrid and interpretable framework for multiclass ECG heartbeat classification that includes self-supervised representation learning. SimCLR-based pretraining enables the extraction of invariant morphological and rhythm-aware representations from unlabeled ECG signals, substantially reducing dependence on annotated data. These embeddings are also used within a broader classification pipeline that includes handcrafted, wavelet, graph-based, and transfer-learning features. A Random Forest classifier serves as the final decision layer. Consistent performance across multiple benchmark datasets indicates that the model does not simply reflect dataset-specific artifacts. Signal quality control is applied exclusively during training rather than as a deployment-time exclusion rule. During deployment, all incoming heartbeats, including noisy segments, are processed without rejection. Robustness beyond high-SNR conditions is validated through noise perturbation experiments and external testing on heterogeneous ECG cohorts (INCART, PTB-XL, Chapman–Shaoxing), confirming that performance does not rely on idealized signal quality. This study is retrospective and based on harmonized public datasets; therefore, label alignment and selection bias may limit generalizability.

Document [7]The goal of this work is to enable the automatic generation of quantum circuits through learned representations that preserve circuit semantics. Traditional approaches relying on unitary matrices or statevectors for analysis are impractical for large-scale applications due to their exponential scaling with the number of qubits. Therefore, we propose an alternative method that leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Contrastive Learning (CL) to learn compact and expressive embeddings of quantum circuits. These embeddings have the potential to allow for efficient downstream tasks such as classification, optimization, and circuit design. A key reason such contrastive features can transfer is that they recover the data's latent spectral or manifold geometry, so structurally similar circuits lie nearby in the learned space. In this work, quantum circuits are represented as graphs, where nodes correspond to quantum gates and edges capture qubit connectivity and gate interactions. A novel CL framework is introduced to learn representations of the circuits in a self-supervised manner, incorporating domain-specific transformations to generate equivalent views of the same circuit. To allow this, an extensive dataset of over 800 non-equivalent quantum circuits is constructed, with a range of qubits going from 3 to 18, and a dynamic depth range based on qubits count. The learned embeddings are tested using a linear evaluation which relies on a linear classifier: with this protocol, we aim at analyzing how effectively the embeddings store information on the circuit structure. Experimental results show that larger embeddings improve the quality of the linear evaluation protocol, achieving high accuracy with a dimensionality significantly smaller than that of the statevector or unitary matrix, respectively scaling as $\mathcal{O}(2^n)$ and $\mathcal{O}(4^n)$. Further analysis on the uncertainty of the linear classifier used in the linear evaluation reveals that increased embedding size not only improves the accuracy of the linear evaluation protocol, but also the confidence in predictions, being more resilient to increasingly complex circuits. By bridging quantum computing and machine learning, this work introduces a scalable and flexible framework for quantum circuit representation. Our findings provide valuable insights into the trade-offs between the size and the quality of the learnt embeddings, offering a foundation for more advanced techniques of automatic generation of quantum circuits.
Document [8]Self-supervised learning (SSL) conventionally relies on the instance consistency paradigm, assuming that different views of the same image can be treated as positive pairs. However, this assumption breaks down for non-iconic data, where different views may contain distinct objects or semantic information. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of SSL when instance consistency is not guaranteed. Through extensive ablation studies, we demonstrate that SSL can still learn meaningful representations even when positive pairs lack strict instance consistency. Furthermore, our analysis further reveals that increasing view diversity, by enforcing zero overlapping or using smaller crop scales, can enhance downstream performance on classification and dense prediction tasks. However, excessive diversity is found to reduce effectiveness, suggesting an optimal range for view diversity. To quantify this, we adopt the Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) as an estimator to measure mutual information between views, finding that moderate EMD values correlate with improved SSL learning, providing insights for future SSL framework design. Humans can effortlessly recognize objects across different viewpoints and contexts. A cat lounging on a couch remains a cat, whether seen from the side or above. Document [0]Unlike contrastive methods, where the presence of explicit negative pairs serves as a primary mechanism for enforcing representational separation, non-contrastive frameworks rely heavily on asymmetry introduced by predictor networks and stop-gradient updates. These elements play a critical role in sustaining representational diversity and structure, even in the absence of pairwise contrastive objectives. The overall findings suggest that collapse is not solely a consequence of the presence or absence of contrastive loss. Instead, successful collapse prevention appears to result from predictor-side asymmetry introduced through stop-gradient updates, together with normalization, which can make feature coordinates compete for limited scale, helping preserve the use of multiple dimensions instead of collapsing into a single direction . It is this combination of asymmetric updates and normalization-driven competition that constitutes the practical key to avoiding collapse and should be regarded as a central design consideration for future self-supervised learning frameworks. 3.4. Theoretical Understanding and Open Challenges of Complete Collapse Despite significant empirical advances in mitigating complete collapse through asymmetric architectural choices and normalization, the theoretical understanding of why these methods work remains incomplete. Most collapse-prevention strategies are empirically observed to be effective, but lack the mathematical guarantees needed to generalize their correctness. Early theoretical efforts to analyze collapse have increasingly focused on the role of symmetry breaking and feature competition. In self-alignment settings, representations can drift toward a constant vector when predictor-side asymmetry is absent and when no mechanism keeps multiple coordinates active. This implies that collapse is not merely a training failure, but depends on whether the learning setup breaks symmetry and preserves diversity across dimensions. Such observations highlight the necessity of understanding how predictor networks, stop-gradient updates, and normalization promote representation diversity and suggest the importance of deriving formal conditions to guide the design of non-contrastive learning frameworks.

Document [2]These practical constraints increase computational complexity and motivate the development of alternative self-supervised learning approaches. Non-Contrastive Alignment Methods: The class of non-contrastive alignment algorithms is a type of self-supervised learning algorithm in which representations are learned by aligning the representations of different transformations of the same input but without using any negative examples explicitly. Rather than forcing differentiation between data points, non-contrastive algorithms ensure that no collapse occurs by making specific architecture choices, such as asymmetric networks, predictor heads, and stop gradients. The BYOL paper first proposed this concept by showing that a student network can predict its target network’s representation without negative pairs . SimSiam further simplified this approach by removing the momentum encoder while retaining a predictor and stop-gradient mechanism . However, despite the efficiency that is gained by not employing contrastive learning, which helps to greatly minimize the computational cost of training as well as the requirement of using large batch sizes and memory banks, the learning target still revolves around aligning representations between views. Repeatedly matching each view to augmentation-consistent targets induces implicit clustering in representation space around those shared targets. Reconstruction self-supervised learning techniques learn representations through reconstruction of the input signal’s missing/corrupted parts. Self-supervised learning is thus introduced by purposefully corrupting the input signal such that the representation learned can recover the signal. Classical self-supervised representation learning was pioneered by autoencoder methods, which have seen substantial development with the introduction of masking in recent years. For example, Masked AutoEncoders (MAE) work on the premise of masking a substantial portion of the input patches and reconstructing them. . Similarly, methods such as BEiT leverage token reconstruction objectives inspired by masked language modeling . Although reconstruction-based SSL effectively exploits partial observability and has demonstrated strong empirical results, these methods operate in input space, which imposes a high-dimensional reconstruction burden and may bias learning toward low-level details rather than semantic abstraction. These limitations motivate alternative approaches that shift the learning objective from input reconstruction to prediction in representation space.

question: Which engineering and theoretical challenges hinder the performance of offline reinforcement learning when training on low-quality or skewed data?
perspectives: Inaccurate value estimates on out-of-distribution actions
Excessive conservatism from behavior constraints or pessimistic penalties
Insufficient trajectory stitching across suboptimal behavioral fragments
Causal confounding and selection bias in logged behavior data

Document [0]In many real-world scenarios, offline-trained agents are later improved further, but effective learning remains sensitive to how values are assigned beyond the actions emphasized during training. Offline RL is particularly vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) action misestimation, where the learned value function assigns inaccurate values to actions outside the data distribution (Fujimoto et al., 2019). These inaccuracies can steer policy updates toward suboptimal or unstable behavior, making subsequent improvement less predictable. Such value errors may also interact with iterative updates in ways that complicate learning (Kumar et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2024). Related concerns about extrapolation error have also been noted in offline settings (Levine et al., 2020). To mitigate these problems, prior work has proposed calibration techniques that aim to improve the reliability of Q-value estimates (Nakamoto et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024).
Document [1]Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning (O20 RL) presents a compelling framework for deploying decision-making agents in domains where online data collection is limited by practical constraints such as cost, risk, or latency. In this paradigm, agents are initially trained on fixed datasets and subsequently refined through limited online interaction. When training relies on logged behavior data rather than randomized interventions, causal confounding and selection bias can make observed action outcomes systematically misleading. However, this transition exposes a fundamental challenge: the misestimation of state-action values associated with out-ofdistribution (OOD) actions, inherited from the offline phase. Such misestimations can severely destabilize online adaptation, leading to suboptimal policy behavior. To address this, we propose an algorithm-agnostic method that regularizes the Q-function prior to fine-tuning by injecting structured noise into dataset actions. This process explicitly bounds Q-value estimates across the entire action space, not just in-distribution actions, mitigating both overestimation and underestimation. We introduce a tunable parameter that governs the degree of conservatism and optimism within the Q-value bounds during the online fine-tuning phase. Extensive empirical evaluations on standard O20 RL benchmarks demonstrate that our method yields substantial improvements over strong baselines, both in terms of stability and final performance. These results underscore the importance of principled Q-function initialization and offer a practical path toward more robust reinforcement learning under distributional shift. By leveraging static datasets, offline RL eliminates the need for online data collection.

question: Which underlying processes drive the degradation of model performance when performing continual test-time adaptation across successive domain changes?
perspectives: Entropy minimization converging to a trivial low-entropy predictor
Catastrophic forgetting from adapting the same parameters across recurring domains
Confirmation bias from self-labeled pseudo-targets during adaptation
Gradient noise from unlabeled online updates under severe shift
context:
Document [0]Of late, test-time entropy minimization has attracted growing interest, as it operates purely unsupervised during inference, without relying on any ground-truth supervision. For example, in test-time adaptation (TTA) (Wang et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2024) it encourages confident predictions to mitigate domain shifts on unseen data streams; in large language models, it helps calibrate uncertainty and improve prediction consistency for alignment (Hu et al., 2025a; Jang et al., 2025). These advances highlight the potential of entropy minimization in unleashing model power during inference, enabling adaptation to novel or out-of-distribution domains and moving toward greater intelligence. However, entropy minimization naturally drives the model to increase the maximum predicted logit, regardless of whether it aligns with the true label. In practice, testing often involves noisy realworld data, domain shifts, or novel environments, where models often tend to be highly sensitive and uncertain, and the predicted maximum class is frequently incorrect. Estos requerimientos son útiles en robots de servicio diseñados para llevar a cabo tareas de vigilancia, inspección, entrega de paquetes, limpieza y exploración. En estas aplicaciones los robots necesitan recolectar medidas de sus sensores en ambientes complejos y extraer información significativa para llevar a cabo sus tareas. Localización y construcción de mapas de manera simultánea (SLAM) es considerada una tarea esencial para los robots móviles inmersos en aplicaciones reales sin requerir información previa acerca del ambiente. La comunidad experta en Robótica ha tratado de solucionar el problema de SLAM de diferentes maneras para representar el ambiente. Esta tesis se ocupa del problema de la localización y construcción de mapas para robots móviles en ambientes complejos. Esto introduce la pregunta de investigación: ¿Cómo un robot móvil puede actualizar su representación interna del entorno y su localización en éste cuando la apariencia del ambiente es cambiante? Este trabajo propone un método de localización y construcción de mapas cuya principal contribución es el Histograma de Estabilidad de las Características (FSH). El FSH es construido usando un sistema de votos: si la característica en el ambiente es re-observada, esta será promovida; de lo contrario, ésta progresivamente disminuye su correspondiente valor en el FSH.

Document [4]A visual-based semantic mapping system can be organized as a process that turns visual observations into object- and place-level meaning. Specific features are first pre-selected based on sensor type, and feature descriptors are computed from the incoming data. Those features or descriptors are then classified in terms of prior knowledge so that objects and places can be recognized. Finally, the resulting properties are endowed with semantic meanings on the basis of topological and metric maps, making the representation a semantic description of the environment rather than only a geometric record. This is the general process for semantic mapping. A metric map in this setting acts as a complementary attribute of the semantic map. Some systems rely on direct image segmentation to obtain semantic information rather than using feature descriptors to represent objects or scenes, but the goal is the same: to recognize objects and places and encode them with semantic labels. Many types of visual sensors have been developed to provide different interpretations of the world, and the subsequent processing methods depend strongly on the data type used. The visual sensor therefore plays a key role in a semantic mapping system, with common visual data ranging from 2D images to 3D point clouds. At an early stage of development, visually recognizing objects or places was commonly done with conventional cameras that record two-dimensional images. In one example, models of indoor Manhattan scenes were acquired from individual images generated from a 2D camera and then assigned semantic labels. Other work captured colour and motion properties with an omni-directional camera for door modelling and detection, and doors were treated as distinguishable landmarks between rooms in indoor environments. Additional studies employed 2D visual data to tackle place recognition in semantic mapping, while object recognition with monocular cameras further enriched the scene representation. Across these examples, previously visited places are represented through recognized objects, labeled scenes, and region-defining landmarks rather than purely low-level visual matches.

Document [8]High-level place representations capture topological relationships and contextual attributes through structured graph-based formats. Graph-based methods model spatial-semantic interactions such as object adjacency and region-level organization, so the description of a place is built from meaningful entities and the way they relate to one another. In this style of representation, a scene is summarized as a structured semantic description rather than reduced to isolated local matches. This abstraction decouples place-recognition systems from any single view of raw appearance and facilitates hierarchical reasoning about place identity. Graphs, including object-based graphs and 3D scene graphs, have therefore emerged as a powerful representation of a place. A graph is a mathematical structure used to model pairwise relations between objects. It consists of vertices, also called nodes, and edges, where the vertices represent the objects and the edges represent the connections or relationships between them. In the context of place recognition, these entities can be landmarks or regions in the scene, and the edges can denote spatial or topological relations between them. Preserving these relationships lets the representation retain contextual structure even when the exact observation changes. Graph representations offer several advantages, including robustness to viewpoint changes, occlusions, and dynamic scenes. They can also store semantic labels to enhance place-recognition accuracy. Recent studies have introduced various graph models to depict places and environments. Co-visibility graphs depict relationships between landmarks and the different viewpoints from which sensors observe these landmarks. Kong et al. constructed a semantic graph that abstracts object instances and their relative position. Topological semantic graphs are designed to organize place structure in a form useful for goal-directed exploration. The Hydra system constructs a hierarchical 3D scene graph that represents places with a hierarchy running from low-level metric support to high-level object semantics. Across these approaches, places are recognized through objects, regions, and their structured relations, while comparing the similarity of two graphs becomes the key challenge in place recognition.

question: Which latent factors constrain the consistency of robotic tasks involving complex physical interactions, such as bending, insertion, or the manipulation of deformable materials?
perspectives: Unobserved contact state and mode transitions
Unknown friction and compliance at the interaction interface
Latent object pose or shape changes during contact
History-dependent material state such as plastic deformation or internal stress

Document [0]Modern approaches to compliant force control emphasize optimizing robot morphology, incorporating compliant actuators, refining transmission mechanisms, and integrating soft materials into end effectors. By physically embedding compliance, these designs reduce computational demands and enhance overall control robustness . This broader literature spans a taxonomy and comparative review of passive, direct, and indirect force-control methods, advanced strategies for robots with complex mechanical structures such as aerial, mobile, cable-driven, and bioinspired platforms, intelligent control algorithms, sensorless force-control approaches, and emerging trends in multimodal sensing and control. Within that landscape, passive compliant control uses a mechanical elastic structure, such as springs or dampers, at the end effector or in the interaction environment so that force control is achieved through the system's inherent elasticity. Because compliance is physically embedded, part of the force-control problem is handled mechanically at the end effector or in the interaction environment itself. This approach remains attractive because it is simple, low cost, and places minimal requirements on the manipulator itself. The passive branch makes the underlying contact mechanics especially explicit because interaction behavior is shaped directly by embedded elasticity rather than by high-bandwidth sensing alone, and the same motivation drives newer hardware trends in robot morphology, transmission design, compliant actuators, and soft end-effector materials. These hardware choices are introduced specifically so that contact behavior becomes safer and more robust before higher-level control is applied, even when more advanced sensing and control methodologies are later added. Even so, passive force-control accuracy remains limited by the complex structure of robotic manipulators, especially nonlinear friction, transmission backlash, and related uncertainties. Those effects prevent precise characterization of the effective compliance along the transmission and at the contact interface, making unknown friction and compliance a fundamental constraint on reliable force regulation.

When direct force/torque sensing is available, controllers can track force references and tighten safety envelopes; otherwise, observers or learned estimators provide wrench/contact-state cues for online monitoring . Across free motion and contact, changing force targets or impedance parameters helps maintain compliant interaction and clearer hooks for runtime safety mechanisms . Finally, high-level task structure and safety rules must be grounded into formal constraints and checked during execution as contact conditions change . Figure 3 provides an overview of this survey. We begin by presenting the background and key definitions in Sec.3 then organize existing approaches from multiple perspectives, covering task characteristics, sensing and policy modalities, data acquisition strategies, simulation environments and benchmarks (Sec.4) and promising future directions (Sec. 5). We summarize how latent contact variables interface with safety in contact-rich manipulation. For variable-impedance forceful skills and insertions, policies must handle changes in contact conditions while preserving compliant interaction. Safety is enhanced by conservative objectives, recovery strategies, and shielded execution (e.g., barrier, reachability, MPC layers) [16, 72–76] Contact sequencing and force behavior (approach, touch, slide) are central in insertion and assembly settings, where the relevant mode switches are often only indirectly observed. Hybrid trajectory-force approaches are prevalent in these settings, and compliant controllers are leveraged during execution . In this survey, we focus on methods with notable online execution concerns, and direct the readers to recent surveys for related methods .

The results reveal three related insights about hidden state in insertion. First, nominally similar end-effector motions can still lead to different outcomes, especially in the real-world setting, showing that the decisive variables are often not directly observed in the commanded pose. Insertion tasks are highly sensitive to contact configuration: even minor misalignments can alter how contact is established at the interface. During contact, small unmeasured shifts in the object's pose or local shape can accumulate, making latent pose or deformation changes hidden variables that determine whether insertion progresses, redirects, or jams. Second, once contact begins, the relevant state is the current contact mode. The system can transition between free motion, sliding contact, and obstructed or wedged contact, and these mode transitions are not fully specified by nominal kinematics alone. Third, across the different proprioceptive conditions, the comparison is most informative as evidence that reliable manipulation depends on tracking these evolving interaction states throughout the task. These interaction states are spatially local, can change abruptly, and become especially consequential on the real robot once physical contact starts. Overall, the table highlights unobserved contact state, together with contact-induced changes in object pose or local shape, as a key hidden variable in contact-rich manipulation.
Document [3]Recent advances in actuator design that emulate the properties of biological muscles, including nonlinear stiffness, damping, and force generation , have improved the ability of bionic robots to interact safely and effectively with complex and dynamic environments . Intelligent control methods have therefore been increasingly integrated into compliant force-control systems to enhance adaptability, robustness, and autonomy when traditional model-based force control struggles with nonlinearities, uncertainties, and dynamic interaction in unstructured environments. Neural networks, fuzzy logic, sliding mode control, and reinforcement learning have all been employed in impedance and admittance control frameworks to achieve compliant interaction with greater flexibility and generalization capability. These intelligent paradigms are introduced precisely because accurate models of the interaction mechanics are hard to obtain when the environment is uncertain. Neural networks are especially well suited for approximating complex nonlinear mappings and compensating for unknown dynamics in robotic systems. Within compliant control, they have been used to estimate system uncertainties and adapt control parameters in real time. Adaptive NN-based controllers have been integrated into impedance control frameworks to enhance compliance and maintain stability under varying environmental conditions . In , a neural-network-adaptive impedance control strategy for manipulators interacting with unknown environments learned nonlinear interaction forces without requiring an accurate system model. Common implementations, including radial basis function and recurrent neural networks, learn dynamic properties while supporting smooth force tracking . Fuzzy logic is also robust for managing uncertainty and imprecision in control systems, and fuzzy impedance control has been applied in uncertain contact settings because its interpretable rule base can be formulated from expert knowledge to dynamically adjust impedance parameters . That emphasis on real-time adaptation reflects the difficulty of fixing the contact model in advance. Across these intelligent compliant-control methods, the central hidden difficulty is uncertainty in contact compliance, stiffness, damping, and force response at the interaction interface.

Typical architectures use a hierarchical split: a languagevision planner selects certified skills/options; mid-level skills expose safety-relevant parameters; low-level safety enforcers (impedance, CBF/MPC, rate limiters) guarantee contact stability and constraint satisfaction during execution [66–69]. In all cases, safety is operationalized through limits on contact forces/pressures and motion, potentially augmented by risk- or semantics-derived rules .
Document [6]Abstract— Contact-rich manipulation requires reliable estimation of extrinsic contacts—the interactions between a grasped object and its environment—which provide essential contextual information for planning, control, and policy learning. However, existing approaches often struggle because the underlying contact state is only partially observed and can change across interactions, which hinders generalization to novel objects and deployment in unstructured environments. In this paper, we present UNIC, a unified multimodal framework for extrinsic contact estimation. UNIC directly encodes visual observations in the camera frame and integrates them with proprioceptive and tactile modalities in a fully data-driven manner. It introduces a unified contact representation based on scene affordance maps that captures diverse contact formations and employs a multimodal fusion mechanism with random masking, enabling robust multimodal representation learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UNIC performs reliably. It achieves a 9.6 mm average Chamfer distance error on unseen contact locations, performs well on unseen objects, remains robust under missing modalities, and adapts to dynamic camera viewpoints. These results establish extrinsic contact estimation as a practical and versatile capability for contact-rich manipulation. The overview and hardware experiment videos are here. Extrinsic contact refers to contact events involving external objects and the environment, beyond the robot’s own body. Estimating extrinsic contact is particularly challenging , as it requires reasoning about interactions that are often indirect, involve multiple objects, and occur under uncertain geometry or dynamics. Nevertheless, extrinsic contact estimation is essential for enhancing robotic dexterity, as it enables robots to perceive and reason about diverse interactions with the environment. From tool use , and non-prehensile manipulation to precise environment interactions , reliable extrinsic contact estimation supports robust performance while ensuring safety and stability in diverse, unstructured settings. Recent research has investigated tactile-based and multimodal approaches for extrinsic contact estimation. However, these methods often must infer latent contact configurations and changes in interaction state from partial observations.
Document [7]Virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness parameters shape the robot's dynamic response so that actual motion follows the desired trajectory while the robot maintains compliant interaction with the environment. In impedance control, impedance represents a measure of the manipulator's dynamic compliance, and the fundamental principle is to generate different levels of compliance to regulate interaction forces during contact. It is the manipulator's measure of dynamic compliance during interaction. Because these virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness settings determine how the manipulator yields against the environment, well-designed impedance parameters significantly influence control performance. These virtual parameters are introduced precisely to tune how the manipulator reacts when it encounters environmental stiffness during force regulation. Traditional constant impedance control remains a simple yet effective approach that is widely used in various fields, including contact force tracking, but it typically assumes a desired constant force and requires prior knowledge of environmental stiffness. That dependence limits its applicability across tasks whose interaction mechanics are not known in advance or do not remain constant. To address this limitation, researchers have explored adaptive variable impedance control for contact force regulation, so that compliance can be adjusted rather than fixed when the environment is uncertain. In , a direct adaptive impedance controller combined a simple filter, an adaptive controller, and an algorithm that maps Cartesian-space control input to physically realizable joint-space torques. In , an impedance controller was introduced to track desired dynamic forces while compensating for uncertainties in the environment's unknown mechanical properties. Ref. considered impedance control from the actuator side and proposed an optimal strategy for a variable-stiffness actuator, with a variable stiffness mechanism aligned in series with the actuator. As intelligent control methods have developed, more studies have focused on learning-based adaptive impedance control for the same reason. Across these methods, reliable force regulation remains constrained by uncertain stiffness, damping, and compliance at the interaction interface, which is why adaptive impedance adjustment is needed.

However, they often center on high-level policy alignment or general-purpose systems, lacking specificity in contact-rich manipulation contexts. This survey also concentrates on the key safety gaps and latent interaction states underlying robot foundation models . Advanced agentic embodied AI sheds light on a generalist robotic system, while the safety issue remains when physical interaction depends on partially observed contact conditions. Safety for VLA robotic generalists lags in physically complex interaction regimes, where contact states are only partially observed and can shift between modes . Hybrid planparameterizefilter stacks that couple semantic/VLM layers with compliant action abstractions and certified online shields improve robustness but remain challenged by contact mode transitions and other unobserved interaction-state changes . Even when geometry is observed, unmeasured history-dependent material state, such as accumulated plastic deformation or residual internal stress, can change the contact response and limit reliable bending or deformable-object manipulation. Advancing VLA safety thus hinges on tighter analytical-data-driven integration for adaptive handling of latent contact evolution and reactive invariance maintenance . Lastly, surveys on human-like manipulation , force/torque control , and safety in robotic manufacturing provide valuable domain-specific insights but remain largely disconnected from the safe learning perspective, especially the standard of safety discussed in . In contrast to the aforementioned surveys, our work uniquely focuses on the intersection of safe learning and contact-rich robotics, where safety must be ensured not only in policy learning but also in dynamic interaction with the environment. We systematically review methods that account for safety during physical contact, discuss open challenges in real-world applications, and outline promising directions for future research. Within that landscape, passive compliant control uses a mechanical elastic structure, such as springs or dampers, at the end effector or in the interaction environment so that force control is achieved through the system's inherent elasticity. Because compliance is physically embedded, part of the force-control problem is handled mechanically at the end effector or in the interaction environment itself. This approach remains attractive because it is simple, low cost, and places minimal requirements on the manipulator itself. The passive branch makes the underlying contact mechanics especially explicit because interaction behavior is shaped directly by embedded elasticity rather than by high-bandwidth sensing alone, and the same motivation drives newer hardware trends in robot morphology, transmission design, compliant actuators, and soft end-effector materials. Extrinsic contact refers to contact events involving external objects and the environment, beyond the robot’s own body. Estimating extrinsic contact is particularly challenging , as it requires reasoning about interactions that are often indirect, involve multiple objects, and occur under uncertain geometry or dynamics. Nevertheless, extrinsic contact estimation is essential for enhancing robotic dexterity, as it enables robots to perceive and reason about diverse interactions with the environment. From tool use , and non-prehensile manipulation to precise environment interactions , reliable extrinsic contact estimation supports robust performance while ensuring safety and stability in diverse, unstructured settings. Recent research has investigated tactile-based and multimodal approaches for extrinsic contact estimation. Document [0]Statistical analysis of 77 relevant publications indicates that the average harvest success rate of robotic end-effectors remains only 76.1%, still far from practical requirements. A central reason is the difficulty of observing the crop and the manipulation scene in natural environments. This limitation stems primarily from the complexity of the natural growing environment. Occlusions by branches or leaves, together with variable lighting conditions, often produce inaccuracies in fruit recognition and positioning, and these perception errors propagate directly into unstable gripping, fruit dropping, and failed harvest attempts during operation. The same observability problem appears in control performance. Despite the diversity of available actuation methods, end-effectors still show limitations in motion planning, real-time obstacle avoidance, and precise execution in complex environments, leading to extended harvest cycles, increased fruit damage, and reduced overall efficiency. The paragraph attributes these shortcomings in large part to limited real-state perception capability: when sensing is inadequate, the robot lacks the reliable scene estimate needed to plan an approach, update its trajectory, and maintain stable contact around the target. Inadequate use of sensors therefore affects both recognition and control, because the robot cannot correct its motion from timely feedback once the scene changes. This lack of dependable feedback is explicitly tied to sensor use. Inadequate sensor integration often leaves the system without real-time feedback during operation, so errors in recognition or positioning are not corrected before they affect grasping and detachment. The broader diversity of fruit and vegetable dimensions and shapes, together with solitary or clustered growth patterns and differing fruit orientations, further raises the burden on perception because the robot must distinguish and localize targets under highly variable visual conditions. Even among fruits of the same variety, differences in size and shape add to the reliability challenge by making target recognition and positioning less repeatable. Under those conditions, fast, stable, and precise harvesting is difficult to achieve when scene understanding is incomplete or delayed.

These observability problems cut across the four tasks considered in this review: monitoring, weeding, spraying, and harvesting. Monitoring and phenotyping depend on spatially referenced estimates of crop state or anomalies, so missed or corrupted observations directly degrade the output. In selective intervention tasks such as weeding and spraying, the robot still depends on dynamic recognition and rapid decision-making in complex natural environments, meaning that weak sensing propagates into incorrect target identification and execution errors. Harvesting is especially sensitive because perception and planning must culminate in a physical interaction that preserves produce integrity, so localisation uncertainty and scene ambiguity turn directly into failed or unstable manipulation. The task set therefore exposes shared autonomy-stack requirements centered on observability rather than any one platform. Whether the robot operates as a UGV, UAV, gantry, or greenhouse system, controlled sensor pose, calibration, and local sensing determine how well it can estimate crop state, remain oriented in the workspace, and place tools accurately. Even when a platform offers repeatability or canopy-level coverage, practical deployment is still bounded by the quality of sensing, recognition, state estimation, and modular sensor capability available in complex field conditions.

question: What is the primary driver of uncertainty that limits the ability to ensure safety in autonomous motion planning for endoluminal or intra-corporeal robotics?
perspectives: I study how anatomical deformation and tissue motion during procedures constrain safe medical robot motion planning.
I study how uncertain tool-tissue interaction forces limit safe autonomous motion inside the body.
I study how imaging and registration errors in localizing anatomy and instruments affect safe medical robotic planning.
I study how partial observability of occluded or subsurface anatomy changes what safe autonomy can guarantee.

Document [0]Together, these contributions create a cohesive framework for perceptually informed, adaptively controlled surgical robotics. The results outline a clear path toward safe, intelligent autonomy in soft-tissue surgery and provide essential building blocks for future deployment in real clinical environments. Toward Autonomous Soft-Tissue Minimal Invasive Surgery: Integrating Learning, Reasoning, Perceiving for Adaptive Surgical Robot Autonomy This thesis investigates the foundations required to achieve adaptive autonomy in soft-tissue surgical robotics. Soft-tissue procedures are defined by continuous, unpredictable anatomical deformation, making autonomous execution dependent on the integration of learned surgical skills, real-time perception, adaptive reasoning, and precise robotic action. To address these challenges, this work develops a unified framework based on four interconnected pillars—Learning, Reasoning, Perceiving, and Acting (LRPA)—and demonstrates its feasibility on clinically inspired phantom scenarios. The first pillar, Learning, focuses on extracting expert surgical competence directly from demonstrations. A domain-adaptive imitation learning framework is developed to recover fine tool trajectories, orientations, and task states for tumor cutting and tissue manipulation. Policies are trained first in high-fidelity simulation, then transferred to real silicone phantoms, achieving an average positional error of 0.2 cm and generalizing to novel anatomical variations. The second pillar, Reasoning, establishes the geometric and anatomical logic needed for autonomous decision-making. This thesis introduces a complete reasoning pipeline for selective vascular clamping in partial nephrectomy, including the extraction of clamping candidates along the arterial tree and the formalization of surgical target points that must remain valid despite intraoperative anatomical motion. The third pillar, Perceiving, provides the system with real-time awareness of soft-tissue behavior. A fast, RGB-D–based deformation tracking method is developed to estimate dense non-rigid motion on organ surfaces. The resulting deformation field enables continuous updates to surgical targets, trajectories, and anatomical landmarks.​ Validation on CT-derived phantoms demonstrates robust performance under external perturbations and visually challenging conditions.
