question: Which reproductive processes account for the decline in crop productivity caused by short-term heat stress during the flowering stage?
perspectives: Disrupted pollen development and viability
Failed anther dehiscence and pollen release
Reduced stigma receptivity or pollen tube growth
Early ovule or embryo abortion after fertilization
context:
Document [0]The world’s leading crops - cereals, oilseeds, and pulses, are produced through sexual reproduction, which involves the fusion of male and female gametes to form seeds. These seeds are the grains or edible parts of the crops that ultimately contribute to the world’s food supply. Successful pollination and fertilization (seed set) play a key role in crop productivity and depend greatly on the environmental conditions in which these processes take place. Transient heatwaves can reduce stigma receptivity and slow pollen tube growth, so fertilization may fail even when pollen reaches the pistil. Reproduction is the most sensitive developmental stage to hot and cold temperatures, drought, combined heat and drought, and salinity stresses (Zinn et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014). Adverse impacts of high-temperature stress on the morphological and quantitative parameters of pollen grains have been reported in many crops, such as maize (Zea mays) (Wang et al., 2019), 2021b), wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Khan et al., 2022), barley (Hordeum vulgare) (Sakata et al., 2010), rice (Oryza sativa) (Endo et al., 2009), field pea (Pisum sativum) (Lahlali et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2015), 2019a, b), common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) (Porch and Jahn, 2001; Prasad et al., 2002), peanut (Arachis hypogaea) (Prasad et al., 1999), cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) (Song et al., 2015), flax (Linum usitatissimum) (Cross et al., 2003), tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) (Giorno et al., 2013), and pepper (Capsicum annum) (Erickson and Markhart, 2002). Drought, like heat stress, can adversely impact male and female organs and contribute to yield reduction in crops (Ishimaru et al., 2022).
Document [1]Anther dehiscence is a pivotal process in the reproductive of flowering plants, enabling the release of pollen for pollination (Figures 1 and 2B). This process begins as the anther matures, triggering changes in endogenous hormone levels, such as JA, auxin, ethylene, and gibberellin (GA), which induce cell wall softening and facilitate dehiscence.43, 44, 45, 46 The inner epidermal cells play a crucial role by undergoing transformation to promote expansion and contraction, generating tension within the anther that prepares it for the final rupture.6, 44 Temperature affects the timing of pollen release, and most plants will crack at a specific temperature threshold. Under high-temperature stress, dehiscence may occur earlier or later than normal, affecting pollen release and potentially compromising pollination success.47, 48, 49 As the anther matures, the epidermal cells within the anther undergo expansion and deposition of secondary thickening. Subsequently, the septum between the two pollen sacs is enzymatically degraded (Figure 2. The anther splits due to the internal pressure from the expanding pollen and dehydration-induced tension.50, 51 The anther wall is typically composed of four layers: the epidermis, endothecium, middle layer, and tapetum.52 Under optimal conditions, the anther wall undergoes PCD to release mature pollen for pollination.
Document [2]HT stress, even for a single day, can alter anther structure in ways that compromise pollen release (Hedhly et al., 2009). The anther is comprised of four pollen sacs, each surrounded by the epidermis, endothecium, middle cell layers, and a secretory tapetum (Figure 4F; Scott et al., 2004; Wilson et al., 2011). Anther opening depends on localized cellular differentiation and degeneration together with changes in anther water status, including enzymatic breakdown of the septum, programmed cell death of the septum, stomium, and endothecium, secondary thickening, pollen swelling, and anther dehydration (Kuriyama and Fukuda, 2002; Sanders et al., 2005; Wilson et al., 2011). Phytohormones, particularly JA and auxin, play important roles in regulating anther dehiscence (Scott et al., 2004; Cecchetti et al., 2008). Deficiencies in JA can delay or prevent dehiscence because JA is involved in tapetal degeneration, septum breakdown, and endothecium thickening, and local increases in auxin can also delay dehiscence by hindering septum breakdown (Ishiguro et al., 2001; Yasuor et al., 2006; Cecchetti et al., 2008.
Document [3]Heatwaves perturb developing anther wall cells and microspores by repressing the expression of *A1 aspartic protease* and its regulator *MYB DOMAIN PROTEIN 80* (Phan et al., 2011; Dündar et al., 2019). The expression of *GIBBERELLIN MYB GENE*, which is located upstream of *PTC1*, *MS1*, and *TDR*, is also sensitive to transient heat stress (Wang et al., 2012). In addition, tapetum cells are equipped with a large number of mitochondria (Wang et al., 2017), and transient heat stress can elevate ROS in tapetum or microspore cells (Mittler, 2017; Xie et al., 2022). Together, these heat-induced molecular and cellular disturbances impair normal microspore development and reduce pollen viability.
Document [4]High temperature is a major concern for the decline in crop growth and productivity (Driedonks et al. 2016 Breeding for plant heat tolerance at vegetative and reproductive stages. Plant Reproduct 29: 67–79")). Heat stress often causes irreversible damage to plant organs and cell structures (Hinojosa et al. 2019 Effect of high temperature on pollen morphology, plant growth and seed yield in quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa Willd.). J Agron Crop Sci 205: 33–45")). Plant reproductive development is more sensitive to high-temperature stress, wherein microsporogenesis and microgametogenesis are severely impacted (Prasad et al. 2017 Field crops and the fear of heat stress—opportunities, challenges and future directions. Field Crop Res 200: 114–121")). Increased temperature disrupts the developmental phases of sexual reproduction by initiating a sequence of physiological, biochemical, molecular, and cellular changes (Lohani et al. 2020 High temperature susceptibility of sexual reproduction in crop plants. J Exp Bot 71: 555–568")). Exposure to high temperatures affects pollen structure, number, cell wall architecture and metabolism, which can lead to reduced plant fertility (Hedhly 2011 Sensitivity of flowering plant gametophytes to temperature fluctuations. Environ Exp Bot 74: 9–16")). Heat stress exposure disrupts the cellular hemostasis of pollen by altering membrane fluidity and protein stability due to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Sharma et al. 2012 Reactive oxygen species, oxidative damage, and antioxidative defense mechanism in plants under stressful conditions. J Bot. )). Pollen has been observed to respond differentially to long-term or short-term heat stress exposure (Bokszczanin et al.
Document [5]This results in increased *RBOHD* gene expression, higher production of H2O2, and consequently a greater accumulation of ROS within the anther.47, 53, 64 Additionally, GAs are involved in regulating the degeneration of the inner layers and initiating dehiscence, thereby influencing anther opening.45 DELLA proteins, the main transcriptional regulators in the GA signaling pathway, inhibit the expression of *Defective in Anther Dehiscence 1* (*DAD1*) genes, suppressing JA and leading to the downregulation of transcription factors *NAC SECONDARY WALL THICKENING PROMOTING FACTORS* (*NST1* and *NST2*), which prevents dehiscence and results in male sterility.53, 65 Recent studies have shown that a decrease in GA levels under heat stress leads to an increase in DELLA proteins, which in turn reduces JA signaling. This suppression of JA signaling ultimately impairs anther dehiscence and causes male sterility.47, 53, 65 Furthermore, heat stress increases ABA levels in the anther, and, in rice, high ABA levels induce ROS accumulation, leading to premature PCD and abnormal degradation of the inner layers.66, 67 Additionally, localized increases in IAA may delay anther dehiscence by inhibiting septum degradation.44, 48 These results suggest that the balanced regulation of hormones plays a crucial role in anther dehiscence under heat stress.
Document [6]HT-induced yield losses during flowering are partly attributable to disrupted flowering behaviors that directly reduce pollen release, especially reduced pollen shedding number due to failure of anther dehiscence in cereal crops (Steinmeyer et al., 2013; Aiqing et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019b; Matsui and Hasegawa, 2019; Chen et al., 2020). When flowering-stage temperatures exceed the HT thresholds of rice, wheat, and maize, seed set and grain number decline significantly, indicating that successful pollen release at anthesis is a major point of vulnerability under short heat episodes (Sanchez et al., 2014). These cereals likely differ in how this dehiscence-related failure is expressed because their floral structures differ. As a monecious crop, maize has separate male tassel and female ear flowers on the same plant, and the tassel is exposed directly to sunlight during flowering. Wheat and rice instead have bisexual flowers, with several florets in each wheat spikelet and a single floret in each fertile rice spikelet (Bortiri and Hake, 2007; Gol et al., 2017). Maize and rice also experience more HT events in space and time than wheat, although temperatures in the paddy field are expected to be more stable for rice growth (Alberto et al., 2009; Matsui et al., 2021). Together, these comparisons keep the paragraph centered on a common flowering-stage outcome: heat reduces seed production in part by limiting pollen shedding through failed anther dehiscence.
Document [7]Prasad et al. (2015 Impact of high temperature stress on floret fertility and individual grain weight of grain sorghum: Sensitive stages and thresholds for temperature and duration. Front Plant Sci 6: 820. ) reported that sorghum showed sensitivity to high-temperature stress 5–10 days before anthesis and 5 days before and after anthesis, highlighting the susceptibility of male reproductive development during these stages. Such loss in seed set can also arise after fertilization, because transient heatwaves can trigger early abortion of fertilized ovules or young embryos before grains develop. They also observed a decrease in the number of grains per panicle under high-temperature stress during flowering and gametogenesis, consistent with injury to pollen development at these stages. Prasad et al. (2017 Field crops and the fear of heat stress—opportunities, challenges and future directions. Field Crop Res 200: 114–121. ) observed that HTs cause impairment of pollen viability and are linked with tapetum layer degeneration. High temperature also reduced pollen germination. Heat stress [42 °C/32 °C (day/night)] at pollen mother cell (PMC) and booting stages disrupts tapetum and pollen development, resulting in decreased grain yield in sorghum. Plants with 9 or fewer days of heat stress showed normal pollen viability, while 12 days caused nonviable pollen grains and loss of grain yield.
Document [8]In addition, Kumar et al. (2013) and Dwivedi et al. (2017) found that the viability of pollen, together with its development and germination, were significantly reduced under high-temperature stress. High-temperature stress during this stage was reported to reduce grain yield per plant, consistent with impairment of pollen function under heat. High temperature had a significant influence on the reproductive growth of wheat plants, and a 1 °C rise above the optimum temperature resulted in a marked decrease in grain yield (Bennet et al. 2012; Yu et al.).
Document [9]During microsporogenesis, microsporocyte (MMC) undergoes two meiotic divisions to form a tetrad of haploid microspores. Then the release microspore divides mitotically to form a large vegetative cell and a small generative cell. Further, the generative cells undergo mitotic division to form 2 germ cells (sperm cells) completing the microgametogenesis phase. Under heat stress conditions, the tapetal cells undergo early degradation and disrupt the sugar-starch metabolism, which leads to pollen sterility or reduced viability. Furthermore, heat treatment affects cell division and significantly alters chromosomal segregation and crossing-over events during meiotic division Heat stress severely affects the morphology of pollen, disrupts cell organelles and pollen wall structure by altering the thickness of intine and exine (Djanaguiraman et al. 2013 Soybean pollen anatomy, viability and pod set under high temperature stress. J Agron Crop Sci 199: 171–177"); Jiang et al. 2015 Seed set, pollen morphology and pollen surface composition response to heat stress in field pea. Plant Cell Environ 38: 2387–2397")). Pollen outer walls originate from tapetal cell, and alteration in pollen morphology during heat stress occurs due to the degeneration of tapetal layer resulting in reduced pollen number and viability (De Storme and Geelen 2014 The impact of environmental stress on male reproductive development in plants: biological processes and molecular mechanisms. Plant, Cell Environ 37: 1–18"); Parish et al. 2012 Tapetal development and abiotic stress: a centre of vulnerability. Funct Plant Biol 39: 553–559")). Morphological abnormalities have been reported in soybean (Djanaguiraman et al. 2013 Soybean pollen anatomy, viability and pod set under high temperature stress. J Agron Crop Sci 199: 171–177")) and common bean (Porch and Jahn 2001 Effects of high-temperature stress on microsporogenesis in heat-sensitive and heat-tolerant genotypes of Phaseolus vulgaris.

question: Which biological processes are responsible for the decline in wheat grain productivity when heat and drought stress occur simultaneously after flowering?
perspectives: Reduced source photosynthesis from stomatal closure and photoinhibition
Impaired grain sink strength and starch synthesis
Accelerated leaf senescence shortening grain filling
Reduced assimilate transport and stem-reserve remobilization
context:
Document [0]The effects of extreme high temperatures on crops have been widely analyzed in several species; wheat , cowpea , soybean , and rice . In the case of wheat, Asseng et al. provided a detailed impact assessment of high temperatures on yield and how critical the adverse effects will be on the production of this crop. Although most of these studies focus on the flowering stage, many evaluations have also been carried out on the other stages of plant development . For example, Wang et al. found differences in photosynthesis and stomatal conductance values between pre-anthesis high temperature acclimated wheat plants and those that had not experienced pre-anthesis heat exposure. As Hay and Walker described, crop yield is affected by heat stress. In this regard, effects on leaf gas exchange and photosynthetic performance have been repeatedly identified in plants . In the first instance, extreme temperatures can affect photosynthesis at the stomatal level under heat stress conditions. In fact, by controlling water vapor and CO2 diffusion, stomata largely contribute to both the rate and the temperature dependence of photosynthesis . Several studies have analyzed plant behavior at the stomatal conductance level under heat-stressed situations, with most indicating inhibition of photosynthesis . Yang et al. also suggested that stomatal responses to high temperature are strongly influenced by water vapor pressure in maize plants.
Document [1]Heat stress also affects plant growth and function (Wahid et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2012). Very little information is available regarding some of these broader effects in crops (Basirirad, 2000; Rennenberg et al., 2006). Overall, drought and heat stresses hamper different physiological functions of plants (Table 2). One of the key physiological phenomena affected by the drought and heat stress in plants is photosynthesis (Farooq et al., 2009b). It is mainly affected due to stomatal limitation, greater susceptibility to photoinhibition and leaf senescence (Wahid et al., 2007). Under combined post-flowering heat and drought in wheat, leaf senescence is accelerated, which shortens the grain-filling period and reduces the time available for assimilate supply to developing kernels. Stomatal closure under drought reduces the CO2 availability, which makes plant more susceptible to photoinhibition (Lawlor and Cornic, 2002). Similarly, heat stress also impairs the process of photosynthesis under these conditions, further reducing assimilate supply during grain filling.
Document [2]Under drought treatment, AGPase activity at 14 DPA was significantly lower than under the control treatment, and in the same period the magnitude of increase in total starch content was also significantly reduced. This close correspondence further supports the conclusion that AGPase activity in the endosperm helps determine the level of starch accumulation during grain filling. The different AGPase activities of the two varieties under the same drought treatment also indicate that genotypes differ in their sensitivity to water deficit, with the drought-resistant variety maintaining stronger AGPase activity than the more susceptible one. It is also important that starch synthases catalyze the next major step of starch synthesis and therefore represent another key factor regulating grain filling. In cereal crops, these starch synthases are subdivided into GBSS, SSS, and SBE. GBSS is mainly involved in amylose synthesis, whereas SSS and SBE are mainly involved in amylopectin biosynthesis. Previous studies have likewise suggested that drought stress can increase amylose biosynthesis in grains. In this study, GBSS activity in both varieties increased under drought stress at 7 DPA but decreased at 14 DPA, and the same stage-dependent pattern was also observed in the proteomics results. The amylose content of Xindong 18, the strongly drought-resistant variety, increased significantly at both 7 and 14 DPA under drought stress, whereas in Xindong 22, the weakly drought-resistant variety, this response was observed only at 7 DPA. These results indicate that drought progressively reduces the endosperm's ability to sustain starch deposition as grain filling advances, even when some early-stage responses transiently favor amylose synthesis. Overall, drought changed the activities of AGPase and starch synthases and reduced starch accumulation in the developing grain sink.
Document [3]Photosynthesis is limited by reduced stomatal conductance under drought stress (Bota et al., 2004). Under heat stress, light-dependent chemical reactions taking place in the thylakoid are among the main sites of damage as a result of high temperature stress. Increased leaf temperature and photon flux density affect the thermo-tolerance adjustment of PSII (Crafts-Brandner and Salvucci, 2002). Together, restricted stomatal conductance and damage to PSII reduce source photosynthesis under combined heat and drought stress.
Document [4]Not much work has been done exclusively on the impacts of dual stress on seed filling and nutritional composition (Awasthi et al., 2014; Sehgal et al., 2017). When combined, these stresses affect various molecular, biochemical and physiological functions, to more severely impair growth, quality, and yield, compared with their individual effects (Rizhsky et al., 2004; Mittler, 2006; Prasad et al., 2008a; Pradhan et al., 2012). Also, the combined heat and drought stress have distinct effects on cellular processes in plants, relative to their individual effects (Rizhsky et al., 2002), 2004; Cairns et al., 2013; Hamidou et al., 2013; Awasthi et al., 2014; Sehgal et al., 2017), suggesting stress-specific responses. Seed filling is a crucial growth stage for all crops, which involves mobilization and transport processes required for importing various constituents, and many biochemical processes for the synthesis of proteins, carbohydrates and lipids in the developing seeds (Barnabás et al., 2008; Prasad et al., 2008a; Awasthi et al., 2014; Farooq et al., 2017a) (Figures 1, 2). Seed filling processes and the accumulation of reserves in the developing and maturing seeds are highly sensitive to environmental changes, which influence the qualitative and quantitative traits of the final yield (Yang and Zhang, 2006) (Figures 3, 4). Heat and drought stress can hinder the accumulation of various seed constituents, primarily starch and proteins (Behboudian et al., 2001; Asthir et al., 2012; Farooq et al., 2017a, b) (Figure 3) through inhibiting the enzymatic processes of synthesis of starch (Ahmadi and Baker, 2001) and proteins (Triboï et al., 2003) (Figure 2).
Document [5]Drought stress severely hampered the gas exchange parameters of crop plants and this could be due to decrease in leaf expansion, impaired photosynthetic machinery, premature leaf senescence, oxidation of chloroplast lipids and changes in structure of pigments and proteins (Menconi et al., 1995). Anjum et al. (2011a) indicated that drought stress in maize led to considerable decline in net photosynthesis (33.22%), transpiration rate (37.84%), stomatal conductance (25.54%), water use efficiency (50.87%), intrinsic water use efficiency (11.58%) and intercellular CO2 (5.86%) as compared to well water control. Many studies have shown the decreased photosynthetic activity under drought stress due to stomatal or non-stomatal mechanisms (Ahmadi, 1998; Del Blanco et al., 2000; Samarah et al., 2009). Stomata are the entrance of water loss and CO2 absorbability and stomatal closure is one of the first responses to drought stress which result in declined rate of photosynthesis. Stomatal closure deprives the leaves of CO2 and photosynthetic carbon assimilation is decreased in favor of photorespiration. Considering the past literature as well as the current information on drought-induced photosynthetic responses, it is evident that stomata close progressively with increased drought stress. It is well known that leaf water status always interacts with stomatal conductance and a good correlation between leaf water potential and stomatal conductance always exists, even under drought stress. It is now clear that there is a drought-induced root-to-leaf signaling, which is promoted by soil drying through the transpiration stream, resulting in stomatal closure. The "non-stomatal" mechanisms include changes in chlorophyll synthesis, functional and structural changes in chloroplasts, and disturbances in processes of accumulation, transport, and distribution of assimilates. In wheat after flowering, simultaneous heat and drought can also slow phloem assimilate transport and weaken remobilization of stem water-soluble reserves to the ears, leaving less carbohydrate available for grain filling.
Document [6]During wheat grain development, high temperature significantly affects starch-related enzyme activities, and these changes directly influence how efficiently the grain sink can synthesize and accumulate starch. Starch in wheat grains is synthesized from sucrose through a coordinated pathway involving sucrose synthase, ADP-glucose pyrophosphorylase, granule-bound starch synthase, soluble starch synthase, starch branching enzyme, and debranching enzyme, all of which regulate the production of amylose and amylopectin. Within this pathway, SuSy is regarded as an important rate-limiting factor in starch synthesis, AGPase catalyzes the formation of ADP-glucose as the primary substrate for starch biosynthesis, GBSS mediates conversion of ADP-glucose into amylose, and SSS, SBE, and DBE collectively regulate amylopectin production. Research on temperature effects on this pathway spans daytime high temperature, nighttime high temperature, and combined day-night high temperature, with daytime heat being the most extensively studied treatment pattern. Lu et al. found that high day temperatures above 30 °C reduced the activities of starch synthesis-related enzymes, including Susy, SSS, AGPase, SBE, and GBSS, while also decreasing starch content. Li et al. showed that similar daytime heat upregulated alpha-amylase activity, enhanced starch degradation, and accelerated starch hydrolysis relative to starch synthase activity, causing starch accumulation to decline. Harris et al. further demonstrated that daytime high temperatures significantly decreased AGPase and SSS activities, with SSS being the most temperature-sensitive enzyme, while effects on SBE, GBSS, and alpha-amylase were comparatively small. Taken together, these studies show that heat depresses grain sink strength by directly impairing the enzymatic machinery required for starch synthesis and by shifting metabolism away from net starch accumulation.
Document [7]High temperature appears to reduce grain biomass mainly through suppression of AGPase and SSS activities, which weakens the grain sink's capacity for starch biosynthesis and ultimately diminishes starch deposition. Heat also altered the timing of starch biosynthesis, inducing earlier peaks in gene expression during this process. Under high-temperature conditions, the transcriptional profiles of starch synthesis-related genes such as AGPase, SSS, and SBE differed across developmental stages, especially at 7 and 14 DPA, showing that the starch-biosynthetic program was disrupted during active grain filling. Lu et al. further demonstrated that high day temperatures above 30 °C downregulated most starch-biosynthesis genes, including AGPL1, AGPL2, AGPS1-a, AGPS1-b, AGPS2, SSI, SSIIa, SSIIb, SSIIc, SSIIIa, SSIIIb, SSIV, GBSSI, GBSSII, BEI, BEIIa, BEIIb, BEIII, ISA1, PUL, PHOL, and PHOH, and this broad suppression led to reduced amylose, amylopectin, and total starch content. Chunduri et al. examined both daytime high temperature at 35/17 °C and combined day-night high temperature at 35/24 °C and found that the starch transporter gene BT1 showed earlier expression under daytime heat but lower expression under day-night heat. The same study also reported decreased expression of AGPL1, AGPS1, GBSSI, GBSSII, SS1, SS2, SS3, ISA1, and ISA2, together with reduced expression of the transcription factors TaRSR1 and OsbZIP58 under both temperature regimes. Even if some starch-degrading enzymes respond differently depending on genotype or temperature regime, the dominant effect described here is that heat suppresses the genes and enzymes required for starch synthesis, leaving the developing grain with lower capacity to accumulate starch.

Document [9]Drought and heat stress causes significant reductions in growth and yield of several important crops; however, the extent of damage depends upon crop growth stage and severity of the stress. In general, the reproductive phase is more sensitive to the stresses causing a substantial reduction in the yield. Water relations are influenced by certain factors including the leaf water potential, leaf and canopy temperature, transpiration rate, and stomatal conductance. Exposure to drought stress disturbs all these factors in plants however, stomatal conductance is affected the most (Farooq et al., 2009b). A significant reduction in the leaf water potential and transpiration rate was observed under the drought conditions which ultimately increased the leaf and canopy temperature (Turner et al., 2001). Another important feature for plant physiological regulation is water use efficiency which is the ratio of the dry matter accumulated to the water consumed (Monclus et al., 2006). Efficient cultivars of wheat have higher water use efficiency under drought stress (Abbate et al., 2004). This improvement in the water use efficiency is mainly due to the accumulation of the dry matter by consuming less amount of water due to the closing of stomata and less rate of transpiration. A reduced water use efficiency was observed in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) when exposed to an early season water shortage and it ultimately resulted in poor biomass accumulation and yield (Costa et al., 1997).

Document [5]Drought stress severely hampered the gas exchange parameters of crop plants and this could be due to decrease in leaf expansion, impaired photosynthetic machinery, premature leaf senescence, oxidation of chloroplast lipids and changes in structure of pigments and proteins (Menconi et al., 1995). Anjum et al. (2011a) indicated that drought stress in maize led to considerable decline in net photosynthesis (33.22%), transpiration rate (37.84%), stomatal conductance (25.54%), water use efficiency (50.87%), intrinsic water use efficiency (11.58%) and intercellular CO2 (5.86%) as compared to well water control. Many studies have shown the decreased photosynthetic activity under drought stress due to stomatal or non-stomatal mechanisms (Ahmadi, 1998; Del Blanco et al., 2000; Samarah et al., 2009). Stomata are the entrance of water loss and CO2 absorbability and stomatal closure is one of the first responses to drought stress which result in declined rate of photosynthesis. Stomatal closure deprives the leaves of CO2 and photosynthetic carbon assimilation is decreased in favor of photorespiration. Considering the past literature as well as the current information on drought-induced photosynthetic responses, it is evident that stomata close progressively with increased drought stress. It is well known that leaf water status always interacts with stomatal conductance and a good correlation between leaf water potential and stomatal conductance always exists, even under drought stress. It is now clear that there is a drought-induced root-to-leaf signaling, which is promoted by soil drying through the transpiration stream, resulting in stomatal closure. The "non-stomatal" mechanisms include changes in chlorophyll synthesis, functional and structural changes in chloroplasts, and disturbances in processes of accumulation, transport, and distribution of assimilates. In wheat after flowering, simultaneous heat and drought can also slow phloem assimilate transport and weaken remobilization of stem water-soluble reserves to the ears, leaving less carbohydrate available for grain filling.
Document [6]During wheat grain development, high temperature significantly affects starch-related enzyme activities, and these changes directly influence how efficiently the grain sink can synthesize and accumulate starch. Starch in wheat grains is synthesized from sucrose through a coordinated pathway involving sucrose synthase, ADP-glucose pyrophosphorylase, granule-bound starch synthase, soluble starch synthase, starch branching enzyme, and debranching enzyme, all of which regulate the production of amylose and amylopectin. Within this pathway, SuSy is regarded as an important rate-limiting factor in starch synthesis, AGPase catalyzes the formation of ADP-glucose as the primary substrate for starch biosynthesis, GBSS mediates conversion of ADP-glucose into amylose, and SSS, SBE, and DBE collectively regulate amylopectin production. Research on temperature effects on this pathway spans daytime high temperature, nighttime high temperature, and combined day-night high temperature, with daytime heat being the most extensively studied treatment pattern. Lu et al. found that high day temperatures above 30 °C reduced the activities of starch synthesis-related enzymes, including Susy, SSS, AGPase, SBE, and GBSS, while also decreasing starch content. Li et al. showed that similar daytime heat upregulated alpha-amylase activity, enhanced starch degradation, and accelerated starch hydrolysis relative to starch synthase activity, causing starch accumulation to decline. Harris et al. further demonstrated that daytime high temperatures significantly decreased AGPase and SSS activities, with SSS being the most temperature-sensitive enzyme, while effects on SBE, GBSS, and alpha-amylase were comparatively small. Taken together, these studies show that heat depresses grain sink strength by directly impairing the enzymatic machinery required for starch synthesis and by shifting metabolism away from net starch accumulation.

question: How do variations in the food matrix account for the divergent bioaccessibility of micronutrients in processed products that share a comparable overall composition?
perspectives: Microstructural disintegration and particle-size effects during mastication and digestion
Protein- and polysaccharide-mediated nutrient binding or encapsulation
Lipid-phase organization and emulsification effects on mixed-micelle formation
Antinutrient chelation and enzymatic release of bound minerals

Document [0]A comparison of not only the nutrient composition but also the way nutrients are assembled in plant cells, which make up tissues and organs, provides insight into how different plant materials are likely to be disassembled during food processing and digestion. For this purpose, plant storage organs represent the highest level of structure described, and typically provide nutrient-rich foods that are grown and harvested for human consumption, including leguminous seeds, cereal grains, tubers, modified stems (e.g. potatoes) and tree nuts. Characteristic multiscale features of plant food span from mm dimensions of the plant organ (e.g. almond seeds) to the nm scale of intra-cellular contents. Mastication is the first stage of the digestion process and consists of breaking down the plant food ingested into smaller particles as well as lubricating it with saliva in order to facilitate its progression through the oesophagus. During mastication, the food matrix becomes greatly transformed with an increase in surface area and formation of a bolus. When subjected to mastication, cells within a plant food tissue can either rupture or separate. For example, the cells of cooked (hydrothermally processed) legumes tend to separate, whereas the cells of raw, hard food structures such as nuts usually rupture.
Document [1]**: ** Due to their combination of featured properties, protein and polysaccharide-based carriers show promising potential in food bioactive ingredient encapsulation, protection, and delivery. The formation of protein–polysaccharide complexes and conjugates involves non-covalent interactions and covalent interaction, respectively. The common types of protein–polysaccharide complex/conjugate-based bioactive ingredient delivery systems include emulsion (conventional emulsion, nanoemulsion, multiple emulsion, multilayered emulsion, and Pickering emulsion), microcapsule, hydrogel, and nanoparticle-based delivery systems. This review highlights the applications of protein–polysaccharide-based delivery vehicles in common bioactive ingredients including polyphenols, food proteins, bioactive peptides, carotenoids, vitamins, and minerals. The loaded food bioactive ingredients exhibited enhanced physicochemical stability, bioaccessibility, and sustained release in simulated gastrointestinal digestion. However, limited research has been conducted in determining the in vivo oral bioavailability of encapsulated bioactive compounds. An in vitro simulated gastrointestinal digestion model incorporating gut microbiota and a mucus layer is suggested for future studies. Food bioactive ingredients are compounds that exert health-promoting properties via modulating physiological or cellular activities, such as antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, and immunomodulating activities . Hence, development of functional foods by incorporating bioactive compounds is a promising strategy to improve human nutrition and health. However, it is challenging to simply add bioactive ingredients into food product matrices owing to the poor water solubility, low physicochemical stability, off-flavor, and limited bioaccessibility and bioavailability of many bioactive ingredients . Designing suitable delivery systems for bioactive ingredients has proven to be an effective approach to overcome these shortcomings. As the two abundant food macromolecules, proteins and polysaccharides have been widely used to fabricate carriers for encapsulating bioactive ingredients .
Document [2]The size of masticated particles varies greatly between food boluses, with particle dimensions ranging from 5 μm to 3 cm(41, 42). However, a degree of similarity was found among plant food categories: nuts, for instance, tend to have smaller particles than vegetables such as cauliflower, radish and carrot. For boluses formed from hard, brittle foods such as almonds, the inter-individual variability in particle size distribution is small, even though individuals can have different mastication strategies(39, 42, 43). However, for certain other plant food boluses, for example cooked rice (i.e. boiled in water), the particle size distribution differs greatly between individuals(44). The bolus particle size distribution, which reflects the extent of deformation and disintegration of a plant food, is an important parameter, as it affects the subsequent digestion processes including gastric emptying and sieving(43) and nutrient digestibility in the small intestine(7, 16). The extent to which these masticated foods disintegrate depends on the structural characteristics of the plant tissue(1). Once masticated, plant foods such as nuts and raw vegetables are swallowed and enter the stomach via the oesophagus. In the antrum of the stomach, the particles of food may be further eroded, increasing the available surface area. The stomach acts as a short-term storage reservoir, and thus controls the delivery of chyme to the duodenum. Simultaneous chemical and mechanical processes facilitate further breakdown of food. For digestion to occur in the stomach, the food ingested should therefore be transformed into particles that have a surface that allows the penetration of the endogenous compounds essential for digestion, such as enzymes (i.e. pepsin and gastric lipase) and acids(45).
Document [3]Substantial research efforts have been made to develop food-grade curcumin delivery vehicles in order to overcome the challenges and effectively deliver curcumin in targeted physiological sites . Different types of curcumin delivery systems have been fabricated using protein–polysaccharide conjugates or complexes as building blocks, including core-shell nanoparticle, composite nanoparticle, microcapsule, emulsion, and hydrogel-based delivery systems. In the past decade, a wide range of protein–polysaccharide complexes have been designed to fabricate core-shell nanoparticles for curcumin delivery, such as casein–soy polysaccharide , pea protein–carboxymethylated corn fiber gum , cationized gelatin and sodium alginate , insect protein–chitosan , native and succinylated pea protein–chitosan , whey protein–gum arabic , and soybean protein isolate–fucoidan complexes . Encapsulation efficiencies of curcumin in these developed core-shell nanoparticles ranged from 30–99% . The curcumin-loaded casein–soy polysaccharide nanoparticles showed long-term dispersion stability after 30 days of storage at 25 °C . Likewise, the chemical, thermal, and photo stabilities of encapsulated curcumin have been significantly improved. Specifically, lysozyme–A. Sphaerocephala Krasch polysaccharide complex nanoparticles increased curcumin stability at physiological pH in aqueous buffer . Approximate 75% of free curcumin degraded in phosphate buffer within 6 min, while 59% and 46% of encapsulated curcumin remained stable after 24 h and 48 h incubation, respectively . Compared to free curcumin (15%), curcumin-loaded pea protein–carboxymethylated corn fiber gum nanoparticles showed a significantly higher thermal stability (95%) after heat treatment (80 °C, 30 min, pH 3.5) .

For example, the comminution of whole nuts, seeds, legumes and cereals upon chewing might possibly be different depending on whether these are provided as such or incorporated in an embedding matrix such as bread or a muesli bar. In general, the implications of certain structural features of plant foods for digestion need to be understood further. For intact plant structures, nutrient release appears linked to particle size and the persistence of residual microstructure during digestion. Plant food material can be disintegrated further in the gastric compartment by the simultaneous action of a low pH, mixing and the enzyme pepsin.
Document [5]The true bioavailability of a nutrient being intrinsically coupled to the specific food matrix in which it occurs remains poorly considered in nutrition science. During digestion, the food matrix and, in particular, the structure of food modulate the extent and kinetics to which nutrients and bioactive compounds make themselves available for absorption. In this perspective, we describe an integrated look at the effect of structure on nutrient bioavailability in plant foods. Based on this integrated look, cell wall integrity and the particle size of the plant material during its transit in the small intestine determine the bioavailability of plant nutrients; in turn, cell wall integrity and particle size are determined by the level of oral processing and, accordingly, what subsequently escapes digestion in the upper intestine and is utilized by colon microbiota. Ultimately, the effect on nutrient digestion is linked to food structure through each step of digestion. A consideration of the structure rather than just the composition of foods opens up possibilities for the design of healthier foods. © 2018 Society of Chemical Industry Keywords: food matrix; structure; digestion; bioavailability; health Nutrition science has traditionally used a reductionist approach to investigate the link between food and health. Based on this approach, the health potential of foods and diets mainly depends on the content of nutrients or bioactive compounds.1, 2 However, we ingest foods, not nutrients, and foods are not simply vectors for nutrients in the human body (such as a pill is for a drug). Despite the concept of bioavailability (ie, the fact that only a fraction of dietary nutrients is actually available to our body) being long recognized, bioavailability studies still often focus on isolated nutrients or simple vector systems. In other words, the true bioavailability of a nutrient being intrinsically coupled to the specific food matrix in which it occurs remains poorly considered.3, 4 In the present study, we define food matrix as “the whole of the food components, their molecular interactions and spatial organization at different scales”.5 Digestion comprises the moment where the food matrix mostly exerts this modulating effect on health.
Document [6]Regarding photo stability, it was reported that after 90 min of UV radiation, the residual levels of curcumin in the free and nanoencapsulated forms (pea protein isolate–high methoxyl pectin complexes) were 4% and 34%, respectively . In addition, the release profile and oral bioavailability of encapsulated curcumin are of great significance for achieving its health-promoting activities. The release kinetics of curcumin from insect protein–chitosan nanoparticles were determined under the simulated oral, gastric, and intestinal conditions . More than 90% of encapsulated curcumin was released after the simulated digestion process, including 6.3% in oral phase, 8.2% in gastric phase, and 78.1% in intestinal phase. A recent study demonstrated that the oral bioavailability of curcumin loaded in casein–soy polysaccharide complexes increased 3.4-fold in blood of mice compared to the curcumin/Tween 20 treatment . Furthermore, encapsulated curcumin in core-shell nanoparticles showed better antioxidant and anticancer activities in vitro compared to free curcumin . Likewise, encapsulation of curcumin in protein–polysaccharide composite nanoparticles has gained significant research attention. The possible encapsulation mechanism of these nanoparticles is that the formation of protein–polysaccharide complexes results in protein unfolding and exposure of the hydrophobic pockets, which facilitate curcumin binding to the protein moiety of complexes via hydrophobic interactions . Encapsulation efficiencies of curcumin in composite nanoparticles are usually higher than 80% . Moreover, curcumin-encapsulated composite nanoparticles have shown great potential in food applications owing to their high dispersion stability and color stability . For example, curcumin-loaded composite nanoparticles (whey protein isolate–sodium alginate nanocomplex) possessed acceptable dispersion stability (no obvious precipitates) in model food processing and storage conditions, such as high concentrations of sucrose and NaCl, and heat treatment at 90 °C for 2 h .
Document [7]Core-shell structure is one of the most common morphologies of protein–polysaccharide hybrid nanoparticles, as shown in Figure 2g. To produce core-shell nanoparticles, particles are first formed by creating protein nanoparticles as the inner core, followed by coating the protein core with hydrophilic polysaccharide as the shell structure . Core-shell nanoparticles are often manufactured to encapsulate and deliver hydrophobic bioactive compounds (e.g., curcumin) due to the mostly hydrophobic interactions occurring with hydrophobic proteins such as zein . Overall, the protein inner core provides good protection for the encapsulated compounds whereas the polysaccharide shell layer prevents particle aggregation and enhances stability by generating strong steric and electrostatic repulsions . Composite nanoparticles are generated by formation of the protein–polysaccharide complexes prior to loading of bioactive compounds, as illustrated in Figure 2h . It was demonstrated that hydrophobic interaction, electrostatic interaction, and hydrogen bonding played vital roles in the formation of zein–propylene glycol alginate composite nanoparticles. These composite nanoparticles functioned as a promising β-carotene delivery system by improving the physicochemical stability and controlled release of the hydrophobic compound . Recently, Chen et al. reported that modification of zein–chitosan composite nanoparticles by atmospheric cold plasma treatment increased the encapsulation efficiency and dispersion stability of loaded resveratrol compared to untreated nanoparticles. The increased encapsulation efficiently was ascribed to the enhanced interaction between zein and chitosan after atmospheric cold plasma treatment . 4. Applications of Protein–Polysaccharide Complexes/Conjugates as Delivery Systems for Food Bioactive Ingredients Food bioactive ingredients commonly loaded in the protein–polysaccharide-based delivery vehicles include polyphenols, proteins, bioactive peptides, carotenoids, vitamins, minerals, and essential oils .
Document [8]During passage through the stomach, the combined action of soaking in an aqueous environment and a low pH may cause swelling of the cell wall and the partial dissolution of pectin from the cell walls of the plant material. This dissolution of pectin from middle lamella may contribute to the disintegration of the plant particles upon mixing induced by peristaltic contractions, such as a decrease in the average particle size, as reported for carrot cubes and raw almonds.49 Clearly, the rate of disintegration is inversely proportional to the particle size because it will take longer for the gastric juice to travel to the core of a comparatively larger particle. In addition, pectin dissolution from primary cell wall may also increase the permeability of the cell wall. Mineral bioaccessibility can also remain low when phytate or other antinutrients chelate iron, zinc or calcium within the matrix, whereas soaking or endogenous phytase activity can enzymatically release those bound minerals. Both particle size reduction and the enlargement of cell wall pores may increase the release of intracellular material even though we did not find any increase in starch digestibility from isolated, intact kidney beans pre-soaked in gastric juice for 2 h, 19 which suggests a limit effect of gastric juice on cell wall permeability. The particle size distribution of boluses at the moment of swallowing and the amount of material released from fractured cells would also affect the extent to which digestive fluids can access the interior of particles during digestion.14
Document [9]However, food classifications based on nutritional composition solely fail to include nutrient release patterns, which significantly affect physiological responses. Therefore, such classifications do not give a complete image of the nutritional quality of the food, hereby insufficiently informing consumers. Therefore, in the last decades, new types of classifications were on the rise, such as the NOVA classification, based on the extent and purpose of processing. The NOVA classification groups foods into four categories from unprocessed over (minimally) processed foods or ingredients to ultra-processed food products . Especially ultra-processed foods gained much attention, also from consumers, as they are often linked with negative health effects . In practice, ultra-processed foods are identified based on the number of ingredients they contain and specifically the presence of one or multiple ingredients not used in a regular kitchen . It should be noted however, that it is not processing itself that causes food products to be unhealthy, but rather the combination of ingredients, created or isolated through processing, into a food product. Those ultra-processed foods are frequently made from individual, disintegrated ingredients so the final product has no or little natural structure, resulting in a (too) fast digestion. In other words, the (micro)structural organization of nutrients within a food product (and the lack thereof in ultra-processed foods) is most probably a determining factor in foods’ nutritional functionality and consequently health effects. For lipophilic micronutrients, the supramolecular organization of the lipid phase and the extent of emulsification during processing govern mixed-micelle formation and thus how efficiently those compounds become bioaccessible, even in foods with similar fat contents. Hence, researchers shifted from studying food composition towards studying food structural properties and their influence on nutrient digestion or bioaccessibility . These structural properties are frequently engineered by targeted food design (e.g. processing and/or formulation) to steer the nutrient functionality. This review will therefore give a brief overview of recent engineering approaches to steer food (micro- )structure and in turn nutrient digestion kinetics and/or bioaccessibility. Specific attention will be given to the cases of food processing and food (re)formulation as strategies to regulate food microstructure and in turn nutrient release, digestibility and/or bioaccessibility.

question: By what processes is the liberation of volatile aroma compounds hindered in food systems with elevated protein or fat content?
perspectives: Partitioning of odorants into the lipid phase
Reversible binding of odorants to proteins or polysaccharides
Diffusion limitation through a viscous or glassy matrix
Saliva-triggered displacement and release only during oral processing

Document [0]This device was composed of two stainless steel pipes, each one adjustable in height and mobile enough to be adapted to the morphology of each subject. Air was drawn in at a rate of 30 mL/min and introduced into the reaction chamber of the PTR-MS instrument through a heated (60 C) Teflon transfer line. The ratio E/N (E is the electric field and N is the number density of the gas in the drift tube) was 150.6 ((1.2) Td (Townsend; 1 Td = 10-17 V 3 cm2 ). The count rate of H20-H3Oþ was 3.1-3.5% of the count rate of H 16Oþ ions, which was (4.3-5.5) 106 count s-1 . The responses for the three compounds sufficiently exceeded the baseline (the signal-to-noise ratio varied from 8 to 12 depending on the measured m/z). Four experienced subjects (female, aged 25-34 years) participated in the in-nose analyses. All subjects underwent one training session, performing at least three practice runs prior to analysis to familiarize themselves with the protocol. The sessions ran over 4 weeks, two sessions per week, and each one lasted 45 min. Eight replicates were performed by each panelist for each product. The samples were presented in a monadic way and were distributed using a Latin quare design for each assessor. After monitoring the air in the room for 10 s, the assessors were asked to connect themselves to the sampling device and to breathe normally for 30 s. After the absence of aroma compounds in the assessors’ breaths had been verified, a 4 g portion of the product served at 13 C was taken into the mouth. Once in the mouth, saliva can displace aroma compounds retained by the matrix, so part of the volatile release occurs only during oral processing. No instructions were given to the assessors regarding how to consume the product. They were only asked to indicate with a beep every time they swallowed.
Document [1]The concentration- and time-dependent release of aldehydes and diacetyl was studied in systems differing in oil content. Dynamic headspace sampling was used to collect the volatile compounds. In the concentration-dependent release experiment, the amounts released decreased with increasing oil content. The volatile compounds were released more rapidly from the aqueous system than from the pure oil. The release over time showed linear or exponential relationships. These results indicate that increasing oil content can retain volatile compounds in the lipid phase and thereby reduce their release. Release of flavour compounds during consumption is a key quality parameter of food and beverages. Several studies have shown that the perceived flavour of a food differs from the odour before ingestion (Taylor, 1996, Taylor and Linforth, 1996), Taylor and Linforth, 1998). Document [0]Here, we summarize the current understanding how ACLY affects the innate and adaptive immune systems, in particular, its roles in modulating metabolic and epigenetic alterations in immune cells. In addition, we discuss alternative sources of acetyl-CoA and their relevance for immune responses. ACLY is a ubiquitous homotetrameric enzyme, which is localized in the cytosol and the nucleus (17). It catalyzes the production of cytosolic acetyl-CoA, generating a substrate for de novo biosynthesis of fatty acids and cholesterol (16). It also provides acetyl-CoA for acetylation of cytosolic and nuclear proteins, such as histones, thus connecting metabolism with epigenetic control of gene expression (17). In mammals, ACLY expression is particularly high in lipogenic tissues, such as adipose tissue, liver or lactating mammary glands (18). Notably, deletion of the Acly gene in mice results in embryonic lethality (19). Moreover, ACLY is known to be highly expressed in many types of cancer cells, supporting proliferation through de novo lipogenesis, and making this enzyme a promising target of anti-cancer drugs (20). ACLY uses an essential intermediate of the TCA cycle, citrate, as a substrate. Citrate is transported out of the mitochondria predominantly through the mitochondrial citrate carrier, SLC25A1, in exchange for malate (21). In the presence of ATP and CoA, ACLY cleaves citrate to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate (22). Acetyl-CoA is then carboxylated to malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), initiating de novo fatty acid synthesis. Oxaloacetate is reduced to malate by cytosolic malate dehydrogenase (MDH), providing a source of NAD+ to support glycolysis. With SLC25A1-mediated transport of malate back into mitochondria, this cycle is known as the malate-citrate shuttle (23, 24) ( ).

Just like hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to effectively trap it inside the cell to commit it to downstream metabolism, acetate is captured by ACSS2 and primed for metabolic use. In addition to taking up exogenous acetate, our results demonstrate that ACSS2 recaptures acetate released by deacetylation processes to retain it in the cell. It is the combination of these two activities that determines the net acetate uptake rate. An important aspect of our work is the determination of acetate utilization fluxes, which makes clear that intracellularly generated acetate is not simply lost to the medium. In hypoxia and low serum, on the other hand, despite reduced growth of both MDA-MB-468 and BT-474 cells, fatty acid biosynthesis is significantly elevated. This may explain the increased efficiency of lipogenic inhibitors under these conditions (Schug et al., 2015; Peck et al., 2016). Acetyl-CoA is also required for protein acetylation reactions, which are important in post-translational modifications. Acetyl coenzyme A may be synthesized in the cytosol from citrate generated in mitochondria. This transfer is dependent on citrate formation and export. For this process, mitochondrial acetyl-CoA is first condensed with oxaloacetate by citrate synthase thus producing citrate and free CoA. Citrate is then exported to the cytosol through the mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1. Here, acetyl-CoA generation is mediated by the activity of the ATP-cytrate lyase (ACL), which catalyzes the ATP-dependent cleavage of citrate into oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA (Chypre et al., 2012). Finally, the malate dehydrogenase 1, NAD (soluble; MDH1) converts cytosolic oxaloacetate by catalyzing the NADH-dependent synthesis of malate, linking this reaction to broader cellular metabolism. Given its key role in the production of cytosolic acetyl-CoA, it is not surprising that ACL serves several and crucial functions in mammal metabolism (Wellen et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2014), 2015; Das et al., 2015; Covarrubias et al., 2016; Deb et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; White et al., 2018). Although ACL resides mainly in the endoplasmic reticulum in mammalian cells (Chypre et al., 2012), it can be found also in the nucleus (Wellen et al., 2009).

Document [0]- Folate metabolism is compartmentalized between the cytoplasm and the mitochondria of mammalian cells. Certain folate-dependent enzymes are present in both of these compartments, such as methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases, which are required to interconvert one-carbon-substituted tetrahydrofolates. In the cytoplasm, there is a trifunctional NADP-dependent methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase-cyclohydrolase-synthetase (DCS). Its mitochondrial counterpart is a bifunctional NAD-dependent methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase-cyclohydrolase (NMDMC), expressed during embryogenesis and in immortalized cells. A comparison of the 3' untranslated region of the NMDMC cDNA with the synthetase domain of the DCS cDNA and gene among different species revealed significant regions of homology. This suggests that the mammalian mitochondrial NAD-dependent DC evolved from an NADP-dependent DCS precursor through a change in cofactor specificity of the dehydrogenase from NADP to NAD. Although the folate pathways are compartmentalized, the mitochondrial folate pathway makes an important contribution to total cellular folate metabolism. Mouse fibroblasts that have a completely inactivated NMDMC gene are glycine auxotrophs. Furthermore, growth of these Nmdmc-/- cell lines is stimulated by supplementation with formate or hypoxanthine. These cell lines also show enhanced incorporation of radioactivity into DNA from formate as compared with serine, demonstrating that formate is a preferred one-carbon donor for the Nmdmc-/- cell lines. This indicates that NMDMC is required for optimal purine biosynthesis during periods of rapid cellular proliferation such as embryogenesis and tumorigenesis. Rescue of these Nmdmc-/- cell lines with NMDMC expression reverses the glycine auxotrophy and shifts the formate-to-serine incorporation ratio back toward the wild-type ratio.

Document [0]- Folate metabolism is compartmentalized between the cytoplasm and the mitochondria of mammalian cells. Certain folate-dependent enzymes are present in both of these compartments, such as methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases, which are required to interconvert one-carbon-substituted tetrahydrofolates. In the cytoplasm, there is a trifunctional NADP-dependent methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase-cyclohydrolase-synthetase (DCS). Its mitochondrial counterpart is a bifunctional NAD-dependent methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase-cyclohydrolase (NMDMC), expressed during embryogenesis and in immortalized cells. A comparison of the 3' untranslated region of the NMDMC cDNA with the synthetase domain of the DCS cDNA and gene among different species revealed significant regions of homology. This suggests that the mammalian mitochondrial NAD-dependent DC evolved from an NADP-dependent DCS precursor through a change in cofactor specificity of the dehydrogenase from NADP to NAD. Although the folate pathways are compartmentalized, the mitochondrial folate pathway makes an important contribution to total cellular folate metabolism. Mouse fibroblasts that have a completely inactivated NMDMC gene are glycine auxotrophs. Furthermore, growth of these Nmdmc-/- cell lines is stimulated by supplementation with formate or hypoxanthine. These cell lines also show enhanced incorporation of radioactivity into DNA from formate as compared with serine, demonstrating that formate is a preferred one-carbon donor for the Nmdmc-/- cell lines. This indicates that NMDMC is required for optimal purine biosynthesis during periods of rapid cellular proliferation such as embryogenesis and tumorigenesis. Rescue of these Nmdmc-/- cell lines with NMDMC expression reverses the glycine auxotrophy and shifts the formate-to-serine incorporation ratio back toward the wild-type ratio.

Document [0]Ferroptosis is described here as a non-apoptotic cell-death program marked by widespread lipid peroxidation, and although the paragraph notes the broader setting of disrupted metabolism, its mechanistic emphasis falls on CPR as a central driver because CPR facilitates ROS generation through its electron-transfer functions. The paragraph ties that CPR-dependent ROS production directly to the peroxidation of PUFA-containing phospholipids, identifying those membrane lipids as the substrates that are oxidized during ferroptotic injury and stating that their oxidation yields lipid hydroperoxides such as PL-PUFA-OOH. Those oxidized phospholipids are then described as membrane-destabilizing species that push the cell into ferroptosis, so the relevant causal chain is CPR-linked ROS formation, phospholipid peroxidation, membrane damage, and cell death. The text also explains why this oxidative process is not restrained once it begins: ROS-induced damage worsens when GSH is depleted, GPX4 activity decreases, and the cellular machinery that would normally neutralize lipid peroxides is impaired. In that setting, lipid peroxide detoxification fails, phospholipid hydroperoxides are allowed to accumulate, and the membrane becomes progressively less stable. The paragraph explicitly says that these combined defects hinder the processes that neutralize lipid peroxides, leading to membrane destabilization and the onset of ferroptosis rather than recovery from oxidative injury. The same description associates ferroptosis with ROS accumulation, GPX4 inhibition, and release of PUFAs as ferroptosis fuel, which fits a CPR-centered account in which radical-generating electron transfer initiates and sustains the oxidative conversion of membrane phospholipids. Read together, these statements present CPR not as incidental background but as the operative source of oxidizing power that drives PL-PUFA peroxidation and thereby produces the membrane-damaging peroxide species that execute ferroptosis.

Document [2]POR is associated with FMN at the N-terminal flavodoxin domain and with FAD at the C-terminal ferredoxin reductase domain. The two cofactors orient toward each other in an alignment necessary for efficient electron transfer, their isoalloxazine rings being only 4 Å apart at the closest . Electrons are brought to POR by NADPH and are transferred in the form of a hydride ion to FAD, passed from FAD to FMN, which then finally transfers them to one of many partner cytochromes P450 in the endoplasmic reticulum. The arrangement between flavins is permissive for the efficient inter-protein electron transfer; however, FMN needs to re-accommodate to donate electrons further. To this end, a more open conformation of the flavodoxin domain is required to position the reduced FMN in the vicinity to the heme-binding site in the cytochrome . A single 21 amino acid-long segment close to the N terminus of the flavoprotein spans the endoplasmic membrane and anchors the reductase in the compartment where the partner cytochromes are localized. Opposite to the anti-ferroptotic roles of other flavoprotein as discussed above, POR was recently shown to possess a pro-ferroptotic activity . Two CRISPR-Cas9-based screens were set up to screen for ferroptosis suppression, whereby intrinsically sensitive clear-cell renal carcinoma and inherently resistant melanoma cell lines were used. The resistant cells were rendered ferroptosis-sensitive by supplementation with ω-6 and ω-3 PUFAs, and ML210 was used to trigger ferroptotic cell death. Inactivation of POR turned out to prevent from ferroptosis in both screens. Mechanistically, lipidome analysis revealed the involvement of POR in the lipid peroxidation .
Document [3]Cell death is an essential component of organismal development and homeostasis which can be characterized by non-lytic and remarkably immunologically silent or lytic and pro-inflammatory . Though the scientific observation of regulated cell death (RCD) historically began in 1842, the rapid growth in RCD research was only started since the term “apoptosis” was introduced in 1972 . Since then, multiple RCD patterns have been identified (Fig. 1), each with unique regulatory mechanisms that influence physiological and pathological processes, including immune responses and tissue damage . However, despite their difference, there are some common features among these cell death pathways. Excess production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is particularly relevant to ferroptotic membrane damage and can influence cell death modalities . ROS are some of the most common oxidants in cells, including oxygen free radicals, e.g., hydroxyl radical (HO•), hydroperoxyl radical (ROO•), singlet oxygen, superoxide (O2-•) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) (Fig. 2). Mitochondrial electron leak is one source of these oxidants, as partial reduction of oxygen generates superoxide and related ROS that can seed downstream lipid-radical chain reactions in membrane phospholipids. Increasing evidence implicates that oxygen free radicals can attack PUFA-containing membrane lipids, and in the presence of bioactive iron this initiates the production of lipid peroxides. If these lipid peroxides cannot be efficiently neutralized and subsequently accumulate in the PMs, they might disrupt PM integrity and drive cells to death [5–7]. Excess lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) containing cell membrane phospholipids (PLs) is the crucial hallmark of ferroptosis. Under these conditions, the PM-PLs can be converted to PL-hydroperoxide (PLOOH) through iron-catalyzed nonenzymatic autoxidation and propagating lipid-radical chain reactions. The continued auto-oxidation of PLs is followed by increased curvature of membrane, thereby stimulating oxidative micellization, pore formation, and subsequent cell membrane damage .

Document [5]Furthermore, ferroptotic cells do not display any hallmarks of apoptosis, and knockdown of necroptosis mediators RIPK1 and RIPK3 do not protect cells from ferroptosis (Dixon et al., 2012; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014). Instead, ferroptosis execution is characterized by an iron-catalyzed excessive peroxidation of PUFA-containing phospholipids (PLs), present in excess in mammalian cell membranes. Supplementing cells with PUFAs promotes ferroptosis, while exchanging PUFAs with deuterated PUFAs that are less susceptible to oxidation or deletion of genes required for the activation and incorporation of PUFAs into PLs inhibits ferroptosis (Dixon et al., 2015; Doll et al., 2017; Kagan et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016b. Mechanistically, double bonds adjacent to methylene groups in PUFAs weaken the hydrogen bond energy of the bis-allylic methylene groups, resulting in increased susceptibility of hydrogen abstraction and consequent oxygenation, which can be monitored through oxidative lipidomics approaches (Else, 2017; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Gaschler and Stockwell, 2017; Repetto et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2016). The deleterious effects of lipid peroxidation in ferroptosis can be neutralized by iron chelators such as deferoxamine (DFO), and a wide variety of lipophilic radical traps such as vitamin E, ferrostatin-1 (Fer1), and liproxstatin-1 (Lip1) (Dixon et al., 2012; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014.
Document [6]The authors suggested that POR can facilitate lipid peroxidation by accelerating the cycling between Fe(II) and Fe(III) in the heme of partner cytochrome P450. At the same time, the participation of other electron acceptors cannot be excluded, because POR can donate electrons to a number of other redox partners, such as cytochrome b5, squalene monooxygenase and heme oxygenase . The discovery is an important advance towards comprehending the diversity of pro-ferroptotic mechanisms. Previously, primarily the arachidonate lipoxygenases (LOXs) were thought to be responsible for lipid peroxidation behind ferroptosis induction . However, lack of LOX expression in some ferroptosis-sensitive cells lines suggested additional lipid damage pathways. The POR-dependent lipid peroxidation offers a possible explanation of this discrepancy. In support, POR was also a hit in a genome-wide ferroptosis screen in the pancreatic carcinoma cell line KP-4 . Because of its many client enzymes, POR defects are expected to result in complex metabolic disturbances, including manifold defects of steroidogenesis. This assumption proved true by the first molecular description of the clinical POR deficiencies that had manifested in the combined insufficiency of 17α-hydroxylase and 21-hydroxylase . Many more mutations in POR have been identified since then. POR deficiency is now classified as a separate form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia independent of Antley–Bixler Syndrome . It affects the biosynthesis of steroids in both the adrenal gland and the gonads. In addition to clinically manifest variants, there are some noticeable polymorphisms in POR not yet linked with disease. Conceivably, they might become relevant phenotypically during environmental variations. One example is the variant A503V, with an average allele frequency of 30%. The high frequency of A503V can also explain its increased detection in tumor samples.

Framed this way, CPR is acting as a pro-ferroptotic source of oxidizing equivalents that can intensify phospholipid damage once the process starts, rather than as a generic marker of cellular stress. The passage then places this effect in the hepatic setting of MASLD, where CPR levels rise in parallel with oxidative stress and where CPR is described as participating in the ROS burden that accompanies lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic signalling. By connecting increased CPR with increased hepatic ROS, continued lipid peroxidation, hepatocyte injury, and reinforcement of ferroptotic signalling, the paragraph supports a self-reinforcing chain in which CPR-driven radical production helps maintain the oxidative conditions that keep membrane lipids under attack. It also frames CPR as part of a vicious cycle of oxidative injury, because ROS production, phospholipid peroxidation, and ferroptotic signalling are described as feeding back on one another rather than remaining isolated events. In this formulation, elevated CPR is not just correlated with liver damage; its electron-transfer behavior is presented as one of the processes that helps propagate ROS and sustain the membrane-directed oxidative chemistry associated with ferroptosis. That framing keeps the causal emphasis on CPR-generated ROS as the force that raises PL-PUFA peroxidation. The closing emphasis on CPR as a possible metabolic regulator and therapeutic target fits that same mechanism, because CPR matters here through its ability to promote oxidative stress and prolong lipid-damaging reactions in the affected tissue. Taken as a whole, the paragraph supports CPR-dependent ROS formation as a driver that amplifies PL-PUFA peroxidation and perpetuates ferroptotic membrane damage in this disease context.
Document [8]In AD, abnormal lipid metabolism and reduced antioxidant defenses promote the susceptibility of hippocampal neurons to ferroptosis . GPX4 deficiency and GSH depletion have also been observed in neurodegenerative models . Notably, several ferroptosis inhibitors have demonstrated neuroprotective effects in preclinical studies. Compounds such as ferrostatin-1 and liproxstatin-1 have been reported to reduce neuronal loss, OS, and neuroinflammation in rodent models of PD and AD. These agents scavenge lipid radicals and maintain cell membrane integrity, thereby preventing ferroptosis-induced neurotoxicity . Furthermore, iron chelators such as deferiprone have been studied to reduce brain iron burden and attenuate disease progression . Despite these promising findings, the clinical application of ferroptosis-targeted therapies in neurodegeneration remains in its early stages of development. Further research is needed to determine the temporal role of ferroptosis, identify biomarkers of susceptibility to its development, and elucidate its interactions with other forms of cell death in the aging brain. Current evidence suggests that ferroptosis is a common pathological mechanism in many neurodegenerative diseases and may represent a viable target for future neuroprotective therapies . Lipidomics has emerged as a critical analytical platform for investigating the biochemical underpinnings of ferroptosis, particularly by enabling the detection and quantification of lipid peroxidation products . During ferroptosis, enzymatic and non-enzymatic oxidation of PUFAs incorporated into membrane phospholipids leads to the generation of PUFA-OOH and secondary reactive species. Lipoxygenases catalyze the oxygenation of PUFA-containing phospholipid substrates, producing phospholipid hydroperoxides that contribute to ferroptosis. These oxidation products not only serve as hallmarks of ferroptotic activity but also play causal roles in membrane disruption and cell death signaling (see Figure 3) .

Persulfides (RSSH) are biologically important reactive sulfur species that are endogenously produced, protect key cysteine residues from irreversible oxidation, and are important intermediates during different enzymatic processes. Although persulfides are stronger nucleophiles than their thiol counterparts, persulfides can also act as electrophiles in their neutral, protonated form in specific environments. Moreover, persulfides are electrophilic at both sulfur atoms, and the reaction with a thiolate can lead to either H2S release with disulfide formation or alternatively result in transpersulfidation. Despite the broad acceptance of these reaction pathways, the specific properties that control whether persulfides react through the H2S-releasing or transpersulfidation pathway remain elusive. Herein, we use a combined computational and experimental approach to directly investigate the reactivity between persulfides and thiols to answer these questions. Using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we demonstrate that increasing steric bulk or electron withdrawal near the persulfide can shunt persulfide reactivity through the transpersulfidation pathway. Building from these insights, we use a synthetic persulfide donor and an *N*-iodoacetyl l-tyrosine methyl ester (TME-IAM) trapping agent to experimentally monitor and measure transpersulfidation from a bulky penicillamine-based persulfide to a cysteine-based thiol, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first direct observation of transpersulfidation between low-molecular-weight species. Taken together, these combined approaches highlight how the properties of persulfides are directly impacted by local environments, which has significant impacts in understanding the complex chemical biology of these reactive species. Document [6]In this way, the dynamic formation and removal of persulfides not only regulates enzyme function and signal transduction pathways but also taps into the body’s broader sulfur pool, linking sulfur signaling to cellular sulfur homeostasis . The mechanisms of protein persulfidation are therefore best understood as reversible sulfur-transfer chemistry rather than as irreversible cysteine blockade. Electrophilic small-molecule drugs classically silence signaling proteins by forging irreversible C–S Michael adducts with sentinel cysteine residues, a covalent cul-de-sac that removes the thiol from cellular redox circuits and locks the target in an inactive state . In stark contrast, HS−-derived inorganic and low-molecular-weight polysulfides perform a far more agile chemistry: these sulfur-rich species donate one zero-valent sulfur atom to a cysteine thiolate, transiently upgrading it to a persulfide (protein-SSH) . Because the transferred sulfur is installed transiently rather than permanently, the modified cysteine remains within cellular redox circuits instead of being removed from them. The reaction completes on the sub-second time-scale and remains fully reversible thanks to the thioredoxin, glutaredoxin and glutathione systems, yet it perturbs the local electrostatics, steric profile and hydrogen-bond network sufficiently to re-route signaling flux . Persulfidation therefore behaves as a dynamic rheostat, whereas S-alkylation functions as a one-way switch . The donor pool is not a terminal by-product but a chemically agile polysulfide reservoir. In other words, the sulfur donor remains poised for exchange rather than locked into an inert adduct. That reversibility distinguishes polysulfide donation from simple covalent blockage and makes inorganic or organic polysulfides suitable sulfur sources for signaling-level persulfidation.
