Document [3]This model is noteworthy because of its multidisciplinary conceptual framework and the resulting variety of experimental approaches that are based on it. The current overall picture of the research in the field is marked not only by experimental approaches but also by the fact that the concept of origin of life (OoL) became less primary due to the unifying concept of emergence of life (EoL) . In this context, the critical role of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and the proposal of a seed condition for the continuous evolution of life is recognized, and has guided not only the hypotheses but also the experimental works. The submarine alkaline hydrothermal vent model for the EoL attempts to give high importance to concepts related to non-equilibrium thermodynamics, highlighting continuity as an important property of the phenomenon of emergence. Thus, the model supports the mechanism of chemiosmosis—universally used in cellular systems—as key for life since its first steps in the transition from non-living matter, while recommending experiments to test the possible components for the emergence of that mechanism . Submarine alkaline hydrothermal vent systems are geologic arrangements that result from serpentinization, a chemical phenomenon that occurs on the seafloor , which basically consists of an oxidation reaction of the mineral content of the seafloor, such as olivine, exposed to water due to deep crustal faults . Examples of these types of arrangements were discovered in the early 2000s, and other hydrothermal fields of the same kind are now known . This broadened the empirical basis for hypotheses and experiments focused on such seafloor systems.
Document [4]Functions emerge as selective pressures present hurdles for populations of protocells undergoing chemical evolution. The hurdles can be surmounted by the stepwise accumulation of functions such as membrane stabilization; osmotic equilibration and transport by transmembrane pores; primitive metabolism utilizing nutrients and energy sources available in the environment; feedback controls; and catalytic cycles enabling replication of polymers. For Darwinian selection to begin to operate, simple self-assembly must be supplemented and ultimately replaced by active processes encoded in informational polymers. The RNA-World hypothesis suggests that transfer of proto-genomic sequence information could be first expressed by simple oligonucleotide templating then later through the combinatorial selection of a pool of functional ribozymes some of which are capable of RNA-catalyzed template-driven synthesis of other RNA sequences by active ribozymes . These laboratory tests of RNA World concepts require cycling, interaction and combinatorial selection of large numbers of polymers encapsulated in glassware. A natural kinetic trap of the kind described above may have supported some version of these powerful laboratory demonstrations of molecular evolution and brought an RNA World, or perhaps more likely, an RNA-Protein World, into existence. It is a common observation that terrestrial microbial life in the form of mats is metabolically most active in a moist, gradually dehydrating state following a short term hydration event such as rain fall . This property suggests a link with an earlier form which can only occur in fluctuating pools: a hydrogel that emerges naturally when sufficiently large populations of stable protocells crowd together next to mineral surfaces as the pool water level drops. Figure 7, center-inset illustrates lipid vesicles (~50% water by weight), which aggregate and form such a “gel phase” during dehydration. In a hydrothermal pool such gel structures would contain concentrated organic solutes and mineral grains along with systems of randomly synthesized functional and inert polymers.
Document [5]An early form of the acetyl-CoA pathway for carbon dioxide reduction would have allowed methanogens and acetogens to produce energy in such hydrothermal systems . One of the merits of the alkaline submarine vent origins of life hypothesis is that these settings provide sustained water-rock interaction and natural chemical gradients . Large impacts would also have created impact-generated hydrothermal systems in and around craters, potentially generating additional submarine habitats with vent-like circulation. These considerations bear on the initial emergence of life rather than its later spread into other environments. Submarine hydrothermal systems were first discovered in 1977 . Thermal anomalies suggest that comparable systems may still remain undiscovered . Among the best-studied white smoker hydrothermal systems is the Lost City Complex . Despite the absence of solar energy, it is teeming with diverse forms of life, from methanogenic archaea up through tubeworms. The seafloor underneath the Lost City Complex is similar in composition to the oceanic crust of the Hadean Earth , which distinguishes it as a realistic analog for ancient alkaline hydrothermal vents. The alkaline water and proton gradients required for an origin of life in alkaline marine vents exist naturally in this system. The oldest known marine hydrothermal sediments on Earth are the Nuvvuagittuq Belt Formation in Quebec, Canada, which have been dated to between 3.77 and 4.28 Ga. Dodd et al. discovered microstructures in these rocks which were interpreted as haematite tubes and filaments similar to those produced by microflora in modern hydrothermal systems. Subsequent experimentation demonstrated that abiotic chemical gardening can also produce similar features . Confirmed Hadean microfossils would strengthen the case for early hydrothermal habitats of this kind; however, additional evidence will be required to determine whether or not microbial life was present in the Nuvvuagittuq Belt.

The concentrated monomers (shown in red) are organized within a two-dimensional reaction space, and reduced water activity drives condensation reactions in which water becomes a leaving group, resulting in synthesis of ester bonds and peptide bonds, the primary links of biopolymers today. Assuming that amino acids and nucleotides are among the potential reactants , the synthesis of peptide bonds and phosphodiesters will occur and this has recently been demonstrated in laboratory simulations . By chance, some of the polymers will have functions that are relevant to selection as components of protocells. Short term dehydration and rehydration of the pool through periodic fluctuations in hydrothermal water supply, rainfall events, and dew from day-night cycles or through changing humidity cause the outer layers of the dried lamellae to disperse large numbers of protocells into the bulk solution. Some of these protocells will contain random sets of polymers (Figure 7, top-inset shows DNA encapsulation). The protocells are then subject to selective processing in which the aqueous environment disrupts some protocells while encapsulated functional polymers stabilize their membranous compartments and thereby increase their robustness . Stabilized protocells would persist and return to deposit their surviving cargos of polymers back into the lamellae as protocells dry down and undergo fusion. In this manner the polymers are “coupled” between phases and cycled within a kinetic trap, permitting generations of polymers to be re-synthesized, tested and, as Darwin intuited, become increasingly complex. The kinetic trap provides scaffolding for the stepwise emergence of encapsulated systems of functional polymers described earlier in the coupled phases scenario proposed by Damer and Deamer .

question: Which mechanisms for the transmission of biological information might have existed prior to the emergence of the current DNA-protein paradigm?
perspectives: An RNA-dominant world where RNA served as both genetic polymer and main catalyst
A mixed RNA-peptide world with coevolving short peptides and RNAs
A pre-RNA alternative-nucleic-acid world using polymers such as PNA or TNA
A non-templated metabolism-first system with compositional inheritance
context:
Document [0]It is often said, again based on first principles rather than historical evidence, that RNA-based life must have entailed some form of cellular compartmentalization70, 71. This would be advantageous for keeping together an RNA replicase ribozyme and its corresponding genomic RNA, and more generally for retaining the fruits of an RNA-based metabolism for the benefit of the system that produced them. In metabolism-first models, such compartments would instead pass on non-templated chemical networks by reproducing overall molecular composition as compositional inheritance. The notion of cellular compartmentalization should not be taken too literally — although all cells in contemporary biology are surrounded by a membrane composed of amphipathic lipids, there are other ways to achieve the preferential association of an ensemble of compounds. What would matter, in either case, is that the relevant molecules remain together through sufficiently persistent associations for catalytic activity and whatever form of heredity is present to stay linked to the same chemical system. This same outcome could arise whenever dispersal is limited and local concentration is maintained, so that products are preferentially retained by the system that produced them. In this sense, the key issue for early heredity is not a fully modern cell boundary, but the maintenance of a coherent chemical unit.

Document [0]The same reactions still fuel life for acetogens and methanogens in the deep crust today (Magnabosco et al., 2018). That kind of continuity from the first forms of metabolism into the physiology of modern cells is undoubtedly what Lipmann (1965) meant with the term "metabolic fossils." In these anaerobes, the acetyl CoA pathway links CO2 fixation directly to energy metabolism; it is linear rather than cyclic, strictly anaerobic, and replete with transition metal clusters (Ragsdale and Pierce, 2008; Martin and Russell, 2007). It is the only CO2-fixing pathway that operates via CO as an intermediate (Ragsdale, 2004), generating carboxyl groups from carbonyl rather than reducing carboxyl groups, which is key to its exergonic nature (Xavier et al., 2018). Such features help explain how CO2-reducing, acetogenic and methanogenic physiology could preserve an early mode of metabolism in modern cells (Berg et al., 2010; Fuchs, 2011; Hugler and Sievert, 2011).
Document [1]Miller and Urey (1959), p. 247) and Morowitz (1968), p. 79) expressed biological free energy in solar terms, but today we know that life in the crust and within hydrothermal vents proceeds in complete darkness through redox chemistry involving H2, CO2, and iron minerals (Corliss et al., 1981; Baross and Hoffmann, 1985). That kind of harsh geochemical environment is much more in line with what Haeckel and Mereschkowsky had in mind. Such settings also contain abundant ferrous iron and ferric minerals, so iron-based redox metabolism could likewise have powered some of the earliest cells. It is also the kind of environment where organisms that live from the reduction of CO2 with electrons from H2, acetogens and methanogens, have what they need for growth. In my view, Probiontes would correspond to LUCA, whereas Archibiontes would correspond to the first free-living cells, which could have been cytochrome-lacking acetogens and methanogens that use the acetyl CoA pathway for H2-dependent carbon and energy metabolism (a grade not a clade). Note the term “Reduction” that Haeckel used to designate the growth of autotrophs (for heterotrophs, he used Oxidation): Bilden Plasma unter Reduction, synthesize plasma reductively. Acetogens and methanogens growing from geochemical H2 are independent of light. Following the lead of Decker et al. (1970) and advice from microbiologists knowledgeable of acetogen and methanogen physiology, I have made a case in recent years that acetogens and methanogens lacking cytochromes could have arisen from reactions of H2 and CO2 at hydrothermal vents ca. four billion years ago and have preserved to this day the founding physiology of the first free-living cells in the bacterial and archaeal lineages (Martin and Russell, 2007; Martin, 2008), 2012).

The simplest answer is perhaps that biologists have always had an intuition that anaerobic bacteria capable of reducing CO2 are ancient. The idea that the first cells on earth were anaerobes and met their carbon needs from CO2 alone without the help of chlorophyll goes back 110 years. In 1902, Haeckel expressed the view that the first step in the origin of life (Archigonie he called it, from Greek archae ancient, gone seed) was the formation of an inorganic formative fluid (“anorganische Bildungs-Flüssigkeit”) containing the essential components, namely, carbonic acid, ammonia, and binary salts (“Kohlensäure, Ammoniak, binäre Salze”) (Haeckel, 1902), p. 361). As shown in Figure 1, Haeckel also saw the very first organisms as synthesizing their cell plasma reductively (“Bilden Plasma unter Reduction”), which today we would call autotrophy. Famous for his classifications, Haeckel placed these first organisms at the top of his system in the class Probiontes, represented by the first order Archibiontes, which contained only hypothetical types named Primordia vitae hypothetica! (Figure 1). Haeckel did not discuss the matter of origins much further in that book, although the exclamation point in Primordia vitae hypothetica!, possibly a punctuational singularity in the history of taxonomy, seems to underscore the importance of the issue. In 1910, Mereschkowsky took the issue of origins in the same direction but several explicit steps further. Mereschkowsky divided Earth’s early history into four phases, Epochs I–IV, as it pertained to origins.
Document [5]At sulfate concentrations below hundreds of micromolar, several sulfur-cycling processes become prominent that are difficult to constrain or quantify at millimolar levels. Under these low-sulfate conditions, the amount of sulfur contained in organic matter and other phases becomes a quantitatively notable pool compared with inorganic sulfur phases, and it can also provide an important source of energy for microbial populations. In many freshwater lakes, for example, organic sulfur exceeds the concentration of the pore-water sulfate pool by orders of magnitude. At tens of micromolar sulfate or less, the production of inorganic sulfur species from organic sulfur in sediments can even exceed rates of sulfate removal from overlying waters. Coupled with oxidation of reduced sulfur species in the oxic layer of the upper sea floor or lake floor, these settings can switch sediments from acting as a sulfate sink to acting as a sulfate source. An important consequence of this in situ sedimentary production of sulfur species is that it alters the sulfur isotope fractionation preserved in sediments. Because production of sulfur species across the redox spectrum does not necessarily involve sulfate reduction, the integrated isotopic signal can instead reflect other sulfur-processing routes, including the isotopic composition of the parent organic compound or fractionation imparted during organic sulfur hydrolysis. The relative importance of these processes is still poorly quantified, but it is clearly relevant for understanding ancient sulfur records. Low-sulfate conditions also increase the importance of intermediate oxidation-state sulfur species. Thiosulfate is especially energetic; even at concentrations below 1 mM it remains an important reactive intermediate for both oxidation and reduction pathways. Microorganisms can also directly take up thiosulfate rather than sulfate or sulfide, and the giant sulfur-oxidizing bacterium Thioploca from Lake Biwa has been shown to possess genes for thiosulfate utilization. This makes sulfur intermediates central players in microbial energetics under low-sulfate conditions.
Document [6]Three main metabolic pathways are particularly important for the sulfur cycle: microbial sulfate reduction, sulfur disproportionation, and sulfide oxidation. Each of these dissimilatory pathways depends on changes in sulfur oxidation state and induces sulfur isotopic fractionation by discriminating against heavy isotopes in the metabolic products. Although isotopic fingerprints can be investigated using all four stable sulfur isotopes, and to a lesser extent oxygen isotopes in sulfate, the relative abundance of 32S and 34S expressed as δ34S remains the most widely used measure in both modern and ancient settings because it captures sulfur fluxes and the relative importance of the processes driving those fractionations. In continental shelf environments, microbial sulfate reduction is responsible for up to half of the oxidation of organic carbon and its conversion back to inorganic carbon in marine sediments, making it one of the dominant sulfur-based metabolisms in anoxic sedimentary environments. Sediments from such settings are therefore major targets for reconstructing ancient sulfur cycling. Microbial sulfate reduction proceeds primarily through organoclastic sulfate reduction and through anaerobic oxidation of methane coupled to sulfate reduction. Current knowledge suggests that the methane-coupled pathway occurs through a syntrophic relationship between methanotrophic archaea and sulfate-reducing bacteria. Because organoclastic sulfate reduction is thermodynamically more favorable than anaerobic oxidation of methane coupled to sulfate reduction, the two pathways are vertically separated in the sediment column: organoclastic sulfate reduction dominates closer to the sediment-water interface where sulfate is relatively abundant, whereas the methane-coupled pathway occurs deeper in sea-floor sediments where sulfate levels and organic matter availability are typically much lower. Sulfide produced by either pathway can react rapidly with iron to form amorphous iron sulfide species such as mackinawite or greigite, and these can later be converted to pyrite through reaction with polysulfide or aqueous sulfide. The precise biogeochemical conditions that favor particular pyrite-forming routes remain uncertain, but the sequence still begins with sulfide generated by sulfur-based metabolism.

Even the origin of photosynthesis is likely to have occurred at hydrothermal vents, taking root in mild thermal radiation rather than from harsh sunlight at the surface (Nisbet et al., 1995). In that scenario, light-driven phototrophy, initially in anoxygenic form, could also have powered some of the earliest cells once pigments and reaction centers evolved. question: Which cellular and signaling processes could contribute to reduced vaccine-induced antibody responses after PFAS exposure?
perspectives: B-cell developmental or secretory dysfunction that limits antibody output
Reduced or altered T follicular helper support for germinal-center antibody responses
Dendritic-cell maturation defects that impair antigen presentation and immune priming
Glucocorticoid-receptor signaling that suppresses antibody production
context:
Document [0]In the human Namalwa B-lymphoma cell model, PFOA, PFOS, PFNA and PFHxS reduced expression of RAG1 and RAG2 in time- and concentration-dependent experiments. These genes participate in assembling antigen-receptor genes during lymphocyte development. Their altered expression provides a possible developmental route by which PFAS could affect the B-cell repertoire available for an antibody response. The measurements were made in a transformed cell line at the tested concentrations; they are not direct measurements of antibody loss after vaccination in people.
Document [1]A PFAS study in human PBMCs linked reduced antibody output to glucocorticoid-receptor signaling. Transcriptomic changes implicated GR-regulated pathways, and pretreatment with the GR antagonist mifepristone reversed suppression of IgG and IgM release after immune stimulation. These results support receptor-dependent regulation as one candidate connection between PFAS exposure and impaired humoral function under the tested culture conditions. They do not establish that changes in circulating thyroid or steroid hormones caused the antibody reduction.
Document [2]In human blood-cell cultures stimulated with SARS-CoV-2 spike peptides, a PFAS mixture reduced plasmablasts and spike-specific IgG at the highest tested exposure, 1000 times the reference blood concentration. This links exposure to a smaller antibody-secreting-cell response, although the mixed-cell culture cannot assign the effect exclusively to B cells. The high exposure and in-vitro setting limit direct extrapolation to ordinary vaccination conditions.
Document [3]Adult mice given PFOA at 7.5 mg/kg/day for 15 days showed sex-dependent changes in splenic B-cell populations. Female mice had fewer plasmablasts and several other B-cell subsets. Remaining isolated B cells displayed increased metabolic responses after stimulation, so the findings do not support a simple claim that all B-cell activation was abolished. The authors linked the altered populations to reduced primary IgM output. This experimental route concerns B-cell development, survival and the supply of antibody-producing cells, with dose and sex limiting its scope.
Document [4]T follicular helper cells support the germinal-center reaction in which B cells are selected and develop effective antibody responses. After gestational and lactational exposure to a PFOA/PFOS/PFHxS/PFNA mixture, female mouse offspring had reduced Tfh and germinal-center B-cell responses during influenza reinfection. This provides an exposure-specific example of weakened cellular support for humoral immunity. It is an animal infection model, so its relevance to vaccine responses is mechanistic rather than a direct human vaccination result.
Document [5]PFOS exposure in mice reduced antigen-specific IgM after challenge with both sheep red blood cells and the T-cell-independent antigen TNP-LPS. The second response does not require the same conventional T-cell help as the first. Suppression of both therefore points to B-cell function as one possible target of PFOS, rather than attributing the entire antibody deficit to helper T cells. The result establishes chemical exposure followed by impaired humoral output in that model; it does not identify every intervening molecular step or a universal human threshold.
Document [6]PFAS exposure can affect the cells that initiate an adaptive immune response. In a THP-1-derived dendritic-cell model, PFOA, PFOS and PFNA impaired maturation responses assessed through markers including CD83, CD86 and HLA-DR. Such changes could weaken antigen presentation and costimulatory support for priming lymphocytes, providing an upstream route to poorer antibody responses. The evidence is from a cell model, and the strength of the response depended on the compound and concentration; reduced vaccine responses in people were not measured directly in this experiment.
Document [7]Germinal centers contribute to the binding quality of antibodies as well as their amount. In female offspring developmentally exposed to a PFAS mixture, influenza-specific IgG showed reduced avidity after reinfection. Together with the reduced Tfh and germinal-center B-cell response in that model, this is consistent with impaired helper-supported antibody maturation. Avidity describes binding strength and should not be confused with antibody concentration. The observation supports a candidate mechanism under the tested exposure conditions, not a universal effect in both sexes.
Document [8]At 1000 times the reference blood concentration, a PFAS mixture reduced circulating Tfh17 cells in human PBMC cultures stimulated with spike peptides. Plasmablasts and spike-specific IgG also declined, while overall IL-21 and CXCL13 did not. The combined findings implicate altered Tfh–B-cell interactions under high exposure. They do not isolate Tfh changes as the sole cause or directly measure lymph-node germinal centers.
Document [9]The Tfh pathway need not explain every PFAS-associated antibody deficit. In the developmental mouse-mixture study, influenza antibody levels declined in both sexes, while the Tfh and germinal-center B-cell decreases were found in female offspring. The sex difference makes helper-cell disruption a supported route in that subgroup, with other processes needed to explain the male response. Several mechanisms can therefore contribute to reduced antibody output without each mechanism being demonstrable in every exposed animal or exposure setting.

Document [9]Once in the bloodstream, particles can be filtered by the glomerulus, reabsorbed in the tubular epithelium or translocated across the nephron. Particle size influences nephrotoxicity: Toxicity does not scale linearly with size, and there is a specific range where renal toxicity is greatest . MPs can reach the kidney through several routes, including ingestion, inhalation, and medical exposure. Ingestion of contaminated food and water is considered the dominant pathway. Chronic ingestion may also disrupt the gut microbiome and impair epithelial-barrier integrity by weakening tight junctions, thereby increasing intestinal permeability and systemic uptake of MPs. Once in the gastrointestinal tract, small particles, particularly those < 10 μm, are able to cross the intestinal barrier and enter systemic circulation. Mechanisms include paracellular leakage through impaired tight junctions, transcytosis by enterocytes or specialized M cells in Peyer’s patches, and transport *via* chylomicrons through the lymphatic circulation . Inhaled airborne MPs may deposit in the lungs, cross the alveolar epithelium, and enter the bloodstream, from which they are subsequently distributed to peripheral organs, including the kidney . In addition, iatrogenic sources have been reported: MPs and NPs have been detected in infusion and dialysis fluids, providing a direct route into circulation without the need to cross epithelial barriers . Once in systemic circulation, the renal fate of MPs is dictated by particle size, surface charge, and protein corona formation . Some particles undergo glomerular filtration and become retained in the glomerular basement membrane, while others are internalized by proximal tubular epithelial cells through endocytosis . The “filtration-reabsorption-translocation” hypothesis suggests that MPs can be filtered at the glomerulus, partly reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, and subsequently translocated to the renal interstitium or back into systemic circulation . At the cellular level, MPs are readily taken up by proximal tubular epithelial cells, as demonstrated *in vitro* with human cultured cells; internalization leads to lysosomal accumulation, defective degradation, and release of reactive oxygen species (ROS), triggering oxidative stress and mitochondrial injury .

question: Which primary triggers account for the occurrence of idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity associated with various major pharmaceutical agents?
perspectives: Reactive-metabolite formation that creates neoantigens or danger signals
Direct pharmacologic interaction with immune receptors such as specific HLA complexes
Mitochondrial stress followed by failure of adaptive hepatocellular responses
Bile-acid transporter inhibition that initiates cholestatic stress

Document [0]Little is known with certainty about the mechanisms of idiosyncratic drug reactions (IDRs); however, there is substantive evidence that reactive metabolites are involved in most, but not all, IDRs. In addition, evidence also suggests that most IDRs are immune mediated. That raises the question of how reactive metabolites induce an immune response that can lead to an IDR. The dominant hypotheses are the hapten and danger hypotheses. These are complementary hypotheses: a reactive metabolite can act as a hapten to produce neoantigens, and it can also cause cell damage leading to the release of danger-associated molecular pattern molecules that activate antigen presenting cells. Both are required for an immune response. There are also hypotheses involving mitochondrial injury. For some drugs, the initiating event may be mitochondrial stress, with injury following when adaptive hepatocellular responses fail to restore energy and redox homeostasis. With some possible exceptions, mitochondrial stress alone is unlikely to be able to completely explain IDRs. However, some types of mitochondrial injury could produce danger signals. Clarifying the contribution of these mechanisms to IDRs has therefore been difficult, and rigorous testing of mechanistic hypotheses was impossible in the past.
Document [1]Consistent with the role of the adaptive immune system, drug-specific peripheral blood mononuclear cell responses can be detected in those who had suffered DILI. Flucloxacillin-responsive CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell clones have been isolated and characterized from patients who suffered DILI, and the drug also activates naive CD8+ T cells from HLA-B*5701-positive volunteers [25: 727-39.]. These cellular findings link susceptibility to a defined HLA background rather than to a nonspecific toxic effect. In addition, a recent meta-analysis of two GWAS identified HLA-A*31: 01 as the main genetic predisposing factor for both hypersensitivity skin reactions and DILI secondary to carbamazepine [26: 1028-36.], further supporting the role of the adaptive immune system in the pathogenesis of DILI. HLA variants associated with toxicity determine the specificity of the peptide-binding groove for the relevant drug antigen, hence enhancing the presentation of that antigen to T cells and leading ultimately to immunological destruction of hepatocytes . A number of studies have confirmed association of co-amoxiclav DILI with the DRB1*1501-DQB1*0602 haplotype; a protective association of the DRB1*07 family with co-amoxiclav DILI has also been demonstrated . In contrast, with regard to flucloxacillin DILI, DRB1*07 has been associated with an increased risk of disease and DRB1*15 with a reduced risk. The relevance of multiple HLA alleles in flucloxacillin DILI therefore fits an antigen-presentation model of pathogenesis. This same pattern of allele-specific susceptibility is seen across drug-associated DILI signals. Together these findings argue that susceptibility depends strongly on the way particular HLA alleles present drug-related antigens to T cells and thereby shape the downstream immune attack on hepatocytes, with different alleles conferring either risk or protection depending on the drug.
Document [2]The prevailing molecular explanation for T-cell involvement in iDILI and in other drug-induced T-cell mediated reactions is that the causative drug is recognized by the TCR after binding to self-molecules. There are two receptor-centered possibilities within this framework. One is a non-covalent, labile pharmacological interaction, the p.i. concept, with immune receptors such as self-peptide-HLA complexes, or even the TCR. In this setting, the drug is recognized through a direct interaction with the immune receptor machinery rather than through nonspecific toxicity. The former mechanism does not require antigen processing . Another possibility is that the drug changes the HLA-binding site for the antigenic peptide, leading to a change in the repertoire of presented peptides . The fact that individuals carrying certain HLA alleles have increased risk to develop DILI when treated with particular drugs can be explained by the preferential molecular association of the drug with certain peptide-carrying HLA alleles, for example flucloxacillin, also known as floxacillin, with HLA-B*57: 01 , and amoxicillin with DRB1*15: 01 and DQB1*06: 02 . These observations place the interaction between drug, HLA complex, and T-cell receptor at the center of the immune trigger. This is an HLA-centered initiating event rather than a generalized cellular stress response. They also explain why risk is concentrated in carriers of particular HLA alleles rather than distributed uniformly across exposed patients. Nevertheless, only a fraction of the drug-exposed individuals having the risk HLA allele develop DILI, suggesting that additional factors are required for disease development. In vitro tests with peripheral blood T cells from DILI patients incubated with the causative drug can give information on the effector function of drug-specific T cells, thus providing insights on the mechanisms of T-cell mediated liver damage .
Document [3]Although the incidence of serious IDRs is low, their unpredictable nature make them scary. Also, because the mechanism of these adverse reactions is poorly understood, there is no specific treatment other than withdrawal of the offending drug and supportive care . While IDRs can affect a multitude of sites in the body, the three most common targets are the liver, skin, and blood cells. Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (IDILI) is the type of IDR most likely to lead to drug withdrawals . In addition, IDILI accounts for 13% of all cases of acute liver failure in the USA . Therefore significant research has been conducted to better understand these reactions in order to prevent future drug candidates from causing IDILI . Unfortunately, as with other IDRs, the mechanism of IDILI is still poorly understood. The liver is a multifaceted organ involved in metabolism, catabolism, and digestion. In terms of metabolism, anything that is absorbed by the intestines must travel through the portal vein to the liver, where it is subject to metabolism before it enters the general circulation. Specifically, the liver plays a major role in decomposition of endogenous products and is the primary site of drug metabolism in the body. The liver is a prime target for IDRs because drug metabolism can result in the formation of reactive metabolites, and injury is most likely to occur where reactive metabolites are formed. The two major types of IDILI are hepatocellular necrosis and cholestatic liver injury. For cholestatic cases, the initiating event may be inhibition of bile-acid transporters such as the bile salt export pump, which causes bile acid accumulation and initiates cholestatic stress. Although a specific drug usually produces a characteristic pattern of injury, it can vary in different patients. Multiple clinical characteristics make the mechanism of IDILI difficult to define. One important characteristic is that the onset of these reactions is generally delayed. Such a delay is consistent with the need for hepatic drug metabolism before injury becomes apparent and, in cholestatic cases, with interference in bile-acid transport.
Document [4]Although inflammasomes are important in innate immunity to fight off infection, excess inflammation can lead to a variety of autoinflammatory conditions. In relation to IDILI, danger signals or drug-modified proteins may signal the activation of inflammasomes and lead to immune mediated liver injury (Figure 3). Figure 3. Inflammasome activation. Drugs have the potential to activate the inflammasome, leading to release of IL-1ß and IL-18, which can further stimulate an immune response. Recently an in vitro experiment was designed to evaluate the ability of certain drugs that cause idiosyncratic skin rashes to activate inflammasomes. THP-1 cells (a human monocyte cell line) were treated with two pairs of chemically similar drugs. Telaprevir has a “black box” warning for severe skin rashes while boseprevir does not, and dimethyl fumarate causes contact sensitization and ethacrynic acid does not cause idiosyncratic reactions even though it covalently binds to proteins. Telaprevir and dimethyl fumarate activated inflammasomes while boseprevir and ethacrynic acid did not . This suggests that inflammasome activation with production of IL-1ß may be a biomarker of IDR potential. Drugs that require bioactivation into their respectful reactive metabolites need to be tested in this model, as well as drugs that cause other forms of IDRs such as IDILI or blood disorders. IDILI may be difficult to study in this model because drugs that cause IDILI generally need to be converted to their reactive metabolite in order to cause liver injury. However, inflammasomes appear to be an intriguing hypothesis of how reactive metabolites activate the immune system leading to an IDR.
Document [5]To build upon this concept, there is evidence that the same HLA allele may increase the risk for one drug and be protective for another one; unrelated drugs may share the same HLA allele too. Overall, these arguments reinforce the leading role of antigen presentation in the genesis of iDILI. Regarding GWAS related to iDILI, most of them have examined the genetic predisposition to a single specific drug or class, whereas more recent studies have revealed some risk variants related to general predisposition independent of drug type . Nicoletti et al. were the first to identify the rs114577328 single nucleotide polymorphism as a risk variant for unselected DILI cases involving different drugs in subjects of European ancestry . Rs114577328 tags the HLA-A*33: 01 allele, which is similar to the HLA-A*33: 03 allele that has been associated with ticlopidine-induced DILI in Japanese individuals. Previous studies had identified examples of HLA alleles associated with structurally different compounds, such as DRB1*15: 01 with amoxicillin-clavulanate and lumiracoxib and DRB1*07: 01 with lapatinib and ximelagatran . Nicoletti and colleagues speculate that their findings, together with the previously available evidence, support the role of adaptive immunity in DILI. Recently, the same consortium also identified a genome-wide significant non-HLA risk allele, the rs2476601 SNP, on chromosome 1 ; the association was not constrained to a specific drug or pattern of injury. Further, the rs2476601 variant added to the risk associated with known HLA alleles, showing epistatic interaction . The same SNP has been associated with increased risk of type 1 diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and several other autoimmune conditions , linking general immune predisposition with the HLA-centered antigen-presentation model of susceptibility.
Document [6]However, recent studies on predictive genetic testing for DILI demonstrated a low positive predictive value of 0.12%, even in the strongest association of HLA-B*5701 with flucloxacillin-induced DILI.28 Therefore, a multidisciplinary approach that relates immune responses to clinical outcomes is required to improve predictability by combining biomarkers with HLA typing tests. The association between particular HLA alleles and susceptibility to DILI drives studies on how small drugs can induce drug-specific T-cell responses that are restricted by the host HLA allele. This focus on HLA restriction keeps antigen presentation at the center of the mechanism and makes allele-specific recognition the dominant mechanistic question. The association of a specific HLA allele with DILI gives rise to several major questions: (1) how are small drugs antigenic, that is, how do they interact with MHC proteins to activate T lymphocytes; (2) how and why do drug-specific T-cell responses arise in only a small portion of patients; and (3) how is a specific immune response restricted by host HLA alleles? T lymphocytes are thought to be involved in the pathogenesis of certain immune-mediated adverse drug reactions, indirectly causing tissue damage through cytokines or directly by the secretion of cytolytic molecules such as perforin, granulysin, and FAS ligand. To stimulate a T-cell response, a drug must act as an antigen and ligate specific T-cell receptors, which ultimately results in the activation of specific T cells. Drugs have also been shown to associate directly with peptides embedded in the MHC to stimulate a T-cell response.30-37 Despite this, very few studies have attempted to define the relevant antigens in patients and then relate those HLA-restricted immune responses to clinical outcome, which is why combining mechanistic biomarkers with HLA typing remains necessary.
Document [7]In addition, it should be possible to design better treatments when drug-induced liver injury does occur. **Keywords: ** idiosyncratic drug reactions, idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury, immune mediated, immune tolerance Idiosyncratic is defined as peculiar to an individual and describes idiosyncratic drug reactions (IDRs) as reactions that only affect specific individuals. In most cases, whether pharmacology, genetics, environment, or all three determine who will develop an IDR is currently not well understood. IDRs pose a significant issue for healthcare and drug development, as these reactions are often not detected in clinical trials . The incidence of these reactions may only be clear after millions of people have taken the drug, where only a small percentage of patients will experience a reaction (generally <1%). In 2004 in the United Kingdom, adverse drug reactions accounted for 6.5% of hospital admissions with an overall mortality of 2% . Although the percentage of IDRs is only about 10% of the total adverse drug reactions , given the total number of drugs prescribed, IDRs are common and represent a major and increasing cause of candidate failure in drug development. Over 10% of drugs approved during 1975-1999 acquired a black box warning or were withdrawn . IDRs are especially difficult to deal with because the mechanism of injury is not well understood, and current testing is not effective in predicting their risk . IDRs are described as type B adverse drug reactions, which means that they do not generally involve the pharmacological effect of the drug and do not occur in most patients. Additionally, most IDRs appear to involve the bioactivation of the drug into a reactive metabolite . This is in contrast to type A reactions, which are generally a consequence of a drug’s pharmacological effect, and therefore more predictable. An example of a type A reaction is excess bleeding caused by warfarin, which is an anticoagulant.

question: Through which mechanisms does arsenic induce cancer when encountered at concentrations typically found in the environment?
perspectives: Epigenetic reprogramming and altered gene regulation
Oxidative stress with indirect genotoxicity
Endocrine disruption affecting growth and differentiation signaling
Altered stem-cell selection or tissue-regenerative signaling
context:
Document [0]Arsenic exposure represents an important problem in many parts of the World. Indeed, it is estimated that over 100 million individuals are exposed to arsenic, mainly through contamination of groundwaters. Chronic exposure to As is associated with adverse effects on human health such as cancers, cardiovascular diseases, neurological diseases and alarming morbidity and mortality in exposed populations. These outcomes underscore the carcinogenic importance of chronic exposure. The purpose of this discussion is to summarize the genotoxic effects of As in cells and to emphasize the importance of signaling and repair of arsenic-induced DNA damage within an oxidative-stress mechanism. Current knowledge on susceptibility factors and biological markers of early effect is relevant because it can help evaluate exposure-response relationships and develop strategies to prevent arsenic health effects. Such biomarkers are useful for detecting early oxidative injury before overt disease and related progression appear. Chronic arsenic exposure is an important problem to human health in many parts of the World. Indeed, over 100 million individuals worldwide are exposed to arsenic, mainly through contamination of groundwaters . Arsenic is a metalloid element and exists in organic and inorganic forms. Inorganic arsenic (iAs) is a class I human carcinogen . Its adverse effects depend on dose, duration and exposure frequency, and they include increased risks of skin, bladder, lung and kidney cancers. In particular chronic exposure to iAs is associated to an increased risk of skin, bladder, lung, kidney cancers, as well as cardiovascular and neurological diseases, diabetes and non-malignant respiratory diseases . One of the principal mechanisms of arsenic toxicity is the induction of a strong oxidative stress with production of free radicals in cells . Indeed, there is increasing evidence that the induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) plays a crucial role in arsenic toxicity and the resulting genotoxic damage.
Document [1]In the last two decades, growing evidence has indicated that epigenetic mechanisms play major roles in the responses, regulation, and alterations associated with cellular As toxicity (Cheng et al. 2012), "Epigenetic targets of some toxicologically relevant metals, " J Appl Toxicol 32: 643–653). There has been growing recognition of the importance of epigenomic mechanisms in maintaining cellular homeostasis and genomic imprinting. Epigenetic alteration, which is certainly not a genotoxic event, denotes processes that govern mitotically and/or meiotically heritable changes in genomic expression through chromosomal marks without changes in the nuclear DNA sequence (Feinberg and Tycko 2004, "The history of cancer epigenetics, " Nat Rev Cancer 4: 143–153; Cortessis et al. 2012), "Environmental epigenetics: prospects for studying epigenetic mediation of exposure-response relationships, " Hum Genet 131: 1565–1589; Ray et al. 2014, "Incorporating epigenetic data into the risk assessment process for the toxic metals arsenic, cadmium, chromium, lead, and mercury: strategies and challenges, " Front Genet 5: 201), and therefore it can serve as a potentially reversible alteration in gene regulation and a priming mechanism for subsequent generations to better tolerate biotic and abiotic stresses.
Document [2]This has been discussed in relation to long-term biological effects and to the development of arsenicosis through control of methylation-related gene expression (Langley-Evans 2006; Nye et al. 2014). As induces hypomethylation which, coupled with poor nutritional status, may disturb gene regulation. Interestingly, DNA methylation genes are upregulated significantly in some settings, suggesting that methylation responses are relevant to arsenicosis (Vahter 2007). The phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEMT) gene regulates the de novo synthesis of phosphatidylcholine, contributing choline for remethylation of homocysteine to methionine and further to SAM, which is critical for methylation processes (Vahter 2007). In this way, epigenomic alterations induced by As can change gene regulation and can serve as an interface between environmental toxicants like As and phenotypic manifestations by translating the As-generated environmental signals to phenotypic responses through altered gene expression. These changes may persist as an epigenetic profile associated with exposure history (Mirbahai and Chipman 2014).
Document [3]One possible mechanism by which arsenical compounds contribute to carcinogenesis is the disruption of normal epigenetic marks at specific loci, which may cause changes in gene expression and carcinogenesis . Although arsenic exposure was found to alter methylation levels in global DNA and promoters of some genes, current research is hard to understand due to the complexity and insubstantial information provided in the current studies. Further investigations are necessary to systematically explore DNA methylation on a genome-wide level in cell lines exposed to arsenic and target tissues from well-characterized arsenic-exposed populations or tumor tissues from arsenic-associated cancers. Such studies will assist in elucidating the possible biological effects of arsenic exposure on DNA methylation and carcinogenesis. Document [4]In this minireview, we discuss the relevance of oxidative stress, generated by metals, metalloid compounds or xenobiotics, for carcinogenesis. Firstly, we summarize the evidence for occurrence of oxidative stress at exposure levels that are relevant for human health. Secondly, we discuss the specific significance of ROS for the toxicity of these ions or organic compounds. In this framework, arsenic is examined as a carcinogen for which ROS-linked damage is relevant to toxic effects at human exposure levels. At the inorganic side we focus on arsenic, chromium, nickel and cadmium, because these species are classified as category 1 carcinogens according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer and the MAK commission . Arsenic is one of the most important toxic metals and is classified as an IARC category 1 carcinogen. Human exposure can occur through contaminated drinking water and constitutes a serious health problem in parts of India and Bangladesh. Other important sources include food, especially rice, cereals or seafood . In 2009, investigations in Germany pointed to elevated levels of arsenic in rice waffles, marketed for nutrition of small children . Arsenic contamination of drinking water has been epidemiologically linked to increased mortality from lung and bladder cancer , as well as cardiovascular diseases . Inorganic arsenic [As(V), As(III)] is efficiently absorbed in the intestine and converted into methylated species. This matters because the methylated metabolites retain genotoxic activity after arsenic biotransformation and remain toxicologically relevant to humans in environmentally exposed populations today worldwide. In fact, methylated metabolites such as monomethyl (MMA) and dimethyl arsonous acid (DMA) trigger genotoxic effects similar to inorganic arsenite , fitting an oxidative-stress framework in which arsenic promotes indirect genotoxicity rather than classical direct DNA reactivity.
Document [5]In addition to cancer, epidemiological studies have associated chronic iAs exposure with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, neurological effects, and detrimental birth outcomes . More recently, studies have also discovered that sociodemographic and regional inequalities for iAs concentrations in public water systems exist across the USA . These studies highlight the importance of iAs exposure as an environmental risk factor that likely contributes to cancer and disease disparities in human health. iAs exposure initiates and promotes carcinogenesis through epigenetic and gene-regulatory mechanisms. At environmentally relevant levels, chronic iAs exposure may also skew stem-cell selection and tissue-regenerative signaling, allowing expansion of cell populations more susceptible to malignant transformation. A growing body of evidence has identified roles for epigenetic reprogramming and altered gene regulation in mediating arsenic-induced malignant transformation of human skin, lung, bladder, kidney, liver, prostate, and breast cells. Document [1]A wide range of nanoparticles have been found to generate free radicals in biological systems, so free-radical generation is proposed as a key mechanism of nanomaterial toxicity in vivo. The unresolved issue is the physicochemical basis for that radical generation in the biomicroenvironment. To address that problem, this study applied comprehensive spectroscopic techniques to probe the origin of free-radical generation induced by iron oxide nanoparticles in biologically relevant microenvironments. The results showed that α-Fe2O3 and γ-Fe2O3 nanoparticles induced hydroxyl radicals through Fenton chemistry, with the balance between homogeneous and heterogeneous pathways depending on pH and on the presence of biological reducing agents. For the target mechanism, the crucial point is that the physicochemical structure of the nanosurface, including the chemical states of oxygen and iron at the surface, was identified as a key factor controlling the catalytic reactions. A notable finding was that in situ surface reduction of Fe2O3 nanoparticles occurred in the presence of physiological amounts of reducing agents such as l-cysteine or NADPH. That surface reduction could enhance, and under low-pH conditions even reverse, the relative capacities of α-Fe2O3 and γ-Fe2O3 nanoparticles to generate hydroxyl radicals, specifically under the acidic pH 1.2 condition highlighted in the study. The study therefore ties differences in nanotoxicity to surface-controlled catalytic ROS generation at the nanobio interface and points to biomicroenvironmental factors that modulate that catalytic behavior. Supporting information reinforced that interpretation with a table of redox potentials for iron oxide and reducing agents at different pH values, detailed calculations for the Fe2O3(s)/Fe2+ couple, and graphics showing physicochemical characterization of α-Fe2O3 and γ-Fe2O3 nanoparticles by X-ray diffraction, EPR spectra, hydrodynamic diameter, and pH-dependent hydroxyl-radical generation.

Amplex UltraRed is presented as a better-suited H2O2-specific assay for mineral slurries because the reagent, 10-acetyl-3, 7-dihydroxyphenoxazine, reacts with H2O2 in a 1: 1 stoichiometry in the presence of horseradish peroxidase to produce highly fluorescent resorufin. Compared with DCFH, Amplex UltraRed is described as 5- to 20-fold more sensitive, and the resorufin product is more stable to chemical and photo-induced oxidation (Zhou et al. 1997). The assay has therefore been used to measure H2O2 production in cells exposed to asbestos (Xu et al. 2002), cancer cells (Wagner et al. 2005), plant cells (Janisch and Schempp 2004), and brain mitochondria (Gyulkhandanyan and Pennefather 2004). ROS analysis in cell cultures presents additional challenges because the initial products generated when minerals react with water and oxygen, as observed in mineral-slurry studies, may themselves become substrates for further reactions catalyzed by enzymes in the cellular environment. The products of those reactions may be highly reactive yet longer lived than hydroxyl radicals, and they can go on to modify proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids within cells. In that sense, the first mineral-derived ROS are not the end of the chemistry but the start of a broader reactive cascade. Assessing the pathological consequences of mineral dust and particulate reactivity therefore requires a panel of assays that detects both the initial mineral-derived reactive species and the secondary species generated by enzymatic conversion in living cells. The need for multiple assays follows directly from that cascade logic. The example given is that hydroxyl radicals formed directly at the mineral surface may trigger formation of superoxide, hypochlorite, and hydrogen peroxide through secondary reactions mediated by cellular components.

Increased production volume will increase human and environmental exposure during normal use, fugitive emissions, accidental spills, and disposal after use. Current environmental and occupational rules are generally based on nominal chemical composition and seldom specify special standards for ultrafine or nano-sized particles, so the occupational and environmental effects of these powders have become a public-policy concern and a direct toxicology research target. Reactive oxygen species, including radicals such as OH• and O2−• and non-radicals such as H2O2, can be generated through both extracellular and intracellular reactions in particle-treated systems . Extracellular ROS generation has therefore been proposed as a mechanism by which particles stimulate cell-surface receptors and initiate inflammatory signaling.

ROS generated by inhaled particulate materials can be active either extracellularly or intracellularly, and within the tightly regulated intracellular microenvironment even small and transient increases in ROS levels can markedly alter cell metabolism. The paragraph attributes the broad spectrum of mineral responses to particle characteristics such as metallic content, surface area, particle size, and morphology, together with cellular characteristics such as embryologic origin, epithelial versus phagocytic lineage, state of differentiation, and pre-existing levels of activation. Even with that biological variation, the common mechanistic thread is mineral-generated ROS production and transformation. Chronic inflammation associated with mineral-generated ROS has been linked to cardiovascular disease (Brook et al. 2003), lung diseases including silicosis and asbestosis (Kamp et al. 1992), and lung cancer (Knaapen et al. 2004). Oxidative stress has also been linked to memory loss and learning impairment (Fujimoto et al. 1996). For that reason, it is important to determine which minerals induce formation of primary ROS or drive transformations to secondary ROS, and from a biological standpoint to study how mineral exposures cause ROS upregulation or impairment of antioxidant defense systems. Even secondary ROS matter because they can amplify downstream cellular injury once the first reactive species has formed. The larger discussion is organized around ROS species themselves, thermodynamic data relevant to those species, analytical methods for detecting ROS in both cell-free and cellular systems, and the set of mechanisms needed to explain how mineral exposure produces disease, including the difficulty of unraveling that relationship in silicosis. Across those topics, reactive oxygen chemistry remains the immediate driver under examination.

The unresolved issue is the physicochemical basis for that radical generation in the biomicroenvironment. Document [0]PM2.5 primarily enters the body through inhalation, with the nose and mouth serving as the primary entry points. When nasally inhaled, a portion of PM2.5 is adsorbed in the nasal cavity, and the remainder reaches the lungs via the airways. Oral inhalation directly leads to deposition in the oral cavity and lungs. Oberdörster et al. demonstrated that exposure of rats to 13C-labeled fine particles via transient inhalation led to an immediate increase in the 13C signal in lungs. However, 1-week post-exposure, the 13C concentration in the lungs had decreased and was similar to that in the olfactory bulb . Notably, the 13C concentration in the olfactory bulb increased 1-day post-exposure and remained stable for at least 1 week. These results suggest that PM2.5 can accumulate in the brain and that clearance from the brain is limited. Elder et al. investigated translocation of Mn nanoparticles to the CNS in rats. They compared animals with both nostrils patent to those with the right nostril occluded. In rats with patent nostrils, Mn accumulated in the striatum, frontal cortex, and cerebellum. In contrast, in rats with the right nostril occluded, Mn accumulation was limited to the left olfactory bulb. These findings indicate that the olfactory neuronal pathway is efficient for translocating inhaled solid nanoparticles to the CNS . The olfactory epithelium is composed of neurons that detect odorant molecules. These olfactory neurons extend their axons to the surface of the olfactory epithelium through the cribriform plate, a porous bone in the nasal cavity, to transmit odorant signals to the olfactory bulb. It is therefore plausible that inhaled nanosized particulate matter is taken up by the olfactory neurons and enters the olfactory bulb via axonal transport.

The elucidation of the molecular pathways linking these exposures to neuroinflammation provides a framework for developing targeted therapeutic interventions. In this account, the pathology is driven by a sequence of events beginning with alveolar irritation, propagating through systemic inflammation, and then producing downstream inflammatory effects in the central nervous system. Accordingly, therapeutic strategies can be stratified into three lines of defense: minimizing exposure, dampening the systemic inflammatory response, and limiting its downstream consequences in the brain. Document [8]The lung-brain axis can propagate inflammation through systemic inflammatory signaling. Alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages, upon exposure to particulate matter, release inflammatory mediators into the systemic circulation . These circulating signals can act at the BBB interface and the cerebrovascular endothelium . In parallel, PM2.5 can injure cerebrovascular endothelial cells and disrupt tight junctions, producing blood-brain barrier dysfunction that facilitates the entry of circulating inflammatory signals into the brain. Once the neurovascular unit is compromised, peripheral inflammatory cues can more readily influence the brain parenchyma, functioning as drivers of pathological signaling . The pathogenicity of this process lies in the diverse mediators associated with systemic inflammation, including oxidized proteins, inflammatory lipids, and DAMPs . For instance, pollution-induced inflammatory signaling has been associated with molecular changes consistent with endothelial activation . By weakening vascular homeostasis, these signals effectively remove the “brakes” on inflammatory activation at the brain interface . Furthermore, DAMPs like HMGB1 (High mobility group box 1) may engage receptors at the neurovascular unit to perpetuate a sterile inflammatory response . This mechanism represents a biochemical link whereby pulmonary stress contributes to inflammation within the CNS . Components of the neurovascular unit do not act in isolation; their responses are shaped by vascular injury and altered barrier function .

Document [7]Experimental and epidemiological data indicate that developmental exposure to certain environmental contaminants poses a threat to the developing brain and may lead to neurodevelopmental disorders. Specific and well-organized cellular and molecular processes, including neural progenitor proliferation, migration, and differentiation, characterize the development of the nervous system. Any incident disrupting the sequence of these developmental steps can lead to permanent or transient structural and functional losses. Another common mechanistic class is cellular stress, in which environmental chemicals induce oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in developing neural cells. The impact that harmful stimuli, such as neurotoxicants, exert on the developing nervous system depends on the timing of exposure that may coincide with region-specific windows of susceptibility. Neurodevelopmental damages may not be evident for a long time (silent neurotoxicity) up until different challenges, including aging, trauma, or exposure to toxicants, disclose and even build up on the existing cellular or biochemical damage. In addition, such alterations may persist once established (see ). We are exposed to a large and increasing number of chemicals and the lack of information regarding their neurodevelopmental toxic potential has generated a growing concern for public health. Experimental animal models and tests have been critical in toxicology to provide fundamental information about potential neurotoxicants. However, animal studies have intrinsic limitations, including variations across species, labor- and time-intensive procedures, as well as ethical issues . Therefore, in vitro assays with cell lines and primary cells, especially those of human origin, have turned out to be good alternatives to live animal experiments for developmental neurotoxicity studies . Document [0]In addition, mechanical disruption of the residual cell envelopes by physical processes, e.g., shrinking and swelling of SOM as well as soil mixing due to bioturbation by macrofauna may also determine the fate (Bohlen et al., 2004; Basile-Doelsch et al., 2020). The ultimate fate of the necromass then depends on many factors: microbial decay, clay content, Fe or Al oxides, water content and pore system of the soil aggregates (Schimel et al., 2007). Microbial necromass (including cell envelope fragments) can be stabilized within the soil matrix through its small size, spatial conformation, and by interaction with itself, e.g., by the formation of stacks of cell-wall fragments that may hamper degradation due to limited accessibility of the interior regions (Miltner et al., 2012; Buckeridge et al., 2020). Necromass may easily be occluded in soil aggregates and therefore not be bioavailable for degradation. Interactions of biomolecules with other organic and mineral matter can occur by ionic or hydrogen bonds or hydrophobic interactions (Galicia-Andres et al., 2021). However, various types of biomolecules are partly stabilized in SOM to different extents: proteins > bulk biomass C > lipids (e.g. PLFA) (Kindler et al., 2006; Kindler et al., 2009; Miltner et al., 2009; Spence et al., 2011; Miltner et al., 2012). An overarching stabilization process of SOM and necromass can also be caused by the formation of hydrophobic domains with a decreased chemical activity of water (Masoom et al., 2016) by drying processes, or by loss of pore water connectivity. The authors impressively provided evidence that around 75% of the necromass-derived SOM material is actually not in contact with water.

Aboveground litter-derived compounds are transported downward through the soil profile in dissolved or colloidal form before sorbing to reactive mineral surfaces. Moreover, this transfer occurs through dissolved or colloidal material moving through the profile. Some of this material interacts with iron oxide mineral particles at reactive surfaces. Others bind strongly to mineral surfaces and thus remain associated with the mineral phase. Fungal biomass, in turn, also contributes substantially to the formation of SOM through necromass that is left behind after cell death. Microbial turnover may also contribute to the formation of stabilized SOM (Lehmann and Kleber, 2015). However, little is known about the forms of organic matter extracted from boreal forest soils. A recent study from our group shows that ca. 40–70% of the total organic C in DOM extracted from boreal forest is present in a colloidal size fraction (Meklesh et al., 2022). Important challenges for future research are to examine how such colloidal fractions move through soils and interact with mineral surfaces. The significance of specific molecular interactions in decomposition processes has been questioned by soil scientists, considering that soil microorganisms may not always have the energy and nutrient resources needed for every proposed mechanism (Lehmann and Kleber, 2015). This may be true in some contexts. However, attention remains on how litter-derived dissolved or colloidal compounds are sorbed to reactive mineral surfaces and how microbial turnover leaves necromass that can persist in mineral soils.

Document [4]The majority of soil carbon (C) is stored in organic matter associated with reactive minerals. These mineral-organic associations (MOAs) inhibit microbial and enzymatic access to organic matter, suggesting that organic C within MOAs is resistant to decomposition. Plant roots and rhizosphere processes are known to transform minerals through dissolution and exchange reactions, implying that MOAs in the rhizosphere can be dynamic. Here we identify root-driven mechanisms and controls that determine how rhizosphere inputs interact with mineral-associated organic matter. We introduce a vulnerability spectrum that highlights how MOAs characteristic of certain ecosystems are particularly susceptible to specific root-driven processes in the rhizosphere. This vulnerability spectrum provides a framework for critically assessing the importance of these root-driven mechanisms at the ecosystem scale. Comprehensive representation of root-driven MOA formation, transport, and disruption will improve model projections of soil C-climate feedbacks and guide the development of more effective soil C management strategies. Plants allocate 40-60% of their photosynthetically fixed carbon (C) to their root systems through dead root cells, tissues, mucilage, and a cocktail of simple organic compounds collectively known as rhizodeposits. This rhizodeposition is a main source of soil organic matter (OM), the largest and most dynamic terrestrial C reservoir on Earth. The proximity of roots to their surrounding mineral matrix is thought to facilitate the chemical association of rhizodeposits with reactive minerals. Because these rhizosphere inputs remain in close contact with mineral surfaces, root-derived compounds can be transformed locally before sorption into stable mineral-organic associations. These mineral-organic associations protect OM against microbial and enzymatic attack, potentially contributing to soil C storage for centuries to millennia. This framing emphasizes root-derived inputs as a central pathway by which rhizosphere C becomes associated with reactive minerals.

Document [6]As microbial necromass decomposition proceeds, more slowly decomposing aromatic components yield more complex molecules for organomineral interactions. For example, condensed aromatic residues can persist for years as particulate matter in litterbags (Fernandez et al., 2019), and related particulate residues have been shown to persist in soils for millennia (Scott et al., 2010). The formation of organo-mineral complexes from these condensed aromatic molecules remains poorly characterized. The formation of organo-mineral complexes from these condensed aromatic molecules remains poorly characterized. In a study of microbial growth in ligninfree model soils, increased mineral-associated phenolic and aromatic compounds were observed after 18 months (Kallenbach et al., 2016), suggesting the accumulation of persistent aromatic material. Document [0]Here, we refer to phases that are formed after either adsorption or coprecipitation as Fe–OC associations. The formation pathway of Fe–OC associations directly affects the properties of the Fe–OC phase. As organic matter accumulates on these associations, organo-organic coatings can develop that shield underlying mineral-associated carbon from enzymatic and microbial exposure. While adsorption of OC changes the surface properties of the mineral, coprecipitation with OC produces a resulting Fe–OC phase with distinct surface characteristics.14–18 During the binding process, part of the OC becomes associated with mineral surfaces. Past studies using forest-floor extracts, plant litter, or humic reference materials have examined Fe binding across different OC sources. These studies involved OC interacting with Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides across a range of source materials.19–22 The binding process thus leaves a fraction of OC associated with mineral surfaces in soils.20, 23 Recently, several studies have shown that substantial fractions of OC may be bound to minerals (30–82%), with the dominant mineral fraction as Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides.12, 24, 25 The amount of Fe-bound OC can also be substantial across different sites.24, 26–28 This suggests that part of the OC may remain unavailable due to binding with Fe minerals despite microbial exposure. However, our systematic understanding of the formation and composition of Fe–OC associations in soils is limited. Across soils, OC can continue to accumulate on existing Fe–OC associations. As this material builds up on Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxide surfaces, organo-organic coatings may become more developed, thereby limiting enzymatic and microbial access to the underlying mineral-associated carbon.
