Document [1]Since terrestrially derived C is a main determinant of freshwater C, any changes in terrestrial primary production and export of organic C will invariably also increase aquatic outputs of CO2. Increased terrestrial productivity has been linked to CO2 fertilization (Huang et al., 2007), and climate-related gains in catchment production can increase the terrestrial organic-matter pool available for export, even though these CO2 effects will be constrained by nutrient availability. Increased export of terrestrially derived DOM to lakes and rivers in boreal regions ("browning") is a widespread phenomenon driven by climate change through CO2 fertilization of forests, warming, and hydrology (de Wit et al., 2016; Creed et al., 2018; Monteith et al., 2023). This climate sensitivity is especially important in boreal landscapes with large terrestrial organic-matter stocks. An empirically based space-for-time model of changes in the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) under a 2 °C climate scenario predicts continued browning of boreal lakes (Larsen et al., 2011b). Forest dynamics are slow, however; hence, space-for-time scenarios projecting increased flux of TOC from catchments owing to increased terrestrial productivity could require centuries to play out. Thus, catchment properties governing production of TOC such as forest size and the fraction of bogs and wetland areas could very well be temporally decoupled from the export, especially considering the large stock of organic matter typically present in boreal catchments. Time series analysis (30 years) of data from 70 Norwegian catchments and lakes provided evidence for a tight temporal coupling between the decadal increase in land greening (with NDVI as a proxy) and lake browning (with TOC as a proxy) (Finstad et al., 2016). Taken together, these results link climate-driven greening and hydrologic change in boreal catchments to stronger terrestrial organic-matter export and darker lake waters over long timescales and over recent decades.

Browning has been attributed to environmental drivers operating on a regional scale, including recovery from atmospheric acid deposition . Changes in soil water acidity and ionic strength are known to affect the speciation and mobility of terrestrially derived constituents; the resulting changes in water chemistry can favour transport of iron together with organic matter . Field, laboratory, and survey studies indicate that recovery from acidic deposition is accompanied by changes in soil solution and inflow chemistry, and the underlying mechanisms can be simulated with physical chemistry models [16–20]. Document [6]Recovery from historical atmospheric acid deposition provides an important explanation for browning of northern waters because it restores the solubility, mobility, and export of dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Sulfate (SO4^2−) deposition has varied tremendously over the last century, with a sharp increase after the Second World War, followed by a sharp decline as a result of international legislation. Since the peak deposition in the early 1980s, SO4^2− concentrations in soils have decreased drastically (Akselsson et al. 2013). The low pH and high ionic strength associated with high S deposition may reduce the solubility and mobility of DOC in soils. Field experiments show that the chemistry of current-day precipitation promotes higher DOC concentrations in organic-rich soil horizons of podzols (Ekström et al. 2011). In contrast, the dominant trend since the late 1980s is declining DOC concentrations in soil solution at 50 cm soil depth in less organic-rich horizons (Löfgren and Zetterberg 2011). In the boreal and nemoboreal landscape, organic-rich riparian soils and peatlands are the most important DOC sources (Laudon et al. 2011). This probably explains why long-term monitoring shows that increases in DOC concentrations in freshwaters correspond with declines in SO4^2− concentrations (Monteith et al. 2007; Erlandsson et al. 2008), although these studies cannot resolve whether current browning is simply a return to a more natural, pre-acidification state.

In general, tipping points become harder to predict in a warmer climate (Kosten et al., 2009). 2.2 Increased loadings of DOM in the boreal biome Over thousands to millions of years, the feedback between terrestrial vegetation and aquatic productivity has been essential for the evolution of the atmosphere and the global climate (Beerling, 2008). Vegetation serves not only as a major C pool and eventually a source of total organic carbon (TOC) in boreal areas, but it also promotes root exudates of CO2 and organic C. This enhances weathering rates, thereby increasing the flux of nutrients (P, N, Si, Fe, Ca, and carbonate (CO3)) (Humborg et al., 2004; Hessen et al., 2009) to surface waters. The availability of nutrients subsequently enhances aquatic productivity and thereby C sequestration. In addition, the carbonate species are important for buffering capacity towards acidification in freshwater and marine systems. On different timescales there is thus a range of feedback mechanisms between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems that demand a better understanding. Tracking past-history (Holocene) tree lines, forest cover, and lake sediments revealed a strong and consistent link between climate, forest cover, and lake TOC (Rühland et al., 2003; Rosén, 2005). Thus, at least on the centennial scale, there is a strong temporal TOC link between terrestrial and aquatic systems. Allochthonous C derived either directly as leachate from litterfall and roots or indirectly via partial decomposition of organic matter in the soils constitutes (by far) the dominant pool of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in boreal freshwaters; hence, forest cover and the fraction of bogs and wetland areas in the catchment are key determinants for the concentration and colour of this terrestrially derived chromophoric DOM (Dillon and Molot, 2005; Larsen et al., 2011a).

Document [3]Our results highlight the importance of the coupled geochemical cycles of P and Fe in the long-term trophic state evolution of stratified, ferruginous, low-sulfate-water lakes, conditions that have been reported to serve as analogs for the Archaean Ocean. Human-induced eutrophication since the 20th century, also known as cultural eutrophication, has become a major environmental threat to freshwater ecosystems worldwide. It can create toxic algae blooms and result in deep-water hypoxia or even anoxia among other adverse effects (Paerl, 1988). In most cases, lake eutrophication is attributed to excessive phosphorus (P) inputs from either external or internal loads because P is often the limiting nutrient for lake primary production (Worsfold et al., 2016). There is increasing recognition that lake internal P loading (i.e. P released from sediments into the water column) can trigger a positive feedback of eutrophication, delaying lake recovery after reducing external P loadings (Orihel et al., 2017). This holds particularly true for seasonally stratified, deep lakes, in which hypolimnetic anoxia caused by thermal and/or eutrophication-related biochemical stratification is expected to trigger effective P recycling from surface sediments back into the water column (Lepori and Roberts, 2017; Tu et al., 2019). Hypolimnetic anoxia or meromixis-induced sediment-P release in deep eutrophic lakes has received increasing attention (Cyr et al., 2009; Nürnberg et al., 2018). In stratified eutrophic lakes, the mineralization of organic matter (OM) tends to cause depletion of dissolved oxygen in deep waters, leading to the reductive dissolution of Fe oxyhydroxides and release of adsorbed P back into bottom waters (Steinsberger et al., 2017).
Document [4]Studies in two seasonally stratified eutrophic lakes in Switzerland (Tu et al., 2019), Tu et al., 2020) have demonstrated that labile P in sediments is sensitive to redox-driven sediment release under stratified conditions. Wastewater and other urban shoreline discharges can provide bioavailable phosphorus that sustains summer phytoplankton production in temperate lakes even when catchment-wide nutrient inputs are otherwise managed. In deep lakes, hypolimnetic anoxia can also enhance phosphorus release from bottom sediments. During periods of strong stratification, prolonged phytoplankton growth can coincide with an elevated risk of eutrophication and anoxia in deep lakes. Furthermore, temperate deep lakes provide an important setting for examining how redox conditions regulate the availability of sediment-derived phosphorus. For decades, many researchers have investigated the potential of sediment-P release using different P fractions in sediments and their potential bioavailability (Gao et al., 2005; Kapanen, 2008). Net burial of labile P fractions in sediments, in combination with productivity, redox, and lake mixing proxies, might shed light on changes in sediment-P retention and related feedbacks in the past prior to human influence. However, most of the empirical and modeling research dealing with sediment-P release has focused on timespans of a few decades (Katsev and Dittrich, 2013) and on shallow, polymictic, well‑oxygenated lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2001). There remains a lack of long-term (i.e., Holocene and longer) records of sediment-P fraction retention, eutrophication, and anoxia history, in particular in stratified, deep lakes.

In eutrophic systems, mineralization of organic matter influences sediment P dynamics, but sediment P release rates are commonly higher under anoxic versus oxic conditions (Beutel, 2006; Osaka et al., 2021). Under highly reduced conditions, microbial sulfate (SO42−) reduction can lead to sulfide accumulation in bottom waters (Beutel et al., 2020), with the subsequent loss of Fe(II) from the water column via FeS precipitation (Balistrieri et al., 1992). The combined release of ammonia, phosphate, and Fe can stimulate HABs, which can produce potent toxins, such as microcsytin and anatoxin, that render water unsuitable for human consumption (Falconer and Humpage, 2005) and for recreational contact (Backer et al., 2010; Brooks et al., 2015). The release of reduced metals from the sediment also creates challenges for potable water management as Fe and Mn degrade water treatability and cause taste and odor issues (Khadse et al., 2015; Betancourt et al., 2010). Maintaining a consistent and safe water supply is particularly important for water resilience efforts in water-scarce regions like Southern California, USA, the focus of this study. This study examined patterns of internal nutrient loading through assessment of nutrient and metal releases to water in experimental bench-top sediment-water chambers under different DO concentrations. The experiment was conducted using the traditional oxic and anoxic phases of typical chamber experiments, as well as a less studied hypoxic phase (DO <2 mg/L), which can show interesting and potentially ecologically important patterns of N and P cycling (Doig et al., 2016; Osaka et al., 2021).

It identifes special importance for the littoral environment as groundwater seepage interacts in the nearshore where shallow pathways directly discharge into lakes. Moreover, its relevance increases in the context of shore benthifcation processes that have been documented in many temperate lakes afer dreissenid mussels’ invasions89–91. Finally, groundwater TP loads around the entire Oneida Lake shoreline exhibited high and widely ranging values but comparable to those reported for internal loading in other temperate lakes45, 46, but this loading is occurring at the sediment–water interface throughout the entire lake shoreline. Indeed, it is possible that a portion of groundwater loading may have been included in internal loading estimations for P budgets, as its diferentiation is empirically very challenging, and studies keep excluding one from the other, albeit acknowledging the potential relevance of both6, 46. From a management perspective it is crucial to diferentiate between the two, as internal loading is related to legacy P, while groundwater seepage is a new, external P source. Te groundwater loads were also comparable to those from Oneida’s tributaries44. Lisboa44 conducted an extensive analysis comparing P loading into Oneida Lake from tributaries vs. groundwater during summer 2020. Cumulative loading estimations from the fve main tributaries into the lake added up to 4744 kg of TP, while groundwater loading throughout a 20 m wide belt around the entire lakeshore was estimated at 3335 kg of TP during the same six summer weeks. Moreover, if only basefow conditions (excluding storm fow events, when the majority of sediment bound TP runof occurs) are considered, cumulative TP loading from streams decreases to 2219 kg (Fig. S2). Other estimates of P loading from tributaries fall within a similar range, such as Makarewicz and Lewis92, whose estimates of TP loading from the same 5 tributaries over the growing season 2002 (March to September) added up to 6216 kg of TP.
Document [8]Groundwater discharge in shallow near-shore margins can interact directly with littoral sediments and plants, so phosphorus delivery to lakes depends on what happens along these seepage pathways. Plant-seepage interactions may precipitate and retain a large fraction of iron in lake-groundwater discharge zones because oxygen released from roots changes local chemistry. In one example, Littorella uniflora was described as an efficient binding agent of phosphate to iron in sediment and therefore an important factor in phosphorus immobilization within the sediment. Even with that littoral retention mechanism, groundwater has been shown to carry significant amounts of dissolved P. Because phosphorus is non-hazardous to human health, it is not routinely monitored in drinking water or groundwater, and for that reason groundwater P concentrations have been much less studied in relation to lakes and rivers. For this and a range of related reasons, phosphorus concentrations in groundwater have not been researched as intensively as those in surface waters. Reported background concentrations in groundwater are usually low, around ~10 µg PO4-P/l in areas without strong disturbance, but groundwater-borne P loads still span a wide range. Meinikmann et al. (2016) reported loads from 0.74 to 2900 mg PO4-P m-2 /year, indicating that groundwater entering lake margins can supply substantial phosphorus. Potentially mobile P, generally orthophosphate, is adsorbed within soil and sediment matrices in the saturated zone, which is why unaffected groundwater was long considered a low nutrient source. Yet groundwater P concentrations can rise appreciably above natural background, and the transport of orthophosphate depends on how much sorption capacity remains in the aquifer and sediment. Background groundwater P also depends strongly on bedrock geology. Bedrock containing large amounts of apatite can produce higher background P concentrations in groundwater, underscoring how local geologic setting shapes groundwater delivery to shore zones.

question: When accounting for littoral fluxes, which types of carbon sources drive the release of carbon dioxide from the pelagic zones of lakes?
perspectives: Terrestrial dissolved inorganic and organic carbon imported from the catchment
Littoral macrophyte carbon exported into pelagic waters
Pelagic respiration of autochthonous organic matter
Groundwater-derived inorganic carbon entering directly to the lake

Document [0]**: ** Lakes are important components for regulating carbon cycling within landscapes. Most lakes are regarded as CO2 sources to the atmosphere, although fluxes vary among systems. The sources sustaining the net exchange of CO2 (FCO2) at large spatial scales, including carbon imported from upstream terrestrial ecosystems and respiration of autochthonous organic matter in the pelagic zone, have not been adequately addressed. We integrated remote sensing and Eddy Covariance (EC) technologies to investigate FCO2 in the western basin of Lake Erie—a large lake. Three years of long-term EC data (2012–2014) at two sites were analyzed. We found that FCO2 at both sites varied over daily and monthly timescales across the study period. Considering the complexity of processes within large lakes and the potential uncertainties that remain in our estimations of FCO2 and chlorophyll-a, additional data and analyses are needed to clarify the underlying regulatory mechanisms. Graphical Abstract Lakes are important regulators in regional and global carbon cycling . Carbon imported from upstream terrestrial ecosystems, as well as organic matter produced within the lake's pelagic zone and respired there, may be stored in the water, transported downstream, released to the atmosphere via outgassing, and/or deposited in sediments . Part of the pelagic CO2 outgassing can be sustained by respiration of autochthonous organic matter produced within the lake's pelagic zone. Throughout terrestrial landscapes, most lakes are sources of CO2 . When integrated into climate models correctly, they may shift the landscape-based predictions of a CO2 flux . Failing to consider the contributions of lake components in remote sensing-based up-scaling efforts could lead to unrealistic estimates of the regional carbon budget.

Document [2]Carbon budgets at both the watershed and global scale use inland-water carbon fluxes to constrain terrestrial ecosystem fluxes. This includes the most recent continental carbon budget, where the lateral carbon flux from land to inland waters is constrained by mass-balance calculations using inland-water carbon outgassing and carbon burial estimates. Unless intense littoral carbon turnover is considered, those inferences can produce biased estimates of the carbon budgets of both inland waters and upstream terrestrial ecosystems, and thus of the continental carbon cycle. In this framework, the net atmospheric carbon uptake by macrophytes can be calculated as the atmospheric CO2 taken up for photosynthesis minus the CO2 and CH4 returned to the atmosphere following macrophyte respiration and microbial decomposition of plant debris. This balance will ultimately depend on how much carbon escapes mineralization and outgassing in the littoral, mainly through carbon burial in sediments and carbon export to the pelagic zone. There is, however, currently no regional or global estimate of littoral carbon burial or carbon export to the pelagic zone, and global productivity estimates of littoral habitats from different aquatic vegetation communities rely on measurements from more than 20 years ago. Hence the only global littoral carbon uptake estimate cited here is based on the assumption that 20% of the carbon buried in pelagic sediments and 20% of the carbon exported to estuaries is derived from macrophyte production. However, this percentage has no clear origin in measured data, which makes the omission of explicit littoral macrophyte fluxes especially consequential. The high areal production rates of macrophytes, combined with the relatively efficient preservation of aquatic plant-derived carbon in anoxic sediments, indicate that both littoral carbon burial and macrophyte-derived carbon available for export could be large. That is precisely why littoral macrophyte carbon has to be treated as a major source term when evaluating pelagic carbon release.

Document [5]The role of lakes in dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) transport and transformation depends on the characteristics of each lake, and lateral CO2 transport can be highly significant in boreal lakes (Weyhenmeyer et al. 2015). Many global carbon estimates, including those currently used for policy decisions (IPCC 2013), assume that in lakes, CO2 is efficiently produced by mineralization of terrestrial dissolved organic carbon (DOC) (Aufdenkampe et al. 2011; Battin et al. 2009; Cole et al. 2007; IPCC 2013; Raymond et al. 2013; Tranvik et al. 2009). Document [9]Macrophytes can strongly influence how dissolved organic carbon is processed within lake water. They release oxygen from their roots, which stimulates bacterial decomposition of DOC (Mann and Wetzel, 2000). Macrophytes also increase the residence time of the water, leading to longer exposure to both photo- and microbial degradation. DOC forms an important food source for heterotrophic bacteria, and macrophytes serve as a substrate for those bacteria as well as for epiphytic algae. The resulting communities of macrophytes and epiphytic bacteria and algae can be very productive and highly efficient with regard to DOC degradation (Wetzel and Sondergaard, 1998). Martin et al. (2005) found that the concentration of chromophoric DOC, the part of DOC that absorbs light in water, decreases as water flows through macrophyte beds. A possible explanation is the high abundance of epiphytic bacteria that degrade DOC there. The interaction between heterotrophic bacteria and macrophyte-epiphytic algae complexes also has implications for the aquatic food web. De Kluijver et al. (2015) found from carbon isotope ratios (δ13C) in a Chinese lake that carbon produced by macrophytes and epiphytic algae contributes to bacterioplankton (55%) and zooplankton (47%). Stimulation of zooplankton can in turn reduce the abundance of phytoplankton and thereby help maintain clear water. The decline in chromophoric DOC through macrophyte beds, together with the isotope evidence, indicates that carbon produced in littoral macrophyte stands is actively transformed and passed into lake microbes and consumers. Taken together, these observations connect littoral macrophyte-derived carbon to microbial and consumer processing elsewhere in the lake, including open-water food webs.

The sources sustaining the net exchange of CO2 (FCO2) at large spatial scales, including carbon imported from upstream terrestrial ecosystems and respiration of autochthonous organic matter in the pelagic zone, have not been adequately addressed. Graphical Abstract Lakes are important regulators in regional and global carbon cycling . Carbon imported from upstream terrestrial ecosystems, as well as organic matter produced within the lake's pelagic zone and respired there, may be stored in the water, transported downstream, released to the atmosphere via outgassing, and/or deposited in sediments . Part of the pelagic CO2 outgassing can be sustained by respiration of autochthonous organic matter produced within the lake's pelagic zone. Throughout terrestrial landscapes, most lakes are sources of CO2 . When integrated into climate models correctly, they may shift the landscape-based predictions of a CO2 flux . Failing to consider the contributions of lake components in remote sensing-based up-scaling efforts could lead to unrealistic estimates of the regional carbon budget.

Document [2]Carbon budgets at both the watershed and global scale use inland-water carbon fluxes to constrain terrestrial ecosystem fluxes. This includes the most recent continental carbon budget, where the lateral carbon flux from land to inland waters is constrained by mass-balance calculations using inland-water carbon outgassing and carbon burial estimates. Unless intense littoral carbon turnover is considered, those inferences can produce biased estimates of the carbon budgets of both inland waters and upstream terrestrial ecosystems, and thus of the continental carbon cycle. In this framework, the net atmospheric carbon uptake by macrophytes can be calculated as the atmospheric CO2 taken up for photosynthesis minus the CO2 and CH4 returned to the atmosphere following macrophyte respiration and microbial decomposition of plant debris. This balance will ultimately depend on how much carbon escapes mineralization and outgassing in the littoral, mainly through carbon burial in sediments and carbon export to the pelagic zone. There is, however, currently no regional or global estimate of littoral carbon burial or carbon export to the pelagic zone, and global productivity estimates of littoral habitats from different aquatic vegetation communities rely on measurements from more than 20 years ago. Hence the only global littoral carbon uptake estimate cited here is based on the assumption that 20% of the carbon buried in pelagic sediments and 20% of the carbon exported to estuaries is derived from macrophyte production. However, this percentage has no clear origin in measured data, which makes the omission of explicit littoral macrophyte fluxes especially consequential. The high areal production rates of macrophytes, combined with the relatively efficient preservation of aquatic plant-derived carbon in anoxic sediments, indicate that both littoral carbon burial and macrophyte-derived carbon available for export could be large. That is precisely why littoral macrophyte carbon has to be treated as a major source term when evaluating pelagic carbon release.

Many studies have documented the important role of cold-season atmospheric rivers in producing heavy precipitation and extreme flooding events. Relatively little research has been conducted on the warm-season atmospheric rivers and their impacts on heatwave events. Here we show an anomalous warm-season atmospheric river moving across the North Pacific and its interaction with the extreme western North American heatwave in late June 2021. ARs are typically associated with a low-level jet stream ahead of the cold front of an extratropical cyclone, and frequently lead to heavy precipitation when they are forced upward by mountains or frontal lift9, 10. Along the west coast of North America (NA), high-impact ARs often arrive in the cold season when weather is dominated by the strong onshore flow of Pacific airstreams2, 9, 11–14. Some of these systems are also known as pineapple express storms for their apparent origin in the tropical area near Hawaii15–17. Their landfall on mountainous areas can produce extremely heavy precipitation and may trigger hazardous floods, mudslides, and avalanches. Intense ARs are rare over the northeast Pacific in the warm season, when a ridge of high pressure tends to reside off the west coast of NA. Such ridged conditions are often accompanied by reduced cloud cover, which increases incoming shortwave radiation to lake surfaces and can sharpen summer temperature extremes.

Document [4]Agricultural irrigation can deliver dissolved salts to a lake even when the irrigation supply is much fresher than the receiving water. Crops and evaporation remove water from an irrigated field, while much of the dissolved mineral load remains. Drainage therefore carries salts in a smaller volume of water, and the returning flow can transport that concentrated load through drains, rivers or groundwater toward the lake. The important quantity for a salt budget is the mass delivered with the flow, rather than the mere presence of an irrigation canal nearby.

The Imperial Valley provides a measured example. A USGS study published in 2003 described irrigation with Colorado River water containing about 850 milligrams per liter of total dissolved solids. Agricultural drainage in the study area contained roughly 3,000 to 15,000 milligrams per liter, with the increase attributed to evapotranspiration. The study investigated treatment of this drainage, but its water-quality measurements also show the concentration process that can occur between supply and return flow. These are historical study values, not an assertion that every drain currently has the same concentration. The same pilot study reduced dissolved solids in treated drainage to about 300-500 milligrams per liter using nanofiltration, illustrating a way to intercept salt before reuse or discharge.

USGS hydrologic investigations describe the Salton Sea as receiving predominantly irrigation drainage, including flows conveyed through the Alamo and New Rivers. Because the lake occupies a closed basin, evaporation removes water without exporting the dissolved salts through a river outlet. Repeated drainage inputs can consequently add to the stored salt mass. Salt loading and observed concentration must nevertheless be distinguished: an inflow less saline than the lake can temporarily dilute it while still adding salt overall. The older USGS water-and-salt budgets document why changes in lake volume and evaporation must be considered alongside inflow. This example connects field-scale irrigation losses, concentrated return drainage and long-term salt accumulation in a receiving lake without requiring all salinity changes to have a single cause.

Document [6]During a “normal” winter, repeated snowfall events should lead to repeated deicing applications (both pre-treatment and post-snowfall removal), resulting in salt accumulations on or bordering impervious surfaces. Roadway and walkway surfaces often develop a whitish appearance as rock salt particles become crushed by motor vehicles and foot traffic. Deicing salts remain stockpiled in this manner until they are cleared off during the next snow removal activity, or until they are flushed off by late-winter snowmelt or spring rainfall. In recent years, “normal” winter weather has shifted to now include both snowfall and rainfall events plus multiple snowmelt events during typical winter months (December–February) in many northern urban areas . Runoff events become intermixed with snowfall events that now produce alternating episodes of deicer application and chloride runoff (see Table 1), possibly reducing the total accumulation of deicers on and near roadways throughout the winter season but extending the potential salt runoff season. We anticipated that gradual seasonal warming leading to snowmelt would gradually mobilize accumulated deicers into the stormwater system for delivery to Lake Winona. However, we expected that late-winter rainfall would more efficiently flush salts from the landscape , particularly from roadways, producing higher chloride concentrations in rainfall runoff than in snowmelt runoff. Our runoff data did not support this expectation, with no significant difference in chloride concentrations in snowmelt-generated versus rainfall-generated runoff. Again, the alternating pattern of snowmelt and rainfall that occurred during both years of our monitoring likely affected the quantity of deicing salts available for conveyance to the lake, with multiple runoff episodes each carrying a reduced load of chloride compared to what might be moved under an idealized single, gradual snowmelt followed by a single cleansing rainfall event. Alternatively, greater runoff flows during rainfall versus snowmelt events potentially diluted chloride concentrations during rainfall events, reducing chloride concentrations in runoff to levels similar to those observed during snowmelt.

Document [9]Deicing salts are a major contributor to freshwater salinization in the Northeastern United States, disrupting ecosystem function, aquatic life, and infrastructure integrity. It is often presumed that surface runoff is the dominant mode of chloride transport from impervious surfaces to surface waters despite empirical evidence for soil and groundwater transport. In urban catchments, weathering of concrete and other built materials and the mobilization of legacy salts from soils are also important sources of salinity that can reach lakes by runoff or groundwater. Our project aimed to (1) estimate the hydrologic pathways for chloride transport in a small, urbanized catchment in the Northeastern United States; and (2) provide a critical evaluation of simulation routines commonly used to guide the management of deicing salts. We investigated possible variations in urban chloride pathways by monitoring stormwater discharge and chloride across a winter season with deicing salt spreading and snow accumulation and melt. We analyzed these time series with US EPA SWMM, which presumes chloride transport occurs exclusively via surface runoff into stormwater systems. We develop two parallel models: one using the base empirical temperature-index snow routines, and a second substituting a process-based snowmelt model. Each model was calibrated via the generalized likelihood uncertainty estimation algorithm to both stormwater volumes and chloride mass. Both models adequately simulated water volumes but failed to reproduce observed chloride dynamics, suggesting substantial deicing salt movement through soils and groundwater as a major urban hydrologic pathway. The results of this study will inform the development of urban hydrologic fate and transport models and chloride best management practices. question: By what processes do the primary drainage divides within tectonically active mountain ranges shift their positions?
perspectives: Gradual asymmetric fluvial erosion and headward channel growth
Discrete river capture events that abruptly reorganize drainage area
Horizontal tectonic advection that shifts topography relative to channels
Landslide-driven divide migration through repeated valley-wall failures
context:
Document [0]In particular, they are often associated with asymmetric reliefs, which are common features of both tectonically active and inactive fold and thrust ranges. Such asymmetry is usually of structural origin, and associated with the uplift of the range along ramp-flat systems or with the development of asymmetric propagation folds. The resulting topography often exhibits a significant difference in slope across ridges, as maintained by tectonic uplift when active, and controlled by the dip direction of underlying strata. The steeper side, which can display bare bedrock cliffs, is most often opposed to the dip direction, whereas a gentler sloping surface on the other side often follows a structural surface set by the dipping strata (Figure 1). This difference in slopes across ridges and associated drainage divides is structurally-controlled and of tectonic origin, and is present since the formation of the ridge, independently of ulterior climatic and geomorphic forcing on the landscape. The asymmetry can induce very contrasted processes and evolution on the two sides, with for example a steep cliff dominated by rock falls on one side, and a gently dipping soil-mantled surface dominated by creep on the other side. Repeated valley-wall landslides can therefore drive divide migration by causing incremental retreat of the ridge crest away from the failing side. Similarly, weathering processes can act at very different paces depending on the respective depths, on each side, of the regolith overlaying bedrock. Such drastic differences in processes between the two sides can have significant implications on how the hillslopes and first-order channels of these ridges respond. In particular, the dynamics of divide migration, where a basin captures part of the drainage area of another, can be modulated by differences in the erosion processes and their response timescales between the two sides of the divide (Whipple et al., 2017; Braun, 2018). In turn, these local processes, at the local scale of the ridge and associated divides, may impact the way the river network adjusts. However, the challenge for coastal regions around the planet is projecting sea-level rise and its impacts into the future. This is an important objective of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), but individual geographic entities (local to national governments) are simultaneously involved in developing future sea-level rise projections for their own regions . Future climate projections are developed through global climate models, which include uncertainties and assumptions of future greenhouse gas emissions (i.e., Representative Concentration Pathways) and model the inputs or factors that will affect global climate, including ice melt and consequently sea-level rise . Today, the predictions or projections for the next few decades are in general agreement but estimates for the end-of-century vary between models and depend on Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs), with increasingly wider uncertainties and ranges by 2100. The latest estimates indicate that values for the end-of-century (2100) range from a low of ~50 cm (~20 inches) to as high as ~310 cm (~10 feet), as a function of greenhouse gas emission scenarios and various probabilities or uncertainties, especially concerning the extent of Greenland and Antarctica ice melt (Figure 3). Understandably, while projections of future sea levels typically only extend out to 2100 due to increasing uncertainties, sea-level rise will not stop then, but will likely continue for decades and even centuries into the future.

Thus, the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta is not doomed to drown under climate change—it is doomed to drown under scenarios of anthropogenic reductions in the sediment delivery needed to sustain the delta83. The upstream component of the problem is therefore the reduced delivery of fluvial sediment needed to sustain the delta plain. The resulting boundary-condition shift therefore involves both diminished sediment delivery from upstream and more aggressive reworking at the delta front and coast. Widespread dam construction, water diversions, and embankment decisions are treated here as human actions that produce or modulate those two retained boundary-condition shifts rather than as separate boundary-condition categories in their own right.

These observations may be more indicative of the importance of salt crystallisation over hydration for the expansion of rocks in this zone. As well as having a critical influence on chemical weathering, biogenic processes, and other mechanical decay mechanisms such as salt crystallisation, thermal regimes can instigate the breakdown rock via the expansion and contraction of minerals in response to temperature. The development of thermal gradients within rock masses and thermally-induced inter-grain stresses in granular rocks are important for decay alongside temperature fluctuations at the rock–air interface (e.g. Warke et al. 1996; Gómez-Heras et al. 2006). Both high-magnitude, rapid changes in rock temperature (‘thermal shock’) and the cumulative effect of repeated lower-magnitude fluctuations (‘thermal fatigue’) can act to weaken rocks making them more susceptible to other decay processes (Yatsu 1988; Mottershead in press). In the coastal zone, temperature appears to be positively correlated to the swelling and shrinking of rocks, at least in the absence of rain (e.g. Hemmingsen et al. 2007). In South Wales, expansion and contraction of coastal limestone and mudstone during periods of dry, warm weather is recognised as an important mechanism of decay (Williams and Davies 1987) and breakdown rates of supratidal greenschist show a positive correlation with summertime air temperatures in southern England (Mottershead 1989). Such relationships may represent enhanced salt weathering during warmer weather alongside any thermoclastic effects. In southwest England, frequent temperature variations in the order of several degrees occur on rock platforms over a timescale of 15–30 minutes, attributed to wind patterns and interruptions to insolation by passing cloud (Coombes 2011b). Such thermal cycling probably contributes to the progressive weakening of coastal rocks to some degree, particularly in association with tidal wetting and drying, and is most pronounced during summer.

However, predicting long-term erosion remains challenging due to the episodic nature of retreat and the limitations of existing models. This study introduces a novel 3D mathematical model that estimates cliff recession by balancing wave energy delivery at the cliff toe against the energy required to erode rock while simulating natural erosion cycles: notch formation, collapse, debris removal, and renewed erosion. The model reduces reliance on historical data by incorporating episodic dynamics and morphologic feedback. The model was validated against a 152-year record of cliff retreat along the Sussex chalk coastline, demonstrating a statistically significant correlation with observed recession rates. The model's ability to capture the complex interplay of beach cover, wave energy, and sea level rise (SLR) was evaluated. As sea level rises, the protective beach sediment cover in front of the cliff can narrow or be stripped away, removing a buffer that otherwise absorbs wave energy and exposes the cliff toe to greater attack. The model showed that SLR substantially accelerates recession under 10–20 mm/year SLR over a century. These results align with empirical studies, highlighting enhanced wave-driven erosion as beach protection is reduced under climate change. This framework provides a critical tool for coastal managers to evaluate erosion risks, prioritize adaptation strategies, and mitigate escalating threats from rising seas and wave attack. Cliff recession is a serious problem in the coastal zones which causes economic loss and sometimes threatens human lives (Doody et al., 2004; Dickson et al., 2007; Westoby et al., 2018; Young et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2024). It is critical to understand coastal change, for coastal zone management and development planning. There has been an interest in develop numerical models and formulations that can be able to predict cliff profile changes, estimate the erosion rate and describe relations between different parameters which are effective on coastal morphodynamics.

Document [1]For rockfall source areas, susceptibility depends on a combination of geology, fracturing, mechanical properties, activity, and hydrogeology. Geological factors include rock types and weathering, variability of the geological structure, bedding, the type of deposit, and whether the slope lies in a folded zone. Fracturing includes the number and orientation of joint sets, their trace lengths, spacing, and the overall intensity of fracturing. Mechanical properties such as cohesion and friction angle influence whether fractured blocks remain stable or detach from the slope face. Hydrogeology matters through permeability and joint permeability, while observed movements or rockfall activity provide direct evidence that the source area is already active. Source-area susceptibility analysis has therefore often used multiple engineering classifications for fractured rock. Within this framework, the joint sets or discontinuities are the anisotropies that mainly control stability, and the geological and mechanical factors are related to those discontinuity properties. The relation between joint orientation and slope orientation is especially important because those discontinuities define potential release surfaces for detached blocks and influence how readily those release surfaces are activated during rockfall failure. This is why approaches such as Rock Mass Rating (RMR), its evolution to Slope Mass Rating (SMR), and the Geological Strength Index (GSI) have been applied successfully to slope-stability analysis. These approaches summarize the quality of the fractured rock mass and make the dependence on joint-slope orientation more explicit when evaluating source-area instability. The link between rockfall activity and the intensity of pre-existing fracturing, including fold hinges with steep limbs, has been demonstrated directly by Coe and Harp (2007). Instability potential can evolve through time as external factors act on the source area, but the controlling theme remains fractured rock releasing blocks from the slope face.

Document [6]At the outcrop scale, instabilities in a rock mass generally involve the mobilization and detachment of discrete blocks bounded by planar discontinuities. The broader slope can be high and complex, but the size of the slope, such as its vertical height, is not by itself a direct indication of the type or size of instability that develops or of the kind of slope damage that will govern motion and kinematics. A small block released as a rockfall from a high, vertical rock slope still involves damage processes that are typical of outcrop-scale instability rather than those of a deep rupture surface located far within the slope. In this setting, the relative orientation and spacing of discontinuities define the shape and size of the blocks, control the geometry of their release surfaces, and strongly influence the way they detach from exposed rock faces. Those blocks displace through simple kinematic mechanisms controlled by discontinuity geometry, and block toppling is one of the characteristic outcomes when fractured bedrock releases individual blocks from the slope. In general, relatively low stress magnitudes, on the order of 100 to 150 kPa for a 4 to 6 m slope and a 25 kN/m3 unit weight, occur along the discontinuities bounding the block, largely as a function of discontinuity orientation and rock-mass unit weight. When the discontinuities are fully persistent, meaning that no in-plane or out-of-plane rock bridges occur along the release surface, the block can displace with limited development of damage, including shearing of asperities along the discontinuity surface (Figure 2a; ). Conversely, even a limited amount of rock bridges along the release surface can effectively stabilize the block and delay or prevent detachment (Figure 2b). Based on a survey of the published literature and online media, it can reasonably be suggested that many large failures are preceded by increasing rates of material detachment from the slope. Those precursory rockfalls decrease the overall stability of the slope and can therefore be considered a form of slope damage that is capable of controlling the detachment and kinematics of blocks within rock slopes. The behavior of those blocks also depends on rock mass quality, a term broadly used to describe the lithological and structural configuration of the rock mass and, in turn, its overall mechanical behavior. High-quality rock masses are generally recognized as having a relatively low degree of fracturing, high intact rock strength, and limited surface weathering, matrix weathering, and alteration. Low-quality rock masses are identified as having a higher degree of fracturing, lower intact rock strength, and more intense weathering and alteration. In the published literature, quantification of rock mass quality using the Geological Strength Index (GSI), originally introduced by Hoek and co-workers to estimate rock mass strength and deformability, has become increasingly popular in practice, and the association between GSI and rock mass quality is widely accepted. The importance of scale, however, cannot be overstated. Methods used for rock-slope damage assessment and for stability analyses focused on structurally controlled block release must take into consideration the size of the investigated or expected instability, because fracturing, intact strength, and weathering condition how readily blocks detach from the slope. In practical terms, poorer-quality rock masses with more fracturing and weathering are more prone to repeated small detachments that progressively prepare larger failures. In this view, repeated small detachments from fractured bedrock slopes are part of the damage evolution that precedes larger block failures, reduces stability, and helps govern rockfall behavior.

Using machine learning, daily fire activity was predicted at 0.05° resolution, about 5 km, across the tropical peatlands of Riau as a function of weather variables alone and then as a function of the same weather variables plus specific hydrologic outputs from the established process-based tropical peatland model ecosys, as summarized in supplementary figures S1 and S2. Those hydrologic outputs were generated using publicly available weather, soil, and management information, and the model was parameterized and benchmarked with available scientific data. Although the coverage and quality of those data were not perfect, the exercise still provided useful insight into the strengths, limitations, and scalability of representing peatland hydrology explicitly at regional scale. The analyses showed that including simulated hydrologic dynamics significantly enhanced the prediction of active fires in Riau compared with using weather variables alone, and the improvement was especially strong during severe drought. In the results and discussion on modeling hydrologic dynamics, the model reproduced drying through desiccation of near-surface peat and mineral soil at 0.05° resolution across Riau during both the short and the long dry seasons in 2015. That pattern explains why prolonged dry periods matter so much: weather variables alone do not fully capture subsurface drying, whereas explicit representation of peat-moisture loss during severe drought gives a better account of when active fires emerge across tropical peatlands and adjacent landscapes. The study therefore ties improved fire prediction to the ability to represent persistent peat drying during severe seasonal drought rather than relying on weather proxies alone during the fire season in Riau.

In drained peatlands, loss of water causes the organic-rich soil to compact and oxidize, producing peat subsidence. Peat soils can shrink by 2–5 cm/year because of water loss and microbial decomposition, and oxidation breaks down organic matter, collapses pore spaces, and permanently lowers land elevation. This subsidence exacerbates drainage problems and accelerates further peat degradation in a self-reinforcing cycle. The broader lithospheric impacts include permanent land loss, reduced capacity to support ecosystems or infrastructure, and saltwater intrusion into freshwater aquifers. In Indonesia, subsidence has rendered 1.2 million hectares of peatland unusable for agriculture or habitation . When peat soils are drained, oxidation also emits 1.9 ± 0.3 Gt CO2/year , shifting peatlands from long-term carbon sinks to net emission sources and degrading their climate-mitigation capacity .

Using machine learning, daily fire activity was predicted at 0.05° resolution, about 5 km, across the tropical peatlands of Riau as a function of weather variables alone and then as a function of the same weather variables plus specific hydrologic outputs from the established process-based tropical peatland model ecosys, as summarized in supplementary figures S1 and S2. Those hydrologic outputs were generated using publicly available weather, soil, and management information, and the model was parameterized and benchmarked with available scientific data. Although the coverage and quality of those data were not perfect, the exercise still provided useful insight into the strengths, limitations, and scalability of representing peatland hydrology explicitly at regional scale. The analyses showed that including simulated hydrologic dynamics significantly enhanced the prediction of active fires in Riau compared with using weather variables alone, and the improvement was especially strong during severe drought. In the results and discussion on modeling hydrologic dynamics, the model reproduced drying through desiccation of near-surface peat and mineral soil at 0.05° resolution across Riau during both the short and the long dry seasons in 2015. That pattern explains why prolonged dry periods matter so much: weather variables alone do not fully capture subsurface drying, whereas explicit representation of peat-moisture loss during severe drought gives a better account of when active fires emerge across tropical peatlands and adjacent landscapes. The study therefore ties improved fire prediction to the ability to represent persistent peat drying during severe seasonal drought rather than relying on weather proxies alone during the fire season in Riau.

Se pronostica a la vez, que muchas regiones donde las condiciones serán más cálidas y secas, experimentarán cambios evidentes en los regímenes de fuegos. Incrementos en las temperaturas, condiciones de sequía, y situaciones meteorológicas predisponentes serán importantes condicionantes en la severidad de los fuegos. Document [1]Forest wildfire severity is strongly shaped by fuels. However, because fuels are also the forest component most altered by the loss of recurring low-severity fire and can be actively managed, quantifying their effects on severity has become an urgent research priority. Here we employed GEDI spaceborne lidar to consistently assess how pre-fire forest fuel structure affected wildfire severity across 42 California wildfires between 2019–2021. Using a spatial hierarchical modeling framework, we found a positive relationship between GEDI-derived fuel structure and wildfire severity, marked by increasing severity as stands shifted away from open conditions toward denser lower-forest fuels. Critically, metrics describing ladder fuels were especially informative for severity patterns. Ladder fuels consistently predicted severity, with sparse understories uniformly associated with lower severity levels. These results confirm that GEDI-derived fuel estimates can overcome limitations of optical imagery and airborne lidar for quantifying the forest structures associated with wildfire severity. Furthermore, these findings have direct implications for designing treatment interventions that target ladder fuels and promote more open stand conditions. Wildfires are an essential ecosystem process that maintains forest productivity, biodiversity, function, and resilience1. Throughout the pre-European Western US, frequent fires were a common phenomenon, including those set intentionally by Indigenous Peoples2, 3. The loss of this Indigenous and other recurring low-severity burning removed a process that had maintained open stand structure and limited ladder-fuel buildup in dry conifer forests. However, elevated tree densities and lower-forest fuel densities relative to the pre-industrial baseline after more than a century of intensive fire suppression have contributed to increasingly severe wildfires4–6. This trend toward historically uncharacteristic high-severity fires has resulted in wildfire regimes that are more destructive to forest ecosystems and more dangerous to human communities7, 8. The occurrence of more severe wildfires has also had an acute effect on post-fire forest transitions.

Document [0]In this short review 1 I discuss how high energy (type I) seesaw models can be nicely embedded within grand-unified models and reproduce the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry with leptogenesis. In particular, after discussing general features and results in leptogenesis, I focus on SO(10)-inspired leptogenesis and on a particular solution, the strong thermal SO(10)-inspired solution, that provides an interesting way to understand neutrino mixing parameters: the non-vanishing reactor mixing angle, the emerging negative sign of sin δ and the slight hints favouring normally ordered neutrino masses and an atmospheric mixing angle in the first octant. I also briefly discuss leptogenesis within two right-handed seesaw neutrino models. In this case a a third decoupled right-handed neutrino can provide a candidate for very heavy cold decaying dark matter produced from right-handed neutrino mixing with a mass in the TeV-EeV range and its decays would give a contribution to the IceCube high energy neutrino events in addition to an astrophysical component. The ΛCDM cosmological model has so far resisted all experimental efforts to unearth sound evidences motivating a modification or an extension. Therefore, it nowadays provides a minimal model able to describe all cosmological observations . However, within the Standard Model of particle physics and fundamental interactions (SM), we cannot explain the nature and origin of some of the features of the ΛCDM, in particular the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry of the Universe and the necessity of a non-baryonic dark matter component. For this reason these cosmological puzzles have to be regarded as strong motivations for new physics beyond the SM. Grand-unified-scale baryogenesis proceeds through out-of-equilibrium decays of superheavy gauge or Higgs bosons that directly create the baryon excess. Neutrino masses and mixing also call for an extension of the SM and it is then reasonable that the same new physics should also address the cosmological puzzles. Here I focus on a simple extension based on the introduction of right-handed (RH) neutrinos with Yukawa couplings, generating a Dirac mass term for neutrinos as for the other massive fermions, and an additional Majorana mass term.

In HTS, instead, the role played by charge order might be more profound and possibly linked or even responsible for the unconventional normal state and superconducting properties. In cuprates the charge order exhibits indeed a strong entanglement with the superconducting order, highlighted by many occurrences, as the depression of the superconducting critical temperature at the doping where charge order is strongest (p ≈ 1/8) , the drop of the CDW intensity and correlation length when entering in the superconducting state , the rise of these two quantities - together with the appearance of a long range threedimensional CDW (3D-CDW) - when superconductivity is depressed under high magnetic fields . Thence, it is not surprising that in several theoretical models, initially proposed by Emery et al and Castellani et al and variously developed in the ensuing two decades [35–45], collective charge density fluctuations are expected to permeate a very broad area of the cuprate phase diagram, being pivotal both to the anomalous properties of the normal state and to the su- perconducting pairing. This is because CDW are localized in a rather narrow region of the phase diagram below the pseudogap temperature: they are absent in strongly underdoped and overdoped samples, even though superconductivity sets in at these doping levels; they are absent at high temperatures, where the strange metal phase dominates the phase diagram.

Document [4]Having stimulated over 100, 000 publications, the question of what causes superconductivity in the cuprates is widely considered to be one of the great challenges of condensed-matter physics . On the twentieth anniversary of its discovery, it was deemed “a mystery that defies solution” . Since then, however, exciting developments have given researchers hope that a solution may in fact be within reach . In particular, a new family of superconductors – the pnictides – was discovered , with critical temperatures as high as 57 K . In this review, I discuss some of the recent developments that shed light on the two major questions of cuprate superconductivity: What causes electron pairing? What is the nature of the pseudogap phase, the enigmatic region of the phase diagram that overlaps with much of the superconducting phase? I do not attempt to review the field but rather explore a particular perspective, based on the conjecture that the pseudogap phase is fundamentally a phase with spin-density-wave (SDW) order, ending at a quantum critical point (QCP), with its fluctuations dominating the scattering of electrons and their pairing. This would make cuprates similar to heavy-fermion, organic, and pnictide superconductors, for which superconductivity is typically found in close proximity to SDW order. While many researchers believe that distinct theories are required for the different families of superconductors, I shall argue here that a fundamentally similar pairing mechanism operates, and this common perspective suggests that a solution may be within reach. Pnictide: iron-based material made of layers of Fe2As2 in which superconductivity can occur, with Tc values as high as 57 K Pseudogap phase: enigmatic region of the cuprate phase diagram delineated by a crossover temperature T\* below which the electronic density of states is partially gapped Spin density wave (SDW): antiferromagnetic modulation of the spin density in a metal; the new periodicity causes a reconstruction of the Fermi surface such that a large hole surface is typically transformed into small electron and hole pockets

The same basic scenario invoked for the hole-doped side applies here on the electron-doped side, with antiferromagnetic correlations providing the relevant organizing framework. On the low-doping side, there is SDW order, broken translational symmetry and Fermi-surface reconstruction. Coming down in temperature, a two-stage evolution occurs, where short-range SDW correlations / fluctuations appear first below T* and long-range order only sets in later. The fact that the SDW order is commensurate, with wavevector Q = (π, π), means that the four-fold rotational symmetry of the lattice is not broken in this case. Near x*, where Tc peaks (in zero field), the resistivity is perfectly linear, almost certainly the result of scattering by antiferromagnetic fluctuations. Stepping back to look at the high-Tc puzzle from a distance, incorporating both sides of the cuprate phase diagram and bearing in mind the broad landscape of unconventional superconductivity as we have come to know it over the past 30 years, the essential ingredient appears to be the antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations that grow strong in this regime. These fluctuations can mediate anisotropic pairing and scatter electrons in a way which is in turn strongly influenced by the pairing correlations.

Weakcoupling renormalization group calculations reproduce the phase diagram – with SDW order giving way to superconductivity – and account in detail for the antiferromagnetic fluctuations observed by nuclear magnetic resonance. This leaves little doubt that pairing and scattering in this material both come from low-energy antiferromagnetic fluctuations. The calculations reveal a fundamental mechanism not considered in previous treatments of non-Fermi-liquid behaviour near an antiferromagnetic QCP: the positive interference between pairing correlations and spin fluctuations . The pairing correlations enhance the spin fluctuations and thereby impart an anomalous linear temperature dependence to the scattering rate , causing the resistivity to deviate from the T2 dependence expected at T → 0 away from the QCP. This interference mechanism operates as long as pairing correlations are significant, and thus provides a natural explanation for the correlation between anomalous (non-Fermi-liquid) resistivity and Tc. The fact that the same correlation is present in cuprates is strong evidence that the same positive interference is at play: spin fluctuations cause d-wave pairing and d-wave correlations enhance scattering. The d-wave-like anisotropy of the linear-T scattering detected by ADMR in overdoped Tl-2201 would then be the fingerprint of that interference, the reason why “electrons scatter as they pair” . As non-Fermi-liquid behaviour and unconventional superconductivity are but two manifestations of the same interference, the observation of a non-Fermi-liquid resistivity tied to Tc emerges as a smoking gun for pairing mediated by antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations. These considerations have motivated the investigation of almost every conceivable mechanism that could create a pairing interaction sufficiently strong to yield superconductivity at these elevated temperatures； strongly correlated models that have been proposed to explain the cuprates have been recently reviewed by Dagotto (1994). In resonating-valence-bond theories, superconductivity emerges when doping mobilizes singlet bonds generated by strong electronic correlations, without any separate pairing glue. The most distinguishing feature of each proposed model is its prediction for the symmetry of the order parameter implied by the specific pairing mechanism. There are many allowed symmetries for the pairing state of superconductors; the full range has been catalogued by Annett, Goldenfeld, and Renn (1991), who also made a comprehensive review of the experimental evidence for different symmetries up to that time. It was first suggested within the framework of a Hubbard model by Scalapino and coworkers (Bickers et al., 1989) that the exchange of antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations could promote pairing in a dx22 channel, but this mechanism was at the time believed to be too weak to explain the high transition tem-peratures of the cuprates. The motivation for this model and the parameters incorporated in it are largely derived from NMR measurements (for a review, see Slichter, 1994). The spin-fluctuation model predicts many of the normal and superconducting-state properties of the cuprates, and is supported by many recent experiments (see the recent review by Pines, 1995).

Document [0]One possibility, albeit indirect, to obtain information on the origins of MBHs is through “archeology” in local dwarf galaxies with stellar mass below ∼ 10^9 M . For this, theoretical predictions need to link the “initial conditions” to what we can observe today: how mass grows through accretion and mergers and the complex dynamics of sinking and ejections become key. Many studies of seeds are instead devoted only to the formation phase and do not evolve a population all the way to today, and even when they do they often include only one type of seeds. The expectation is that measuring the masses of MBHs and their occupation fraction in the smallest dwarf galaxies can help infer the origin of MBH seeds132, 133. In primordial-black-hole scenarios, the seeds would have formed directly from overdensities in the early Universe before stars or galaxies existed. However, many seed models predict similar initial masses, ∼ 10^3 M (see Box 1), limiting the value of this probe, but the discovery of a ∼ 10^5 M MBH in a dwarf galaxy with stellar mass ∼ 10^6 M — if shown to belong to a genuinely low-mass system — would hint at the existence of direct collapse. Furthermore MBH formation mechanisms predict that only a fraction of dwarf galaxies host MBHs, and this fraction depends on the specific mechanism. Because direct collapse and some flavors of primordial black holes predict rare seeds, the occupation fraction of dwarf galaxies, especially those with stellar mass as low as ∼ 10^6 M , provides a useful test of these channels, as shown in Box 1. This is reflected in the shape and normalization of the MBH mass distribution, known as mass function, 134: heavy-seed scenarios would be truncated at higher masses. The number density also reflects the frequency, or rarity, of such seeds: to explain today’s MBHs we need models that predict at least the observed number density.
Document [1]LSBHs can grow into SMBHs if they can either sustain near-Eddington accretion for Gyr time periods, or more likely experience short bursts of super-Eddington accretion 15–18. In this vein, many theoretical studies argue that the formation of a thick disk around a BH may facilitate super-Eddington accretion even in the presence of feedback 19–23. This pathway is further supported by recent observations of SMBHs that accrete at super-Eddington limits 24, 25. However, even if LSBHs can accrete at super-Eddington rates, it is still unclear whether LSBHs encounter regions of sufficiently high density to allow super-Eddington accretion to develop efficiently and frequently. This is particularly true at mass scale of the LSBHs since the lighter a BH is, the more difficult it is to attract mass and accrete. Previously, it has been shown that LSBHs can grow in idealised, isolated galaxy simulations, using extremely high resolution hydrodynamic simulations26–28. Depending on the properties of the surrounding gas, it was shown that LSBHs can grow on timescales of 500 Myr 15 or even achieve rapid runaway accretion episodes 26, 28, 29. Several studies have shown that super-Eddington accretion onto light black hole seeds is possible across a wide range of parameters, including feedback efficiencies, seed masses, and accretion models, and that sustained growth can occur even when thermal feedback is included 27, 30. However, more realistic, large-scale cosmological simulations have consistently failed to demonstrate LSBH growth 16, 31 In this study, we run a suite of high-resolution cosmological simulations to investigate the small spatial scale dynamics (sub-pc) around LSBHs and study their growth in a fully cosmological setting, including both SNe feedback and BH feedback. Our goal is to investigate if LSBHs (similar to their behaviour in idealised isolated systems) can grow in a self-consistent cosmological environment.
Document [2]*Context*. We present simulations of a massive young star cluster using the codes Nbody6++GPU and MOCCA. The cluster is initially more compact than previously published models. It contains one million stars and has a total mass of 5.86 × 105 M⊙ and a half-mass radius of 0.1 pc. *Aims*. We analyzed the formation and growth of a very massive star (VMS) through successive stellar collisions and investigated the subsequent formation of an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in the core of a dense star cluster. We used direct *N*-body and Monte Carlo simulations that incorporated updated stellar evolution prescriptions for single and binary stellar evolution (SSE and BSE) tailored to massive stars and VMSs. These include revised treatments of stellar radii, rejuvenation, and mass loss during collisions. While the prescriptions represent reasonable extrapolations into the VMS regime, the internal structure and thermal state of VMSs that formed through stellar collisions remain uncertain, and future work may require further refinement. *Results*. Runaway stellar collisions in the cluster core produce a VMS that exceeds 5 × 104 M⊙ within 5 Myr that subsequently collapses into an IMBH. We stress that further work on stellar astrophysics is needed, particularly in the context of VMS formation. The VMS formation currently represents strong uncertainties. Our model suggests that dense stellar environments may enable the formation of VMSs and massive black hole seeds through runaway stellar collisions. These results provide a potential pathway for early black hole growth in star clusters and offer a theoretical context for interpreting recent observations with the James Webb Space Telescope of young compact clusters at high redshift. In addition, the larger dynamical mass strengthens the effect of dynamical friction by a small fraction, improving the likelihood of the black hole migrating toward the galactic centre.43, 44. Interesting, the final masses of our growing light seeds 103 − 104 M⊙ are the seed BH masses in larger cosmological simulations 45–47. Many of these studies found that their seeds grow into SMBHs at lower redshifts and are likely to be progenitors of the SMBHs observed at lower redshifts. But for these seeds to sustain growth, their host galaxies stellar mass must typically exceed masses of 109 − 1010 M⊙ at which point feedback is no longer efficient at expelling gas. Our simulations therefore provide a bridge between the light seeds expected from the first stars and the black holes seeded in large-volume cosmological simulations, linking the earliest formation pathways to the long-term growth into the SMBHs observed at low redshift. This, of course, is a non-trivial task in the mainstream of cosmological simulations. PopIII remnant black holes are typically not modelled in a cosmological context due to the high resolution required to resolve their birth environments and secondly the required resolution to correctly model the growth of their remnants is typically not achieved (i.e. the BHL radius is not resolved). Our simulations achieve both but at the cost of being unable to evolve the system beyond a few hundred Myr post Big Bang. Although our high-resolution simulations are limited in runtime and cannot trace the long-term evolution of these seeds, the early growth that these select few BH undergo positions them as compelling candidates to be the dominant channel for the origin of SMBHs.

Instead of taking the whole spectrum into account, we assume that the typical energy of an ionizing photon is hν0 = 20 eV (∼ 60 nm) (Murray-Clay et al. 2009a). Once the protoplanetary disk dissolves, a planet orbiting a young star becomes exposed to high energy radiation from the host star. For orbital periods less than 100 days, this is expected to drive the erosion of the planetary atmosphere. As stars age, rotational spin-down causes a decrease in magnetic activity and with it their high-energy X-ray and ultraviolet emission (e.g. Gudel et al. ¨ 1997; Ribas et al. 2005; Booth et al. 2017). Young stars with ages less than a Gyr emit XUV radiation that can be several orders of magnitude higher than for the present-day Sun. For planets, the XUV irradiation level thus is much higher in the early stages compared to more mature ages. As a result, their atmospheres are hotter, more expanded and therefore more susceptible to mass loss. When investigating the atmospheric erosion of planetary atmospheres it is thus important to account for changes in the mass loss rates induced by changes in the received XUV flux. In this study, we take into account the observed spread in X-ray luminosities of stars in open clusters with ages below a gigayear by modelling the host star activity evolution with a range of spin-down ages (Tu et al. 2015; Johnstone et al. 2021). By spin-down or saturation time, we mean the age until which a star emits intense XUV flux at a constant level before decreasing.

A major advantage of our model is that it is analytic, so it can provide insights into planetary science without being obscured by the details of numerical modeling. There are, however, some disadvantages that warrant discussion. In the following, we list the atmospheric and geophysical limitations of our framework. Our model assumes an ideal gas with constant opacity, heat capacity ratio, composition, and no chemistry. Real systems are, however, dynamic, as can be seen by the geological history of the terrestrial planets in our solar system. Adopting a more complex numerical prescription, such as an atmospheric general circulation model (e.g., Leconte et al. 2013; Lefèvre et al. 2021), wavelength-dependent opacities (e.g., Fortney et al. 2007; Nettelmann et al. 2011), and a comprehensive atmosphere-interior chemical model (e.g., Kite et al. 2020; Ito & Ikoma 2021), would increase the accuracy of our model, though it would be computationally demanding. As of writing, more detailed atmospheric evaporation simulations assume a priori that a thermosphere exists and that mass loss is driven by XUV irradiation (e.g., Kubyshkina et al. 2020). Our analytic framework provides a stepping stone for more thorough photoevaporative mass-loss models by clarifying the thermodynamic conditions under which XUV-driven escape operates.
