In RS memory devices, the HfO layer is used as a switching layer between an inert and a reactive metal electrode, which illustrates RS operation through the electroformation of an oxygen-vacancy-rich filament and its later rupture or re-connection during switching. Te subsequent switching characteristics after electroformation are also strongly correlated with this vacancy-mediated filamentary process. Several outstanding properties of HfO-based RS memory devices, such as large memory window, multi-level storage ability, low power consumption [13–15], and CMOS compatibility with possible high-density or three-dimensional integration, have attracted a considerable research strong interest for their application in neuromorphic computing [17–19], in particular for the development of artifcial synapses or neurons in neural networks. Most studies that reported such RS behavior in HfO focused on electroformation and the subsequent switching performance to realize high-precision multilevel operation, and on the analog weight update in the synaptic application to exploit the resistance dynamics of memory devices. Similar to biological synapses, nonvolatile RS devices act as memory components, storing the strength of synaptic connections without power. However, for these RS devices to fully mimic synaptic behavior, they must meet specifc requirements, including forming voltage, variation, switching behavior, switching speed, switching voltage, conductance modulation, endurance, and retention. As this filamentary switching in an RS device signifcantly afects these multiple performance aspects, improving control of filament formation and rupture is crucial to accurately implement synaptic operations in artifcial systems.
Document [2]This review article summarized the recent understanding of resistance switching (RS) behavior in several binary oxide thin film systems. Among the various RS materials and mechanisms, TiO2 and NiO thin films in unipolar thermo-chemical switching mode are primarily dealt with. To facilitate the discussions, the RS was divided into three parts; electroforming, set and reset steps. After short discussions on the electrochemistry of ‘electrolytic’ oxide materials, the general and peculiar aspects of these RS systems and mechanism are elaborated. Although the RS behaviors and characteristics of these materials are primarily dependent on the repeated formation and rupture of the conducting filaments (CFs) at the nanoscale at a localized position, this mechanism appears to offer a basis for the understanding of other RS mechanisms which were originally considered to be irrelevant to the localized events. In some oxides, however, the resistance change is attributed to a bulk insulator-to-metal transition or other phase transformation of the switching layer rather than to a single dominant filament. The electroforming and set switching phenomena were understood as the process of CF formation and rejuvenation, respectively, which are mainly driven by the thermally assisted electromigration and percolation (or even local phase transition) of defects, while the reset process was understood as the process of CF rupture where the thermal energy plays a more crucial role. This review also contains several remarks on the outlook of these resistance change devices as a semiconductor memory.

Document [0]By constructing a 2D/3D/2D sandwich architecture that incorporates photo-ferroelectric 2D perovskites at both interfaces, the polarization-induced internal electric field can be maximized and more uniformly distributed across the absorber layer (Figure 14g) . This photo-ferroelectric interface effectively suppresses nonradiative recombination and enables *V*oc approaching the Shockley-Queisser-limit, representing a conceptual shift from device-level performance tuning to ferroelectric-interface-driven photovoltaic physics. Upon applying a brief pre-bias prior to the *J–V* measurement, the ferroelectric dipoles in the 2D layers become preferentially aligned, leading to a simultaneous enhancement of all photovoltaic parameters compared with the biased control device (Figure 14h-k). As a result, the perovskite solar cell based on the 2D/3D/2D sandwich architecture achieves a PCE ~ 24%, a FF ~ 84%, and a *V*oc as high as 1.21 V. Overall, the integration of ferroelectric halide perovskites introduces a new degree of freedom for solar cell design, spanning from device-level performance tuning to interface-driven suppression of voltage losses. Such ferroelectric and photo-ferroelectric strategies open new opportunities for realizing perovskite solar cells that simultaneously achieve high efficiency, mechanical robustness, and long-term stability. Ferroelectric halide perovskites uniquely combine switchable polarization with defect-tolerant semiconducting behavior, enabling neuromorphic devices with highly controllable synaptic weights, robust endurance, and low-energy operation . These characteristics make them particularly attractive for scalable and energy-efficient artificial synapses, offering a promising route toward next-generation brain-inspired computing architectures beyond conventional von Neumann systems. By applying a voltage across two electrodes, the charge current flow through the defect was generated which induces the electrical pumping of the emitter luminescence. In the heterostructure, the combination of NbSe2, a hole-like van der Waals metal, 21, 22 and graphene is chosen to form an asymmetric electrical junction with h-BN in between, enabling the efficient injection of electron and hole carriers into the defect sites for the generation of light emission. In addition, the edges of two metallic electrodes were aligned with minimal overlap, confining the path of the tunneling current flow to go through the defects positioned within the aligned edges. Reducing the number of participating defects in the tunneling current generation further stabilizes the photon emission and allows the direct comparison of the emission intensity to the tunneling current. With fabricated devices, we measured the electroluminescence (EL) from h-BN defect sites using an optical set-up equipped with a cryostat kept at 6.5 K while varying the applied voltage. Figure 1b shows the electrically induced emission spectrum measured from one of the devices showing several narrow emission peaks brightened as a function of voltage. We name this device as Device 1. We note that Device 1 has the total thickness of h-BN corresponding to 7 nm between electrodes (Optically active h-BN: 5 nm, spacer h-BN: 2 nm). Above a threshold, the emission intensity of individual peaks gradually increases with the applied voltage. The spatial image measured by the charge-coupled device (CCD) imaging mode is shown in Figure 1c. From the image depicting the reflection of a white light source, the boundaries of graphene and NbSe2 electrodes can be identified and the localized EL is found at one corner of the stacked region. Such spatially confined EL plausibly originates from edge- or interface-localized states in the heterostructure. Although position-controlled QEs are routinely fabricated using static strain gradients, the use of dynamic strain fields to control the brightness of QEs has not been explored yet. Here, we address this challenge by introducing a novel device in which WSe2 monolayers are integrated onto piezoelectric pillars that provide both static and dynamic strains. The static strains are first used to induce the formation of QEs, while their energy and brightness are then controlled via voltages on piezoelectric pillars. Numerical simulations show that these effects are due to a strain-induced modification of the confining-potential landscape, which leads to a net redistribution of excitons among the different QEs. The first seminal works reporting single photon emission in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs)1–5 have stimulated an explosion of research activities aimed at investigating the possibility to use quantum emitters (QEs) in TMDs for ultra-compact quantum photonics6, 7 . Compared to other established solid-state-based quantum-light sources, such as semiconductor quantum dots, QEs in TMDs have the clear advantage of being relatively simple and cheap to fabricate, and their spatial position across the substrate can be controlled with high precision8–12.
Document [5]Recent experiments in TMD moire heterostructures uncovered the formation of moire-trapped trions, namely charged interlayer excitons localized by the periodic potential landscape of twisted bilayers. In H-stacked MoSe2/WSe2 heterobilayers, electrostatic doping allowed electrons or holes to fill moire potential minima, and narrow photoluminescence peaks emerged about 7 meV below the neutral moire exciton emission. Those lower-energy peaks were assigned to positively and negatively charged moire trions and were observed to obey valley-dependent optical selection rules, tying them to the same moire-confined excitonic framework as the neutral states. The charged states inherited valley Zeeman splittings and g-factors similar to those of their neutral exciton counterparts, which supported their identification as moire-confined species rather than as unrelated localized emitters. Polarization-resolved photoluminescence further revealed a striking helicity reversal between the positive and negative trion branches. That reversal was attributed to competition between spin-conserving valley-flip and valley-conserving spin-flip relaxation channels during trion formation, again emphasizing that the optical response is governed by the moire-trapped valley landscape. Coulomb staircases were also observed, appearing as stepwise changes in trion emission energy caused by Coulomb interactions with carriers occupying nearest-neighbor moire sites. Because these trions remain localized in moire traps, they open a route to engineering fermionic many-body states in an optical-lattice-like platform. Unlike neutral excitons, these trions are fermions, so moire localization combines discrete optical emission with tunable spin, valley, and charge degrees of freedom in the same periodic trap landscape. Their long-lived populations, on the order of hundreds of nanoseconds, together with gate-controlled polarization tuning and Stark-effect sensitivity, make these moire-confined charged excitonic states relevant to dynamically controllable quantum-emitter arrays in twisted heterostructures. The relatively shallow confinement potential of about 30 meV and the small trion binding energies further underscore that the localized emission arises from the moire potential itself.

Document [9]ABSTRACT: Atomic defects in solids offer a versatile basis to study and realize quantum phenomena and information science in various integrated systems. All-electrical pumping of single defects to create quantum light emission has been realized in several platforms including color centers in diamond and silicon carbide, which could lead to the circuit network of electrically triggered single-photon sources. However, a wide conduction channel which reduces the carrier injection per defect site has been a major obstacle. Here, we realize a device concept to construct electrically pumped single-photon emission using a van der Waals stacked structure with atomic plane precision. Defect-induced tunneling currents across graphene and NbSe2 electrodes sandwiching an atomically thin h-BN layer allow robust and persistent generation of non-classical light from h-BN. The collected emission photon energies range between 1.4 and 2.9 eV, revealing the electrical excitation of a variety of atomic defects. By analyzing the dipole axis of observed emitters, we further confirm that emitters are crystallographic defect structures of h-BN crystal. Our work facilitates implementing efficient and miniaturized single-photon devices in van der Waals platforms toward applications in quantum optoelectronics. KEYWORDS: Hexagonal boron nitride, single-photon emitters, quantum light sources, van der Waals heterostructures, electrical pumping Defects in solid-state systems provide a rich platform to study not only the fundamental properties of materials and their modifications but also the quantum nature of the isolated carriers, which find applications in quantum technologies.1–5 Among various systems, twodimensional materials provide an exceptional playground to study fundamental properties of defects regarding the dimensionality of the host material as well as their quantum nature for developing highly integrated quantum circuitries.6–8 For example, defects in ultrathin hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) have been shown to exhibit bright single-photon emission which can be used for quantum communication.9, 10 Also, single spins in h-BN defect sites have been found to probe minute physical quantities of proximate specimens in nanometer distance.11–13 However, implementing quantum operation of h-BN defects in previous works has largely relied on the optical pumping source for the generation of carriers which imposes difficulties on the targeted and controlled manipulations of defects in integrated structures.

All-electrical pumping of single defects to create quantum light emission has been realized in several platforms including color centers in diamond and silicon carbide, which could lead to the circuit network of electrically triggered single-photon sources. However, a wide conduction channel which reduces the carrier injection per defect site has been a major obstacle. The cobalt-based Fischer−Tropsch (FT) catalysts usually consist of metallic cobalt nanocrystallites dispersed on a support material. The present review surveys the progress that has been made over the last couple of decades in the area of the effect of the support and its surface modifications in cobalt-based FT synthesis.
Document [3]The cobalt/TiO2 catalyst is an intricate system. As briefly discussed before, TiO2 is a reducible metal oxide that actively participates in the formation of the active phase under FTS reaction conditions. The three most common crystal phases of TiO2 are anatase (tetragonal), brookite (orthorhombic), and rutile (tetragonal). The phases can be distinguished, for example, with vibrational spectroscopy or XRD, and mixtures of the two tetragonal crystal phases, such as P90 (90% anatase, 10% rutile), are often used in heterogeneous catalysis. Both anatase and rutile TiO2 can already be reduced to TiO2-x suboxide species in H2 at temperatures above 300°C. These suboxides interact electronically with the cobalt nanoparticles, leading to the formation of cobalt-TiO2 interfaces with special properties, including enhanced FTS activity. Under FTS conditions, the catalytically important behavior is therefore associated with these electronically modified cobalt-support interfacial sites. However, if these metal-support interactions are too strong, TiO2-x suboxide species may block active sites or CoTiO3 may be formed. This inactive metal-support compound is more likely to be formed at high CO conversions and when cobalt oxides are present in the catalyst under reaction conditions. The latter is because positively charged Co2+ more readily accepts an electron than Co0. With the cobalt/TiO2 system, it is thus only a fine line between enhanced activity and deactivation. This balance depends on preserving interfacial promotion without crossing into deactivation. The first step toward understanding these special interfaces is detecting and characterizing them in detail, preferably under relevant reaction conditions.
Document [4]A number of theoretical works have attempted to give some insight into the phase transformations induced by carbon. Sautet and Cinquini [102 ChemCatChem 2: 636] explored periodic trends in subsurface C migration on flat metal terraces for some of the most common transition metals and calculated the carbon chemical potential for a series of reactions at different temperatures. According to this publication, under FT reaction conditions both cobalt and iron undergo carbide formation, at least at the uppermost surface layers. That conclusion places cobalt carbide formation directly in the near-surface region where Fischer-Tropsch catalysis occurs. In another publication, Pan and coworkers [103 Phys Chem Chem Phys 12: 7848] presented a diffusion mechanism of C atoms through the lattice array of bulk fcc and hcp Co during the first stages of carbide formation. Their work showed that fcc-Co(111) and hcp-Co(0001) substrates present similar thermodynamic and kinetic properties for carbide formation, since the activation energies for carbon penetration are 1.17 and 1.12 eV, respectively. However, further penetration into deeper layers appears to be unfeasible, with barriers of 2.21 and 1.85 eV for fcc-Co(111) and hcp-Co(0001), respectively, unless cobalt vacancies promote carbon diffusion by reducing the activation barriers of inner-layer migration. This means the transformation to a carbide state is most accessible at or near the cobalt surface, not uniformly through the whole bulk. Moreover, the infiltrated carbon atoms alter the electronic structure of surface Co atoms by depleting some of their valence 3d electrons used for the activation of the C-O bond during FT synthesis. These calculations therefore support cobalt carbide formation in the catalytically relevant near-surface region and describe how that carbide chemistry changes the cobalt centers participating in Fischer-Tropsch reactivity.

Document [7]This model study that attempted to delineate structural effects from electronic effects should serve as a guide to develop next-generation catalysts in FT synthesis. The alumina support is the most extensively studied support in FT synthesis, and the above-discussed surface modification techniques help to improve either the activity or selectivity or both in FT synthesis. For further improvements, studying surface modification with a combination of organic and inorganic species to tune the dispersion and electronic effects of the active phase and performing FT catalytic tests for long duration (time on stream) to establish the catalytic stability would enable their implementation in industry. Next to alumina, silica is another widely used support in cobalt-based FT catalysts, as it possesses suitable chemical and physical properties to serve as a perfect support. The nature of hydroxyl groups (silanols) and their concentration and distribution on the silica surface play vital roles in the dispersion of cobalt particles. The high surface area of silica favors moderately high metal dispersion at reasonably high metal loadings. Furthermore, its surface chemistry enables high reducibility of cobalt precursors to the metallic state under favorable conditions. It was reported that the degree of cobalt reduction was higher on silica compared with other supports, i.e., SiO2 > TiO2 > α-Al2O3 > γ-Al2O3. 70 Though metal− support interactions are weaker on silica compared with alumina, the preparation and pretreatment conditions must be carefully chosen to avoid the formation of cobalt silicate (Co SiO ), which is inactive in FT synthesis and can be reduced to metallic cobalt only at temperatures above 700− 800 °C.71−74 The interaction between cobalt and silica that yields cobalt silicate was stronger for the catalysts prepared in basic media than for those prepared in acidic media.74 The ease of reduction to metal species on silica supports was found to decrease with decreasing Co3O4 particle size.75 Noble metal promoters such as Ru, Pt, or Pd were added to cobalt catalysts supported on SiO to improve the reducibility and/or dispersion of cobalt.76 In the following sections, the effects of the textural properties, surface modification with different metal oxides or organic molecules, and acid/base properties of silica on the catalytic activity/selectivity in FT synthesis are discussed.

Document [0]Details of catalyst-coated membrane (CCM) fabrication and morphological characterization can be found in previous work . Briefly, the CCM was prepared using RSDT, where anode and cathode catalyst layers were directly deposited onto a piece of Nafion® (N117) membrane. The active area of the CCM was 86 cm2. The anode catalyst comprised iridium oxide (IrOx) nanoparticles with an average particle size of 2 nm embedded in Nafion® ionomer. Cross sections of post-test MEAs were analyzed with scanning electron microscopy (SEM), scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), and X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (XEDS) to obtain the catalyst distribution in the MEA and investigate degradation mechanisms. The cross section of the degraded CCM shows both anode and cathode catalyst layers wrinkled due to compression during cell assembly and drying upon disassembly. The anode thickness is 2–2.5 μm, while the cathode thickness is 14–22 μm. XEDS maps show strong Ir and Pt signals at the anode and cathode catalyst layers, respectively. Electron microscopy and chemical analysis indicate that iridium dissolves in the anode during MEA tests, with only 30% remaining at EOT.

The formation of these oxidized states suggests an oxidative environment that promotes Ir instability. According to Kasian et al., 99 this anodic oxidation is a critical factor contributing to Ir dissolution, as the surface becomes less stable in acidic media. Under such conditions, dissolved Ir can enter the electrolyte. This dissolution significantly reduces the active Ir content of the catalyst and impairs its OER activity. The reversible nature of some surface-oxide transformations also indicates ongoing restructuring of the anode during operation. Over time, this dynamic behavior is consistent with progressive catalyst loss. Yu et al.100 discovered that dissolved Ir species can migrate through the Nafion 117 membrane, affecting the anode/membrane interface. Recent work utilizing ex situ ICP-MS analysis and detailed physicochemical characterization of the CL/membrane interfaces has further advanced the understanding and accurate quantification of anode catalyst losses under realistic PEMWE operating conditions.101, 102 Gas-bubble formation also impacts CL stability. As the catalyst layer morphology evolves and its pore network becomes less favorable for oxygen removal, bubbles are retained more readily, increasing gas-transport losses and driving the cell to higher voltage at high current density. Limiting bubble size can significantly increase stability.100

question: By what processes is the tissue-specific distribution of nucleic-acid-carrying lipid nanoparticles determined following systemic administration?
perspectives: Apolipoprotein-driven receptor targeting after protein-corona formation
Endothelial anatomy and local hemodynamic filtration in target organs
Direct interactions between nanoparticle surface chemistry and cell membranes
Preferential uptake by resident phagocytes that sets downstream tissue accumulation

Document [0]One issue is how particle surfaces are interpreted after exposure to blood. For example, liposomes containing phospholipids with high phase transition temperature display differences in blood behavior.78, 79 It will be interesting to investigate whether these differences can be attributed to distinct protein adsorption onto the nanoparticle surface. Figure 3. Effect of blood-protein association on LNP systemic fate and biodistribution. PEG lipids can be incorporated into LNPs, but the resulting particles are defined biologically by the proteins that associate with their surface. Following intravenous LNP injection, surface lipids can exchange while proteins present in the blood, including apolipoproteins such as ApoE, associate with the nanoparticle, allowing receptor-mediated interactions with cells. LNPs therefore present biomolecular coronas in blood. A common surface component in this literature is a hydrophilic polymer with a neutral charge at physiological pH. The most commonly used polymer is polyethylene glycol (PEG). PEGylation has long been discussed in simplified terms, but it is now recognized that the proteins associated with PEGylated nanomedicines are important determinants of their biological identity (Figure 3). These interactions shape how nanoparticles are encountered by cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system.80−82 Conversely, avid capture by resident phagocytes such as Kupffer cells and splenic macrophages can dominate the initial fate of circulating LNPs and thereby determine their downstream tissue accumulation. However, it is now recognized that it is the presence of certain proteins, such as clusterin (apolipoprotein J), in the corona of PEGylated nanomedicines that is central to their biological identity.83, 84 These observations emphasize that the surface-presented protein corona, rather than the bare material alone, is essential to understanding LNP fate (Figure 3).85, 86
Document [1]Not all NPs are equivalently hazardous; stable, non-ion-releasing or robustly coated formulations show reduced toxicity, underscoring the role of surface chemistry in safe-by-design strategies . In summary, these cases reveal significant design criteria—measurements, electrostatic forces, ligand orientation, and peptide secondary arrangement—that govern the level to which membranes face remodeling, incursion, or destabilization. The evolution of these mechanistic findings into calculable design doctrines can integrate therapeutic advantages with safety in significant biological realms. A conceptual overview of current applications, technical challenges, and future directions is encapsulated in Figure 15, providing a structural framework for the advancement of safe and effective nanomedicines. Nanoparticle–membrane interactions underpin a broad spectrum of therapeutic delivery strategies, in which controlled adsorption, partial insertion, or membrane remodeling govern cellular uptake and subsequent intracellular trafficking . Recent mechanistic studies further demonstrate that membrane lipid composition and nanoparticle surface chemistry act cooperatively to regulate translocation efficiency and endocytic routing, with subtle variations in interfacial charge distribution or lipid packing leading to pronounced differences in delivery outcomes . The efficacy of nanoparticle–membrane interactions derives from physicochemical attributes such as size, charge, shape, elasticity, and surface functionalization, which govern engagement with lipid bilayers and cellular barriers . In drug and gene delivery, cationic nanoparticles bind strongly to lipid bilayers and promote penetration , while anionic particles interact more weakly but modulate bilayer diffusivity. Geometry also matters, i.e., oblate nanoparticles display enhanced uptake compared to rigid spheres due to increased deformability . Partner-assisted uptake further illustrates cooperative effects . Because hydrophobic bilayers restrict hydrophilic drug permeability , electroporation and cell-penetrating peptides are often exploited to enhance cytosolic delivery .
Document [2]Overcoming these barriers will require cross-disciplinary advances in polymer chemistry, nanofabrication, and clinical testing. PGI2, nitric oxide (NO), and hydrogen sulfde are examples of vasodilators released by endothelial cells that increase vessel size by relaxing smooth muscle cells, while selectins and intercellular adhesion molecules (ICAMs) are examples of surface proteins that facilitate extravasation of immune cells out of the blood circulation and into the surrounding tissue [9–21] (Figure 1A). Document [1]Organoids are self-organizing, three-dimensional cell clusters that are often derived from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) (Rossi et al., 2018). They form with minimal direction from exogenous biochemical factors and create a tissue-specific niche where cells replicate some aspects of organ function or complexity (Qian et al., 2019). Embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived organoids provide a rare window into early cellular events that give rise to tissues and diseases (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014; Pasca et al., 2015). Because organoids are generated from PSCs, strategies to prevent uncontrolled tumorigenicity, such as confirming the absence of pluripotent markers in differentiated cells or incorporating a suicidal gene to eliminate residual pluripotent cells, must be employed. Additionally, brain organoid protocols are still quite variable and thus, strong quality controls are necessary to reduce the experimental heterogeneity. Nevertheless, brain organoids have proven particularly useful for studying the human brain, which we have limited opportunities to observe and differs from those of animal models (Marshall and Mason, 2019). The cerebral cortex is perhaps the most interesting region of the human brain, as it is significantly larger and more complex than that of our evolutionary predecessors and regulates higher order functions like consciousness and thought. Cortical organoids (COs) have been used to study human-relevant neurodevelopment (Trujillo and Muotri, 2018), disease pathophysiology (Di Lullo and Kriegstein, 2017), and brain evolution (Giandomenico and Lancaster, 2017). Despite these advances, the absence of vasculature in organoid models leads to numerous problems beyond a lack of tissue complexity. A primary issue faced with organoids is the formation of a necrotic core due to insufficient mass transfer of oxygen and nutrients.

In the cited work, a fibrin hydrogel scaffold increased the efficiency and quality of hiPSC-derived endothelial differentiation, and the authors interpret this as evidence that a three-dimensional physical environment and its associated surface tension are important for guiding cell fate. The same section states that differentiation outcomes change with substrate stiffness, implying that lineage commitment depends on whether cells experience the appropriate mechanical resistance from their extracellular matrix. It further notes that not only stiffness, but also ECM type and ligand density, influence mechanotransduction and can even reverse the effect of stiffness alone. Taken together, the paragraph supports a mechanistic explanation in which stem-cell-derived tissues remain immature when their extracellular matrix is too simplified, too two-dimensional, or mechanically incorrect. In that framework, failure to reach adult-like maturity arises because the organoid does not yet recreate the proper matrix composition and mechanical cues needed to stabilize mature differentiation programs.

It emphasizes that the surrounding matrix supplies both biochemical and biomechanical information, and that extracellular-matrix stiffness and composition are critical cues that shape stem-cell behaviour and fate by being sensed at the cell surface, altering cytoskeletal tension, and transmitting signals to the nucleus. In other words, maturation is not limited simply by missing soluble factors; it is constrained when the cells are placed in an immature or non-native matrix environment that fails to provide adult-like mechanical instruction. The same logic is used to motivate new differentiation strategies based on synthetic and natural extracellular matrices, because changing matrix composition and mechanics can change lineage progression and functional state. Applied to stem-cell-derived organoids, this supports the view that incomplete adult-level maturation persists when the extracellular matrix remains developmentally immature, with the wrong stiffness, ligand context, and physical microenvironment to drive fully mature tissue identity.

It notes that immature SC-CMs grown on conventional planar surfaces remain relatively round, with isotropic organization of myofilaments and no mature membrane architecture, whereas adult cardiomyocytes are elongated and structurally anisotropic. The surrounding framework of the review identifies extracellular matrix, decellularized extracellular matrix, three-dimensional cardiac tissue constructs, and other mechanical strategies as maturation tools precisely because the baseline culture environment does not supply the adult-like geometric and material cues that native tissue provides. Document [8]**: ** The use of patient-derived tumor tissues and cells has led to significant advances in personalized cancer therapy and precision medicine. The advent of genomic sequencing technologies has enabled the comprehensive analysis of tumor characteristics. The three-dimensional tumor organoids derived from self-organizing cancer stem cells are valuable ex vivo models that faithfully replicate the structure, unique features, and genetic characteristics of tumors. These tumor organoids have emerged as innovative tools that are extensively employed in drug testing, genome editing, and transplantation to guide personalized therapy in clinical settings. However, a major limitation of this emerging technology is the absence of a tumor microenvironment that includes immune and stromal cells. The therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors has underscored the importance of immune cells, particularly cytotoxic T cells that infiltrate the vicinity of tumors, in patient prognosis. To address this limitation, co-culture techniques combining tumor organoids and T cells have been developed, offering diverse avenues for studying individualized drug responsiveness. By integrating cellular components of the tumor microenvironment, including T cells, into tumor organoid cultures, immuno-oncology has embraced this technology, which is rapidly advancing. Recent progress in co-culture models of tumor organoids has allowed for a better understanding of the advantages and limitations of this novel model, thereby exploring its full potential. This review focuses on the current applications of organoid-T cell co-culture models in cancer research and highlights the remaining challenges that need to be addressed for its broader implementation in anti-cancer therapy. Recent progress in our understanding of the tumor microenvironment (TME) has led to the development of effective therapies for advanced cancer in recent years. Treating numerous patients with cancer with monoclonal antibodies that target the inhibitory receptors expressed by immune cells (immune checkpoint blockade, ICB) has shown remarkable response rates in various solid tumors and hematologic malignancies . Therefore, it is crucial to develop preclinical models that can investigate the TME and guide clinical precision therapy .
Document [9]Hence, organoids can be defined today as 3D cell aggregates derived from stem cells or organ progenitors that are able to differentiate into organ-specific cell types and self-organize into structures mimicking the in vivo tissue arrangement, compartmentalization and functionality . To date, hPSC-derived organoids (hPSC-Orgs) have been generated that resemble the small intestine , kidneys , brain , liver , pancreas , and others. These organoids are considered a promising model suitable for studying the mechanisms underlying human development, drug discovery, modeling diseases and regenerative medicine . However, two main limitations remain: i) the size of the organoids is limited to a couple of millimeters due to the passive diffusion of nutrients and oxygen that threatens the survival of the cells at the organoid core, and ii) the functionality of hPSC-Orgs remains immature and resembles embryonic and fetal tissues rather than adult organs, probably due to missing developmental cues that are still unknown . These absent cues likely include systemic endocrine signals and long-range neural inputs that developing tissues receive in vivo but isolated organoids cannot access. Endothelial cells (ECs) may play a key role in overcoming the aforementioned limitations. Here, we review the progress achieved in the generation of hPSC-Orgs derived from the three primary germ layers (endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm), which are exemplified by the pancreas, liver, kidneys and brain. We discuss the role of ECs during tissue and organ development, and we analyze the state of the art in vascularized hPSC-Orgs (vhPSC-Orgs), the source of ECs employed for this purpose and the challenges remaining in the creation of ex vivo functional and vascularized organs. Most current hPSC differentiation protocols are based on the events of in vivo embryonic development that lead to organ formation .

Document [1]A critical aspect of EV biology is their glycosylation, which involves the addition of carbohydrate moieties (glycans) to proteins and lipids on the EV surface. The types of glycans present on EVs significantly influence their properties, including targeting and uptake by recipient cells. EVs are primarily decorated with two main types of glycans: N-linked and O-linked glycans. N-linked glycans are attached to the nitrogen atom of asparagine residues and are often complex structures that can include various modifications such as fucosylation and sialylation . O-linked glycans, on the other hand, are attached to the hydroxyl group of serine or threonine residues and can also exhibit considerable diversity, including O-GalNAc and O-GlcNAc modifications . The specific glycan profiles can vary depending on the cellular origin of the EVs and the physiological or pathological state of the producing cells. The glycosylation of EVs has profound implications for targeting and uptake. The presence of specific glycans on EVs can dictate their targeting to particular cell types. For example, glycan-binding proteins (lectins) on recipient cells can recognize and bind to specific glycan structures on EVs, facilitating selective uptake (Figure 2). This targeting is crucial in pathological contexts, such as cancer, where tumor-derived EVs may carry distinct glycan signatures that promote their interaction with tumor-associated cells . The uptake of EVs by recipient cells is influenced by their glycan composition, consistent with glycan-dependent recognition at the cell surface. Studies have shown that alterations in glycosylation can modulate the efficiency of EV uptake.

Document [9]Passive targeting is the foremost mechanism by which nanocarriers and drug-bearing macromolecules deliver their payload selectively to solid tumors. An important driver of passive targeting is the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, which is the cornerstone of most carrier-based tumor-targeted drug delivery efforts. Despite the huge number of publications showcasing successes in preclinical animal models, translation to the clinic has been poor, with only a few nano-based drugs currently being used for the treatment of cancers. Several barriers and factors have been adduced for the low delivery efficiency to solid tumors and poor clinical translation, including the characteristics of the nanocarriers and macromolecules, vascular and physiological barriers, the heterogeneity of tumor blood supply which affects the homogenous distribution of nanocarriers within tumors, and the transport and penetration depth of macromolecules and nanoparticles in the tumor matrix. To address the challenges associated with poor tumor targeting and therapeutic efficacy in humans, the identified barriers that affect the efficiency of the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect for macromolecular therapeutics and nanoparticle delivery systems need to be overcome. In this review, approaches to facilitate improved EPR delivery outcomes and the clinical translation of novel macromolecular therapeutics and nanoparticle drug delivery systems are discussed. Improved clinical outcomes in the treatment of some cancers have not been observed despite tremendous efforts in the development of new chemotherapeutic agents. This is largely due to the failure to deliver these agents selectively to tumors and the lack of precision in targeting cancer cells . This poor targeting to tumors greatly increases the propensity for debilitating off-target consequences and minimizes the magnitude of therapeutic efficacy. Innovations in the field of nanotechnology, immunology, chemistry, and pharmaceutical technology have led to the development of a variety of drug delivery systems aimed at improving the plasma half-life, biodistribution, and the target-site accumulation of chemotherapeutic drugs . Nanoparticles for drug delivery are carrier systems in the nanometer size range, composed of biocompatible and biodegradable natural and/or synthetic polymers, self-assembled lipids, or inorganic materials, capable of carrying payloads such as small molecule therapeutics, peptides, proteins, or nucleic acids and delivering their cargoes in a controlled manner at the target site .

Improved clinical outcomes in the treatment of some cancers have not been observed despite tremendous efforts in the development of new chemotherapeutic agents. This is largely due to the failure to deliver these agents selectively to tumors and the lack of precision in targeting cancer cells . This poor targeting to tumors greatly increases the propensity for debilitating off-target consequences and minimizes the magnitude of therapeutic efficacy. Innovations in the field of nanotechnology, immunology, chemistry, and pharmaceutical technology have led to the development of a variety of drug delivery systems aimed at improving the plasma half-life, biodistribution, and the target-site accumulation of chemotherapeutic drugs . Nanoparticles for drug delivery are carrier systems in the nanometer size range, composed of biocompatible and biodegradable natural and/or synthetic polymers, self-assembled lipids, or inorganic materials, capable of carrying payloads such as small molecule therapeutics, peptides, proteins, or nucleic acids and delivering their cargoes in a controlled manner at the target site .

These materials were selected during the early EFDA phase of the ITER project due to their advantageous plasma compatible properties . Be was considered an excellent candidate as a PFC for ITER due to its high thermal conductivity, low Z, good thermo-mechanical properties and high melting point (1560 K) . Be was first tested in a fusion environment during the early stages of the JET project, where it was used as a plasma limiter. The results showed that its use led to a significant reduction of plasma instabilities. Later, in 2008, it was used in JET to replace the graphite PFC in the first wall area of the vessel to test the ITER blanket . Compared to graphite, the use of Be PFC proved to be crucial, leading to a reduction of the oxygen levels inside the reactor. Furthermore, the absence of chemical sputtering leads to a reduction of H isotope retention in comparison to graphite. At the same time, it was showed that Be presence in fusion plasma does not influence significantly the plasma performance . However, despite its plasma compatible properties, Be has an increased sputtering yield when subjected to intense D and T particle bombardment and this will consequently lead to the erosion, migration and re-deposition of Be layers.
Document [7]It is well established that H isotope retention in W is governed by the trapping in lattice defects . Dislocations are common defects in W as large amounts of dislocations are introduced during the manufacturing process . Furthermore, dislocations can also be formed in W components during transient events (e.g., edge localized modes) via a plastic deformation caused by high thermal stresses . Stresses caused by high local concentrations of solute H during plasma operation can also induce a plastic deformation . Although H interactions with dislocations have been extensively studied for various metals and alloys , the data for W is scarce. In the experiments of Ogorodnikova et al. defects with a rather low H detrapping energy of 0.85 eV were attributed to dislocations and grain boundaries. Concurrently, Manhard ascribed defects with the H detrapping energy of 1.25 ± 0.11 eV to dislocations. Anderl et al. observed a correlation between the reduction of the concentration of defects with the H detrapping energies in the range of 1.34–1.56 eV and the reduction of the dislocation density, although it was admitted that these energies seem to be too high for dislocations. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations predict different H detrapping energies for various types of dislocations in W: An edge dislocation has a considerably higher H detrapping energy (1.28–1.36 eV) compared with that of a screw dislocation (0.92–0.96 eV)‡. Most of the previous experimental studies on this subject employed annealing of as-received dislocation-rich W samples at various temperatures, which resulted in the decrease of dislocation density, and investigated its influence on deuterium (D) trapping .

Oxide-rich or impurity-modified near-surface regions can also act as strong trapping sites for tritium because their altered local chemistry binds hydrogen isotopes close to the surface. One often discussed possibility results from the evolution of irradiation defects within the implantation range. Irradiation of the W matrix in the near-surface layer is assumed to result in bubble and void formation. A review of bubbles in metals by Condon and Schober outlines some possible cavity formation mechanisms. During irradiation the implantation zone develops voids and vacancy clusters that can retain hydrogen isotopes. In sputter-depth profiling after high flux D implantation combined with residual gas analysis molecular D2 was found to be released from surface near layers, consistent with deuterium associated with near-surface cavities . However, direct observation of such bubbles was not possible at low ion fluxes and fluences in ion beam experiments, even in high resolution TEM. Typically a dense defect network resulted from the irradiation . Only post-irradiation annealing resulted in the formation of gas bubbles . After 8 keV D irradiation and annealing to temperatures above 873 K D agglomerated into nano-size cavities. Recently, at much higher fluxes and fluences surface and sub-surface structures could be resolved. Recrystallized polycrystalline tungsten was exposed to a deuterium plasma with high flux of 10^22 D/m2 s at about 38 eV up to fluences of 10^26 and 10^27 D/m2 and temperature between 320 and 800 K.

In the case of simultaneous irradiation of PCW by 500 eV helium and deuterium ions, the presence of He enhanced D retention in the near surface . In the case of low-energy helium-seeded deuterium plasma exposure, the deuterium retention in polycrystalline W was modified compared to pure deuterium plasma . At high fluxes and fluences above 10^26 D/m^2, seeding of helium ions into the D plasma significantly modifies D retention at elevated temperatures (400-700 K) (Fig. 5) and prevents the formation of blisters (Fig. 6). Overall, these observations indicate that helium irradiation creates a modified near-surface microstructure in the implantation zone that is associated with deuterium accumulation in that region .

Document [7]Fission gas release is impacted by grain growth in two ways. First, the moving grain boundary aids in the collection of gas at the grain boundary (grain boundary sweeping) since the low solubility of the fission gas prevents it from redepositing in the newly formed crystal. In the second way, as the grain grows, the average diffusion distance for the fission gas increases, which tends to slow down the rate at which gas is transported to the grain borders (Pastore, 2012). Hence, one way of improving fuel performance is to increase the grain size and therefore the diffusion path of the gas atoms (Turnbull, 1974). Different mechanisms for fission gas release are known as the diffusion of fission gases out of the fuel, direct releases, such as recoil and knockout releases, and release by fuel cracking. Recoil release is the release of fission gases with a high kinetic energy right after fission near the external surface. Knock-out release is the release of the fission gases near the external surface by collision with fission products or primary knock-on atoms (Lee et al., 2008). Figure 1 shows a schematic of the recoil and knock-out processes. In diffusion process, fission gas atoms generated in the fuel grains partly precipitate in intra-granular bubbles and coincidently, a fraction of the gas atoms diffuse to grain boundaries through trapping in and irradiation-induced resolution from intra-granular bubbles. Fission gas behavior in grain is illustrated in Figure 2. The diffusion of fission gas release models for low to moderate burnups typically consider three basic processes: volume diffusion within the fuel matrix including the precipitation of single atoms into intra-granular bubbles, precipitation and growth (and shrinkage/destruction) of grain boundary gas bubbles and inter-linkage of grain boundary bubbles resulting in release to the pin free volume (Blair et al., 2006). Document [9]Uranium dioxide (UO2) has been typically used as a nuclear fuel material for the light water reactor (LWR). LWR is currently the most prevalent reactor type used for a power production. The thermal conductivity of nuclear fuel materials is one of the most important properties for evaluating a fuel performance in a nuclear reactor, because this property affects the fuel centerline temperature, operating power efficiency, safety, release of the fission product, etc. For example, a decrement of the thermal conductivity reduces the efficiency of the operating power, and increases the fuel centerline temperature. And the increment of the fuel temperature can affect a release of the fission products. Solid fission products decrease the thermal conductivity of oxide fuel materials when they are present as dissolved species in the matrix or as precipitated solid phases. Unfortunately, under reactor operating conditions, a decrease of the thermal conductivity is unavoidable. To minimize the decrease of the thermal conductivity of fuel materials, the thermal conductivities of UO2 and various elements added-UO2 (Gd, Dy, Cr, etc.) have been widely studied by many investigators , , , , , , , , , . In a nuclear reactor, the fission products have several kinds of physical or chemical states . The solid-state forms emphasized here can be classified into three groups , , : (a) fission products dissolved as oxides in the fuel matrix, (b) fission products forming metallic precipitates and (c) fission products forming oxide precipitates. This classification can be applied to the case of a uranium base oxide fuel as well as a UO2 fuel. It was intended to show the effects of the physical states of solid fission products on the thermal conductivity of UO2 and (U0.924Ce0.076)O2.

Document [5]Chen et al. introduced the PD model for pitting corrosion, proving the applicability and unique advantages of PD in corrosion. Therefore, in this study, the PD method is employed to simulate the dissolution corrosion process of 316L in liquid LBE. This study proposes a PD model to simulate the dissolution corrosion behavior of 316L in LBE, based on the PD diffusion framework from Ref. . For the key parameters in the model, a universal calibration method is developed. Using the experimental data from Ref. , the relevant parameters for solution annealed (SA) and cold drawn (CD) processing of 316L stainless steel were successfully calibrated. The established dissolution corrosion PD model for 316L in LBE not only allows for the systematic analysis of the synergistic effects of processing methods (such as SA and CD), temperature, and oxygen concentration on corrosion behavior, but more importantly, it fills the current gap in the dissolution corrosion kinetics model for 316L in liquid LBE environments. The dissolution corrosion mechanism of 316L in liquid LBE can be primarily classified into two types : selective dissolution and non-selective dissolution. Selective dissolution involves the preferential leaching of Ni, Mn, and Cr due to their significantly higher solubility in LBE compared to Fe. This elemental depletion destabilizes the austenitic matrix, promoting localized ferritization (formation of an α-ferrite layer) and consequent material degradation, representing the dominant pathway for 316L corrosion in LBE. In contrast, non-selective dissolution, characterized by uniform dissolution of all elements including Fe, occurs primarily in solution-annealed steels. Therefore, it is evident that the dissolution corrosion of 316L in liquid LBE predominantly follows selective dissolution, with non-selective dissolution occurring only under specific conditions. We now discuss the influence of Cr, Mn, and Ni on the selective dissolution corrosion of 316L.
Document [6]Dissolution corrosion, a primary degradation mode, arises from the inherent solubility of constituent metal elements (e.g., Fe, Ni, Cr, Mn) in LBE. The dissolution corrosion process mainly consists of two steps: 1) the breaking of metallic bonds between metal atoms under the influence of LBE (considered as the reaction process); 2) diffusion into the liquid LBE driven by concentration differences until saturation concentration is reached (considered as the diffusion process) . Document [0]These practices should also be consistent with applicable ride-through and reconnection expectations in standards and grid codes . Many protection functions rely on fundamental-frequency phasor estimates. During faults, inverter limiting, control saturation, and filter resonance interactions can introduce waveform distortion and harmonics . Converter dynamics can evolve on millisecond time scales, while relay measurements often use cycle-based windows, potentially masking fast transitions or producing misleading phasor estimates. These effects can degrade protection dependability, particularly for elements sensitive to angle, impedance trajectories, or sequence quantities . Mitigation options include robust estimation and filtering approaches, careful selection of measurement windows for inverter-rich feeders, and validation of settings and algorithms using EMT waveforms representative of inverter limiting and ride-through behavior . Overall, the dominant protection challenges in inverter-dominated power systems stem from limited fault current magnitude, control-defined current angle, altered sequence behavior, and recovery dynamics that differ from synchronous-source assumptions. These characteristics affect overcurrent coordination, directional dependability, distance reach, and reclosing practices. 6. Mitigation Strategies for Protection in Inverter-Dominated Power Systems Mitigating protection challenges in inverter-dominated grids requires coordinated action across three layers: (i) protection-side solutions that improve dependability and selectivity under low and controller-shaped fault currents, (ii) inverter/control-side solutions that shape fault responses within semiconductor and grid-code limits, and (iii) system/architecture-side solutions that improve overall fault visibility and coordination by design . The intent is not to force inverter-dominated systems to “look like” synchronous systems, but to ensure that protection remains reliable under the fault-current envelopes and ride-through behaviors mandated by modern practice and standards . (i) Adaptive settings and supervision logic: A practical first step is to adapt pickup thresholds and timing to the reduced fault-current levels expected with current-limited inverter-based resources (IBRs).
Document [1]Nevertheless, through advanced control algorithms—such as those based on VSM models or Synchronverter frameworks—virtual inertia can be synthesized by power electronic converters, enabling them to actively support system frequency stability . This emulation relies on control strategies that replicate the inertial response of synchronous machines. Crucially, for these controllers to operate effectively, the converter must be able to exchange power rapidly during transient frequency events. Consequently, virtual inertia emulation has become a key technique to enhance the dynamic performance and resilience of inverter-dominated power systems . The VSG strategy emulates the rotational inertia and damping characteristics of a synchronous generator through a power electronic inverter. This approach makes it applicable to photovoltaic systems, wind generation, and ESS for enhancing frequency support in microgrids. During an imbalance between power generation and demand, different frequency response mechanisms are triggered across various time intervals, as illustrated in Figure 3. Following a disturbance, such as a sudden generation loss, the inertial response occurs, typically lasting less than 10 s. During this phase, the kinetic energy stored in SGs is released to counteract the energy shortfall, thereby limiting the frequency nadir and reducing the ROCOF; in low-inertia settings, insufficient inertial support after such an imbalance leaves these frequency excursions less effectively restrained.
Document [2]Standard compliance constraints. Grid codes specify LVRT/HVRT and current injection envelopes; negative-sequence capability may be constrained. Protection must operate with mandated inverter behavior. Update protection philosophy consistent with standards; coordination with interconnection requirements. Implement standards-compliant current injection (including negative sequence where required). Traditional overcurrent protection assumes that fault current is substantially higher than load current and that short-circuit current magnitude provides reliable discrimination across protection zones. With current-limited inverters, fault currents may be only slightly above rated current and may not scale proportionally with fault proximity or fault severity . Consequently, definite-time and inverse-time elements may fail to pick up, operate with excessive delay, or lose coordination selectivity . Coordination margins can compress, especially in feeders where multiple inverter sources contribute bounded current and where upstream devices see reduced incremental current during downstream faults . In addition, current limiting can introduce time-varying behavior (brief inception transients followed by sustained clamped current), which complicates pickup and time grading . Mitigation measures typically include re-evaluating pickup levels using realistic fault signatures, applying supervision logic (e.g., undervoltage or directional supervision) to preserve security with lower pickups, and using more selective protection principles in critical zones. Where protection reach and sensitivity cannot be ensured by magnitude-based methods, communication-assisted or differential schemes are often preferred . In practice, time-domain EMT-informed validation is increasingly used to confirm that operating times remain dependable across the range of plausible inverter-limiting behaviors . Directional elements depend on the relationship between current direction and a polarizing quantity and are commonly based on voltage, sequence components, or memory voltage . In inverter-dominated systems, fault current angle can be strongly influenced by control objectives (e.g., reactive-current priority during ride-through) and by limiter behavior, rather than being determined primarily by passive network impedances .
Document [3]In weak grids, increased grid impedance amplifies the coupling between PLL dynamics and the network, potentially inducing low-frequency oscillations or system instability . Analyses indicate that higher grid impedance modifies the effective feedback of the converter current loop, enabling the PLL to influence the closed-loop system through voltage-current coupling and causing eigenvalue migration. When the impedance ratio or short-circuit capacity falls below a critical threshold, PLL phase regulation may become a source of instability, leading to loss of phase lock and amplified oscillations . During frequency disturbances or other large transients, GFL's dependence on an external voltage reference produces pronounced transient oscillations and degraded dynamic response under voltage sags or phase jumps . Collectively, these findings demonstrate that GFL stability challenges in weak grids arise from intrinsic PLL-grid impedance interactions rather than mere parameter-tuning errors. Measures such as reducing PLL bandwidth, adding damping, or enhancing filtering can partially mitigate these risks, but they only provide local improvements and cannot fundamentally overcome the mechanism-level constraint created by the control architecture. In practical terms, the weak-grid problem emerges because the converter current loop, PLL, and surrounding network no longer behave as separable elements once grid strength drops, so synchronization control feeds back through the electrical interface and shifts closed-loop dynamics toward oscillatory behavior. The same mechanism explains why short-circuit weakness, impedance ratio, and transient voltage disturbances all worsen the response of a GFL converter through the synchronization channel rather than through an independent disturbance pathway. It also explains why apparent tuning fixes remain conditional on network strength, since the basic control-network coupling is still present after those adjustments. The instability is therefore rooted in how synchronization control and weak-grid impedance shape one another during operation. The evidence identifies converter synchronization and control coupling with a weak network as a direct trigger for significant instability events, rather than as a secondary consequence of some other disturbance mechanism.
Document [4]2024 is confirmed to be the warmest year globally since records began and the first calendar year that the mean global temperature exceeded 1.5°C above its pre-industrial level , a threshold set by the Paris Agreement to reduce the risks and impacts of climate change. This record-breaking level of global warming underscores the urgency of addressing climate change through rapid and systemic shifts, especially in the energy sector, which is the largest source of CO2 emissions . In globally modeled pathways that limit warming to 2°C, in 2050, almost all electricity will be supplied from zero or low-carbon sources, such as renewable energy sources (RESs) or fossil fuels with CO2 capture and storage . Furthermore, an increased electrification of energy demand through, e.g., electric vehicles and heat pumps is expected . As a result, electricity grids worldwide will undergo a profound transformation in the coming decades, replacing conventional, synchronous generators and aiming for nearly 100% RES integration. Wind and solar photovoltaic systems, the most significant RESs, are predominantly integrated into electricity grids via power electronic inverters. As a result, future power grids will be primarily dominated by inverters and their control strategies. This transition introduces significant challenges to power grid stability, as RESs and inverters inherently do not provide inertia, reducing the inertial response available after power imbalances . The loss of inertia is seen as the most prominent challenge for the stability of the power grid by European transmission grid operators . Poorly damped inter-area oscillatory modes across major transmission corridors can drive distant areas to swing against each other and escalate into system splits or other large disturbances. In January of 2021, the European power grid saw a system split into two synchronous areas; it has been found that the system had been close to its dynamic stability margin , underscoring the importance of adequate inertial response and sufficient damping of inter-area modes.

The evidence reviewed in Section 4, Section 5, Section 6 and Section 7 leads to a clear conclusion: protection in inverter-dominated systems cannot rely on classical “high-current + Thevenin source” assumptions, because inverter fault responses are current-limited, control-shaped, and mode-dependent . We note that several mitigation concepts discussed in this paper are also applicable to other low-fault-current contexts. However, inverter-dominated grids introduce additional, technology-specific challenges, because fault responses are current-limited and control-shaped, may change abruptly during limiter mode transitions, and depend on synchronization behavior and sequence-control capabilities . Furthermore, ride-through requirements can enforce sustained but bounded current injections, altering relay-visible quantities (e.g., apparent impedance trajectories and directional polarization signals) beyond what is typically assumed in classical low-fault-current systems . At the same time, standards increasingly require inverter-based resources (IBRs) to ride through and provide defined support during faults, so protection must be designed to work with limited but sustained inverter contributions rather than expecting fast DER disconnection . Although the research community is advancing rapidly, several gaps must be addressed before utilities can apply consistent, validated protection “design rules” for mixed GFL/GFM networks at scale . (i) Non-Thevenin modeling for protection studies: Short-circuit and distance-protection reasoning still often assumes a Thevenin source and impedance-dominated current angles. Inverter behavior violates this through hard current limits, reactive-current priority, PLL dependence (GFL), and limiter/virtual-impedance transitions (GFM) .
Document [6]Research on GFL grid-connected control has primarily focused on improving synchronization stability and damping characteristics under weak-grid conditions, aiming to enhance operational adaptability in scenarios with low short-circuit capacity and strong impedance coupling. Existing studies commonly improve the PLL structure to strengthen phase detection accuracy and synchronization robustness, including adaptive-bandwidth PLLs, enhanced second-order generalized integrator PLL (SOGI-PLL), and synchronization methods based on state observers or frequency estimation, thereby improving the inverter's capability to suppress grid phase noise, voltage distortion, and frequency disturbances . Simulation analyses and field operation data indicate that appropriately reducing PLL bandwidth, introducing grid-frequency disturbance filtering, and implementing virtual damping control can mitigate PLL-induced phase oscillations and negative damping effects, thereby enhancing synchronization stability under weak-grid conditions . Meanwhile, some studies introduce virtual impedance, supplementary damping control, and online grid-impedance identification with adaptive tuning strategies at the inner current-loop level to reduce strong inverter-grid coupling and alleviate stability risks associated with resonance amplification and control-parameter mismatch . These approaches have significantly improved the local robustness of GFL control in engineering practice under weak-grid conditions, providing effective technical solutions to weak-grid synchronization difficulty and PLL-induced instability. However, most of these enhancements still rely on parameter tuning or auxiliary control loops and do not fundamentally alter the GFL paradigm's strong dependence on external grid phase angles. As a result, synchronization uncertainty under weak-grid conditions cannot be eliminated at the mechanism level. Even when local damping is improved, the stability margin still depends on how PLL bandwidth, inner-loop tuning, virtual impedance, and grid-impedance adaptation interact with the surrounding network during disturbances, distorted voltages, and resonance-prone operating points. The same body of work therefore treats weak-grid instability as a control-interaction problem rather than as an isolated hardware deficiency. The underlying evidence points to converter-control interaction with a weak network, especially through PLL behavior, impedance coupling, and resonance-sensitive tuning, as the direct source of the instability problem being managed.

For example, converter outer control loops have an operating frequency range of 1–10 Hz and converter switching frequency is in the kHz range . This wide frequency range leads to interactions between converter control dynamics and various dynamics of power systems, such as electromechanical dynamics of machines, dynamics of nearby converters, and electromagnetic transients of the network, leading to various oscillations in the power network . The oscillatory events due to these interactions are categorized under converter-driven stability. Fast-interaction converter-driven stability events can be the result of interactions between fast inner control loops of converters and passive components of the system causing high-frequency oscillations . High-frequency switching of converters can also cause high-frequency resonances with LCL power filters, causing a fast-interaction converter-driven stability issue . The interactions between controllers of nearby converters can also cause high-frequency oscillations classified under fast-interaction converter-driven stability category . Interactions between outer control loops of power electronic converters and slow-response components of the power network, such as electromechanical dynamics of SGs, are categorized under slow-interaction converter-driven stability. Studies of show that the system strength at the connection point of converters affects these low-frequency oscillations. Interactions between direct-drive permanent magnet generators of wind turbines and weak AC grids has resulted in low-frequency oscillations and slow-interaction converter-driven instability issues in Xinjiang, China, since 2014 . The rating of converters and their control strategies are among the factors that affect slow-interaction converter-driven stability . Document [9]Historically, synchronous generators have dominated the power system; therefore, inertia was often ignored in planning studies. Inertia is an inherent property of synchronous generators that provides additional time for control mechanisms to respond to changes. This inertia can be understood as the stored kinetic energy in rotating generators, which is released or absorbed during frequency events and limits the rate of change of frequency (RoCoF). As the carbon-neutral system demands more renewable energy, these sources, in particular wind and solar, have been extensively added to the grid in recent years. These sources are connected to the grid via inverters; hence, the grid frequency is decoupled. The majority of the inverters used are in gridfollowing configuration, therefore these inverter-based resources (IBRs) cannot provide any inertia during frequency events. As a result, the grid lacks synchronous inertia, and low-inertia systems may experience load shedding or widespread blackouts when RoCoF values exceed safe limits. Advanced control mechanisms, such as virtual synchronous machines (VSM), allow IBRs to provide virtual inertia. This thesis examines the integration of inertia constraints in long-term capacity expansion planning, which aims to ensure the stability of frequencies in future low-inertia power systems, taking into account sources that provide virtual inertia. A large-scale convex optimization model, adapted from , which is implemented for the European transmission system, divided into seven synchronous areas, is used in this thesis for the comparative study. The model co-optimizes investment in generation, storage, and transmission while explicitly linking operational decisions to inertia provision. Inertial response from different technologies is used according to their properties. A unit commitment relaxation enables high spatial and temporal resolution while maintaining tractable computation. Stability is enforced via RoCoF constraints reflecting realistic contingency sizes. Two planning scenarios are analyzed: a 'Brownfield' configuration with existing conventional assets and a 'Greenfield' low-carbon configuration excluding coal, lignite, oil, and nuclear plants. Each scenario is assessed under unconstrained 'Base' and stability-constrained 'RoCoF' methods, and three experimental cases are tested to compare the effect of allowing both battery energy storage systems with grid-forming inverter (BESS GFM) and virtual inertia enabled wind turbine, only BESS GFM, or only wind system with virtual inertia technologies.

This record-breaking level of global warming underscores the urgency of addressing climate change through rapid and systemic shifts, especially in the energy sector, which is the largest source of CO2 emissions . In globally modeled pathways that limit warming to 2°C, in 2050, almost all electricity will be supplied from zero or low-carbon sources, such as renewable energy sources (RESs) or fossil fuels with CO2 capture and storage . Furthermore, an increased electrification of energy demand through, e.g., electric vehicles and heat pumps is expected . As a result, electricity grids worldwide will undergo a profound transformation in the coming decades, replacing conventional, synchronous generators and aiming for nearly 100% RES integration. Wind and solar photovoltaic systems, the most significant RESs, are predominantly integrated into electricity grids via power electronic inverters. As a result, future power grids will be primarily dominated by inverters and their control strategies. This transition introduces significant challenges to power grid stability, as RESs and inverters inherently do not provide inertia, reducing the inertial response available after power imbalances . The loss of inertia is seen as the most prominent challenge for the stability of the power grid by European transmission grid operators . Document [9]Historically, synchronous generators have dominated the power system; therefore, inertia was often ignored in planning studies. Inertia is an inherent property of synchronous generators that provides additional time for control mechanisms to respond to changes. This inertia can be understood as the stored kinetic energy in rotating generators, which is released or absorbed during frequency events and limits the rate of change of frequency (RoCoF). As the carbon-neutral system demands more renewable energy, these sources, in particular wind and solar, have been extensively added to the grid in recent years. These sources are connected to the grid via inverters; hence, the grid frequency is decoupled. The majority of the inverters used are in gridfollowing configuration, therefore these inverter-based resources (IBRs) cannot provide any inertia during frequency events. As a result, the grid lacks synchronous inertia, and low-inertia systems may experience load shedding or widespread blackouts when RoCoF values exceed safe limits. Advanced control mechanisms, such as virtual synchronous machines (VSM), allow IBRs to provide virtual inertia. This thesis examines the integration of inertia constraints in long-term capacity expansion planning, which aims to ensure the stability of frequencies in future low-inertia power systems, taking into account sources that provide virtual inertia. A large-scale convex optimization model, adapted from , which is implemented for the European transmission system, divided into seven synchronous areas, is used in this thesis for the comparative study. The model co-optimizes investment in generation, storage, and transmission while explicitly linking operational decisions to inertia provision. Inertial response from different technologies is used according to their properties. A unit commitment relaxation enables high spatial and temporal resolution while maintaining tractable computation. Stability is enforced via RoCoF constraints reflecting realistic contingency sizes. Two planning scenarios are analyzed: a 'Brownfield' configuration with existing conventional assets and a 'Greenfield' low-carbon configuration excluding coal, lignite, oil, and nuclear plants. Each scenario is assessed under unconstrained 'Base' and stability-constrained 'RoCoF' methods, and three experimental cases are tested to compare the effect of allowing both battery energy storage systems with grid-forming inverter (BESS GFM) and virtual inertia enabled wind turbine, only BESS GFM, or only wind system with virtual inertia technologies.

At the technology-comparison level, a life-cycle-cost meta-analysis across storage options found that application and duty cycle (bulk shifting vs. peak shaving vs. regulation) dominate relative economics, with hydrogen storage becoming comparatively attractive at long durations, provided utilization and charging costs are favorable (Zakeri & Syri, 2015). Extending that logic to power-to-X, techno-economic assessments of power-to-liquids identify electricity price, full-load hours, and plant scale as first-order cost determinants, mirroring the sensitivity seen in hydrogen-only pathways and underscoring that operational context often matters more than nominal efficiency differences (Fasihi, Bogdanov, & Breyer, 2018). As mentioned earlier, the HHS system is a form of GS suitable for bulk storage and capable of providing multi-day energy capacity to compensate for the significant temporal variations inherent in solar and wind power generation. This technology converts electrical energy into gravitational potential energy by vertically moving a large rock piston. This massive cylindrical piston of rock, typically excavated from solid bedrock such as granite, is housed within a deep, subterranean cylindrical cavern.
Document [2]Unlike PHS, which requires two large water reservoirs at different elevations, HHS utilizes a single large cylinder of rock cut directly from the local geology. To store energy, water is pumped beneath this rock piston using a standard pump-turbine system, creating hydraulic pressure that lifts the massive rock block. To discharge energy, the pressurized water is released back through the turbine as the rock piston lowers under its own weight, generating electricity. This mechanism allows the system to function as a virtual battery with the operational characteristics of a hydroelectric plant, but without the need for mountains or valleys . While the concept itself is mentioned briefly in several review articles, e.g., , the available literature on this technology is scarce and brief, basically in the form of one article and two reports. The first study by Heindl introduced the foundational concept of HHS, proposing the excavation of large rock pistons with diameters between 60 and 160 m to achieve grid-scale energy storage capacities between 26 MWh and ∼ 1.3 GWh. A preliminary cost breakdown of the installation process was provided, including tunnel system, drilling, wire sawing, rock removal, and floor separation, as well as coverage, waterproofing, and sealing. The specific energy storage cost was found to decrease rapidly from 512 to 51 EUR/kWh. However, the study remained a conceptual introduction without detailed hourly operational modeling or integration with renewable generation sources. Rudresh and Elsaraf performed a site-specific feasibility study for an HHS system on the Bonavista Peninsula, Canada, integrated with a wind farm.

The first strategy replicates a basic power-to-power system designed to meet the electricity demand exclusively through solar energy, without any connection to the electrical grid.
