Document [2]Physical19, 20 and numerical experiments21-23 reveal that drainage divide mobility is strongly influenced by differences in erosion rates across opposing flanks. In tectonically inactive regions, divides shift toward the side with lower erosion rates30. For instance, in a symmetrical mountain range, more rapid erosion and headward channel growth on one side of the mountain will push the main drainage divide[G] toward the less erosive side19. The migration of drainage divides was first recognised in the Rocky Mountains around the 1870s30. Since then, the advancement of remote sensing, geologic dating, and numerical simulations have triggered a proliferation of research into the dynamics of divide movement21, 31. For example, a novel and effective method to predict the direction of divide movement in 201432 boosted divide migration to become a trending research topic in geomorphology33. Thereafter, the number of methods used to decode divide migration histories, predict their future mobility32, 34, 35, and constrain the rates of divide horizontal migration3, 4, 36 has rapidly increased. However, a synopsis is required to understand and consolidate these methods and the controls on divide motion. In this Review, we aim to provide an overview of drainage divide migration and explore its implications on climate and biodiversity[G]. To better understand the dynamics of divide migration, we evaluate their steady-state position and migration rate. Additionally, we provide an overview of the methods used for decoding divide migration history and predicting their future mobility. We build on the growing evidence showing how divide migration influences regional biodiversity13, 15, 37, and explore the mechanisms of how the position and movement of drainage divides impacts regional rainfall, temperature, and ecosystems. Finally, we advocate for a research agenda integrating divide migration with ecosystems, geohazards, and planetary sciences.

Several studies have shown differences in chi-index values between opposite sides of a divide and, consequently, hypothesized divide instability and the predicted direction of divide migration from an area characterized by lower values towards an area typified by higher values . However, this approach works best if the uplift pattern, bedrock erodibility, and climatic conditions are uniform, which is hardly the case for long mountain ranges and prominent orographic barriers. Moreover, the choice of reference base (base level) was shown to dramatically influence the results and, hence, interpretation . The review above shows that the divide itself at the mountain-range scale is seldom characterized. Much more often, its history and future behaviour are inferred from indices calculated for drainage basins or topographic metrics of the belt adjoining the divide. In this contribution, we intend to present a range of DTM-derived measures, both simple and more complex, which may be used in an analysis of the first-order (main) drainage divide of a mountain range (MDD) at a large spatial scale. They help to evaluate symmetry/asymmetry of the mountain range, along-divide topographic variability, and morphometric properties of areas adjacent to the divide. However, most of these measures can be also applied to lower-order drainage divides within a larger area of interest. The mountain-range scale is defined as relevant to terrain elevations of the length between ~102 km and ~ 103 km, thus being long enough to have varied topography and a perhaps complicated history that reflects both exogenic and endogenic influences. All numerical values and visualizations can be easily derived from digital elevation models. Some of these measures have already been used, whereas other solutions are proposed here for the first time.

Thereafter, the number of methods used to decode divide migration histories, predict their future mobility32, 34, 35, and constrain the rates of divide horizontal migration3, 4, 36 has rapidly increased. However, a synopsis is required to understand and consolidate these methods and the controls on divide motion. In this Review, we aim to provide an overview of drainage divide migration and explore its implications on climate and biodiversity[G]. To better understand the dynamics of divide migration, we evaluate their steady-state position and migration rate. Additionally, we provide an overview of the methods used for decoding divide migration history and predicting their future mobility. We build on the growing evidence showing how divide migration influences regional biodiversity13, 15, 37, and explore the mechanisms of how the position and movement of drainage divides impacts regional rainfall, temperature, and ecosystems. Document [0]When fluids are extracted from porous subsurface layers compaction ensues as the overburden compresses lower sedimentary layers, resulting eventually in land subsidence 34, 158 . Subsidence related to groundwater pumping can lead to subsidence rates which exceed rates for SLR by an order of magnitude 8, 158, 159 . Additional shallow subsidence can be triggered when drainage leads to lowering of the surface water table, triggering shallow compaction and volume loss following oxidation of soil organic material and peats 32, 160, 161 . Satellite-based estimates of subsidence in the Mekong Delta, where the phenomenon has been relatively well studied, range from 10 – 40 mm/yr between 2006-2010 78 and up to 60 mm/yr between 2014-2019 162 with contemporary rates associated to groundwater pumping alone modeled to be on average around 11 - 16 mm/yr 78, 79 , with continued acceleration into the future as groundwater extraction keeps increasing 28 . Also in other deltas, rates of subsidence in areas with known major groundwater extraction can reach similar rates, e.g., localized up to 18 mm/yr in the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta 103, and up to 9.8 mm 163 over parts of the Nile Delta. Typically, rates are highest around cities 78, 158, 164, and particularly cities in Asia 68, 165 , which greatly increases potential socioeconomic impacts of land subsidence. Where deltas hold reserves of hydrocarbon such as oil and gas, such as in the Niger 82, 166 or Mississippi Delta 81, 167 , hydrocarbon extraction can further accelerate land subsidence. Total land subsidence, especially in unconsolidated deltaic settings, is the cumulative result of various subsurface processes acting at different depths, time scales and spatial extents 6, 168 . As a result, land subsidence can be highly spatio-temporally variable, which makes modeling and projecting it not straightforward and current models tend to focus on a single driver or process only.

Geological factors include rock types and weathering, variability of the geological structure, bedding, the type of deposit, and whether the slope lies in a folded zone. Fracturing includes the number and orientation of joint sets, their trace lengths, spacing, and the overall intensity of fracturing. Hydrogeology matters through permeability and joint permeability, while observed movements or rockfall activity provide direct evidence that the source area is already active. This is why approaches such as Rock Mass Rating (RMR), its evolution to Slope Mass Rating (SMR), and the Geological Strength Index (GSI) have been applied successfully to slope-stability analysis. These approaches summarize the quality of the fractured rock mass and make the dependence on joint-slope orientation more explicit when evaluating source-area instability. The link between rockfall activity and the intensity of pre-existing fracturing, including fold hinges with steep limbs, has been demonstrated directly by Coe and Harp (2007). Instability potential can evolve through time as external factors act on the source area, but the controlling theme remains fractured rock releasing blocks from the slope face.

The link between rockfall activity and the intensity of pre-existing fracturing, including fold hinges with steep limbs, has been demonstrated directly by Coe and Harp (2007). Near population centers, humans are often responsible for the majority of wildfire ignitions, and they provide ignition sources in highly predictable areas and seasons of the year, when natural ignitions are rare (Balch et al. 2017), Keeley and Syphard 2018). Ignition pattern and frequency interact with fuels, weather, and topography to influence fire occurrence, leading to heterogeneous burn probabilities across a landscape (Ager et al. 2012), Povak et al. 2018). Using prior knowledge of human and lighting-caused fire starts coupled with knowledge of the probability of fire spread and likely severity, managers can identify the areas of any landscape where uncharacteristic or impactful fires will likely occur (Parisien and Moritz 2009), Parisien et al. 2012), and decrease the proportion of the landscape that requires treatment. There are a number of available tools and approaches to identify areas that would benefit from strategically placed fuel treatments. In general, fuel treatments are not implemented at random, and for good reason (Finney et al. 2007). A comparison of random vs. strategically placed treatments showed that a significant reduction in area could be achieved with strategic placement (Ager et al. 2013), 2016), where that opportunity exists. Quantifying the probability of high-severity wildfire across a given landscape and focusing thinning treatments on high-probability areas can decrease the required treatment area by >50% (Krofcheck et al. 2019). However, the success of these strategies depends on maintaining the treatments and reintroducing fire to a larger portion of the landscape (Agee and Skinner 2005), Barros et al. 2018). Where reserved areas are abundant or widely distributed, opportunities for spatially optimizing fuel treatments are limited, and considerably more treated area may be required outside of reserves (Finney et al. 2007). In summary, justifying inaction based on the scale of the problem is too large is highly circular.

Fire Weather Season Length (FWSL) is one indicator used to describe the duration of these conditions. The interdependency between wildfires and the prevailing weather is well established. On the one hand, the prevailing weather conditions in a specific area can potentially affect ignition as well as propagation. For instance, prolonged heat and dryness can create an ideal scenario for the occurrence of extreme wildfires.

question: Which factors determine the longevity and subsurface propagation of fires in tropical peatlands?
perspectives: Lowered water tables from drainage and land-use change
Prolonged drought that creates severe peat-moisture deficits
Peat bulk density and porosity that sustain smouldering combustion
Buried woody roots and subsurface fuel continuity
context:
Document [0]Smouldering combustion in organic soils propagates laterally and downwards through an overall exothermic sequence composed of dehydration, pyrolysis, and char oxidation, so sustained subsurface fire depends on whether the peat structure can keep that sequence going across the fuel bed. First, the smouldering front gradually preheats the medium ahead at dehydration temperatures of about 50-100C. Once dehydrated, the dry medium undergoes endothermic pyrolysis at temperatures above 150C, and the chemical breakdown of the solid fuel yields char, pyrolysate gases, and ash. In smouldering combustion, in situ char oxidation dominates gas-phase oxidation, so the reaction remains closely tied to the solid structure of the fuel. Last, char oxidation reactions take place once ignition temperatures above about 210C are reached and sufficient oxygen transfer is guaranteed, producing heat together with CO2, CO, and water vapour as the main combustion products. For a subsurface wildfire front, the intensity and rate of spread are primarily controlled by heat losses to the environment and by oxygen transfer to the combustion zone. In peat, those controls are set by the physical structure of the soil rather than by an external flame front. Bulk density, porosity, and related permeability determine whether the peat can sustain smouldering ignition and propagation, because those properties govern how effectively the porous fuel bed dries, chars, retains heat, and keeps oxygen reaching the hot reaction zone. When those structural properties maintain the balance between oxygen supply and heat loss, the peat layer can continue burning laterally and downward as a smouldering wildfire. This is why the physical fuel-bed architecture of peat directly controls persistence below the surface. In that sense, peat longevity and subsurface spread follow from the way bulk density and porosity organize the internal combustion environment of the burning layer.

Elevated levels of carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and particulate matter (PM10/PM2.5) triggered a surge in respiratory emergencies, particularly among children, with asthma cases rising sharply across the region . In Indonesia’s extensive peat swamp forests, falling water tables dried out organic peat, enabling deep smoldering combustion that destroyed standing biomass and ignited subsurface layers. Buried woody roots create subsurface fuel continuity that lets smoldering fronts spread laterally through the peat and persist below ground. These underground fires persisted for weeks, releasing toxic compounds and contributing to a tropospheric ozone spike recorded at Watukosek, Indonesia—a phenomenon linked to large-scale biomass burning . Tropospheric ozone is an important air pollutant and greenhouse gas, which plays a key role in atmospheric chemistry. The haze’s bioclimatic impacts disrupted ecosystems, reduced visibility, and strained public health systems, underscoring the vulnerability of peatlands to human-induced degradation and climate variability. The 1997–1998 peatland fires, intensified by severe El Niño drought conditions, devastated 3.4 million hectares of land in Indonesia, including 750, 000 hectares of peatlands in Kalimantan, and 300, 000 and 400, 000 ha in Sumatra and West Papua, respectively . These fires released 0.81–2.57 gigatonnes (Gt) of carbon—equivalent to 13–40% of global fossil fuel emissions at the time—primarily from the combustion of ancient peat deposits . This catastrophic event temporarily elevated Indonesia to the world’s third-largest greenhouse gas (GHG) emitter in 1997, surpassing industrialized nations like Japan and Germany . Tropospheric ozone (O3), was significantly elevated during the 1997 Indonesian peatland fires due to photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emitted by burning vegetation and peat.
Document [2]Smouldering fire is a slow, low-temperature, flameless form of combustion that differs from flaming fire in its chemistry, transport processes, and time scales, and it is one of the largest and longest-lasting combustion phenomena on Earth. It is a heterogeneous process sustained when oxygen directly attacks the hot fuel surface, so the physical structure of the fuel strongly matters for whether the combustion can keep moving once ignition has occurred. Smouldering is the dominant burning behaviour of porous and charring fuels such as wood, char, peat, and polyurethane, and that classification places peat squarely in the kind of material that can support persistent subsurface burning. In peatlands, a porous fuel bed can hold a hot reaction zone and allow oxygen to reach the fuel surface without requiring open flaming, which helps explain why smouldering wildfire becomes a significant disturbance, contributes substantially to global carbon emissions, and can provide positive feedback to climate change. Compared with flaming fire, smouldering can be initiated by a much weaker ignition source and can also provide a shortcut to flaming through smouldering-to-flaming transition, but its usual behaviour is creeping spread rather than rapid flame advance. Traditionally it spreads on the order of 1 cm per hour, at least two orders of magnitude slower than flaming fire, yet it can still be sustained at extremely low oxygen concentrations of about 11%. Those features are consistent with peat acting as a porous, charring medium whose structure supports long-lived combustion beneath the surface, making peat porosity and the resulting oxygen access central reasons these fires can persist for long periods after ignition. The fact that very low oxygen is still sufficient for continued smouldering reinforces the same point: once a peat layer has the porous structure needed to feed the hot surface, subsurface combustion can survive in conditions that would not sustain rapid flaming. That same porous, charring character is what makes peat especially capable of sustaining flameless combustion after the initial ignition event.

Document [0]Smouldering combustion in organic soils propagates laterally and downwards through an overall exothermic sequence composed of dehydration, pyrolysis, and char oxidation, so sustained subsurface fire depends on whether the peat structure can keep that sequence going across the fuel bed. First, the smouldering front gradually preheats the medium ahead at dehydration temperatures of about 50-100C. Once dehydrated, the dry medium undergoes endothermic pyrolysis at temperatures above 150C, and the chemical breakdown of the solid fuel yields char, pyrolysate gases, and ash. In smouldering combustion, in situ char oxidation dominates gas-phase oxidation, so the reaction remains closely tied to the solid structure of the fuel. Last, char oxidation reactions take place once ignition temperatures above about 210C are reached and sufficient oxygen transfer is guaranteed, producing heat together with CO2, CO, and water vapour as the main combustion products. For a subsurface wildfire front, the intensity and rate of spread are primarily controlled by heat losses to the environment and by oxygen transfer to the combustion zone. In peat, those controls are set by the physical structure of the soil rather than by an external flame front. Bulk density, porosity, and related permeability determine whether the peat can sustain smouldering ignition and propagation, because those properties govern how effectively the porous fuel bed dries, chars, retains heat, and keeps oxygen reaching the hot reaction zone. When those structural properties maintain the balance between oxygen supply and heat loss, the peat layer can continue burning laterally and downward as a smouldering wildfire. This is why the physical fuel-bed architecture of peat directly controls persistence below the surface. In that sense, peat longevity and subsurface spread follow from the way bulk density and porosity organize the internal combustion environment of the burning layer.
